[ingratit]ude is detestable and punishable by the same. And truly, a pious soul would rather die honorably than live among the living with the shameful branding of an ingrate.

High-Noble Lord, it has now been eleven years and several months since the Congregation at *Obdam* extended to me a lawful calling, reinforced by your High-Nobility's favorable approval, upon which—having been released from the Congregation in the *Hague by Breda*—I came over to those of *Obdam*. The many polite encounters and the goodwill with which your High-Nobility has deigned to honor my humble person during the time of my residence in your High-Nobility’s Lordship of *Obdam*, but primarily your High-Nobility's great zeal in defending and promoting the true Religion, and in preventing all public idolatrous and soul-seducing practices of blind Popery <note>The author uses "blind Popery" as a common 17th-century Protestant polemic against the Roman Catholic Church.</note> (*O God, have mercy on those poor people, and let them be illuminated by the enlightenment of the Gospel of the glory of Jesus Christ!*), has not only obligated me to offer zealous prayers for the well-being of your High-Nobility's person and entire lineage, but also moved me to dedicate this Book to your High-Nobility. I have spent many of my leisure hours within your High-Nobility’s Lordship on the translation of this work; and just as it was completed, that great God, through the special guidance of His all-governing providence, was pleased to call me to the ministry of that flourishing and renowned Mother-church of the City of *Emden* <note>Emden was a major center for the Reformed faith and often called the "Geneva of the North."</note>, to which I cannot depart without leaving this work for your High-Nobility as a token of heartfelt gratitude, especially since it was finished exactly at the end of my service in your High-Nobility’s Jurisdiction. Receive it then, High-Noble Lord, with a favorable eye; read through it with a devoted soul. You shall find herein, by God’s grace (who has so exceptionally exalted your High-Nobility in this life), a shown path to come, in this time, to a powerful assurance of God’s favor, and after this life to that eternal exaltation in God’s glory at God’s right hand, upon those Heavenly Thrones. There, all believers being placed, shall then judge the world with Christ, the Son of God; which, just as it is holily promised to the believers in *Matthew 19 verse 28* and *1 Corinthians 6 verse 2*, I heartily wish that the great God may grant this honor to your High-Nobility out of grace, and also to all who are dear to your High-Nobility, along with all those who love the appearance of Jesus Christ.

...has distributed various works in a holy order among various people, according to His pleasure; He has assigned commerce to you as your civic calling and practice, being a calling that is neither of today nor of yesterday, not forbidden, but confirmed by the most holy laws of that eternal Law-giver and Lord of Heaven and earth. <margin>Leviticus 25:14, etc.</margin> Kings and Princes were also formerly merchants, and traders the most glorious in the land. <margin>Genesis 42:6. O foolish merchants! What is this in the end, in the final balancing of the books, other than great effort for the profit of wind—mere damage, all-lost, a <term>Surrender of the Estate</term> <note>original: "Cessie"; a legal term for declaring bankruptcy or surrendering one's assets to creditors</note> to Hell. If I knew, dear Brother and Brothers-in-law (as I do know through God’s grace), of a chance to make a great and honest profit with a small amount of capital, God and nature and all your demonstrations of friendship have long since obligated me to give you the first opening thereof. And this is what I have had in view in the translation of this outstanding Book: that alongside the High-Noble Lord of Obdam, I might also dedicate the same to you as an eternal token of remembrance and gratitude. # To the Reader.

Among all the duties I have previously proposed, I have omitted one, which I now see as the chief and most excellent of all others: *This is the duty I call Looking unto Jesus. And if I must reveal by what occasion I happened upon the same, I shall do it sincerely, and clearly, and in the simplicity of the Gospel; thus:* In the Spring of the year 1653, I was visited with a severe illness, and as the Lord began to restore my health, it came to my mind what the Lord Jesus had done for my soul, was still doing, and would yet do for the same, until He should have made it perfectly blessed. In my meditations on these things, I could find no beginning of His works except in that eternity before the creation of the world; nor could I find any end to His works except in that eternity after the world's end; yet between these two extremes, I have understood several of Jesus Christ's dealings, both past, present, and to come. In the multitude of these thoughts within me, my soul took great delight, and that delight ignited other desires in me, since a desire cannot exist alone. I began to meditate on these Scripture passages, which at first seemed to set the working of my affections upon such a blessed object as a <term>Gospel duty</term> <note>A "Gospel duty" refers to a spiritual practice or obligation required of a Christian under the New Covenant of grace, as opposed to the legal requirements of the Old Testament law.</note>; thereupon I resolved, if the Lord Jesus would only restore my health and prolong my life, that I would do my best to gain more insight into this Gospel duty than I had ever known before. And to the end that my other necessary labors would not be hindered by this effort, my intention was to take up this subject in my usual sermons, through which I would have the opportunity to search both the Scriptures, various writers, and my own heart. In the course of time, I began this work, praying to God that He would help me complete it, just as He had caused me to begin it, and that all might serve for His glory and for the best of His church. In the progress of my labor, I found a world of spiritual comforts, both in respect to the subject I had at hand, Jesus Christ, as well as in respect to the act in which my duty toward Him consists: in looking unto Jesus. 

1. Concerning the object, that was the proper subject to which I was especially bound to preach; "Christ among you the hope of glory," said Paul to his <term>Colossians</term> <note>The people of Colossae to whom the Apostle Paul wrote the Epistle to the Colossians.</note>, adding immediately thereafter, "Whom we preach." *Colossians* 1:26, 28. And to me, the least of all the saints, is this grace given—what grace? To preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ. *Ephesians* 3:8. God’s servants are bound by their office to preach Jesus Christ richly. <term>Dr. Sibbs</term> <note>Richard Sibbes (1577–1635), an influential English Puritan theologian known for his "sweet" and comforting preaching style, often nicknamed "the Heavenly Doctor."</note> says well, that the special duty of Christ's ministry is to lay Christ open, to hold up the tapestry, and to explain the unknown mysteries of Christ; and for this reason, he exhorts that we should labor at all times to speak something of Christ, or that which leads to Him; speaking of the Law, let us let that drive us to Christ; of...

<summary>In this preface, the author describes how a near-fatal illness in 1653 led him to contemplate the eternal works of Jesus, inspiring him to write a treatise on the spiritual discipline of "Looking unto Jesus." He argues that the primary duty of a minister is to "hold up the tapestry" of Christ's mysteries for the congregation.</summary>
<keywords>Looking unto Jesus, Gospel duty, illness and recovery, Richard Sibbes, Christology, ministry, preaching, Colossians, Ephesians</keywords>

# To the Reader.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter O containing a woodcut scene of figures in a landscape.</image-desc>Among all the duties I have previously presented, I have omitted one, which I now regard as the foremost and most excellent of all others: This is the duty I call <term>Looking unto Jesus</term> <note>original: "Sien op Jesus"; the central theme of this work, focusing on the soul's continuous gaze upon Christ as the source of salvation</note>. And if I must reveal the occasion by which I came upon this, I shall do so sincerely, clearly, and in the simplicity of the Gospel; thus: In the Spring of the year 1653, I was visited with a severe illness, and as the Lord began to restore my health, it occurred to me what the Lord Jesus had done for my soul, was still doing, and would yet do for it, until He should have made it perfectly saved. In my meditations on these things, I could find no beginning to His works except in that eternity before the creation of the world; nor could I find any end to His works except in that eternity after the end of the world. Yet between these two extremes, I perceived several of Jesus Christ’s actions, both past, present, and future. In the multitude of these thoughts within me, my soul greatly delighted itself, and that delight ignited other desires in me, for a desire cannot exist alone. I began to meditate on those Scripture passages which at first seemed to place the workings of my affections on such a blessed Object as a Gospel duty. Thereupon I resolved that, if the Lord Jesus would but restore my health and prolong my life, I would do my best to gain more insight into this <term>Gospel duty</term> <note>an obligation or practice required of a Christian under the New Testament "Good News"</note> than I had ever known before. And so that my other necessary labors would not be hindered by this effort, my intention was to fall upon this subject in my regular preaching, through which I would have the opportunity to research both the Scriptures, various writers, and my own heart. In the course of time, I began this work, praying to God that He would help me finish it, just as He had caused me to begin it, and that everything might serve His honor and the best interests of His church. In the progress of my labor, I found a world full of spiritual comforts, both in respect to the Object I had at hand—Jesus Christ—and in respect to the act in which my duty toward Him consists: looking unto Jesus. 1. ...modest duties, let those teach us to walk worthily of Christ. Christ, or anything that leads to Christ, must be our proposal, or the target for our eyes to aim at. **Sibbes’ [Commentary on] Canticles** <note>original: "Sibs Cantic."; 'Canticles' is another name for the Song of Solomon. Richard Sibbes (1577–1635) was a famous Puritan theologian.</note> **p. 428**. And I can say with feeling, *that it is the sweetest subject that was ever preached upon; and is this not like a poured-out ointment, whose scent is so fragrant, and whose taste is so sweet, that all the Maidens love him for it?* <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:3.</note> *and is it not a gathering of all glory, beauty, and excellence, both of things in Heaven and of things on earth? and is it not a mystery as sweet as it is deep? Truly, great Books have been written about Jesus Christ, there is rule upon rule, Sermon upon Sermon, Book upon Book, and piece upon piece, and yet the mystery is such (as someone clearly said) that we are all still only as if on the first page of the simple Catechism of Jesus Christ: yes, Solomon reached only as far as "what is his name?"* <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:4: "What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?"</note> *and I fear that many of us understand neither the name nor the matter.* It is a worthy study to make further and further openings of this blessed mystery; and it were to be wished that all of Christ’s servants would consume themselves in spelling out, reading, and understanding the same. See, just as a certain great point requires the skill of many school-teachers (and even when joined together, it is still barely enough) to give a good explanation of it; so is this main chapter, this holy and glorious mystery, worthy of the labor of all the learned; and if they should all bring their observations together, and stack all their studies upon one another (which I have somewhat attempted to do in the following treatise), they would still find that only a little of this mystery is known, in comparison to that which still remains and is unknown; yet this they must know, *what is difficult to understand is delightful to investigate* <note>original: "quod difficile intellectu, dilectabile inquisitu"</note>, as **Bernard** <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note> says; that which is hard to understand is sweet to search out, and so I have found it. 

2. Concerning the act of looking unto Jesus, just as it is a combination of knowledge, desire, hope, faith, and love, so also of joy; how could I then be otherwise than filled with unspeakable and glorious joy while I was busy studying, writing, and especially working upon my soul in the exercise of this "looking"? If there is any duty on earth that mirrors the duty of the saints in Heaven, I dare say it is this one. **Mr. Rutherford** <note>Samuel Rutherford (c. 1600–1661), a Scottish Presbyterian theologian and author.</note> in his **Epistle to the Dying Christ** <note>original: "Sendbrief aen de stervende Christus"; likely referring to a portion of his letters or his work on Christ's death.</note> writes thus:

> An act of life in Christ, and upon Christ, in the works of seeing, enjoying, embracing, loving, and resting upon him, is that noonday Divinity, and the theology of the <term>Beatific Vision</term> <note>The "Beatific Vision" is the ultimate direct self-communication of God to the individual person in Heaven, allowing them to see God as He is.</note>; there is a general assembly of immediately-enlightened theologians around the Throne, who study, read, preach, and praise Christ night and day. Oh, what rays, what irradiations and flashes of intellectual enjoyment, beholding him, possessing him, and living in him, and what a fire of love comes from that face, from that Face of God, from the Lord the Almighty God, and from the Lamb that is in the midst of them? And oh, what returns and reaching out of the mind's sight—embracing, loving, and wondering—fall back to him in a circle of glory.

Now if this is the duty of the perfected saints in glory, do we then not follow them, and feel something Heavenly in our imitation, in our looking with them upon Jesus? I write of that which I have in some measure felt, and of which I still hope to feel more; and therefore, whoever you are that reads this, I pray you,

> *An act of living in Christ, and upon Christ, in the works of seeing, enjoying, embracing, loving, and resting upon him, is that midday Divinity, and Theology of the blessed vision; there is a general assembly of immediately-enlightened theologians around the Throne, who study, read, preach, and praise Christ night and day. <meta>This page concludes the author’s preface to the reader. The previous page discussed the inexhaustible mystery of Christ, comparing our current understanding to only the first page of a catechism. This page invites the reader to begin the practical exercise of "looking unto Jesus" and provides a specific 81-day spiritual schedule.</meta>

...come and warm your heart by this holy fire! O come, and smell the precious ointment of *Jesus Christ!* <note>The "precious ointment" is a common Puritan metaphor for the name and graces of Christ, drawn from Song of Solomon 1:3.</note> O come and sit down under this shadow with great delight! <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 2:3: "I sat down under his shadow with great delight."</note> Oh, that all men (especially those into whose hands this Book shall come) would immediately apply themselves to the exercise of this Gospel-art of looking unto *Jesus!* If they find nothing *Heavenly* herein, then my art shall deceive me; yet let them pray that, just as they look upon him, a power may also go out from him and fill their souls.

Reader, I have but one more thing to say to you: if you wish to know how you shall continually perform this duty, just as you do your morning and evening prayer; it would not fail if you took a portion of it every day, either in the morning or in the evening, at one time or another—at least for some part of the time together. I know some who, in a steady daily course, fulfill these two necessary duties of meditation and prayer; what the subject matter of their meditation is, I cannot know for certain. Only our experience can tell us—be it *Heaven* or *Hell*, sin or grace, or whatever it may be—that if we keep ourselves to the exercise of the same single subject, we are prone to negligence, coldness, or formality. The reason is that we soon grow weary of a thing, unless that one thing is everything; but that is *Christ*, for he is everything. *Colossians 3:11.* <note>The verse states: "...but Christ is all, and in all."</note> If you then would make this *Jesus Christ* your subject only once a day—to know, consider, desire, hope, love, believe, rejoice, call upon, and be conformed to him, in the various aspects of his work of redemption: as it was designed, promised, and performed in his birth, life, death, resurrection, Ascension, sitting [at the right hand of God], intercession, and second coming—and if one of these parts were to be your exercise for a single day, and you proceeded thus every day from the first to the last to look upon *Jesus*, I trust that you would never weary yourself. And why so? O, there is variety in this matter upon which you must look, and there is variety in the manner of looking upon the same. For instance, one day you could employ your knowledge of *Jesus* in the execution of the great work of your salvation in his eternity; the second day you come to meditate upon *Jesus* in that regard; and the next day you come to desire *Jesus* in that regard; and the following day to hope in *Jesus* in that regard; and so on, until you come to the last day of the work; which (besides * the subject matter treated at length in each part, even in these workings upon the subject) would in total amount to a number of 81 days. 

But will this variety not be delightful? It is *Mr. Lockyer's* observation on *Colossians 1:16* <note>Nicholas Lockyer (1611–1685) was an English Puritan clergyman and chaplain to Oliver Cromwell.</note> that a holy soul cannot weary itself in the contemplation of *Jesus*; how much less then shall it weary itself in looking unto *Jesus*, which involves much more than the contemplation of *Jesus*? Come, visit this duty and persevere in it, at least eighty-one days in a year; and so 81 days in each year of your life. And I shall not then entirely draw you away from your meditation on any other subject, but shall leave the remainder of the year—being still more than three parts—to your own pleasure. If you have so resolved, I have nothing more to say; but the Lord be with you, and if you sooner or later perceive any good through this work, give God the glory, and remember in your prayers him who has taken this trouble for the honor of *Christ* and for the good of your soul. Thus rests

->Your Servant in *Jesus Christ*<-
->*I. A.*<- <note>I.A. stands for Isaac Ambrose (1604–1664), the author of this work.</note>

***

* I trust that the Reader will be willing to read through the entire Book at least once; and then for this steady daily exercise, lasting 81 days in a year, I have left the subject in each part to be read or not read at one's pleasure; unless the whole or a part of it should lead to that single act of knowing *Jesus* in this or that respect.

### To
# LOVERS OF CHRIST.

## Worthy, truly God-fearing and Jesus-
## loving READER.

<image-desc>The text begins with a large decorative initial 'D' contained within a square border, decorated with floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>

**The eye is not satisfied with seeing,** said he who saw through all things under the Sun in his *Ecclesiastes* <note>original: "Predicker"</note> Chapter 1, verse 8. If this is true, as the wise Solomon found it to be regarding the world’s vain and empty shadows—which pull the eyes and hearts of their lovers with such insatiable desire that they, forgetting both God and themselves, their soul and their salvation, chase and follow them to their own eternal shame and loss—then I know, and I feel it through God’s grace in my soul, and I testify to it before God and men, that God and Jesus, and Heaven’s firm and glorious and eternal treasures, snatch away the spiritual eye and the soul of a child of God with such a holy and insatiable desire that they, forgetting and despising the world’s vain and empty trifles, do not rest from looking upon Jesus Christ until they have passed into that blessed communion with him. To thus behold Jesus (who is the fairest of all the children of men, and who is all in all), the maker of this edifying Book has presented Jesus most gloriously to us. And if you truly love Jesus, I do not doubt that his labor, which he has performed to the honor of Jesus, will be pleasant to you; nor will you despise that I tell you in **Dutch** <note>original: "Duyts," which in the 17th century referred to the Dutch language</note> what he has spoken of Jesus in the English tongue. A Bride can never hear too much of her beloved Bridegroom. The smallest message brought to her from him, even by the smallest child, will not weary her to hear or to receive. Let me be one of the least of Jesus Christ’s servants; if you truly love my Lord and Master, I know that you will receive my message with joy, even if I come to speak to you with only a stammering tongue, following the pattern of one of his most worthy Servants. I pray you then, for the love of your Jesus, read, read through, and re-read this Book, which Isaac Ambrose has made for the honor of Jesus, and which has also been translated by me for that purpose; you shall not regret the effort. It will indeed do you good in your life for its improvement; yes, it will do you good in the time of your death, and by **Looking unto Jesus** you shall not only overcome all fear of death, but also be kindled with a holy desire to pass through a blessed death to your Jesus, and to behold him in his glory, and to rejoice eternally in *Looking unto Jesus*.

<summary>In this preface, the translator introduces Isaac Ambrose's work to a Dutch audience, arguing that while worldly sights never satisfy, the spiritual act of "looking unto Jesus" provides eternal peace and comfort in death.</summary>
<keywords>Isaac Ambrose, Looking unto Jesus, spiritual discipline, Solomon, Ecclesiastes, Dutch translation, salvation, comfort in death</keywords>

**H**eavenly light, which *Ambrose* <note>Isaac Ambrose (1604–1662), a prominent English Puritan minister whose works were highly influential in the "Nadere Reformatie" (Dutch Second Reformation).</note> first through this paper kindled,
**E**ven sharing it with England, was kept under a narrow roof,
**T**ill by this candle a *Lamp* <note>A pun on the translator’s surname, Johannes Lampe.</note> was lit.
**S**o now the *Netherlands* <note>original: "Neerlandt"</note> sees it too, and finds for its failings,
**I**n these pages the very best counsel,
**E**ven the most necessary. O soul-sick *Netherlands*, let
**N**ot this English Book pass by without reading it with attention,
**O**r suchlike works: if you would gladly be healed.
**P**raise *Lampe* not only for the light he has hung up,
**I**n the darkness of this age, but exercise your own sight,
**E**re it fades away. The eye of your faith
**S**hould see above all earthly things, and turn itself upward,
**U**nto your Jesus sitting at his Father’s right hand
**S**howering better gifts down upon the whole *Netherlands*.

# Upon the glorious Book of
## ISAAC AMBROSE, <note>Isaac Ambrose (1604–1662) was a prominent English Puritan. His work *Looking unto Jesus* became a devotional classic in the Dutch "Nadere Reformatie" (Further Reformation).</note>
### Translated by JOHANNES LAMPE; Called Minister from Obdam to Emden.

<margin>*Song of Solomon 5*</margin>
The Bride, once wishing to recount her Beloved’s praise,
Begins from head to toe, to depict *Him* most beautifully
And portrays Him as if with a seraphic quill:
> My beloved is white and ruddy, what fairer could one desire?
> He is the fairest among the countless number of men,
> And Angels; *He* is my *Savior*, *Head*, and *Lord*,
> And further His *Head*, His *Hair*, His lovely *Dove-like eyes*,
> His *Lily-white Mouth*, His *Hand* of power,
> His *Legs* and everything that concerns my *Beloved*,
> Is naught but *Gold*, *Turquoise*, and *Marble*, and *Sapphires*,
> Yea, more is that which comes to adorn my *Beloved*,
> It is glorious, fair, and sweet; in short, it is perfect.

But where can the finite describe the infinite?
Who must not remain mute here, or at least stammering?
What Eagle does not find itself blinded by such a Sun?
What foot can ever tread such a mountain of radiance?
So also the *Bride* stammers, and thus ends her speech:
"Everything one finds in my *Beloved* is altogether lovely." <note>A paraphrase of Song of Solomon 5:16: "He is altogether lovely."</note>

So shall I also, along these ivory steps,
Follow the dear *Bride* in the praising of this Book,
And say, stammering, that the end and the beginning
Is sweet and fair; all that one shall find in this *Scripture*,
It serves for the Praise and Honor of JESUS our *Beloved*,
It is glorious and it is sweet, for JESUS is within it.

---

## ANOTHER.

No thing tasted sweet to *Bernard’s* <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a medieval mystic famous for his intense devotion to the person of Jesus; he famously said that the Name of Jesus was "honey in the mouth."</note> holy mouth,
Where he did not find the lovely *Name* of *Jesus*;
Who is there then who does not love this glorious Book,
Since one finds the name of *Jesus* on every page?
He who loves *Christ* does well to praise the *Author*,
And him who through his *Lamp* <note>A play on the translator’s surname, Lampe.</note> points us to this *Savior*.

...a Sun to enlighten him, a Physician to heal him, a fiery wall to protect him, a friend to comfort him, a pearl to enrich him, an ark to carry him, a rock to support him in the most sorrowful pressures;

Christ alone is the ladder between heaven and earth, the Mediator between God and man, a mystery into which the angels of heaven desire to peer, to look, and to see. <note>The author alludes to Jacob’s Ladder and the "mercy seat" where angels are depicted as looking down.</note>

Here is a truly blessed subject; and who would not be eager to look into it, so that they might have knowledge of it?

<margin>John 17:3</margin>
*This is eternal life, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.* Come then, and let us behold this Sun of Righteousness. We can receive nothing but good, and in no way any harm, through such a beholding. It is true that if we look at the natural sun for a long time, our eyes are darkened and our faces become blackened; but by looking upon Jesus Christ, our eyes shall become clearer and our countenances more beautiful.

<margin>Proverbs 15:30</margin>
Since the light of the eyes rejoices the heart, how much more so when we have such a blessed object to behold? Just as Christ is more excellent than the whole world, so does this looking far surpass all other sights. It is a brief summary of a

<column-break/>

Christian’s happiness, the greatest strength of the duties of the Gospel: *Looking unto Jesus.*

In the text we have an act and its object. The act stands very expressively in the original Greek text as *aphorontes eis* <note>original: "ἀφορῶντες εἰς." This is the present participle of "aphorao," meaning to look away from all else and fix one's gaze upon a single thing.</note>. The English <note>The author likely refers to the English translations of his time, such as the King James Version, which he uses as a scholarly reference alongside the Dutch.</note> does not express it completely; it signifies a turning away or a diverting of the eye from one object to another. There are two expressions here: *apo* [away from] and *eis* [unto]. One implies a turning away of the eye from all other objects, and the other a fixing of the eye upon such an object, and upon it alone. Thus, it is both a "looking off" and a "looking on." Upon what? That is the object: a looking unto **Jesus**. This is a title that expresses His mercy and bounty, just as "Christ" indicates His office and ministry. I shall not be so curious as to inquire why He is named *Jesus* and not *Christ* here; I understand that the focus is on the Person, whom both names signify. It may only be noted that *Jesus* is the purest of all the names in the Gospel. *Jesus* was not the language of the Old Testament; the first place where we read of this title being given to Christ is Matthew 1:21.

<margin>Matthew 1:21</margin>
> *Thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins.*

Some have noted that this Name, Jesus, was given to Him twice: once at His death <note>The author may be referring to the inscription on the Cross or the fulfillment of His saving work.</note> (Matthew 1:21) and thereafter for eternity (Philippians 2:10). The first was a sign of His entry into the covenant with God, to [fulfill] the law...

### Edifying contemplations of Jesus.

<margin>Gen. 19:17.</margin>
This was the Lord's command to Lot: "And do not look behind you." He was to forsake and loathe the wickedness of Sodom so greatly that he would not even deign to cast a glance back toward it.

<margin>Isa. 17:7, 8.</margin>
"In that day shall a man look to him who made him, and his eyes shall look upon the Holy One of Israel, and he shall not behold the altars, the work of his hands." This was the fruit of God's discipline over His chosen Israel; they were not to cast a glance at their false altars, lest those idols turn or twist their eyes away from their Maker.

<margin>2 Cor. 4:18.</margin>
"We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen," says Paul. A Christian’s focus passes over and beyond all earthly things. Once a soul learns what an eternal God is—what an eternal Jesus is, and what an eternal crown is—and when it understands the great work of Christ in saving poor sinners and sharing Himself forever with such lowly creatures, then all desire for these visible earthly things loses its power. What are they to be compared to this?

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
But what are those things from which we must look away in this "looking"? I say they are: 1. good things; 2. evil things.

### I. Good things. 
In the preceding chapter, the apostle tells us of a "cloud of witnesses" <note>Referring to the heroes of faith listed in Hebrews 11.</note> whom we must undoubtedly look upon at

<column-break/>

the proper time. But when he catches sight of this second object <note>Jesus</note>, he scatters the cloud and presents Jesus Himself. The Apostle desires that we should *look away* <note>original Greek: "ἀφορᾶν" (aphoran) - to look away from all other things in order to focus on one.</note>, turning our eyes from the witnesses and directing them to Jesus Christ. It is as if he were saying: "If you truly wish to see a sight once and for all, look at Him." Although the saints are guides who go before us, they are nonetheless only His followers. He is the Chief Leader—the leader of them and of us all; look to Him! There is a time when <margin>James 5:10.</margin> James could say, "My brothers, take as an example the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord." But <margin>John 13:15.</margin> when Jesus comes, He says, "I have given you an example"—an example above all examples. Then "all flesh is silent before the face <margin>Zech. 2:13.</margin> of the Lord." Let all the Saints and the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels.</note> cover their faces with their wings, so that we may look only unto Jesus and let all other sights pass.

### II. Evil things, 1. in general; 2. in particular.

#### I. In general, 
we must look away from all things that stand on this side of Jesus Christ, and from evil things. In a word: we must look away from all that is of "self," whether it be our sinful self, our natural self, or even our religious self. In this matter, we must turn our eyes away from all these things.

we must look away from all that is in the world; and that

# Looking unto Jesus.

<margin>James 4:4.</margin> ...that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? Lust in Christians is spiritual adultery; when we have enough in God and Christ, and yet desire to place our happiness in created things, that is true harlotry. Now, there are three steps in this spiritual harlotry:

I. **The mindset of this world:** You know that adultery can exist in one’s affections without the body being defiled: impure glances are a step toward lust. In the same way, the children of God can have certain worldly "glances" and straying thoughts; when temptation is strong, the world can indeed become great in their judgment and imagination.

II. **The setting of the heart upon the world:** This is a higher step of spiritual adultery. Our hearts belong to Christ and are His own; now, to set them upon the world, when they ought to be kept chaste and faithful for Jesus Christ—what <margin>Matthew 6:24.</margin> an adultery is that? *You cannot serve God and Mammon:* A housewife who does not keep herself satisfied with one husband must necessarily be a harlot.

III. **The preferring of the world before Christ Himself.** This is the highest peak of lust and the height of this adultery. What? To make the members of Christ the members of a harlot? Well, worldly ones! These wondering thoughts belong to Christ; these difficulties belong to Christ; this love is Christ’s; this time, this

<column-break/>

care, this earnestness is Christ’s; it is all Christ’s. And will you give that which is Christ’s to the world? And will you prefer the world over Christ with what is His own? What? To live like public harlots who love everyone more than their own married husbands? Well, how despised shall you become because of this among men and Angels; at the last day they shall point <margin>Psalm 52:7.</margin> <note>The source text cites Psalm 52:9, but in most English Bibles, this verse corresponds to Psalm 52:7.</note> their finger at you and say, *See the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.* See that <margin>Mark 5:17.</margin> Gadarene <note>The Gadarenes were the people who, after Jesus healed a demon-possessed man by sending the demons into a herd of swine, asked Jesus to leave their region because they feared the loss of their livestock more than they valued His presence.</note>, who loved his swine more than Jesus Christ. *Do not love the world,* says John. <margin>1 John 2:15.</margin> Christ is never precious in our judgment so long as the world appears glorious to us. As <margin><note>original: "Cui Christus incipit dulcescere, Neæsse est amarescere mundum. Bern."</note> "To whom Christ begins to become sweet, the world must necessarily become bitter." — Bernard of Clairvaux</margin> we begin to taste sweetness in Christ, then the world begins to become bitter to us: the more sweetness we taste in the one, the more bitterness we shall find in the other.

IV. **We must look away from the World regarding its sinful honor;** what is this honor other than an inordinate desire for men to think well of us, speak well of us, and to praise and boast of us? It is just like a person running up and down the streets chasing a bubble <note>original: "beere" - likely referring to a "blaas" or "bel," an air-filled bladder or soap bubble used as a metaphor for something hollow and fleeting.</note> that flies in the air, tossed here and there by the winds and the breath of many men’s mouths: it is still in doubt whether he shall catch it; and if it happens, it is but a bubble. Such is the pride of life, of honor, and of vain glory: it falls hard.

It uses the metaphor of marriage and the biblical example of the Gadarenes to illustrate how the pursuit of worldly honor is as hollow and fleeting as chasing a bubble in the wind.</summary>

Now there are three stages in this spiritual harlotry, namely:

I. The disposition of this world: you know that there can be adultery in the affections even if the body is not defiled: impure glances are a step toward lust. In the same way, the children of God can have certain worldly glances and wandering thoughts; when temptation is strong, the world can indeed appear great in their judgment and imagination.

II. The setting of the heart upon the world: this is a higher stage of spiritual adultery; our hearts belong to Christ and are His own. You cannot serve God and Mammon: A wife who is not satisfied with one husband must necessarily be a harlot.

III. The preferring of the world before Christ Himself. This is the highest peak of covetousness and the summit of this adultery. What? To make the members of Christ the members of a harlot? §. 2.

### An exhortation to look away from all other things.

A word of exhortation.
**C**hristians! I beg you, look away from all other things, especially from all evil things. I know that I have pleaded with you regarding a difficult matter: I would certainly need the eloquence of an angel to move you to turn your eyes away from these things; indeed, even if I possessed such speech, it would still not be enough; it is God alone who must persuade Japheth <margin>Gen. 9:27. <note>This refers to a biblical blessing where God "enlarges" Japheth; the author uses it here to mean that only divine grace can persuade a person to find their home in spiritual matters.</note></margin> to dwell in Shem’s tents: and yet I offer you a few meditations intended to move you, leaving the outcome to God.

I. Consider that all other evil things are a mere nothing in God’s judgment: For truly, every <margin>Ps. 39:6. <note>In English Bibles, this is Psalm 39:5: "Verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity."</note></margin> man, no matter how firmly he stands, is mere vanity: not only some men, but every man: not only man in his worst state, but every man in his best state: nor is it simply that every man in his best state is of little value; rather, every man in his best state is vanity, emptiness, nothing: and was he only so in part? No, he is so in all parts, entirely and completely, mere vanity. Would we ever think that a powerful, rich, and prominent man, whom we often gaze upon with such high and wondering thoughts, would be considered so empty in God’s judgment? O wonder! wonder! yet it is not so great a wonder, for one day or another you shall have the

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where "looking unto Jesus" was defined as an "excellent Gospel-ordinance." Here, the author explains why it qualifies as a divine law (ordinance) and specifically why it is an ordinance of Christ, rather than a mere human rule or a natural duty.</meta>

### Book the First. Chapter 3. Section 2.

Reasons why this is 1. an ordinance, and 2. an ordinance of Christ, can be these:

<margin>Matt. 11:25</margin>
I. Why an ordinance? Here there is only this reason: the will of the Lord. **"Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in thy sight."** Ordinances are certain charges, given by an external command of a Lawgiver who has the power to command. It is Christ’s will to impose this law upon all the children of men: that they shall look upon him. And what need have we then to ask for reasons concerning this? It is our duty to obey, and not to know why he commands. If "He himself said it" <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς ἔφα* (autós épha) — a phrase famously used by the students of Pythagoras to mean that the master's word is the final authority, requiring no further proof.</note> was enough in the school of Pythagoras to settle the disputes among his scholars: I am certain that it ought to go much more so in Christ’s School; and therefore we shall not search further for reasons.

2. Why an ordinance of Christ? It is this: because all spiritual ordinances, laws, and institutions depend upon Christ, so it does not lie in any man’s power to establish any new spiritual ordinances in Christ's church. I do not wish to deny that human power also has a role in the ordering of such things which the church does not possess uniquely, but holds in common with other assemblies—such as meeting in a certain place and at a certain time, etc., according to that rule: **"Let all things be done decently and in order."** For this is not an institution <note>term: institution — In this religious context, an "institution" refers to a sacred rite or law specifically established by God, whereas "order" refers to practical arrangements made by people.</note>, but only the dictate of right reason. But when it comes to an ordinance, law, and institution—that

<margin>1 Cor. 14:40</margin>

<column-break/>

is, when something more is given to a matter than nature itself has given to it; when, through the power of the institution, there is added some power to work upon the soul—that depends only on Christ. Consequently, because in the preaching of the Word and in the administration of the Sacraments we expect a power, a spiritual working, more than they could otherwise have and give by nature, therefore we say: this is Christ’s ordinance. So also because in this looking unto Jesus we expect a power, a spiritual working that accompanies it, more than nature can give, therefore we call it an Ordinance, and an Ordinance of Christ, to distinguish it from all other Ordinances, rules, and institutions of men, by whatever name they might be called.

**Jesus Christ**. Some give a loving glance toward **Christ** every now and then, but their eyes are immediately turned away again. **Magor-Missabib**, <note>A Hebrew name meaning "Terror on Every Side."</note> a terror all around, in every sense a terror to himself.

# Looking unto Jesus.

I. They do not possess the wisdom, knowledge, and discernment of Christ that they might otherwise have. Through the beholding and earnest consideration of Christ, we obtain more and more knowledge of Christ; but if we will not look, how shall we then understand this great mystery of grace? However, I speak not only of a theoretical <note>original: "beschouwelicke"</note> knowledge, but primarily of a practical and experiential knowledge. Without looking unto Christ, we cannot expect that any power shall emanate from Christ: there is but a bare letter, or a mere token of Christ upon those who are such; they do not possess a clear, comforting, inward, and experiential knowledge of Jesus Christ.

II. They do not taste the goodness of Christ as they might otherwise do. Christ is nothing else to them, so long as they neglect Him, but a darkened star, by whose light they are not moved. Christ is not sweet to them in His ordinances; <note>The "ordinances" (instellingen) refer to religious practices like prayer, the sacraments, and the preaching of the Word.</note> they do not find that delight and that refreshment, that comfort and satisfaction therein, which He otherwise serves to us. ### The First Book. Chapter 3. Section 5.

<margin>Exodus 14:25.</margin> service; they are just like Pharaoh’s chariots without wheels <note>A reference to the biblical account where God removed the wheels of the Egyptian chariots so they drove with difficulty.</note>; O, they do not perceive Christ's love, neither in the clear revelation of His mysteries, nor in the joyful communication of His gifts of grace, nor in the sanctification and comfort of their trials, nor in the sealing of the forgiveness of their sins: O, they do not feel those uplifting comforts which Christ commonly speaks to the heart when He speaks from His own heart in love. O, that deficiency! O, the misery of this deficiency.

**V.** They do not have that experience of Christ’s power which those have who exercise themselves in this duty. Would you know wherein the power of Christ consists? I answer: in the casting down of the strongholds of sin; in the overcoming of Satan; in the humbling of man’s heart; in the sanctifying of their souls; in the cleansing of their consciences; in bringing their thoughts into the obedience of Christ; in strengthening them to endure tribulations; in making them grow and increase in all heavenly grace. And those who properly and effectively look unto Christ shall share in this power. But if this duty is neglected, there is nothing of all such things: for this reason, we call this the **duty of duties**, the **chief duty**, the **singular duty**. And regarding all other duties, means, and ordinances <note>The "ordinances" refer to established religious practices such as prayer, the sacraments, and the preaching of the Word.</note>, if Christ is not in them, they are of no value. In all duties, this is the essential part: that we—

<column-break/>

—look through them all, unto Jesus. It comes from Christ alone that power and efficacy are communicated to the spiritual ordinances; there were many people in the crowd around Christ, but it was only that weak woman who touched Him who felt that a unique power went out from Him. We see that there are many who take heed of the ordinances, who come into the assembly, but only a few find that the inward power of Christ is brought upon their souls. Those who neglect, or are grossly ignorant <note>original: "hottelyck onwetende"</note> of this great mystery of **looking unto Jesus**, are no better than strangers to Christ’s power.

**VI.** They have no sense of the worthiness and excellence of Christ who keep no acquaintance with this duty; they are not so drawn by His beauty; they are not so taken with the sweetness and delight of Christ’s countenance; He is not the *fairest among ten thousand* in their eyes; and this is why they have neither desire nor longing for Him, why they do not delight or rejoice themselves in Christ. Truly, these stirrings are the proofs of our high esteem: those who do not rejoice in Christ, nor have any longing for Christ, set an altogether lowly price upon Christ.

**VII.** They have no feeling either of their own deficiency, nor of the world's vanity, who do not practice this duty. In that—

In this glass <note>The author uses "glass" here in the seventeenth-century sense of a looking-glass or mirror. By looking at Christ, the believer sees a true reflection of their own state.</note> we see that man is blind, and that no other Sun but Christ can enlighten him; man is naked, and no other garment but Christ can cover him; man is poor, and no other treasure but Christ can enrich him; this man is drowning in debt, and no one else but Christ can pay for him; this man is empty, and no one else but Christ can fill him; this man is restless, dejected, and tormented, and no one else but Christ can set him at rest. Well, all this, and even more than this, is seen in this mirror of Jesus: the soul that looks here can do no other than come to an end of all other "perfections"; indeed, the further the soul looks upon the creatures, the more and more it discerns their vanities. But alas! there is no consideration, no judgment or feeling, neither of man's defects, nor of the world's vanity, nor even of any desirable good in Christ, for those who are not occupied in this divine and spiritual contemplation.

Thus far concerning the lack of those who neglect this duty of looking unto Jesus.

# Looking unto Jesus.

### §. 7. More moving reasons to strengthen us in this work.

I. Consider that your looking upon Jesus will maintain your communion with Jesus: and is this not well worth the effort? What, Christians! what is this communion with Christ other than a truly Heavenly prelude? Through this we enjoy his person and all delightful relationships to his person, to his death, and all the soul-saving fruits, privileges, and outflows of his death: through this we are led into Christ’s wine-house <note>Original: "wijn-huys." A reference to the "banqueting house" in the Song of Solomon, symbolizing a place of spiritual intimacy and abundance.</note>,

<margin>Song of Sol. 2:4.</margin>
held up in his galleries, and love is his banner over us: through this we are brought onto the Mount with Christ, so that we may see him as if changed in form <note>A reference to the Transfiguration of Jesus on the mountain.</note>, and say with Peter, "Lord, it is good that we are here, let us build tabernacles here." Oh, what a blessed thing it is to have Christ dwelling in our hearts, and hear us as we rest in Christ’s bosom! Oh, what a blessed thing it is to maintain the mutual communication of works between Christ and our souls! As for example: he bears our sins; let us take up his healing. He was wounded for our sake; let us drink the spiritual balsam that flows from his wounds; he has taken upon himself our unrighteousness; let us clothe ourselves with his righteousness; he has accepted our curse and damnation; let us accept his justification, blessing, and salvation. To this

<column-break/>

end we look unto Jesus, even when he hides his face through desertion; and let us not rest until we have bound him; when we bind him, let us hold him fast, and not let him go, and not drive him away from our hearts through our numbness <note>Original: "verdooventheden." Refers to a state of spiritual insensibility or being "dull of hearing."</note>. If we value the presence of Christ thus, how shall we maintain and increase the communion with Christ for our comfort?

II. Consider that your daily necessities require you to look often upon Jesus: you have need of Christ; you have need that he pray in you, and you have need that he pray for you to your Heavenly Father; you have need that he work in you, and work for you his own holy will; you have need that he present you and yours unblemished before the face of his Father in life, in death, and on the day of judgment; there is not one moment in your life in which you do not <margin>2 Tim. 1:8.</margin> continually have need of Jesus Christ. And can a hungry man forget bread? Can a heart that pants with thirst fail to desire the water-streams? Can a bound man forget freedom? Can a child in his distress forget his Father who lives in glory and luxury? Oh, let your necessities likewise drive you to Christ, and think upon Christ: is he not the fountain that fills all our deficiencies? Christians! ask your own experience: when you look upon Jesus, and lean upon Jesus, are you not best

# The First Book. Chapter 3. §. 7.

at rest: sometimes you say, how sweet is his bread, and how pleasant is his drinking-cup, and how lovely is his presence? At such a time you cannot wonder at him enough: Oh, what sweet insights are then in your souls! Well, why then do you not always look upon him? Or at least, why do you not often place yourself in the state of his Disciples, who kept their eyes toward <margin>Acts 1:10</margin> Heaven, while Christ ascended? <note>Referring to the Ascension of Jesus, where the disciples watched him rise into the clouds.</note> How richly could you employ your idle hours and spare minutes here for the restoration of all necessities of body or soul?

III. Consider that the eye and the heart set upon Christ is one of your most certain testimonies of <margin>Matthew 6:21</margin> sincerity: *Where your treasure is, there your heart shall be also.* If Christ is your treasure, your heart will also be with Christ; and certainly a heart in Christ set upon God is a sincere testimony of saving grace. External works are easily recognized, but those of the heart are the most certain testimonies: if your teaching is not a sufficient proof of your grace, if the arguments of your tongue and hand can be refuted, yet this proof of the affection of your heart will show that you are sincere. Take a poor Christian who has a weak judgment, an unstable memory, a stammering tongue, yet if his heart is set on Christ, I would rather die with that person and have my soul in the place of his soul, than in the place of those who

<column-break/>

do not have such a heart, even though they possess the most excellent gifts, and portions, and abilities that anyone in the world could have. Christians! If you want to have a certain testimony of God's love, and a firm proof of your right to glory, labor to set your hearts upon Christ. O look then unto Jesus. You can be assured that Christ will judge that you truly love him when he sees that your hearts are set upon him.

IV. # Looking unto Jesus.

This is worthy to be reflected upon and meditated upon. If **Christ** does not have your hearts, who or what shall have them? O, that a Christian should find more pleasure in letting their heart dwell among thorns and thistles than in the bosom of their precious **Jesus**! What? Would you run after the droplets and pass by the fountain? Why would you chase the shadow and abandon Him who is the substance itself? If the mind takes its course away from **Christ** toward other things, those things are not only of lesser value, but also lead to destruction: <margin>Jeremiah 2:5</margin> *They have gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and have become vain.* <note>The author uses this biblical quote to warn that turning away from the "fountain" of Christ leads to a life of emptiness or "vanity."</note> How unworthy the world is to be looked upon by a Christian, of that we have spoken before. And thus the exhortation is concluded; henceforth I shall specifically open to you the way of this duty, to which I have sought to move you until now.

But note first in this work these two parts of the text: the act and the object. The act is *looking*, and the object is **Jesus**.

I. By *looking*, as you have heard, we understand an inward, experimental knowledge, desire, hope, faith, love, invocation of **Jesus**, and conformity with **Jesus**. It is not merely a bare knowledge swimming in our brains; it is not such a vain remembrance of **Christ**. Just as **Christ** has various excellencies in Himself, so He has also adorned the soul with the power to comprehend in various ways, so that we may be capable of enjoying to our delight those various excellencies which are in **Christ**. Just as creatures have their various uses, so God has given us various senses, so that we might enjoy the pleasure of them all. What pleasure would we have had in fragrant flowers or pleasant perfumes if we did not have the sense of smell? Or what good would we have had from the tongue or from music if God had not given us the sense of hearing? II. By **Jesus**, who is the object of this act, we understand a **Savior**, who has carried the great work of man's salvation from the first to the last. In His second coming, the true end of time, into all eternity. O, what a blessed object there is for us in each of these stages! O, what a wondrous love it is that we shall look upon! Before I show you how you must look upon Him in these respects, I will first set the object before you: I shall quietly lay out the colors of this wonderful beauty before your eyes, and then point out the art of how you must look upon it.

"You have called us here" (they say in the **Song of Solomon**) "to look upon your **Shulammite**." <note>The Shulammite is the bride in the Song of Solomon, often interpreted in this period as a type of the Church or the soul in relation to Christ.</note> What shall we see in Him? What does the Bride answer? Nothing less than "a company of two armies" <note>original: *een reye van twee heyren*. A reference to Song of Solomon 6:13, interpreted here as a vast multitude of perfections.</note>; that is, several legions of goodly sights; a sea of bottomless depths of manifold, excellent perfections. Or if these words are understood as referring to the Bride, and not to Christ—well, what many words do we nonetheless find in the **Song of Solomon** expressing that in Him is a multitude of divine sights? Myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon, all kinds of perfumes, all kinds of incense trees, all kinds of the merchant's powders are in Him. He is altogether lovely: all that is in Him and about Him is nothing but a flowing together, a bundle, an army of glorious sights; all appearing at once in a cluster and growing upon one stem. There is many a noble sight in **Jesus**; I shall not, then, bind myself only to these two in particular, but shall treat of all those I have now proposed.

And if ever, then now, awaken your hearts. Say to all—

<margin>The essence of the Son is of itself, and for this reason He can be called God-of-Himself. <note>original Latin/Greek: *Essentia Filii est à se ipsa, & hac ratione dici potest αὐτό-ϑεος* (*autotheos*). ### I. Concerning the matter itself, which is Jesus Christ, who must be considered in two ways: both as He is a Son, and also as He is a God. Now, insofar as He is a Son, He is the thing that is born, but not insofar as He is a God. Insofar as He is God, He is of Himself, being neither born nor proceeding; the Divinity of the Father and the Divinity of the Son is but one and the same; and therefore the Son, insofar as He is God, is God of Himself, without beginning, just like the Father:

<margin>Yet the essence of the son is not from himself, therefore in this way he is not God-of-himself. <note>original: *Essentia tamen filii non est à se ipso, ideo sic non est αὐτό-ϑεος*. The author is making a fine theological distinction: Christ's *nature* is divine of itself, but His *personhood* as "Son" is received from the Father.</note></margin>

but insofar as He is a Son, He is not of Himself, but the Son of the Father, being generated by Him; and from this it follows that the Son is generated by the Father insofar as He is a Son, but not insofar as He is God.

### II. Regarding the time of this birth, it has no beginning, middle, nor end, and therefore it is eternal, before all the world: this is one of the wonders of our Jesus, that the Father generating, and the Son being generated, are equally eternal. Wisdom in the book of Proverbs (who, according to the unanimous saying of all theologians, is Christ) speaks thus:

<margin>Proverbs 8:24, 25, 26, 27.</margin>

I was born when the depths were not yet there, when there were yet no fountains, heavy with water: before the mountains were settled:

And a little before: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His way, before His works, from that time on: I have been anointed from eternity, from the beginning, from the ancient times of the earth; that is to say, from eternity: for before the world was made, there was nothing but eternity. Against this it might be brought forward that the saying of God the Father,

<margin>Hebrews 1:5; Psalm 2:7. <note>original: *He-Ps. 2, 7*</note></margin>

"You are my Son, today I have generated you," is explained by Paul as referring to the time of Christ’s resurrection. "We declare unto you the promise," (says Paul) "which was made unto the fathers, that namely God has fulfilled the same unto us their children, when He raised up Jesus: as it is also written in the second Psalm, You are my Son, today I have generated you." <note>Referencing Acts 13:32-33.</note> But we make a distinction between the generation itself and its revelation or declaration. Jesus the Son of God is generated from all eternity, but when He became man, and especially when He rose again from the dead, then He was powerfully proven to be the Son of God by nature. And the words of the Apostle must be understood as referring to this proof, or to this revelation.

# The Second Book. Chapter I. §. 1.

Counsel and Essence are mine (says Christ) I am understanding. <note>original: "Raedt ende Wezen zijn mijne (seydt Christus) ick ben het verstandt." This is a reference to Proverbs 8:14, where Wisdom—traditionally identified by theologians as Christ—describes her nature.</note>
What the Father is, the Son is also; yet in man the understanding and that which is understood are often not one and the same; but in God these are one together: God's conceptions and generations are the most inward; the Father conceives from Himself, and in Himself, and His conception is a generation, and His generation remains constantly in Himself, because His understanding can unite with no other thing corresponding to Him but with Himself; and that procreation of Himself, or that generation of Himself, is the second subsistence <term>selfstandigheyt: a person or individual existence within the Godhead</term> in the Trinity, whom we call the eternal Son of God.

IV. Regarding the mutual kindness and love of Him who generates, and of Him who is generated, we say that from this comes forth a third person or subsistence in God. But to better understand this matter, we must observe two things; first, that in the essence of God, besides His understanding, there is also a will. Secondly, that His will works eternally upon Himself, just as His understanding does.

¶ The first, that in God's essence, besides His understanding, there is also a will, is entirely clear, for He who gives a will to all rational creatures cannot Himself be devoid of it: how could He be without a will, whose will it is that we will: it is entirely necessary that there must be a certain first or supreme will, to whose will all that wills is fixed; but the Scrip-

<column-break/>

<margin>Isaiah 45:9, 10. <note>The text quoted actually aligns more closely with Isaiah 46:9-10.</note></margin>
-ture says clearly, I am God, and there is no God more, and there is none like me. My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

¶ The second, that this will in God works eternally upon Himself, is also clear: for just as the understanding works, so also works the will; but God's understanding works upon Himself as the first and most complete truth: therefore also God's will wills Himself as the first and most perfect good. And truly, what other suitable object can the will of God have, but Himself? An infinite will must necessarily have an infinite good, and in this sense, as our Savior tells us, no one
<margin>Matthew 19:17.</margin>
is good but one, namely God; and from here it is that the will of God strikes upon Himself, and has a well-pleasing <note>original: "welbehagen," a state of perfect satisfaction or delight</note> in Himself, as in an infinite good.

¶ And now we proceed to the manner of this high, hidden, and spiritual proceeding of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Just as God's will works and strikes upon Himself from all eternity, so it works this effect, that it delights itself in that infinite good which it comprehends in itself, for the act of the will is a rejoicing and well-pleasing: and even this delight, which God or His will has in His own infinite goodness, brings forth a third person or subsistence in God, whom we call the Holy Spirit. ->§. 2. Of<-

...Holy Spirit is / I shall answer / He is the mutual kindness, and love, and rejoicing, and pleasure of the Father and the Son: The Father rejoices and delights Himself through this act of the will in His Son / and the Son delights and rejoices Himself through this act of the will in His Father; and this is what the Son says of Himself and of the
<margin>Prov. 8:30</margin>
Father / I was daily His delight, playing always before His face; <note>original: "Ick was dagelicks sijne vermakingen, t'aller tijdt voor sijn aengesichte spelende." I shall explain this through a certain likeness or illustration; As when a person looks into a glass <note>A mirror, typically made of polished metal or glass during this period.</note> / if he laughs, his image laughs as well; here is but one true face / and yet in this unity we can find a Trinity: the face is one / the image of the face in the glass is the second / and the laughter of both together is the third / and nonetheless they are all three but in one face / and they are all of one face / and are all but one face; so the understanding that is in God /

<column-break/>

is one, the reflection or image of His understanding / seen in Himself as in a glass / is a second / and the love and delight of both together / perfected through the power of the will / is a third; and yet they are all in one God / they are all of one God / and are all but one God. In this Trinity there is neither first nor last / in respect to time; but they are all together / and at one time: just as in a glass the face; and the image of the face / when they laugh, they laugh together / and the one is not before / nor the other after the other. ——— To conclude all this, Just as we have the Son from the Father through His eternal will working through His understanding / so we have the Holy Spirit from the love / and pleasure and delight of them both / through the united working of the understanding and the will together; whereupon we conclude three distinct persons / or subsistences <term>self-standighede: individual existences or 'persons' within the one divine nature</term> / which we call the Father / the Son and the Holy Spirit / in one spiritual / but nonetheless unspeakable being / which is the true God Himself. — My intention is not to dwell upon the Father and the Holy Spirit / but only upon the Son. But nevertheless I have added this / so that you might better understand the manner of the generation of the Son of God; and also the mutual kindness / love / pleasure / and delight between the Father and the Son / even from all eternity.

### §. 2.
### Of our election in Christ before the world began.

Let us now look upon Christ in his relationship to us before the whole world was made. God thus being from eternity in himself / and there being nothing else besides him; the first thing that he did (outside of what you have already heard <note>This refers to the internal generation of the Son and the Spirit described on the previous page.</note>) or the first thing that he could do according to our understanding / was a decree within himself to reveal his glory: Or a purpose in himself to communicate <note>In this context, to "communicate" means to share or impart His divine qualities to something else.</note> his glory to something else outside of his eternal unity. I say, to *something else*, for what is communication other than an outflowing / a coming forth from / or a movement between two ends? I have now brought you to God's deeds and workings in relation to his creatures; follow me a little / and I shall shortly bring you to Christ in relation to yourselves.

These dealings or workings of God were and are: 1. The decree. 2. The execution of the decree of God. These words I must explain a bit more closely.

I. The decree is an act of God / according to the counsel and purpose of his own will / governing all things / and all circumstances / and the order of all things from eternity in himself surely / and unchangeably /
<margin>Ephesians 1:11.</margin>
but nonetheless freely. *Who works all things* (says the Apostle) *after the counsel of his own will*; and this work / or this act of God is in-

<column-break/>

# The Second Book. Chapter 1. Section 3.

intention is not to enter into this dispute; it is simply granted that this ancient love that God has shown us in Christ is not from today or yesterday, but from <margin>2 Timothy 1:9</margin> before all the world; Paul speaks of the grace that was given to us before the ages of eternity began. But what is most worthy of notice in our text, as it serves our purpose, is that we are chosen in him. We read of three phrases in the Scriptures speaking of Christ: sometimes we are said to be blessed in him, and sometimes because of him, and sometimes through him. Sometimes **in** <margin>Philippians 1:29</margin> **him**, as here: *he has chosen us in him*; sometimes **because of him** (or for his sake), as elsewhere: *It is given to you for Christ's sake, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him*; sometimes **through him**, as in the words <margin>1 Corinthians 15:57</margin> of Paul: *Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.* But the blessings come **through** Christ, in the respect that Christ is a Mediator <term>Middelaer: A "go-between" or legal representative who reconciles two parties—in this case, God and humanity.</term> not only of merit, but also of execution; obtaining and receiving from grace not only every good thing for us, but also carrying it out and powerfully applying the same to us. And the blessings come **because of Christ's sake**, in view of the fact that Christ, through his obedience, obtains all good things which are granted to us in his time. And we have the blessings **in Christ**, because in Christ—as in a common storehouse <note>original: "ghemeen Magazijn"</note>—all things are first laid away, which shall afterwards be shared with us. And so we are in Christ

<column-break/>

This grace of election first began in Christ our Head, and has thus descended downward to us, his members. Christ is the firstborn among all his brothers, having the preeminence; or Christ <margin>Romans 8:29</margin> was the firstborn among many brothers, the first who opened the womb. Christ was sealed and set apart to be the Prince of our salvation before (in the order of nature) we were chosen. In the order of actual existence, we admit that Christ is revealed, promised, and given after sin, and that we repent, believe, and persevere before we are saved; but in the order of God’s purpose, Christ is before sin, and salvation is before repentance, faith, and perseverance. And thus, in consideration of us, we say that the "end" must in nature be before the "means" to that end; now the permitting of the fall, repentance, faith, and perseverance are used by God as means to bring some to salvation; therefore God also first designs our salvation, and then the means; and both the end and the means are the product of God’s election or pre-ordination. ### The Second Book. Chapter 1. § 5.

...that God would much rather have trees for their fruit / than for firewood : for this reason He purposed that the human race / notwithstanding sin / should not perish entirely.

Upon this the **Trinity** held counsel; and the question was / what shall be done with poor man? The learned set forth here a certain conflict between God’s holy attributes / and through a freedom which the Holy Spirit allows them by virtue of the language of the Holy Scriptures / they speak of God in a human manner / as if He had come into certain distresses and anxieties / through the competing desires of His various attributes. **Justice** urges Him for the damnation of a sinful / and consequently rightfully cursed creature; which desire is strengthened by His **Truth** / in order to make good that threat / *in the day that you eat thereof / you shall die the death* <note>The original Dutch uses "den doodt sterven," a literal translation of the Hebrew idiom for "surely die," emphasizing the absolute certainty of the sentence.</note>: **Mercy** pleads on the other side for grace / and compassion toward men / being wretchedly deceived and overcome by Satan / and this plea <term>pleydop|A legal term for a formal argument or case made in court; here it refers to the metaphorical trial between God's internal qualities.</term> is accompanied by **Love** and **Goodness** and other such attributes; finally, the matter having to come to a conclusion / **Wisdom** finds a way out / which the Angels of Heaven look upon with wonder and amazement / seeing how these differing pleas of His attributes are to be reconciled with one another. # The Second Book. Chapter 1. §. 7.

...and the motives for Divine <term>election|The doctrine that God sovereignly chooses individuals for salvation.</term>.

6. Because election based on foreseen faith—or the election of people because they are seen to be believers who persevere in faith and holiness until their final breath—brings with it many absurdities. Specifically: 1. This would mean choosing people who are viewed neither in a state of innocence nor in a state of misery, but already in a state of grace, which contradicts the very nature of the choice. 2. This does not produce faith, holiness, and perseverance out of the gracious benefit of election; rather, it produces election out of the foreseen works of faith, obedience, and perseverance. This is directly contrary to the <term>Scripture|The Bible</term>, 
<margin>Ephesians 1:4.</margin>
which says: *He has chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love.* 3. This would be as much as saying that election, or <term>pre-ordination|God’s act of deciding or ordaining outcomes beforehand.</term>, does not help a person at all on the path to eternal salvation. For how could something be a cause leading us surely on the way to eternal life if it does not even come into consideration until a person has finished their course of faith and godliness (at least in God's foreknowledge) and has arrived at the gates of Heaven? Such a falsely-named "pre-ordination" could more rightly and properly be called a "post-ordination" <note>The author is mocking the idea of "choosing" someone after they have already succeeded; "pre" means before, while "post" means after.</note>. But I

<column-break/>

have stood too long upon this dispute, and it is directly against 
<margin>1 Timothy 1:4</margin>
my intention, which is not to bring forth controversial questions, but rather <term>edification|The process of building up a person's faith and spiritual understanding.</term>, which is in faith. I remember what I have read, and I already begin to feel in practice, that these conflicting points only disturb our spirit and destroy our zeal, our love, and our delight in Jesus (as we look upon this lovely subject and object), even by distracting and changing our gaze; not one word more, then, of this kind.

### §. 8.
#### The Decree.

God’s decree concerning man’s salvation before the foundation of the world is evident from these texts: "I will declare the decree" (says God); what was that?

<margin>Psalm 2:7, 8.</margin>

As concerning Christ and the Church: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you; ask of me and I shall give you the heathen for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession." It was God's decree to give a Congregation <note>original: "Gemeente," referring to the body of believers or the Church.</note> to Christ from among the Jews and the Gentiles; and this decree was made in that day of eternity when the Son of God was begotten of his Father. This decree has various names in the language of Scripture:

1. This is the same thing that we commonly call **pre-ordination** <term>pre-ordination|In this context, it refers to predestination: the divine foreordaining of all that will happen, especially with regard to the salvation of some and not others.</term>! For what is pre-ordination other than a decree of God concerning the various preparations of grace, through which some are infallibly brought to salvation? Pre-ordination is a decree of both the means and the end; a decree to give certain people here a powerful grace, and to bring those same people after this life to glory.

# The Second Book. Chapter 1. Section 9.

I 3

The reason for this dispute lies in these words: *Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed: he does not say, and to seeds, as of many, but as of one, and to your seed, which is Christ.* <note>This is a central argument from Galatians 3:16, where the Apostle Paul uses a grammatical point—the use of the singular "seed"—to argue that the Old Testament promises point specifically to Jesus.</note> 1. Some conclude from this that no <term>covenant<note>A formal agreement or contract between God and humanity.</note></term> or promise has been made to us directly, but only to Christ or with Christ. In this view, Christ stands in our place and deals with God on our behalf, fulfilling all the conditions regarding life and heavenly glory; so that all the promises are made to him. Nevertheless, it is practically admitted that because we belong to Christ and are included in the covenant, it is therefore sometimes called a covenant made with us. <margin>Jeremiah 31:32</margin> *I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah.* This does not mean that the covenant is strictly made with us, but only with Christ for our sake; and when we feel the power of the promise working within ourselves, then we begin to remember that we are also included in that same covenant. But it is better (they say) that we feel ourselves to be included in the covenant that God made with Christ, than to think that we ourselves had entered into a covenant with God.

2. Others wish to prove from this that there is no covenant or promise made with Christ for his own person alone, but only with Christ in a spiritual manner—that is, with those who are members of Christ’s body and thus united with him. For notice the words (they say): the promises were 

<column-break/>

first made with Abraham and then with his seed. This "seed" is the kind of seed that has a right to the promises in the line descending from Abraham; now, this cannot be Christ in his own person, but Christ within his spiritual body <note>The "spiritual body" refers to the Church or the community of all believers united under Christ.</note>. And when the text says that the promise was not spoken to "seeds" (plural), but to one "seed," which is Christ, they make a distinction between a twofold seed of Abraham. First, there is a fleshly, natural seed according to the physical lineage; and in this sense, Christ speaks to those godless, unbelieving Jews who had come out to kill him: <margin>John 8:37</margin> *I know that you are Abraham's seed, but you seek to kill me.* Second, there is a spiritual seed that walks in the faith and footsteps of Abraham; thus you understand that those who live by faith are Abraham's children. <margin>Galatians 3:7, 29</margin> *And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.* Now the promise was made to Abraham and his seed, not seeds: that is, not to both types of seeds—the fleshly as well as the spiritual—but only to the one, which is the spiritual. And this seed is "Christ," meaning the Spiritual Christ—the body of Christ, the believers who are united with Christ through a sincere and living faith.

3. Others conclude from this that this covenant is made both between God and Christ, and between God and us. First, it was between God and Christ: the entire work of redemption and salvation was between God and
