and Christ settled these matters before the foundation of the world; but this does not prevent the same promise from being fulfilled for us later in the fullness of time: Consider how it works in covenants among men; when a child is not yet born, the Father obtains a deed of inheritance for his child, which he keeps in his hand until the child is born and comes of age, and then he places the child in possession of it. This is how the matter stands here; for a time, we were enclosed in the womb of God’s election <note>The theological concept of God choosing individuals for salvation before time began.</note>, until we were brought forth through the grace of rebirth; but during this time, we are not capable of receiving any promise of life made to us; rather, those promises are made to Christ on our behalf, and he has received the promise from the Father in our place. Yet it happens in such a way that, once we are reborn, the promises are applied to us ourselves, and then we are placed in possession of them.

This is then the meaning of the words: the covenant is made with Christ; that is, with Christ and his heirs; primarily with Christ, and with Abraham’s offspring in Christ, and yet specifically with the believers, who are also Abraham’s seed. The entire distinction lies in the little word *Christ*, and what is understood by it: whether Christ in his own person, or Christ’s spiritual body, or Christ through representation: And we say—

<column-break/>

I. Not Christ in his own person; I mean, not Christ considered as a private individual, because 1. that would contradict the aim of Paul, whose purpose is to prove that the promise of eternal life is made to all believers; and then 2. it would follow that the promise of eternal life would be given to Christ alone, and not in the least to those who believe in Christ.

II. Not Christ in his spiritual body <note>Referring to the "body of Christ," or the collective community of all believers.</note>, because 1. <margin>verse 17.</margin> The promise was made to Christ, in whom the covenant was confirmed. 
<margin>verse 8.</margin> 2. In whom the nations were blessed. <margin>verse 14.</margin> 3. In whom we obtain the promise of the Spirit through faith. 
<margin>verse 13.</margin> 4. Who became a curse for us. Now all of this cannot be applied to Christ when viewed spiritually <note>The author argues that these actions require a specific historical person—the Mediator—rather than just the collective group of the Church.</note>, for the spiritual Christ did not confirm the covenant, nor bless the nations, nor give the Spirit, nor did he become a curse.

III. It is Christ through representation; Christ as <term>Mediator<note>One who negotiates or acts as a bridge between two parties; here, between God and humanity.</note></term>, Christ as a public person, to whom the promises are made; for Christ and his heirs are all but one united household; and just as the Covenant of Works was made with Adam and all his descendants, and there were not two separate covenants; so also here the covenant is made with the second Adam <note>A title for Jesus, contrasting him with the first man, Adam, who failed the original "Covenant of Works."</note> and with his children. But each in his own order: <margin>1 Cor. 15:23.</margin> Christ the first-fruits, afterward those who belong to Christ.

...to communicate outside of His eternal unity, He made this design <note>original: "beworp". A draft, blueprint, or architectural plan.</note>: that all He would do in this regard would be to the praise of the glory of His

### The Second Book, Chap. 2. §. 2. ###

His grace and loving-kindness, and yet also satisfy His truth and justice? Finally, God’s wisdom found that glorious and wonderful means, the Lord Jesus Christ. And is this not <margin>Romans 3:25</margin> the meaning of the Apostle? Whom God set forth to be a propitiation <note>A "propitiation" is an offering that turns away anger or fulfills a legal requirement; here, it refers to Christ’s sacrifice.</note> through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness, through the forgiveness of sins. Ponder and consider these words! God did not set forth Christ as a propitiation only to show His mercy in the forgiveness of sins: how? Is there anything other than mercy in the forgiveness of sins? Yes; there is something else, there is also justice. And therefore He set forth Christ to be a propitiation, so that He would demonstrate His righteousness; <margin>Verse 26.</margin> yes, look at the account: to demonstrate, I say, His righteousness, that He might be just, and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Not [only] so that He might be merciful, but that He might be *just* in justifying the one who has faith in Jesus. This text gave <term>Luther</term><note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German reformer, famously struggled with the phrase "the righteousness of God" until he realized it referred to the righteousness God *gives* to believers, rather than just the justice that *punishes* them.</note> much work to understand, and he prayed for a long time before he was able to grasp its true meaning.

This is the great mystery of the Gospel; it is no wonder that a poor human being cannot reach it. This is what the infinite wisdom of God has been working on from all eternity: how a way might be found to make sinners

<column-break/>

blessed, and yet remain perfectly just. Yes, O my soul, think a little further; not only is God's mercy glorified in this manner, but also the glory of His justice—truly as much, yes, even more than if the sinner had been eternally damned. And that is proven thus:

1. When God ordained a <term>surety</term><note>A "surety" (borg) is a legal guarantor who takes responsibility for another person’s debt or obligation.</note>, His Son, and laid our debts upon Him to satisfy His justice: wherein God, not wanting to spare His Son even unto the last penny—I mean, not even to the slightest degree of punishment—thereby God has shown a greater love for justice than if He had damned ten thousand times a thousand creatures. Suppose a criminal comes before the judge; the judge does not want to excuse the criminal, but commands that the law be satisfied; this is proof that the judge loves justice. But if the judge’s own Son is a wrongdoer, and it is evident to the whole land that the judge will not excuse him; in that, the judge shows more honor to justice than in the sentencing of a thousand others. Likewise, when the Lord God throws many thousands of sinners into hell, to be tormented there forever, forever, forever; this is a sign that God loves justice. <meta>This page continues the exploration of God's "Design" for salvation, specifically focusing on how Christ satisfies the demands of divine justice. The previous page discussed the tension between mercy and righteousness; here, the author uses a financial analogy—a creditor and a debtor—to explain why Christ's sacrifice is superior to eternal punishment for the sinner.</meta>

->### Looking unto Jesus.<-

<margin>Romans 8:32.</margin> Scripture [says], he did not even spare his own Son) this, yes, certainly this is a greater proof of God’s love for justice than if the whole world were to be condemned. 

2. Suppose that the reconciled sinner had been condemned; then God’s justice would only have been in a state of seeking satisfaction, and in eternity it would never have been fully satisfied. But in the way that God has invented to make sinners blessed, his justice is not only receiving a <term>satisfaction</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, "satisfaction" refers to the legal payment or restitution required to balance the scales of justice after a law has been broken.</note>, but it is fully satisfied. As an example: suppose someone is another's creditor, who owes him a hundred thousand pounds, but this person is poor, and the most he can pay is only a penny a day. Suppose that the creditor were to put him in prison until he had paid even to the last penny; it is true that he would receive something day after day, but as long as the debtor lived, he would never be [fully] paid. Now, if a rich man were to come and present him with a hundred thousand pounds all at once, then the creditor would be paid immediately. 

Well, such is the difference between God satisfying his justice upon the sinner and upon Jesus Christ: God comes to the sinner and demands the debt of punishment because he has not paid the debt of obedience. God throws him into prison, and the most he can pay is,

<column-break/>

speaking figuratively, only a penny a day; and for this reason the poor sinner must do nothing but constantly pay, and pay, and will have to pay for all eternity. This is the cause of their eternal punishment in hell: because they can never pay enough in a time that has an end. But now our Lord Jesus Christ has come, and has paid the debt in full all at once, so that justice says: "I am content; I am satisfied." Certainly, this is a greater honor even for the justice of God.

This was God’s counsel from all eternity: how he would find a way for his love and kindness, and yet also satisfy his truth and justice. Oh my soul, reflect and wonder! Jesus Christ has been the means, and in Christ, not only is God’s mercy exalted, but also his justice; yes, it is more exalted and more glorified in your salvation than it ever could have been in your eternal condemnation.

# Looking unto Jesus

<margin>Romans 8:32</margin> (Scripture: He also did not spare His own Son) <note>original: "hy heeft oock sijnen eygenen Sone niet gespaert"</note>—this, yes indeed this is a greater proof of God’s love for <term>justice</term> <note>The Dutch *gerechtigheyt* implies both personal righteousness and the judicial standard of justice.</note> than if the whole world were to be condemned.

2. Suppose that the reconciled sinner had been condemned; then the justice of God would only have been in a state of seeking <term>satisfaction</term> <note>The term *voldoeningh* refers to the full payment of a debt or the completion of a legal penalty.</note>, and in all eternity it would not have been fully satisfied. But in the way that God has devised to make sinners blessed, His justice is not merely receiving a partial payment, but it is fully satisfied. For example: suppose that someone is a creditor to another who owes him a hundred thousand pounds, but this person is poor, and the most he can pay is but a penny a day. Suppose the creditor were to cast him into prison until he had paid even to the last penny; it is true that he would receive something day after day, but he would nonetheless never be fully paid as long as the debtor lives. Now if a rich man were to come, and at once lay down a hundred thousand pounds for him, then the creditor would be paid immediately. Just so is the difference between God satisfying His justice upon the sinner and upon Jesus Christ: God comes to the sinner and demands the debt of punishment because he has not paid the debt of obedience. God throws him into prison, and the most he can pay is—

<column-break/>

—to speak figuratively, but a penny a day; and for this reason the poor sinner must do nothing but continually pay, and pay, and shall have to pay for all eternity. This is the cause of their eternal punishment in hell: because they can never pay enough in a time that has an end. But now our Lord Jesus Christ has come and has paid the debt in full at once, so that justice says: *I am content, I am satisfied.* Certainly this is a greater honor even for the justice of God.

This has been the counsel of God from all eternity: how He would find a way for His love and kindness, and yet also satisfy His truth and justice. O my soul, reflect and wonder! Jesus Christ has been the means, and in Christ not only is God’s mercy exalted, but also His justice; yes, it is more exalted and more glorified in your salvation than it could have been in your condemnation throughout eternity.

All the saints of God, from the first to the last, were then present before Him, and He regarded them in His well-beloved Son, Christ. Before there was anything in the world—neither man nor any creature therein—He had from <meta>catchword: before</meta>

### §. 3.
#### Of desiring Jesus in this respect.

III. We must desire Jesus, just as He took upon Himself the great work of our redemption and salvation in that eternity. It is not enough that we know and meditate; but we must also 

<column-break/>

desire. Now, desire is a movement of the mind looking forward to obtaining some good that we do not have, and which we judge to be useful to us. In this respect, we cannot desire Jesus as if He were still to take upon Himself the work of our salvation before the ages began, for that work is already perfectly completed. But we may be desirous of these things: namely, 1. For the revelation of that work in us. 2. For God and Christ, those great <term>allies: bondgenooten, referring to the partners in the divine covenant</term> and negotiators of this work for us. 3. For a complete and ultimate execution, through which God actually works in time according to all His operations or decrees before time.

1. We must have a desire for the revelation of this work in us. We have heard what wonderful, excellent, and glorious things have been done by Jesus Christ for His saints from all eternity; and O, what a desire ought there now to be in us to know that we also are of that number? # Looking unto Jesus.

It is not enough that we know, and reflect, and desire, but we must also **hope**, and hold fast to our hope as for our own best interest. Now, hope is a movement of the soul <note>original: "ghemoedt" — referring to the inner disposition or heart</note>, by which we expect some future good, whether by appearance or with certainty. The whole question is: does that salvation—concerning which that great transaction between God and Christ took place—also concern me now? And what are the grounds and certainties upon which my hope is built? I know that some greatly abuse this doctrine: [they say] "If God has ordained me to salvation before the whole world existed, then I may well live just as I please; I then have no need to hear God's word, or to pray, or to hold edifying conversations, or to fulfill any other holy duties, for I am assured that I shall be saved." And thus they at once overthrow all the grounds of hope. It stands firm that God's decrees are unchangeable: but they do not lead to even the least of such conclusions or <term>reasonings</term> <note>original: "reden-kavelinghen" — often used to describe deceptive logic or sophistry</note>. For you might just as well say: "The Lord has ordained that I shall live so long, and after that time I shall not, nor can I, die; and therefore I have no need of food or drink or clothing or any other things." Oh foolish, senseless, devilish reasoning! God's decree concerns the **means** just as much as the **end**; those whom God has decreed to make blessed, He has also decreed to call, to justify, to 

<column-break/>

sanctify, before He makes them blessed.
O my soul, see upon what grounds your hope is built: if these are weak, your hope is weak; but if these are strong, then your hope shall also be strong, and certain, and prudent.
<margin>Romans 10:6</margin> In examining these grounds, *do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven? or who shall descend into the abyss?* Seek it neither above nor below: it is impossible for you to ascend into heaven with your body and to look upon the thoughts of eternity, or to read your name in the **book of life**, but seek it in these fruits and workings of your <term>election</term> <note>original: "uytverkiesing" — the theological concept of being chosen by God for salvation before time began</note>. For—
1. If you are included in God's decree for salvation, God will, sooner or later, cause the power of His Word to work upon your conscience with authority and conviction: <margin>1 Thessalonians 1:4, 5</margin> *knowing, beloved brothers, your election by God: for our Gospel was not among you in words only, but also in power.* The Apostle speaks thus of others; he was able to know that they were God's chosen ones, either through the <note>original: "oordeel der liefde" — judgment of charity; assuming the best of a fellow believer</note> or through a spirit of discernment, with which some were gifted in the times of the Apostles: but how could he know this truth so infallibly? By this glorious operation: *our Gospel was not among you in words only, but also in power.* Oh, it is so good that you notice with what power the preached word comes to fall into your hearts:

2. **If God has also foreordained you to salvation, then He shall, sooner or later, powerfully call you.** "Those whom He foreordained, these He also called": this calling is a calling of our soul from sin, out of the midst of the crowd of the world to Jesus Christ; it is such a calling that gives the soul power to follow Christ; <margin>Matthew 9:9</margin> just as Matthew, being called by Christ, stood up and followed Him. They are people of a different disposition of mind, <note>original: "beheerdigheypt" – refers to the state of being governed or directed; the internal "management" of the soul</note> of different movements, inclinations, and of a different walk of life; <margin>Acts 26:18</margin> they are called from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. **As the Apostle [says]:** <margin>Ephesians 5:8, 7</margin> **"You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord... There is some difference between hope and faith; just as hope looks upon what the word promises, **the matter of the word** <note>original Latin: "rem verbi"</note>; so faith looks upon the word itself, **the word of the matter** <note>original Latin: "verbum rei"</note>; hope looks primarily at the mercy and kindness of the promise, but faith looks mostly at the authority and truth of the promiser; hope looks at its object as something in the future, but faith alone looks at the object as present; both make a particular appropriation to themselves; but hope as expecting the same, and faith as possessing such in a certain manner. # Looking unto Jesus.

...made a promise from all eternity, that I want to send my Son into the world to be a curse for sin; yes, and if you believe, for your sin; and this is the greatest work of all that is to be done in all eternity. Surely, if I had wanted to deceive you in anything, it would have been in this; it is not such a great matter for me now to bring you into heaven, or to make your souls blessed, as it was to send my Son into the world to be made a curse for sin. <note>The author uses a "greater to the lesser" argument: if God did the hardest thing (sacrificing His Son), He will surely do the "easier" thing (bringing the believer to heaven).</note> But since I have already done such a great work, and have already been so faithful in that promise, what can you do but believe my faithfulness in the fulfillment of all other promises? If but a man were to owe you a thousand pounds, and paid you nine hundred and ninety-nine, you would surely think that he would not remain behind with the rest. Well, God has already paid His nine hundred and ninety-nine, and all the glory of heaven is, by comparison, no more than one compared to all that He has already done; we may well believe then, that He who has done so much for us will not leave that little bit undone.

Come then, and rise up, **O** my soul, and believe that you have a part in these eternal dealings between God and Christ: is there not enough stability here for your faith? If only you are called, the promises of God are yours; or if you do not

<column-break/>

dare lean upon His promises (which God forbid), you have His written conditions, His seal, and witnesses of every kind, both in heaven and on earth. Or if you still do not believe, you have the oath, the pledge, and the greatest part of your salvation already given into your hand. Yes, my poor soul, I say to you even more than this: Christ Himself has bound Himself for you from all eternity, that you shall believe. **O**, then, do not act through your rejection of the Gospel so that Christ would have to be summoned because of His bond! <note>A legal metaphor: the author warns that by refusing to believe, the soul is "suing" Christ or making Him default on the legal contract He made with the Father.</note> Certainly, if you believe, you shall make Christ's word true; he who does not believe makes God a liar—though in another sense, and because he understands it so—even in this, that he nullifies Christ's undertaking in the covenant. Therefore, do believe; yes, cry out: *Lord, I believe; help thou my unbelief;* increase my faith, until I shall have come to the full assurance of faith. Faith is, in this sense, the true eye of the soul, reading that its name stands written in the book of life; it is an acceptance of our particular election. **O**, so believe then, until you come to a complete conviction of God's love in Christ.

### The Second Book. Chapter 2. Section 6.

[He who] has taken salvation upon Himself in eternity. ### The Second Book. Chapter 2. §. 6. ###

...riches of His love to be presented in Jesus Christ. Doubtless He also had other great designs in working such great things as He has done, but above all the designs that God has had in all His works, this is the chiefest: to honor His mercy, to glorify the riches of His love and grace. Had it not been for this, He would never have created the world; and therefore in the world to come, it shall be God’s delight to show His Saints and Angels what He can do for a creature; yes, throughout all eternity He shall demonstrate to them to what a height of excellence and glory His love and mercy can exalt poor souls, so that even the Saints and the Angels shall wonder at it, and shall worship and exalt the name of God for all eternity.

# Looking unto Jesus.

...and miserable sinner such as I am? Has such a love ever been seen? Has such a mercy ever existed? And must not heaven and earth stand amazed at this? Oh, what shall I do to show proper gratitude to this glorious God? Thus you, who know that you have a part in Christ, must diligently apply yourself to praise and thank God. Say to yourself: who has distinguished me from these rejected souls? Alas! we are all made of the same material, and hewn from one rock. It is told of one of the recent Kings of France <note>Likely referring to a story popular in 17th-century devotional books about a king's humility regarding his birthright</note>, that in a serious meditation and reflection on his own state, as being a King and Judge over that Nation, he said: "Oh, when I was born, there were surely a thousand other souls born alongside me in this Kingdom, and what more have I done for God than these?" Oh my soul, what distinction has there been between you and so many thousands of the rejected, who live in the world alongside you this day? Nothing, truly nothing other than the free mercy, kindness, and love of God in Christ Jesus. Oh, then praise that God; yes, let the praise of the glory of His grace resound. Remember that God intended this, and that this is your duty.

### §. 9.

->On the conformity with Jesus in this regard.<-

IX. **W**e must become conformed to Jesus: we must keep our eyes on Jesus for our imitation: this is also the meaning of this "looking" in our text. And in respect to our pre-ordination <term>pre-ordination: the theological concept that God determined the salvation of believers from eternity</term>, the Apostle clearly says:
<margin>Rom. 8:29</margin>
He has pre-ordained us to be conformed to the image of His Son. This is also one of the ends <note>purposes</note> of our pre-ordination; this is one of the ends of our looking unto Jesus; yes, it is included therein. A true looking unto Jesus has a power in it to make us conformed to the image of Jesus Christ. We are changed into His likeness by beholding [Him],
<margin>2 Cor. 3:18</margin>
says the Apostle. Oh, when I consider the love of God in Christ toward me, even from all eternity, how can this do otherwise than stir up my soul to be like Jesus Christ? Even among men it is so; where there is an attachment, there is also a desire to be like one another; how much more, considering my attachment to God in Christ, must I desire to be like Christ in His form? Now the whole question is, what is this image of Christ, to which we must become conformed? I give as answer, that it consists in holiness and glory: but since the latter is our reward, and the former our bounden duty, therefore you must look upon that.

Thus far we have looked unto Jesus as our Jesus, in that eternity before all time until the creation: after this we shall look unto Jesus, as he took upon himself that great work of man’s salvation <term>salvations (saligheydt): the state of eternal blessedness and deliverance from sin</term> in the creation / in the beginning of time / until his first coming.

In this part / just as in the preceding / we shall first set before you the object; and then we shall direct you how you must look upon it.

The object is Jesus, as he took upon himself the work of man's salvation / in that dark time / before his coming in the flesh. <note>The "dark time" refers to the era of the Old Testament, where Christ was seen through shadows and types rather than in person.</note>

No sooner was the world made / and all that is therein; than man was created / so that God might have the opportunity / to show his grace in the salvation of his elect. And it was then / that God's eternal design / and counsel / and foreknowledge / and purpose / and decree / and covenant with Christ began to be carried out. It is

Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a highly influential Latin Church Father whose writings shaped much of Western Christian thought on original sin.</note> writes among others that they remained standing for only six hours; but although we cannot determine the exact time / it is nevertheless probable enough / that it was but a short time: This we find / that Moses having presented the creation of man / without relating anything else in between,

### The Third Book, Chapter 1, Section 1.

...going before the Gospel / and are fulfilled under the Gospel / so that such a great good would be earnestly desired / before it would be given. In the time of darkness, people are very eager for the light; just as the morning-watchman <note>original: "morgen-wachter" — a reference to Psalm 130:6, where the soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning.</note> watches and longs for the morning / so the dark revelation of Christ in the promises / has kindled the hearts of the Patriarchs to a heartfelt desire for the coming of Christ in the flesh. But in this darkness we have some stages to observe: before the giving of the law through Moses the promise was somewhat darker; the law having been given / the promise in the times of the Prophets was a little clearer; in the times of the Prophets up to John the Baptist / the same was even clearer: just as the coming of the Messiah gradually drew nearer and nearer / so the promise also became clearer and clearer: Just as the coming of the Sun is closer or further away / so also the preceding light is greater or smaller: in that same way was also the Revelation that went before Christ / somewhat darker or clearer / according to whether the rising of the Sun of righteousness <note>A common historical metaphor for Christ, based on Malachi 4:2.</note> was either further away / or closer by. It was God’s good pleasure / to reveal the riches of his grace by stages / and not all at once; we see even on the bright day <note>original: "hevigen dagh" — referring to the intensity and clarity of the New Testament era.</note> that God in various appearances of his fine mercy

<column-break/>

and kindness descends more and more to his Church: Even now in this wonderful light of the Gospel / we have our divine Ceremonies and Sacraments / we see him from afar / we know but in part; but the time shall come (even before his second coming) that we / or our children / shall see him with greater clarity and perfection / and somewhat from closer by. My present work is to set forth Christ in the covenant of grace / as it was promised / and because the promise has its distinction of stages / according to the various dawnings <term>voor-brekingh</term> <note>Literally "breaking-forth," as of the dawn or light through clouds.</note> of the same in the dark world / so shall we observe the same as it has been revealed.

1. From *Adam* to *Abraham*.
2. From *Abraham* to *Moses*.
3. From *Moses* to *David*.
4. From *David* to the Babylonian captivity, or thereabouts.
5. From the captivity or thereabouts to Christ.

In each of these parts we shall find some nearer and nearer revelations of God’s mercy in Christ / of the covenant of grace / of our Jesus taking upon himself that great work of man’s eternal salvation in those dark times. Regarding the meaning of the words / we shall open these things somewhat more closely / as 1. what the **Serpent** is. 2. who the **woman** is? 3. what is the **seed of the Serpent**. 4. what is the **seed of the woman**? 5. who is **He** / it being translated in our Bible as *the same*? <note>This refers to the masculine pronoun used for the Messiah who will crush the serpent, which was a point of translation debate between Protestants (who used "He" or "the same") and Catholics (who used "She").</note> 6. what is the **Head of the Serpent** / and the crushing of the same? 7. what is the **heel of the woman’s seed** / and the bruising of it? 8. between whom the **enmity** <term>enmity: a state of deep-seated ill-will or hostility, here used to describe the spiritual war between good and evil</term> was / or rather the enmities? for in the words we find several armies / *I will put enmity between you, and the woman, and between your seed, and her seed,* etc.

1. **Who is the Serpent?** I find various opinions among the interpreters: Some say / that it was only the **Serpent** / and that which concerns **Satan** / is only to be understood spiritually: others say / that it was only **Satan** under the name of the **Serpent** / as he is also sometimes called the **great Dragon** /
<margin>Revelation 12:9.</margin>
*And the great Dragon was cast out, namely the Old Serpent, which is called Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, he was, I say, cast down to the earth.* Others say / that it was both **Satan** and the **Serpent**; just as people are said to be possessed by **Satan** / so the **Serpent** was possessed by the **Devil**. **Satan** could not

<column-break/>

seduce our first parents to sin through any internal temptation / as he indeed does now through the help of our corruption: nor could he bear [influence] in their bodies or souls / because of their holiness and glory that was in them / and therefore he intended to take some beast of the earth / and through the steering of its tongue he spoke through it. But how? should then the **Serpent** be punished / who was only **Satan’s** tool in the temptation? Yes:

Such was God’s love for man / that he cursed both the master-worker and the tool of that evil: just as someone in his anger breaks the sword into pieces / with which his Son / or friend was wounded; so God broke **Satan’s sword**: the **Serpent** is punished according to the words of the text / and **Satan** is punished in the spiritual meaning of the Lord.

2. **Who is the woman?** Some understand it all figuratively / and they want to tell you / that the **Serpent** and the **Woman** are the highest and lowest powers of the soul; and that always after the fall there has been a continuous war between these: but I note this explanation as vain and trifling / although the same is also found by some **Church Fathers** / of great standing: <note>Refers to allegorical interpretations by early Christian theologians like Origen or Augustine.</note> others say / that this woman was the **blessed Virgin** / in which regard they then read these last words thus, *she shall crush the head*: <note>The author is referencing the Latin Vulgate translation "ipsa conteret," which attributes the crushing of the serpent to Mary rather than Christ.</note>

**II.** In what sense is the law a covenant of grace? I answer, that the Law can be considered in several meanings; as:

1. Sometimes it is taken in a broad sense for any heavenly teaching, whether it be a promise or a commandment; and in this sense <margin>Rom. 3:27.</margin> the Apostle speaks of a *law of works*, and of a *law of faith*.

2. 3. 4. Sometimes it is taken as a summary only for certain works of the law / against such <column-break/> things the law is not. <margin>Gal. 5:23.</margin>

5. Sometimes it is used only for the Ceremonial Law / the Law having a shadow of the good things to come. <margin>Hebr. 10:1.</margin>

6. Sometimes it is also used in regard to the Jews; as being able to save without Christ; and so the Apostle generally takes it in his epistles to the Romans and to the Galatians.

7. Sometimes it is also understood as that part of the Moral Law / which deals with simple commandments and orders / without any promises.

8. Sometimes it is also taken for the entire Moral Law / with its preface and accompanying promises. And in this last sense it is taken by us / when we say / that the Law is a covenant of grace.

### The Third Book. Chapter 1. Section 4.

<margin>Deuteronomy 7, 8, 9</margin>
Moses said to Israel: Because the Lord loved you, and because he kept the oath which he had sworn to your fathers, the Lord has brought you out with a mighty hand and has redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh, King of Egypt. You shall know then that the Lord your God is God, the faithful God, who keeps the covenant and mercy to those who love him and keep his commandments, even unto a thousand generations.

**2.** In respect of us; God preferred to deal with us in the manner of a covenant, rather than in a singular, eminent way of majesty <note>The author distinguishes between God acting as a distant, absolute Sovereign and God acting as a partner in a legal and relational agreement.</note>, based on these grounds:

**1.** That he might bind us more firmly to himself: a covenant binds on both sides; the Lord does not bind himself to us while letting us go our own way; No, 
<margin>Ezekiel 20:37</margin>
"I will bring you," says God, "under the bond of the covenant." God sees how slippery and unsteady our hearts are, how ready we are to turn aside from our duties toward him; 
<margin>Jeremiah 14:10</margin>
we love to wander, and therefore, to prevent this instability and unsteadiness, and to make our hearts more and more firm in our obedient walk before him, it has pleased God to bind us in the bond of the covenant. Thus, while we reach for any blessing from God, we are also compelled to keep the covenant with God. You might say, "A commandment binds as well as a covenant." This is true, but a 

<column-break/>

covenant twines <note>original: "twijnt." This refers to the process of twisting two strands of thread together to make a stronger cord. The author suggests the covenant doubles the strength of the legal obligation.</note> (so to speak) the bonds of the Law and doubles the command upon the soul; when it is only a commandment, God alone imposes the burden, but when I have given a promise in return, then I impose and bind that burden upon myself.

**2.** That our obedience might be the more willing and free; an absolute Law might seem to extort obedience, but a covenant and agreement clearly show that such obedience is more voluntary and willing. This is the nature of the covenant of grace: first, God promises mercy, that he will be our "exceeding great reward"; and then we promise obedience, to be his free and willing people. Thus, we become God’s property, not only by right of his Sovereign power and love, but through a possession arising from our own voluntary consent. We are not only his people, but his *willing* people; we give him our hand when we become his and enter with him into the covenant. 
<margin>Ezekiel 17:18</margin>
See this expressed in Ezekiel 17:18: *He despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand.* <note>To "give one's hand" was a formal gesture of pledge or agreement.</note> We are his, just as a Wife belongs to her husband; 
<margin>Ezekiel 16:8</margin>
*I entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became mine.* Now, in marriages, as you know, there is always a free and mutual consent; and so it is here also.

**3.** That our comfort might be the more powerful; that we, in all our troubl— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "moepe-", likely intended to be "moeyelyckheden" (troubles or difficulties).</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Preface to the Ten Commandments. ### The Third Book, Chap. 1. §. 4.

Do we not see clearly that God said to <margin>Gen. 15:7</margin> Abraham, *I am the Lord, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans*? and once more, <margin>Gen. 28:13</margin> *I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham, and the God of Isaac*? How then is it said that he was not known to them by his name Jehovah? This passage has perplexed many of the learned; but it seems to me that this is the meaning: although he was known to the Patriarchs <note>The foundational fathers of the faith, specifically Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> by this name, **Jehovah**, as it exists in its letters, syllables, and sound, he was nevertheless not yet known to them through experience in his steadfastness to fulfill his promises—specifically, to lead them out of the land of Egypt. This name Jehovah signifies both his essence in himself and his giving of "being" or fulfillment to his word and promise; thus, in reality, he was not yet known or revealed to the Patriarchs in this way. They were held up only through faith in God’s almighty power, without receiving the promised things. Of Abraham it is said, while he still lived, <margin>Acts 7:5</margin> that God gave him no inheritance in the land of Canaan, not even a footstep, but he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring after him. And now that his offspring has obtained the promise, and has had a full knowledge and experience of his power and goodness, how they have known the power of his name Jehovah! So,

<column-break/>

regarding the fulfillment of his future promises, he has said that they shall know him, that he is the Jehovah: *you shall know that <margin>Isa. 49:23</margin> I am the Lord.* —— *Therefore <margin>Isa. 52:6</margin> my people, therefore shall they know my name in that day, that I myself am he who speaks; behold, here I am.*

2. **I am the Lord God**, this signifies the plurality of persons; God, in the delivery of the law, has not only shown his essence but also the manner of his essence; that is, the three manners of existence in that one, simple, and eternal being—or the Trinity of persons in the Unity of essence. The word <note>The author is referring to the Hebrew name 'Elohim', which is grammatically plural.</note> signifies strong, powerful, mighty; or, if we express it in the plural number, it signifies the "almightinesses," or the almighty powers. For this reason, the Scripture attributes the common name God to the individual persons: the Father is God (Heb. 1:1-2), the Son is God (Acts 20:28), and the Holy Spirit is God (Acts 5:3-4). Now, God is said to be the giver of these laws, which were delivered by Moses <term>covenant-wise: in the form of a binding legal agreement or treaty</term>, so that their authority might be all the greater; and for this reason, all law-givers have labored to persuade the people that they received their laws from God.

3. **I am the Lord your God**: herein is the appropriation <note>The act of taking something for one's own; here, the personal claim a believer has on God.</note>, and in truth, here is the mercy—that God speaks thus to every believing soul: *I am your God.* Through this appropriation

4. In the confirmation of the Law, we find something of Christ. It was confirmed by seals and sacrifices, etc. What were all these but foreshadowings <note>original: "voorbeelden," referring to theological "types" or patterns that point to a future reality</note> of Christ? In the first expression of the covenant, we find the seal of circumcision; but now it has pleased God to add another seal to the first to strengthen their faith, namely: the Passover <note>original: "Pascha"</note>; and was this not a foreshadowing of Christ, the spotless Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world? Again, in this revelation, Moses introduced the Priesthood as an established ordinance to offer sacrifices for the people; and was this not a foreshadowing of Christ, our true and unchangeable High Priest? From time to time, I have seen the articles of a believing Jew’s Creed, gathered together from the Law of Moses, reading thus: *I believe that the Messiah shall die as a satisfaction for sin:* this they observed from their constant bloody sacrifices; and the slaughter of the Lamb at their deliverance from Egypt taught them no less.

<column-break/>

And thus we can go further: beyond all doubt, Christ's death and resurrection, Christ's priesthood and Kingdom, were portrayed and indicated through the sacrifices, and the bronze serpent <note>A reference to the "koperen slange" from Numbers 21, which Jesus identifies as a type of Himself in John 3:14</note>; and the Priesthood of Aaron, and the Kingdom of Israel; and I cannot think otherwise than that the godly, spiritual Jews understood this well, and they did not find rest in the sacrifices or Sacraments themselves, but every one of them truly possessed Christ through faith.

by demanding such a perfect obedience, [God intended] to humble and abase the Israelites, so that they might flee more earnestly to Christ. In this sense, the Law <margin>Galatians 3:24</margin> is our schoolmaster <note>The original Dutch uses *tucht-meeſter*, referring to the Greek *paidagōgos*, a guardian or tutor who led a child to their teacher; here, the Law leads the believer to Christ.</note> to bring us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. A schoolmaster (as you well know) does not only discipline and punish; he also teaches and instructs. Likewise, the Law does not only threaten and curse when its work is not done, but it also points out where we can obtain the strength and help—namely, from the Lord Jesus Christ. This being the case, how much are all those to be rebuked who, under the pretext of free grace and Christ, abolish the Law? Let us rather uphold it, for this is the way to uphold free grace and Christ. Surely, he who discovers his failings through the perfect rule of the Law, and whose soul is embittered and humbled because of these failings, must necessarily prize Christ, desire Christ, and exalt Christ in his thoughts above all the men of the world.

### §. 5.
### Concerning the covenant of promise, as revealed to David.

The further breaking-through of this gracious covenant occurred with David; and in this revelation, even more of Christ is seen. The expression of it is primarily in these words: *Although my house be not so* <margin>2 Samuel 23:5</margin> *with God; yet He hath made with me an everlasting covenant, that is in all things well-ordered and sure.*

To understand this well, we shall examine the following points:

1. Who the author of this covenant is.
2. Through whom this covenant is made.
3. What it means to say that the covenant is "established"?
4. How the covenant is "ordered"?
5. Wherein the covenant is "sure" or preserved?
6. Whether Christ is more clearly revealed in the breaking-through of this covenant than in any of the previous ones?

1. Who is the Author of this covenant? David says, *He has established it.* "He" is God; the Rock of Israel, the eternal Rock, their Rock and Redeemer <note>original: "Pſal. 19. 15" — in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 19:14.</note>, the Rock of their strength <note>original: "Pſal. 62. 8" — modern Psalm 62:7.</note>, the Rock of their heart <note>original: "Pſal. 72. 26" — modern Psalm 73:26.</note>, the Rock of their refuge <margin>Psalm 94:22</margin>.

The Psalmist uses this manner of speaking frequently and regularly to show that God is a mighty, constant, and

# The Third Book. Chap. 1. §. 6.

<margin>Job 2:4</margin> Life is a completely internal and deep matter in man; it lies entirely close to the heart—"skin for skin" (the Devil once spoke in truth) and all that a man has, he will give for his life. But he who does not hate his Father <margin>Luke 14:26</margin> and Mother—yes, even his own life, says *Christus* <note>original: "Christus" — Latin for Christ.</note>—he cannot be my disciple. For this reason, the Apostle, wishing to express this innermost and internal life of grace <margin>Galatians 2:20</margin>, says: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me;* and that which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the *Son of God*, who has loved me and given Himself up for me. What a powerful and strange expression is in these words: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me?* I do not live the life of birth; I do not breathe any physical breath—that is, in comparison to the life of faith. Even his natural life, although that is internal, he says he does not live, in respect to this life of grace, which is even more internal. And let this serve as a resolution to this question.

4. What is it that we have the Law written in our hearts? This writing encompasses the preceding, and is even somewhat more; the Transfer is expressed in these particular things:

1. It is said to be written, so that there might be something internal, corresponding with the Law from without: it was written externally, and so it is also written internally. This writing is as much as co-

<column-break/>

pying, or transcribing <note>original: "co-pperen / of uytschrijven" — the author uses the metaphor of a clerk or engraver copying a master text onto a new surface.</note>. This internal writing is entirely in agreement with the external writing. Oh, what a mercy this is, that the same God who with His own finger wrote the Law on the stone Tables, also writes the same Law by the finger of His Spirit in the Tables of our hearts? Just as you see in a seal: when you have pressed the seal into the wax, and you pull it away again, then you find in the wax the same impression that was in the seal. So it is in the hearts of the believers; once the Spirit has softened them, then He writes the Law therein; that is, He imprints an internal capability, an internal inclination into the heart, corresponding with all parts of the Law. This is what the Apostle calls the *Law of the mind*: *I see* <margin>Romans 7:23</margin> *another Law in my members*, which wars against the *Law of my mind*. Now, what is this Law in the mind other than an internal disposition to keep, in some measure, all commandments of the external Law? And this is the writing of the Law; (or if you will) the copying and transcribing of the Law into our innermost part.

2. It is said to be written, so that it might be rooted and driven into our hearts, like letters that are engraved in marble; such is the manner of God's writing. When God writes, it cannot be put out or erased; the letters that are written in marble shall not easily wear out again; so also the writing of God's Spirit is even less to be [un]done <note>The catchword "doen" at the bottom suggests the sentence continues on the next page, likely to say "undone" or "erased."</note>:

5. How are we so taught by God that, by comparison, we have no need for any other manner of teaching? I answer:

<meta>This page continues the meditation on the Covenant of Grace, specifically focusing on the "mother-promise" made to Abraham and moving into the promise given to Moses and the Israelites. ### The Third Book. Chapter 2. Section 2.

Just as it was with the nations who were friends with *Rome*: if they at any time desired it, the *Romans* were bound by honor to protect them, and they did so with such zeal as if they were protecting their own city of *Rome*. So it is with those people who are friends with God; He is bound by His honor to protect His people, and He will certainly do so if they desire His help. And how could it be otherwise? Is it even possible that God should break His covenant? And will He not stir Himself to scatter <note>original: "verstropen," meaning to plunder, destroy, or scatter</note> His and our spiritual enemies? He will surely do so. Thus sound the words of His covenant:
> *I will be a God to you, and to your seed after you.*

This is the general promise, which I may call the **mother-promise**, which has all other promises enclosed within her. And we find a *Jesus* in this promise; meditate upon that: it is God in *Christ* who is presented to us in this promise, *I will be a God to you, and to your seed after you.* Oh, how sweet! Here is the greatest promise that was ever made. *Christ-God* is greater than grace, forgiveness, holiness, and Heaven; just as the Bridegroom is worthier than the wedding garment, the bracelets, and the rings: the Well and fountain of life is more excellent than the streams. *Christ* is the objective blessedness <term>objective blessedness: the source of happiness that exists outside of oneself, namely God Himself</term>, far exceeding the created and essential blessedness that takes its origin from Him. Oh, my soul, is this not well worthy of your innermost meditation? But more on this in the next section.

<column-break/>

3. Meditate upon *Jesus* in the promise that was made to *Moses* and the children of *Israel*:
> *I am the Lord your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.*

Much has been said before about this promise as a subject for your meditation; but to be brief, meditate in this promise on the **fullness** and the **ownership**. Here is a fullness: it is a promise of infinite worth, a hidden treasure, a rich possession, an overflowing blessing that no one can properly value. It is nothing less than the great, and mighty, and infinite God. If we had a promise of a hundred worlds, or of ten heavens, this one is more than all of those. Heaven is undoubtedly beautiful, but God is yet much more beautiful, for He is the God of Heaven. and it is for this reason that the Saints in Heaven itself are not satisfied without their God. It is very sweetly expressed by *Bernard* <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic</note>:
> *Just as all that we give You, O Lord, cannot satisfy You unless we give ourselves to You; so also all that You give us, O Lord, cannot satisfy us unless You give Yourself to us.*

And this is why, just as God makes the Saints His portion, so God is the portion and the inheritance of His Saints. Meditate upon the greatness, the goodness, and the all-sufficiency of this promise: *I am the Lord your God!* Without doubt, *Moses* had many other rich promises from God, but without God Himself he could not be satisfied.
<margin>Exod. 33:15.</margin>

Oh, meditate on this and wonder! What? That the great and glorious God of Heaven and earth is willing to enter into a covenant; that is to say, to make a contract with us, so that He is willing to make Himself our debtor? Oh, my soul, meditate on this very attentively; He is in Heaven, and you are on earth; He is the Creator, and you are His creature. Oh, what are you, or what is your father’s house, that you are exalted thus far? Even the covenant itself is a wonder, as it relates God to us; what is it other than a contract, a comparison, a knitting together, and a binding of God to us? When Jehoshaphat and Ahab were in a covenant, see how Jehoshaphat spoke of himself: <margin>1 Kings 22:4.</margin> *I will be as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.* So it is also between God and us. When He once grants us this covenant, then His strength is our strength, His power is our power, His hosts are our hosts, and His attributes are our attributes; we have a share in all of them. There is a covenant for both damaging <note>In the sense of an offensive alliance against spiritual enemies.</note> and for protecting (if I may speak thus) between God and us; and if we hold this up to Him in all our distresses, He will not be able to forsake us.

### The Third Book. Chap. 2. §. 2.

Just as it was with the nations who were befriended by Rome—if they ever desired it, the Romans were bound by honor to protect them, and they did so with such zeal as if they were protecting their own city of Rome; so it is with those people who are befriended by God: He is bound by His honor to protect His people, and He will do so if they desire His help. And how else? Is it possible that God would break His covenant? And will He not drive Himself to scatter His and our spiritual enemies? He will surely do so. Thus read the words of His covenant: *I will be a God to you, and to your seed after you.* This is the common promise, which I may call the **mother-promise** <note>The author uses this term to describe the foundational promise—God giving Himself to His people—from which all other spiritual blessings and secondary promises grow.</note>, which has all promises enclosed within it; and we find a Jesus in this promise—ponder that—it is God in Christ who is presented to us in this promise: *I will be a God to you, and to your seed after you.* Oh, how sweet! Here is the greatest promise that was ever made; Christ-God is greater than grace, forgiveness, holiness, and Heaven; just as the Bridegroom is worthier than the wedding garment, the bracelets, and the rings: the well and fountain of life is more excellent than the streams. Christ is the objective happiness <term>objective happiness: "voorwerpige gheluckſaligheydt," referring to the theological concept that true bliss is found in the "Object" (God/Christ) rather than just the subjective feelings of the believer.</term>, far surpassing created and essential happiness which has its origin in Him. O my soul, is this not well worthy of your deepest meditation? But more on this in the next [section].

Here is a fullness: it is a promise of infinite worth, a hidden treasure, a rich possession, an overflowing blessing that no one can properly value; it is nothing less than the great, and mighty, and infinite God. If we had a promise of a hundred worlds, or of ten heavens, this one is more than all of them; Heaven is undoubtedly beautiful, but God is even more beautiful, for He is the God of Heaven. 1. **An everlasting covenant**: Meditate on this in its internal power and not merely in its outward administration. 3. **It is guarded, or sure**: God is not fickle or loose in His covenants; heaven and earth shall pass away before one jot or tittle of His word shall fail. not as merely a shadow of grace in comparison to the love and the richness of God’s grace in Christ in the justification <note>The theological act of God declaring a sinner righteous.</note> of a sinner.

If you have any right to this promise—*I shall forgive your iniquity, and I shall remember your sins no more*—then you are freed from eternal death and you have a share in an eternal Kingdom; O, truly know your blessedness! Remember how you are so infinitely bound to God, to Christ, to God’s mercy and free grace! This promise echoes nothing but grace and blessing; grace from God and blessing upon us. It is grace, because nothing but grace and mercy can forgive; it is grace, because God has the power in His hands, if He wills, to take vengeance. He does not overlook sin as men overlook an injury when they feign forgiveness; they may forgive because they lack the power to avenge. But it is different with God; <margin>Deut. 32:35</margin> *Vengeance is mine, and recompense,* says God. He is powerful enough to destroy, and yet He would rather forgive; <margin>Exod. 34:6</margin> this is His Name: *Strong and Merciful.*

O my soul, you are ready to complain: "What? Would the Lord forgive my sins? What reason would God have to look upon me, to forgive me, to snatch me like a burning branch <note>Original: "brandt-hout" — a reference to Zechariah 3:2, meaning someone rescued from destruction at the last moment.</note> out of the hellish fire?" What? Would God forgive me? But now (if only your heart is humbled) consider that the Lord shall do it.

<column-break/>

<margin>Micah 7:18</margin> 1. Because He delights in loving-kindness; it is God’s pleasure to forgive sin. Never have we had more pleasure, or even as much pleasure, in the doing and committing of sin as God has in the forgiveness of sin. He is the Father of mercies; <margin>2 Cor. 1:3</margin> He has a delight in mercy, just as a father delights in his children. It does Him good to see the fruits of His own loving-kindness in the taking away of the sins of His own people.

2. Because it is His purpose, which He has purposed in Himself from all eternity. This was that great purpose of God (as you have understood) to glorify His grace in those whom He had purposed to save; He desires the prize of the glory of His grace. <margin>Ephes. 1:6</margin> He will not be deprived of His glory. He will be wonderful in His saints; <margin>2 Thess. 1:10</margin> <note>The OCR says 1:16, but this refers to verse 10.</note> He wants the world to be amazed when it becomes known what sins were committed by them which have been forgiven by Him. And it is for this reason that God’s people are called "vessels of mercy," <margin>Rom. 9:23</margin> so that He might make known the riches of His glory upon the vessels of mercy. For just as vessels are, or can be, filled up to the brim, so shall the vessels of mercy be filled up to the top with mercy, so that the richness of His glory in the forgiveness of sins may be seen and known as a wonder before all the world.

<summary>This page explains that God's forgiveness is not a sign of weakness but a deliberate act of grace from a powerful Deity who delights in mercy. It emphasizes that God planned this forgiveness from eternity to demonstrate the "richness of His glory" through His people, described as vessels filled with mercy.</summary>

<column-break/>

the desire for that same thing, in so far as it can have any assurance or increase: Just as we see in outward, physical riches, that they are desired more vehemently by no one than by those who possess them; and the more grace-filled a soul is, the more the heart is also desirous of a greater measure of grace, just as water poured into a pump draws more out of it: <note>This refers to 'priming' a manual water pump; you must add a little water to create the suction needed to draw up a great deal more.</note> no one is so fervent in praying, *Lord help my unbelief*, as he who can say, *Lord I believe*; things may be desired in order of their assurance, and higher degrees of the same. Again, present things can be the object of our desires, so that they may continually remain with us; just as a person taking pleasure in something good that he has, desires the continuation of that pleasure; so the soul of man, having a reach as great as immortality, may desire the permanence as well as the presence of those good things which it possesses.

2. As the **substance**; the true essence of the covenant consists in this: "I shall be a God to them, and they shall be a people to me"; now *Christ* is both of these in Himself; He is the God of His people, and through His representation, He is the people of God, and before God. 
3. As the **equivalence**: many parts or fruits of the covenant must be fulfilled for the believers in their own time; but as soon as they are justified, *Christ* is said to be the covenant, being handed over as a present pledge or hand-gift <note>original: "handt-gift"; an "earnest" or down payment given to seal a contract, proving the rest will follow.</note> into the hands of man at the very moment of his justification: and this pledge is of equal value and esteem as that which is finally fulfilled. And so *Christ* is, in each of these respects, the covenant itself; He is the true peace and reconciliation itself, "and this man shall be peace, when 
<margin>Micah 5:4.</margin>
*Assyria* <note>original: "Assur"; the historical enemy of Israel, used here as a symbol for all spiritual enemies.</note> shall come into our land." Just as heat is hot by itself, and all other things become hot through it when they are united with it; so is *Christ* the covenant itself, and we are all only in the covenant insofar as we [are united with Him].

# The Third Book. Chap. 2. § 4.

### §. 4.
### Concerning Hope in Jesus in Such a Regard.

WE must hope in Jesus, just as he has taken upon himself that great work of our salvation in the manner of a covenant: now, what is hope other than a good feeling <note>In this context, "feeling" refers to a spiritual perception or sense of assurance.</note> regarding the possession of its object? Certainly, a good feeling is so necessary to hope that it mostly constitutes all its types and distinctions; depending on whether this feeling is greater or lesser, it causes the strength or weakness, the excess or the lack of this passion of hope. This good feeling determines whether hope is either doubtful or certain; being certain, it produces either confidence or <term>presumption</term> <note>Theological term for an unwarranted or arrogant hope of salvation without true faith.</note>. Presumption is nothing other than an immoderate hope without foundation; but confidence is, in a certain way, such an assurance of the things hoped for as if we already held them in our hands. Therefore, we generally say that we have great, strong, and good hope when we wish to speak of its certainty; which has given some cause to portray it thus: Hope is a certain, well-grounded confidence that the desired good shall come. To not dwell on this: the whole question is, do these promises, which are included in the covenant of grace, also pertain to me? And what are the grounds and foundations upon which my hope is built? If the grounds are weak, then the hope is doubt-

<column-break/>

ful or presumptuous; but if the grounds are sound, then the hope is good, and I may cast my anchor and build upon it.

In the examination of these grounds, we shall look only for the qualities which the Scripture says are provided to those with whom the Lord enters into the covenant of grace; and these we shall bring: 1. To the condition of the covenant. 2. To the promise of the covenant: as —

1. If you are in the covenant with God, then God has wrought in you that condition of the covenant: a true, and living, and <term>saving</term> <note>Specifically, faith that leads to "salvation" or "blessedness" (saligheid).</note>, and justifying faith.

<margin>Acts 16:31.</margin>
> Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall be saved.

<margin>Rom. 10:9.</margin>
If you believe, then you shall be saved. The promise of life, which is included in faith, is made only to the believer. This is such a certain way of testing that the Apostle himself has directed us toward it:

<margin>2 Cor. 13:5.</margin>
> Examine yourselves, whether you be in the faith.

But how shall I examine myself, since in these days there are so many who boast of faith? Well, thus: 1. True faith will bring you out of yourself into Christ,

<margin>Gal. 2:20.</margin>
> I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me:

a believing person does not have his life in himself, but in Jesus Christ: he has his spiritual being in the Father, and in his Son Jesus Christ; he is united with the Lord, and is one Spirit with him: he sees the Father in the Son, and the Son

Poor soul! You stand greatly amazed at this grand agreement of God: "What? That God would enter into a covenant with me? What? That God would make such great and precious promises to me? Surely these promises and these benefits are too high for me, or for any living soul."

Let that be so; but take heart nonetheless / for God shall glorify His grace / and for that reason He shall perform this great work. All that is required of you / and all that God demands of you in this case / is only to believe. Assuredly, you have no part in Christ / no part in the covenant of grace / if you will not believe. Faith is the essential value <note>The "high value" or core requirement.</note> of the covenant of grace; and therefore, either believe / or there is no covenant.

I know that it is no light matter to believe / indeed / it is one of the very hardest works under Heaven to move a soul to faith. "What? Will that great God of Heaven make a covenant with such a miserable human as I am? I cannot believe it." Well? What is the cause? "Ah, my sins, my sins! God is a consuming fire against such as I; He cannot look upon unrighteousness; there is little hope that God would ever want to come into a covenant with me." ### The Third Book. Chapter 2. Section 5:

Consider Him as one who has made it His ministry to heal, and refresh, and restore, and reconcile? It reminds me that merchants have among themselves a ministry of insurance <note>original: "bedieningh van versekeringh." ### §. 6.
### Of the loving of Jesus in this respect.

<margin>Dr. Preston on love.</margin>
VI. We must love *Jesus*, as he has taken upon himself this great work of our salvation in a covenantal manner <note>original: "verbondts-wijse." This refers to the theological framework where God's relationship with humanity is structured as a series of formal agreements or "covenants."</note>. I know that love, of all other motions of the soul, is held to be the first and foremost; some call it the first springing or outgoing affection of the soul, and therefore I might well have placed it in the first position before hope or desire; but I have preferred to place it in this order, as (in my judgment) most corresponding (if not with the order of nature, yet) with the spiritual workings as they manifest themselves in my soul: when a good thing is presented, then I first desire, and then I hope, and then I believe, and then I love. And some describing this spiritual love, tell me that it is a holy affection of the heart, springing from faith. But to pass over these delicate matters like a spider’s web (which is indeed artistic, but thin), this is certain: that I cannot believe that all these dealings of *God* through *Christ* are for me in a covenantal manner, without necessarily loving that *God*, and also loving that *Christ*, who has thus first and willingly loved me; go then, my soul, bring the fire to the hearth, stir up your small

->On Loving Jesus in This<-

<margin>Dr. Preston on Love.</margin>
VI. **WE** must love Jesus, just as He has taken upon Himself this great work of our salvation in the manner of a covenant. I know that love is considered the first and foremost of all the motions of the mind; some call it the first springing or outgoing affection of the soul. <column-break/>

O my soul, I cannot express the love of God in *Christ* toward you. I paint the Son only with a piece of coal <note>original: "kole." A metaphor for a crude or dark sketch that fails to capture the brilliance of the subject.</note>, when I attempt to express God’s love in *Christ*.

2. Regarding the properties of this love: 1. God’s love toward you is an eternal love. He has had thoughts of you in His eternity in this manner; *At such a time there shall be such a man, and such a woman living on earth; in the latter times such a one (I mean you who read this, if you believe) and to that soul I shall reveal myself, and share my love; to that soul I shall offer Christ, and to that soul I shall give the hand of faith to hold fast to Christ; and to that end I now write the name in the book of life, and no one shall be able to erase it again.* O eternal love! O those blessed dealings between the Father and the Son from all eternity, to reveal His love even to your soul.

<margin>Malachi 1:2, 3</margin>
2. God’s love toward you is a choice love; it is a selecting and distinguishing love; as He, passing by many thousands whom He has left lying there, even then set His heart upon you: *Was not Esau Jacob's brother? says the Lord; yet I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau.* So also, were you not the brother of such a one,

<column-break/>

or the sister of such a one who remained evil and godless? Were you not from such a household, of which several, or some, have been passed by, and yet God has loved you, and set His love upon you? Surely this is an extraordinary love.

<margin>Hosea 14:5</margin>
3. God’s love toward you is a free love: *I will love them freely,* says God. And <margin>Deuteronomy 7:7, 8</margin> --- *The Lord did not set His affection on you, nor choose you, because you were more numerous than any other people... But because the Lord loved you;* there can be no other reason why the Lord has loved you, than because He has loved you; we are accustomed to say, this is a woman’s reason <note>In the 17th century, this was a common idiom for a decision made purely by one's own will or desire without external necessity—here used to describe God’s sovereign grace.</note>; *I will do this, because I will do this;* but here we find that it is God’s reason; although it seems a strange proof, yet *Moses* can go no higher; He has loved you; why? because He has loved you.

4. God’s love toward you is a love of all relations: mark what the love of a friend is to his friend; or what the love of a Father is to his Child; or what the love of a husband is to his wife, such is God’s love to you; you are His friend, His son, His daughter, His Bride; and God is your all in all.

### §. 7.
### Of rejoicing in Jesus in this regard.

VII. We must rejoice in Jesus just as he has taken that great work of our salvation upon himself by way of a covenant. I know that our joy here is only in part; so great is the excellence of spiritual joy that it is reserved for heaven; God does not allow it to be pure and

<column-break/>

perfect here below; and yet / such as it is (though mixed with care and pain) / it is a blessed duty; it is the light of our souls; and if it were entirely taken away / our life would be nothing but terror and confusion. Oh my soul / if you had no hope that some joy would meet you in all your doing / you would become powerless and motionless / you would be without movement and strength / you would no longer speak of Jesus / or of a covenant of grace / or of God / or of Christ / or of life / or of grace / or of glory.

Well then, my soul, go up and rejoice in Jesus / if you love him / what should hinder your joy in him? It is a common rule / that when love proceeds / and desire has no hindrance / it always passes from love to joy. The first movement of desire toward the good / is to be united with it / and the next desire toward the good / is to enjoy it: now love consists in union / and joy in enjoyment; for what is enjoyment but a joy that we have in the possession of that thing / which we love? There is quite a bit of debate among the philosophers <note>original: "wijsgieren," meaning those who seek wisdom.</note> regarding the distinctions between love and joy. Some put it thus: just as is the movement of flowing bodies / that run toward their center / thinking to find their rest there; but

VIII. **W**e must call upon Jesus, or God the Father in and through Jesus in relation to this covenant of grace / now this calling upon God consists in praying and thanking.

# Looking unto Jesus.

...dness and mercy that has been revealed to her. O my soul, have you thus approached penitently at His feet to touch the tip of Christ's golden scepter? <note>A reference to the Book of Esther, where Queen Esther approached the King at the risk of her life; his extending the golden scepter was a sign of mercy and acceptance.</note> Well then, your hand is given to God; then you have entered into the covenant of peace. Christ’s offering and your acceptance of the covenant of grace give birth to a sweet agreement and a harmonious conformity.

2. God in Christ keeps the covenant with us; so must we also, through Christ, be careful and diligent to keep the covenant with God. In worldly matters, people pay very close attention to the agreements that are made. Now, it is not enough for us that we have entered into the covenant with God; we must also keep it. The Lord shall never, nor has He ever, broken the covenant on His side; but alas, we have broken the first covenant—the covenant of works—on our side. <note>In Reformed theology, the "Covenant of Works" refers to the agreement with Adam (based on obedience), while the "Covenant of Grace" refers to the salvation offered through faith in Christ after the Fall.</note> Let us take good care that we do not break the second one as well, for then there is no place left for any other covenant. Just as the Lord keeps the covenant with us, let us also keep the covenant with Him, for in this is the blessing:
<margin>Ps. 103:17, 18.</margin> *The lovingkindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting... to those who keep His covenant.*

Much depends on us keeping this covenant; therefore, permit me to expand on this a little: several acts of faith are required for this keeping of the covenant. As—

<column-break/>

1. In keeping the covenant, faith always has its eye upon the rule and the commandment of God. Just as faith looks upon the promise regarding things that must be believed, so faith looks upon the commandment regarding those things that must be done. Faith does not wish to bring "strange fire" <note>The OCR reads "bier" (beer), but in this theological context, it is almost certainly "vuur" or "vyer" (fire), referring to the biblical story of Nadab and Abihu who were punished for offering unauthorized "strange fire" before the Lord in Leviticus 10.</note> before the Lord; it knows that God will accept nothing other than that which accords with His will.

2. Just as faith takes its direction from the rule, so it directs us in the keeping of the covenant toward the right end—that is, to the glory of God. We are from Him and live in Him, and through faith we must live for Him and because of Him; for none of us lives for himself,
<margin>Rom. 14:7, 8.</margin> and no one dies for himself: for whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord. Whether we live, therefore, or die, we are the Lord’s. Again, He died for
<margin>2 Cor. 5:15.</margin> all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them. God demands this as His
<margin>Psal. 50:15</margin> right and [our] duty: *You shall honor me,* says God; yes, says
<margin>Psal. 86:12</margin> faith, *I will honor Your Name forever.*

3. Faith arms the soul in the keeping of the covenant against all obstacles that it encounters. For example: sometimes we are tempted on the right hand by the bait and the seductions of the world. *All this I will give you,* says the world,
<margin>1 John 5:4.</margin> *if you will be mine*; but then faith overcomes the world, set-

4. Through faith we seek God, and seek the fulfillment of his promises according to our need; do we lack wisdom, gentleness, patience, or any other grace? Faith shall bring us to the fountain through prayer, and by this means it expects and waits to receive the grace that we lack. Just as a child sucking the breast draws the milk for its own nourishment from it, and becomes stronger thereby, so we suck from Christ through the prayer of faith, and from the promise of grace, and by that means we obtain strength for our inner man <note>The "inner man" refers to the spiritual nature or the soul, a concept rooted in Paul’s epistles (e.g., Ephesians 3:16).</note>, to fulfill the covenant that we have made with God.

6. Just as faith strengthens us, so if we should at any time fail in our covenant-keeping through the power of temptation, faith also brings us back to the right path, and restores us to our former state: I do not say that the covenant between God and us can be broken; we can anger God, and fail in God's service, but as long as we do not displace God, and leave him, and choose another Master, another Lord, and husband besides God, then the covenant of grace is not yet broken: but a true believer cannot do this; he can fall, and fall often, and yet not fall away,

<column-break/>

but he rises again: he may turn aside, but he nonetheless returns to the way of the covenant. How sweet is this doctrine! Christians! we can, and indeed we sometimes walk a bit weakly in the keeping of the covenant, our foot slips, and we step aside from the way of the Lord, but faith makes us return to God; it brings shame to our face, that after so much grace shown to us we give God such wicked repayment; it makes us mindful of these promises; <margin>Zech. 1:3.</margin> *Return to me, and I will return to you.*

<margin>1 Sam. 12:20, 22.</margin> *You have done all this evil, yet do not turn away from following the Lord: for the Lord will not forsake his people for his great Name's sake, because it has pleased the Lord to make you a people for himself.* By contemplating these and other similar promises, faith makes us courageous to return to God, to take words to ourselves <note>original: "woorden tot ons te nemen" — an allusion to Hosea 14:2, meaning to prepare a sincere confession and plea for mercy.</note>, and to plead the covenant of grace to our advantage; this working of faith brought Peter back to Christ, whereas Judas, lacking this faith, lay down in despairing worry, in no way able to rise again, or to restore himself.

O my soul, are you provided with these workings of faith, which greatly strengthen you to keep the covenant with God? Then there is a sweet conformity between you and Jesus.
