Let us nonetheless consider it honor enough that God has exalted us to be his people. Christians: even if we should not be esteemed at all, we can nonetheless rest satisfied in this, that God is our God; should we be persecuted, taken prisoner, and oppressed, we can nonetheless say with Jacob, *I have enough, because the Lord is gracious to me*, <note>original: "Ick hebbe genoegh," referring to Genesis 33:11.</note> and has accepted me into the <term>covenant</term> <note>A formal, binding agreement between God and His people.</note> with him: surely then we testify of God before Heaven and earth, that he is better to us than corn, or wine, or oil, or anything else that the world could ever provide.

3. We must place ourselves under the power of every word of our God, and we must make our-

<column-break/>

selves conformable to the example of our God; that is, we must labor to become imitators of God, and follow his virtues; it is a part of that honor which children owe their parents, that they are obedient to their commands, and follow their Godly example; we can show God no greater honor <margin>Deut. 33:3</margin> than that we humble ourselves at his feet, to receive from his words, and that we <margin>Ephes. 5:1</margin> deny the essence of this world to become his imitators as beloved children. O remember this! for then we are indeed made conformable to him, then we are holy just as he is holy, and pure just as he is pure; and how can this do otherwise than serve to the honor and glory of our good God?

In this part, as in the previous ones, we shall first set forth the object <note>In 17th-century devotional writing, the "Object" refers to the specific divine person or event that the soul should focus its attention upon during prayer or study.</note>, and afterward direct you on how you should look upon it.

Angels have been sent to various people, such as to Gideon, Manoah, David, Daniel, Elijah, Zechariah, and others. <column-break/>

takes away the sin, then He even blesses our blessings, and He sanctifies even our afflictions; He brings peace out of turmoil, riches out of poverty, honor out of shame, freedom out of slavery; He pulls out the sting of death, and the fire of hell is extinguished by Him; just as all evil lies coiled within sin, so He who saves us from sin saves us from all evil, whatever name that evil might have.

But is not *Christ* as precious a name as *Jesus* is? I answer, No, because: 1. *Christ* is not the name of God; God, as He is God, cannot be anointed <note>The title 'Christ' comes from the Greek 'Christos,' meaning 'Anointed One,' referring to a specific office or role</note>, but *Jesus* is the name of God, and that in which He takes a more particular delight. 2. *Christ* is shared with others, for Princes are called *Christi* <note>Latin for 'anointed ones'</note>, but *Jesus* is His own, for there is no Savior besides Him. 3. *Christ* is anointed—to what end other than to be a Savior? *Jesus* is consequently the end, and the end is always above the means.

# The Fourth Book. Part 1. Chapter 1. § 2.

described it thus: / <margin>Luke 1:35.</margin> the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.

Observe from these words first the agent or worker, and then the fruit or the work: 1. The agent or working cause of Christ's conception is the Holy Spirit: this agrees with that <margin>Matt. 1:20.</margin> saying of the Angel to Joseph, *that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Spirit.* Here it may be asked why Christ's conception is attributed to the Holy Spirit, which is nonetheless common to all three persons in the Holy Trinity? I answer, that it is done not to exclude the others, but:

1. To show that it was God's free grace, which is frequently called the Holy Spirit. 2. Because the Father and the Son worked it through the Holy Spirit, whose work it was immediately and in a special manner; we have great reasons to be thankful to all three persons: to the Father who ordained this <term>garment</term> <note>The author uses the "garment" as a metaphor for the human nature that Christ "wore" over His divinity.</note>; to the Holy Spirit who prepared it; to the Son who wore it; to the whole Godhead, who clothed us with it, and through it has made us righteous.

---

But nonetheless, the Holy Spirit is not Christ's Father; He did not generate Him, but formed Him; He did not bring any substance from His own being from which Christ was made, but He took from the human nature of the Virgin, and from that

<column-break/>

prepared the body of Christ within her: away with all gross errors, and old heresies! This conception of Christ did not happen through any fleshly outpouring of seed, but through preparation, that is, through the operation or power of the Holy Spirit; or otherwise by the powerful command and disposition of the Holy Spirit, or otherwise by the blessing of the Holy Spirit, whereby that part of the blood or seed of the Virgin, from which the body of Christ was prepared, was so purified and sanctified that therein could be no stain or blemish of the original impurity <note>This refers to the doctrine that Christ was born without "Original Sin," which was believed to be passed down through natural generation.</note>.

2. The fruit or the work has been Christ's humanity, in which we have to consider the substance and the manner. 1. Regarding the substance, note the substance of the body and of the soul of Christ: 1. The substance of Christ's body was the true flesh and blood of the <margin>Gal. 4:4.</margin> Virgin; *He was made of a woman*, says the Apostle; that is, of the flesh, and blood, and essence of the woman; and He was <margin>Rom. 1:3.</margin> *made of the seed of David*, says the Apostle, *according to the flesh*; otherwise He would not have been able to be a Son of David according to the flesh: and if it be the truth, what the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>Likely referring to Aristotelian biological theories prevalent in the 17th century regarding reproduction.</note> say, that the seed of the man does not enter into the essence of the child, but only disposes the seed of the woman (just as a master-craftsman disposes and prepares his work) to make that into the form of a human; well then, I do not know in what [regard]...

### Looking unto Jesus

the conception of Christ in its substance would be entirely different from our conception; except only in the preparer or worker of His being, who was the Holy Spirit. 2. The substance of the being of Christ's soul did not proceed from the soul of the Virgin as a part of the same, but it was made like the souls of other men; that is, out of nothing, through the power of God; and thus infused into the body by God's hand. But of these things (of His body and soul, and human nature) we shall speak more broadly in the next section.

2. Regarding the manner of the preparation of Christ’s human nature, which was wondrous: the Angel attributes two workings to the Holy Spirit in this great work; the one that He would come over the Virgin, the other that He would overshadow her. By the first is indicated the unusual working of the Holy Spirit in the preparation of the human nature of Christ, <margin>Judges 14:6</margin> just as it was said of Samson, *the Spirit of the Lord came upon him*, that is, the Spirit of the Lord inspired him with an unusual power. So also the Spirit of the Lord came over her; that is, the Holy Spirit worked in her in an unusual manner. As for example, in ordinary procreation our being and parts are prepared sequentially by degrees: as first the seed becomes a fruit, then an unformed body <note>original: "on-werck-tuyghigh", meaning a body without functioning organs</note>, and then the liver, the

<column-break/>

heart, and the brain are prepared, and the others subsequently; and there are at least forty days before the body of the child is perfectly prepared. But with the body of Christ it was entirely different, for in that very moment of His conception, He was perfectly prepared in soul and body, empty of sins, and full of grace; even in the moment of His conception He was perfectly formed, and immediately united with the eternal Word, perfect God and perfect man. Truly this was unusual, and this is the characteristic of the Holy Spirit *to work suddenly* <note>original: "subitò operari"</note>, to work quickly, and perfectly; <margin>Augustine, *Book on Faith, to Peter*, ch. 18.</margin> as soon as the flesh was conceived, it was immediately united and made the flesh of the Son of God; it was quickly made, perfectly made, and holily made.

The second working attributed to the Holy Spirit is the overshadowing of the Virgin: this teaches us that we must not investigate too much into this great mystery. Alas! It is too high for us. If the course of ordinary procreation is a mystery, how far then does this unusual working exceed all our understanding? ### §. 4.

->*Of the distinction of the two natures in Christ.*<-

IV. There is indeed a clear distinction between these two natures. 1. In respect of their essence / the Divinity cannot be the humanity / and the humanity cannot be the Divinity. 2. In respect of the attributes / the Divinity is most wise / righteous and almighty / indeed wisdom / righteousness and almightiness itself / and such the humanity is not / nor can it be. 3. They have a distinct will / *not my will, but your will* Luke 22:42 *be done, O Father*, differing entirely as the will of the creature / from the will of the Creator. 4. Even the operations in the work of redemption are indeed inseparable / and yet distinct / *I lay down my life and take it up again:* John 10:18. To lay it down was the work of the man / and not of God / and to take it up was the work of God / and not of the man: in these respects we say that each nature remains in its entirety / without any change / composition / mixing / or confusion: there is no changing of the one into the other / just as water was once changed into wine; no composition of both / no annihilation <note>original: "vernietingh"</note>

I answer / A thing can become another / either through change / just as water was changed into wine / but in this way Christ is not changed / the Godhead was covered for a time / but not annihilated: or a thing can become another through union / as when one self-standing entity <term>subsistence; an independent existence</term> is joined to another / and is nonetheless not transferred or changed into the nature of another: just as a Soldier having put on his weapons / is a weighted man; or a man having put on his clothes / is no longer a naked / but a clothed man; and yet the weapons and the Soldier / the man and his clothes are distinct things; and so it has been with Christ: the flesh is said to have become God

<column-break/>

and the Godhead is said to have become man / not by the change of one into the nature of the other / but by the assumption or addition of the human nature to the Divine / and nonetheless the human and the Divine nature are always distinct things; both natures in Christ remain whole and unmixed; truly the humanity is greatly glorified by the Godhead; but the Godhead is in no way changed by the humanity; and so much for the distinction of the two natures.

---

### The Fourth Book. Part I. Chapter I. §. 5.

1. That human nature <term>human nature: the physical and psychological essence of being human, which Christ took upon himself</term> has its very existence in the second Person of the **Trinity** <term>Trinity: the Christian doctrine that God is one being in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term>, and is of itself devoid of a separate, independent existence.

<margin>Colossians 2:9</margin>
2. That this human nature is a unique Temple for the **Godhead** <term>Godhead: the divine nature or essence of God</term> of Christ to dwell within; it is the place where the Divine reveals itself far more clearly and gloriously than in any other creature. It is true that through His providence He shows Himself in all His creatures, and through His grace in His Saints; but He dwells most gloriously and eternally—according to the fullness of His Godhead and through a personal union—only in the humanity of *Jesus Christus*. In Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Some emphasize this point: that just as in this life no one comes to God except through *Christus*, so in the life to come, no one shall see God otherwise than in the face of *Jesus Christus*.

3. That the humanity of *Christus* stands in a closer friendship with the Godhead than any other creature, whether humans or Angels. Just as He once said, "My Father and I are one" <note>John 10:30</note>—meaning one in essence—so may He also truly say, "humanity and I are one," meaning one person forever.

4. That the humanity of *Christus*, according to its capacity, is a co-participant with the Godhead in the work of **redemption** <term>redemption: the act of saving or being saved from sin and error</term> and **mediation** <term>mediation: acting as an intermediary or bridge between God and humanity</term>. Just as He is *Immanuel* <note>original: "Immanuel", a Hebrew name meaning "God with us"</note> in respect to His person, so is He *Immanuel* in respect to His 

<column-break/>

ministry. <margin>John 20:17</margin> He had to be both man and God to be capable of bringing His comforting message to the children of men: *go hence to my brothers, and tell them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.* <note>original Latin/Dutch citation: John 20:17</note> In the work of redemption and in the work of mediation, I am man as well as God; my flesh is truly the bread of life.

5. That the humanity of *Christus*, together with the Godhead, is worshipped and served with divine honor. Similarly, the honor shown to a King also extends to the Crown upon his head. We do not worship the humanity alone as a mere creature, but we worship the Person of *Christus*, consisting of both the human and the divine nature.

<margin>Luke 2:52</margin>
6. That the humanity of *Christus* has an uncommon measure—indeed, without measure—of indwelling grace poured out upon it. In this, He surpasses even the Angels; for grace is given to them only in measure, but to the humanity of *Christus* it is given without measure, as much as a creature can possibly contain. 1. It is a **completely actual union**: it is not a mere conceptual or intellectual union, existing only in the understanding, and being nothing without the understanding; it is not an imaginary thing, having no other being than in the brain: no; no; it is a true, actual, essential, and substantial union. I confess that in natural unions there is a greater clarity, but there can nevertheless be no greater truth; spiritual workings do not, for that reason, bring forth less power because the senses cannot distinguish their manner of operation; even the **lodestone** <term>lodestone: (Dutch: *zeyl-steen*, literally "sailing-stone") a naturally magnetized piece of mineral used as a compass. The author uses it to show that invisible forces are still physically real.</term>, being but an earthly substance, when it is yet out of our sight, or under the table, or behind some solid part, it moves the needle just as powerfully as if it were in our sight. And shall he not contradict his own senses, who would say, "it has no operation, because I do not see it"? O my **Savior** <term>Savior: (Dutch: *Salighmaker*) literally "Blessed-maker," a common Dutch title for Christ focusing on his role in bringing eternal happiness.</term>! you are more mine than my body is mine; my senses feel that at present, but in such a way that

<column-break/>

I must lose it; but my faith sees and feels you so present with me, that I shall not be separated from you for all eternity.

2. It is a **very close union**; you ask, how close? If an Angel were to speak to you of this, he would not be able to satisfy you; yet, as far as our understanding can reach, and the creatures can serve to enlighten us, take it thus. All that can be brought forward by way of comparison regarding the joining with any other thing; that and much more can be said of our union with Jesus Christ. To give some examples from the Scripture,
<margin>1 Corinthians 6:17</margin>
see what one stick is with another, when they are glued together;
<margin>1 Samuel 18:1</margin>
see what one friend is with another, like **Jonathan and David**, who are said to be bound and knit together;
<margin>Isaiah 62:5</margin>
see how near the **Father and the Child** are to one another; how much the **husband** is bound to the **wife**; see
<margin>Ephesians 5:31</margin>
what union there is between the
<margin>John 15:5</margin>
**branches and the vine**; the
<margin>1 Corinthians 12:12</margin>
**members and the head**; yes, even something more! See what the **soul** is to the **body**; so is Christ, and so near is Christ, and even nearer to the person of every believer. *I live, yet not I,*
<margin>Galatians 2:20</margin>
says **Paul**, *but Christ lives in me*; as if he said, just as the soul is to the body of a natural man, that it moves it naturally and makes it living, so is Jesus Christ for my soul and body. O there is a wonderful, close...

### The Fourth Book. Part 1. Chapter 1. §. 5.

...eternity in this spiritual union!

3. It is a **complete union**; that is, the whole Christ is united with the whole believer, soul and body. If you are united with Christ, then you have Christ wholly and entirely; you are one with him in his nature, in his name; you have that same image, grace, and spirit in you that he has; the same precious promises, the same access to God through prayers as he; you have the same love of the Father; all that he has done or suffered, in that you have your part; you have his life and death, it is all yours; and likewise on your side, he has you wholly and entirely—your nature, your sins, the punishment for your sins; your wrath, your curse, your shame; yes, your understanding and wealth and strength, all that you are or have, or that it is possible for you to do for him. It is a complete union: *My beloved is mine, and I am his*: <note>original: "Mijn beminde is mijn, ende ick ben sijn" — a reference to Song of Solomon 2:16.</note> the whole Christ from head to foot is mine, and all that I am, have, or eternally can do is his.

4. It is an **inseparable union**, which in eternity <margin>Jeremiah 32:40.</margin> cannot be broken. *I will* (says God) *make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them to do them good; and I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me.* This is a glorious promise; a troubled soul might say: "Dear God, you might not want to depart from me, I know that you will not; but oh, I fear that I shall depart from you! Oh alas! I

<column-break/>

turn every day to sin and Satan!" But no, says God: *I will put my fear in your heart, that you shall not depart from me*: as if he would say, "We shall be held together eternally and nevermore be separated." For this reason, Paul triumphantly challenged all enemies on earth (or rather in hell) to do their best to break this knot: *Who shall separate us from the love of God in Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?* Romans 8:35. Let come all that can, and see if this blessed union between me and Christ can be broken in eternity by anything you can do.

And this concludes this union.

2. There is a **spiritual communion** with God in Christ. Both of these are the workings of Christ’s personal or substantial union; first union with his person, and then communion with his benefits: in a proper manner of speaking, the union is not with any of the benefits that flow down to us from Christ; we are not united with the forgiveness of sin, holiness, or peace of conscience, but with the **Person of the Son of God** himself: and then, secondly, follows this sharing of all his benefits, proceeding without intermediary from this union with the Lord Jesus Christ; so that just as Christ was a **Priest, Prophet, and King** <term>Priest, Prophet, and King: known as the *munus triplex* (triple office), this theological concept describes the three roles of Christ's ministry which believers are said to share through their union with him.</term>, we also in a certain way are priests, prophets, and kings;

### §. 6.

## Of the Birth of Christ.

VI. Now follows Christ’s birth. Now it was that the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>original: "Sonne der gerechticheyt"—a title for the Messiah from Malachi 4:2.</note> would break forth from her bed, where he had hidden himself for nine months as if behind a fruitful cloud. This was a wonder of the world; a thing so marvelous that it was given to the believers as a sign seven hundred and forty years before <margin>Isa. 7:14.</margin> it was fulfilled: *Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign: behold, a Virgin shall become pregnant, and she shall bear a Son.* A wonder in truth, and great beyond all comparison: that the Son of God shall be born of a woman; that he, being the true **Melchizedek** <note>Melchizedek is a biblical figure described as having "no genealogy," serving as a "type" or precursor to Christ's eternal nature. See Hebrews 7.</note> 
<margin>Hebr. 7:3.</margin>

<column-break/>

—without Father and without mother—yet must have a mother-Virgin; that he who existed before Abraham nevertheless had to be born two thousand years after Abraham; that he who was a **Son of David** <note>A traditional title for the Messiah, emphasizing his royal lineage.</note> and therefore was born at **Bethlehem**, yet is also a **Lord of David**. Wonderful things are spoken of you, O Son of God! Before he was born, the Prophets sang and prophesied of him, the Patriarchs foreshadowed him, the **types** <note>original: "voorbeelden"—historical figures or events in the Old Testament believed to symbolize or "prefigure" the coming of Christ.</note> foretold him, God promised him, and the Son of God finally accomplished it. When he was born, the Angels ran to and fro, Gabriel brought the message, the glory of Heaven shone, a star announced it, and the Wise Men were the Heralds who proclaimed his birth. But come a little closer; let us go to Bethlehem (as the shepherds <margin>Luke 2:15.</margin> said) and let us see the word that has come to pass there! As soon as we set the first foot in his inn, we shall see Heavenly wonders before our eyes. Now **look upon Jesus!** Look upon him as he, in the fullness of time, took upon himself that great work of our salvation. Here you can now read the contents of **Adam’s covenant**, of **Abraham’s promise**, of **Moses’ revelation**, and of **David’s succession**. These have been but coverings, but now we shall push aside the curtain; come and behold the truth itself. O wonder above wonders! Whom do we find in this Inn? A Child in the manger.

-> ### Looking unto Jesus <-

...with the sinful man? He has violated my Law, broken my commandment, and as far as it lies within him, disrupted the structure of the world; he has robbed my glorious work of Heaven, of Earth, of the Sea, and of everything that is therein; he has disfigured himself for ever, ever, and ever. O, what shall be done with this sinful, rebellious, lost, and miserable creature, man? For a time, all things in Heaven were still and amazed, because they saw the great God of Heaven was angered; finally, **Mercy** <note>original: "goedertierenheydt"</note> and **Peace** arose, and sought to appease God's wrath through sweet and friendly pleadings; but **Justice** and **Truth** were on the other side, and they moved Almighty God to proceed and to show himself (as he indeed is) a "consuming fire," a God who visits sin <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:29 and Exodus 20:5, emphasizing God's role as a judge who cannot ignore wrongdoing.</note>. This plea is drawn out at length and recounted by Bernard, Andrewes, and others <note>The author cites Saint Bernard of Clairvaux and Lancelot Andrewes, famous theologians who popularized the "Four Daughters of God" allegory.</note>.

1. **Mercy** made a beginning, for through her willingness to do good, she is always the first; her inclination tends toward compassion—or rather, she herself is an inclination to have compassion over the miserable; and if she can but redeem them, no matter what it may cost her, rest assured that she will redeem them; for she does not look at who the party is, nor what he has done, nor what he has deserved; but (which is a powerful

<column-break/>

comfort for us poor sinners) she looks at what he suffers, and in what a miserable and wretched state he is. Her advocacy was as follows: "What, Lord, have you then created all men in vain? Do you wish now to destroy him for whose sake you made the world? Shall the householder be cast out and thrown into prison, and remain there until he has paid the last penny? <note>A reference to Matthew 5:26, suggesting the impossibility of man paying his own debt to God.</note> Shall then all men and women, from the first to the last in the world, be damned for always and ever? Alas! What profit is there in their blood? What will it avail, that men and devils alike shall be driven toward the hellish flames? And will not the Devils, those great enemies of God, rejoice over this? And what then will become of your great Name on earth? And is this not your Name: *The Lord, Lord, merciful and gracious, longsuffering and great of mercy and truth, showing mercy to thousands, forgiving iniquity, transgressions and sins*? <note>This is the "Name of God" as revealed to Moses in Exodus 34:6-7.</note> Will God then annihilate his own Name? Will he cast off for eternity? And no longer be favorable? Does his mercy cease forever? And will he no longer let himself be entreated? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he shut up his mercies through wrath?" With these and similar holy whispers and murmurings, **Mercy** has pressed herself into God's bowels <note>In 17th-century language, the "bowels" (ingewanden) refer to the deepest seat of emotion and compassion.</note> and moved them to pity.

#### [Concerning some consequences after Christ's birth.]

VII. We shall touch upon some consequences after Christ's birth, so long as He was but a child of twelve years. As ———

1. Being only eight days old, He was circumcised and named Jesus. <column-break/>

tion which sin would otherwise bring upon our souls; therefore are this name **Jesus**, and this sign of circumcision joined together, for through the shedding of His blood He had to be our **Jesus**, our Savior; <margin>Hebrews 9:22.</margin> *for without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness:* and there is no salvation for our souls. <margin>Romans 4:11.</margin> Circumcision was the seal. # The Fourth Book. 1. Part. Cap. 1. §. 7.

<column-break/>

"Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord" <note>This is a reference to the Law of the Firstborn found in Exodus 13:2 and Luke 2:23.</note>: O wonder! there was no uncleanness in the Son of God, and yet He was first circumcised, and thereafter He was brought to the Lord and presented to Him; He who had come to be a sacrifice for our sin, wished to be considered "unclean" in our place according to the Law, so that by fulfilling the Law, He might take away our uncleanness; He who was above the Law, wished to come under the Law, so that He might free us from the Law. We are all born as sinners; but O, the unspeakable loving-kindness of our Jesus, who has provided a remedy as early as our sin begins! First He was conceived and then born, to sanctify our own conception and birth; and after His birth He was first circumcised, and then presented to the Lord, so that through these two holy acts, that which was by nature unholy might be sanctified unto God. Christ did not even leave our childhood without improving it, but through such an offering of Himself, He immediately cleansed us from our impurity. Now Christ is brought in His mother’s arms to His own house, the Temple; and as a man He is offered up to Himself as God. O, how gloriously did the Temple shine when its true Owner was now within its walls? Now the hour and the Guest had come, in whose presence the second Temple would surpass the first <note>A reference to the prophecy in Haggai 2:9, suggesting that the presence of Christ gave the Second Temple greater glory than Solomon's original Temple.</note>; this was the house that was built for Him and dedicated to Him,

and in which He had long dwelt under the "types" <note>original: "voorbeelden." ### The Fourth Book. Part 1. Chapter 1. Section 7.

...operation of the Godhead, with which the nature of the Child was united; just as the birth of Christ was, so also was the childhood of Christ exceedingly humble; Oh, how we ought to exalt Him, or to humble ourselves before Him, who for our sake was willing to humble Himself so greatly?

5. Being twelve years old, <margin>Luke 2:42</margin> He went up with His parents to Jerusalem, according to the custom of the Feast. Through this holy deed of His young years, He has a high desire to raise our first years to a proper godliness; <note>The author suggests that Jesus’s actions as a child serve as a model for how young people should be raised in faith.</note> but I shall not dwell upon this: I would rather <margin>verse 46</margin> observe Him sitting in the midst of the Teachers, hearing them, and questioning them: while the other children of His age ran and played in the streets, His parents found Him sitting in the Temple; not to look at the outward glory of that House, at the Golden Candlesticks, or Tables, or Cherubim, or Pillars, or the molten Sea <note>The "molten sea" was a massive bronze basin in the Temple court used by priests for ritual washing.</note>, or the Golden Altar, or the vessels of its gold; Oh no, but to hear the Teachers and to question them. He who, as God, had given them all their wisdom, now listens as a Son of Man to the wisdom He had given them; and having heard, He questioned, and thereafter He undoubtedly also answered; even His questioning was a form of teaching; for I do not think He intended so much to learn, as to instruct these Teachers of Israel.

<column-break/>

Certainly these Rabbis had never heard the voice of such a Protector; <note>original: "Beschermer"</note> they could see nothing else in this Child but the very Wisdom of God, and therefore the text says, <margin>verse 47</margin> they were all amazed at His understanding and answers; their eyes saw nothing but a Child, but their ears heard the wonders of God’s Law; because of that which they saw and that which they heard, they could not but be carried away and astonished. But (O you Jewish Teachers) why did you not now think of the Star, of the Wise Men, of the Angels, and of the Shepherds? Why did you not now remind yourselves of Herod, and of his question, and of your answer, that the Christ should be born in Bethlehem of Judea? You brought forward the Prophets, so why did you not now think of that prophecy, that *unto us a Child is born, and unto us a Son is given, and His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty <margin>Isaiah 9:5</margin> God, Father of Eternity, Prince of Peace?* <note>The verse numbering follows older translations; in most modern English Bibles, this is Isaiah 9:6.</note> In vain is the wonder that does not end in faith; no light can help when the eyes are held shut by unbelief and prejudice.

Assuredly, Christ did not spend all that time, from His twelfth to His thirtieth year, in idleness; just as He was raised by His parents, so He learned from His supposed father <note>original: "genoemde Vader"; literally "named father," referring to Joseph’s role as the legal rather than biological father of Jesus.</note> to be a carpenter. I know that Matthew has recounted it thus: *Is this not the son of the carpenter? and is His mother not named Mary?* But notice this: *Is this not the carpenter, etc.*

Some explain it thus: as long as Joseph lived, Christ worked with him in the carpenter’s trade; and Joseph having died—which happened before the revelation of Jesus to Israel—He worked alone, and was then no longer called the carpenter’s son, but the carpenter Himself. Herein is comfort for people of the lowliest condition; just as the rustic life was honored in the person and state of the first Adam before his fall, so here is the life of the laborer <note>original: "handt-wercker"; referring to skilled manual labor or craftsmanship.</note>. <column-break/>

boring, and working, and hewing of wood, and the like. Here is a sharp rebuke for all those who spend their time in idleness, or without a particular calling; who do no other work than chasing after vain, foolish, unnecessary, and sinful things. What? Are they wiser than Christ? Our Jesus did not wish to waste His time in this way at all. It is true that before that time He had done nothing great, nor of public notice; but even this was not without mystery. By doing nothing public,

->§. I.<-

->*Of the knowing of Jesus as He took upon Himself that great work of our salvation in His birth.*<-

What "looking" means has been explained to you previously. And so that we may have an inward, experiential looking upon Him, for which our soul longs, let us put all these particular things into practice. Such as—

1. Let us know Jesus, who took upon Himself the great work of our salvation in His first coming, or incarnation. Come, let us learn what He has done for us when He came among us. There is not the slightest matter in His first ap-

<column-break/>

pearance that does not notably concern us. Is it possible that the great God of Heaven and earth would humble Himself so infinitely (as we have heard) for anything other than a great cause? And what could He intend other than His own glory and the best for His creatures? O my soul! if you have any part in Christ at all, then all this concerns you; the Lord Jesus had an eye on you in this whole transaction; for your sake He became man; and for your sake He was conceived and born. Do not look upon these things as merely intellectual or common; do not look only at the bare narrative of the events, for that is but fruitless. The chief duty is in observing the end, the meaning, and the intention of Christ; and especially as it regards you—not others, but your very self. ### The Fourth Book. Part 1. Chapter 2. §. 2.

<margin>John 1:14</margin>
**In Jesus Christ:** the Word became flesh; no sooner was he conceived than he was God-man and man-God; he was perfectly prepared and immediately united with the eternal Word:
<margin>Galatians 4:4</margin>
God sent his Son—there is the divine nature; born of a woman—there is the human nature. Truly, this mystery is great: that the Word became flesh; that the Son of God was born of a woman; that a star gives light to the Sun; that a branch bears the Vine <note>The author uses these paradoxes to highlight the supernatural reversal of the Incarnation: usually the vine supports the branch, and the sun illuminates the stars.</note>; that a creature gives essence to the Creator; that the mother is younger than the one she has born, and much smaller than the one she has enclosed. O my soul, marvel at all of this! But above all, consider that this was for you, and for our salvation; he was man so that he could die for us, and he was God so that his death would be sufficient to save us; had he been only man and not God, he might well have been able to suffer, but throughout eternity he would not have been able to make satisfaction for sin; he would not have been able to be a Jesus, a Savior <note>The Dutch term "Saligh-maker" literally means "One who makes blessed," the standard term for the Savior.</note> of souls; and had he been only God and not man, he would not have been of the race of our sinful nature, and so he would not have been able to satisfy God’s justice in the same nature in which it had been offended; nor could he, as God

<column-break/>

alone, have been able to die for sin; for the decree had gone forth that our Redeemer must die for sin, because without the shedding of blood there is
<margin>Hebrews 9:22</margin>
no forgiveness: but no shedding of blood, nor any suffering, could happen to the Divinity of Jesus Christ. I shall not argue over God's power—whether he could have brought about another kind of human redemption than through the Incarnation <note>original: "mensch-weerdingh," literally "becoming human."</note> of the Son of God: without contradiction, this was God’s will, and he ordained no other way because he did not desire to. O my soul, contemplate this in relation to yourself; he is God-man, so that he might suffer and satisfy for your sins; he is God-man, so that he might be powerful and capable enough to perfectly carry out the work of your salvation; as God he is powerful, and as man he is capable of fulfilling the office of a Mediator; as God he was powerful to bear the punishment of sin, and as man he was capable of suffering for sin. O the wisdom of God in this dealing! Human nature can indeed suffer death, but cannot overcome it; divine nature can overcome death and all things, but cannot suffer it; and for this reason, there are two natures in Jesus Christ; O think upon this; it is a matter well worthy of your attentive meditation.

->### Looking unto Jesus.<-

<columns>
**Christ.** Just as the unapproachable light of the Godhead was placed in the dark and obscure lantern of human flesh; so these two natures have remained whole without any change, mixture, or confusion: they were not like wine and water which become one through mixing; there is no such mixing of the divine and human natures; they are not like snow and water, which become one through dissolving; there is no such change of the human nature into the divine, or of the divine nature into the human. Some say that after the resurrection, the Godhead was more perfectly communicated to the humanity than at his conception; but although that would do nothing but swallow up the truth of his humanity, just as an entire sea swallows a little drop of oil; notice that just as he was God and man from the first moment of his conception, so these two natures have always remained distinct in subsistence, attributes, and operations. Well, meditate on this, O my soul, in relation to yourself; O, here is comfort to be found! By this means you now have free access to the throne of grace, to find help in your needs; and just as you have free access, so you may also approach with boldness; his Godhead indeed causes a holy shame, <note>The Dutch *beschaemtheydt* suggests a sense of bashfulness or awe-struck unworthiness when facing the majesty of God.</note> but his humanity comforts the

<column-break/>

faint-hearted and weak souls; his divine nature may startle <term>startle<gloss>The original Dutch *verschickt* implies being "moved" or "unsettled" by the overwhelming presence of the divine.</gloss></term> a person, but his human nature makes us courageous to come to him; even after his resurrection, it pleased him to send this comforting message to the children of men, 
<margin>John 20:17.</margin>
*go hence to my brothers, and tell them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God:* now as long as he is not ashamed to call us his brothers, 
<margin>Hebrews 11:16.</margin>
so God is also not ashamed to be called our God. O, what sweet fruits we may pluck from this tree, from the actual distinction of the two natures in Christ. <margin>1 Timothy 2:5.</margin>

IV. The Prophet tells us that *unto us a child is born, and unto us a Son is given.* <margin>Isaiah 9:5</margin> <note>In modern English Bibles, this is Isaiah 9:6.</note> But how may I hope that this child was born for me, and that this Son was given to me? What King would want to leave his throne and go to become a **toad** <note>The author uses the "toad" as a symbol of something repulsive and lowly to emphasize the vast distance between the Creator and the sinner.</note> to save other toads? And do I not differ much more from God than a toad does from me? And has sin not made me even more hideous in God’s eye than any ugly toad can be in my eyes? Oh, I am less than the very least of all God’s mercies. I am more worthy of hell and the devils than for union and fellowship with God and Christ; I cannot believe.

**2.** The **infinite severity of divine justice**, which must be satisfied; a soul thinking somewhat deeply and seriously upon this shrinks from it and cries out: Oh, what shall become of my soul? One of the least sins of which I am guilty deserves death and God’s eternal wrath; *the wages of sin is death* <note>original: "de besoldingh der sonde is de doot" — a reference to Romans 6:23.</note>: and I cannot satisfy that debt. Although I have several **millions of talent-pounds** <note>The "talent" was an ancient unit of weight and money; here it refers to the massive, unpayable debt of sin mentioned in Jesus’s parables.</note> of transgressions, I nevertheless do not have a single **mite** <term>Mite: the smallest possible coin, representing a negligible amount of value</term> of my own to pay with. Oh, how then could I believe? What thoughts could I have of God’s mercy and love toward me? God’s Law condemns me, my own conscience accuses me, and justice demands its due.

**3.** The **lack of a Mediator**, or of any suitable Person who may stand between God and the sinner. If there is unworthiness on my side,

<column-break/>

and on God’s side a sharp and strict and narrow justice, and I see no <term>Mediator: a "go-between" or bridge-builder; in Christian theology, Jesus Christ is the only one who can reconcile God and humanity</term> to whom I can go and first unite myself with Him before I deal with the infinite Majesty of God Himself, how can I do otherwise than despair and cry out? Oh, what a wretched man I am! Oh, that I had never been! Or if I indeed had to exist, oh, that I had been a toad, or a snake, or rather some other poisonous creature instead of a human; for when those die, they perish and have an end; but the end of a <term>reprobate: a person who is rejected or cast off by God</term> sinner is torment without end. Oh, woe is me, alas! I cannot believe; there is no place for faith in this situation! These are the hindrances.

## 2. The aids to faith in this sorrowful state are these.

What soul would not have risen up at these words, even from the abyss of hell? I know that a poor soul would have called this into doubt and said / what then will become of infinite justice? Shall it be bent to make my soul <term>salvation-ready</term> <note>original: "saligh"; often translated as blessed or saved, referring to the state of being reconciled with God.</note>? This would have been no small doubt / considering especially that great conflict (as we have heard) between loving-kindness and truth, and righteousness and peace <note>This refers to the "Four Daughters of God," a common medieval and early modern allegory based on Psalm 85:10, where Mercy, Truth, Justice, and Peace debate the fate of humanity.</note>: but to take away all conflict / God has not only spoken from Heaven by Himself / but He Himself has come down from Heaven to the earth to speak to us. Oh, see this wondrous work of <term>loving-kindness</term> <note>original: "goedertierenheydt"; a term for God's tender mercy and grace.</note>! God has come down in the flesh / He has come as a price; He Himself shall

pay Himself according to all the demands of His righteousness and justice before our eyes; and all this being done / He now comes Himself to offer and dedicate your soul. ### §. 6.
#### On Loving Jesus in this Looking.

VI. Let us love Jesus as he has taken upon himself the great work of our salvation in his first coming or **incarnation** <note>original: "mensch-weerdingh"; literally "man-becoming," referring to the theological concept of God taking on human flesh.</note>. Now, what is love other than a reaching out or a going out of the heart toward the beloved object, or toward the object by which it is drawn and attracted? Notice, O my soul, that everything that has a drawing power in this looking-up is an object or a common cause of love; and could you ever fall upon any object that is of greater attraction than the incarnation of Jesus Christ? If love is the **lodestone** <term>lodestone</term> <note>original: "zeyl-steen"; a naturally magnetized mineral used as a compass; here a metaphor for an irresistible attraction that pulls the soul toward God.</note> of love, what a powerful attraction is this for you! It

<column-break/>

seems to me that the mere sight of Christ’s incarnation is powerful enough to carry you away with the contemplation of his infinite **loving-kindness** <note>original: "goedertierenheydt"; a term used to describe God’s tender, fatherly mercy and grace.</note>: see how he calls out, or (as it were) draws out the soul to union, contemplation, and enjoyment of his glory! O come, and surrender yourself to him; give yourself to him, and see that all your inclinations and works agree with his will: O love him, not in part, but with your whole heart.

But to awaken this love, I shall only present the object, which shall be a sufficient reason. Love awakens love: now just as God’s first love was revealed in this, that he made man after his likeness; so his second, excellent love has consisted in this, that he made himself like unto man; dwell then a while on this love, for (I think) that this is the greater love of the two; yes, if I may speak freely, I believe that this is the most perfect visible display of God’s love that has ever been; the Evangelist has described it to us thus: <margin>John 3:16</margin> **God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son**: <note>original: "alsoo lief heeft Godt de werelt gehadt, dat hy sijnen eenigh-geboornen Sone gegeven heeft"</note> he gave him to become human, to become flesh, and to die the death; but the magnifying of his love is in this expression, [**so loved**]—so? how? indeed, so perfectly, so Fatherly, so voluntarily, as no

It is commonly said that it is a greater act of God's love to save a soul than to create a whole world; and I believe that it is an even greater love of God to take on our nature than simply to save our souls. For a King to dispense with his own Law, and by his own power to deliver a murderer from the gallows, is not as great an act of love and mercy as if he were to take the murderer’s clothes and wear them as his most precious livery <term>livery</term> <note>original: "levereij"; a distinctive uniform worn by the servants of a monarch or noble. Well, God has done exactly this in taking on our nature, and even more than this; he did not want to save us by his bare power alone, but he took our clothes—our flesh—and in this flesh he has carried our Persons, and in that flesh he was willing to die for us, so that we would not die, but that we might live eternally through him. Truly this was love, that God no longer (so to speak) wanted to be God alone <note>original: "enckel Godt"; meaning God in His pure divine essence, without the addition of human nature.</note>, but that he wanted to take on another nature, rather than let the luster of his glory destroy our souls.

I shall not do wrong (as I am busy tracing a line of God’s love in Christ from the beginning to the end in the saving of souls) if we look back here a little, and preciousy set together the dealings of God’s love from eternity, before the foundation of the world, until this time.

IX. Let us become conformed to Jesus <note>To be "conformed" means to be shaped or molded into the same likeness or character as Christ.</note> in relation to this great matter of his <term>Incarnation</term> <note>Original: "mensch-weerdingh," literally "becoming-human."</note>. Looking unto Jesus brings this about and causes it; the sight of God

<column-break/>

shall make us like God, and the sight of Christ shall also make us like Christ: for just as a mirror cannot be held toward the Sun without giving off a reflection like it; so God allows no one to behold his face without changing them into his own likeness through the radiance of his light. And Christ allows no one to descend into the depths of his glorious and blessed Incarnation without them bringing away some sweet impressions of an attached and transformed nature. Come then, and let us look once more upon Jesus in his Incarnation, so that we may become conformed and made equal to Jesus in this looking.

But in what does this conformity or likeness with Jesus consist? I answer, in these and similar parts: —
1. Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit; so too must Christ be conceived in us by the same Holy Spirit. To that end, the seed of the Word is cast into us, and the beginnings of grace are poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit;
<margin>James 1:18.</margin>
"He has begotten us through the Word"; however poor, and contemptible, and weak people may judge it to be, God has nonetheless ordained no other means to bring spiritual life into us but in this way: "where there is no prophecy, the people perish." Where there is no preaching, there is a heavier judgment than that of Egypt, when in every house a dead person was found— <note>Original catchword "von-" refers to the plague of the firstborn in Egypt, where a dead person was "found" (gevonden) in every home.</note>

# Looking unto Jesus.

found. Through the Word and Spirit, the seed of all manner of grace is simultaneously sown in our hearts, and once enclosed within our heart, Christ is immediately conceived in our heart.

Regarding this spiritual conception or the receiving of Christ within us, a weighty question is posed: is it possible for a person to discern how such a thing is brought about? Those who deny it use these passages: <margin>Colossians 3:3.</margin> "our life is hidden with Christ in God"; and "the wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes"; <margin>John 3:8.</margin> It is a wonderful, hidden, and secret conception. The Holy Spirit has expressed the state of our un-regenerate nature, in which Christ found us, by the name of "the dead" <margin>Ephesians 2:1.</margin> so that it must necessarily be as impossible for us to know how it is wrought, as it is impossible for someone to know how they received their own physical life. Some say that the first act of the <term>infusion</term> <note>Original: "instortingh." A theological term referring to the way God "pours" grace or spiritual life into a person's soul.</note>, or the receiving of Christ, or of grace (it all comes to the same thing), is wrought in a single moment and not by degrees, and therefore it is impossible to discern the manner of it.

And yet we maintain that we can discern both the preparations for grace and the first workings of grace. 1. The preparations for grace can be discerned; these are the dread and spiritual conflict that often precede the work of <term>regeneration</term> <note>Original: "weder-geboorte," literally "again-birth" or being "born again."</note>; that can be compared to the heating of metal before it is melted and poured into the earth to take its form; now, by the help of natural reason, one can discern these things. 2. Much more can the first movements and workings of grace be discerned by someone who

<column-break/>

is truly born again, because his spirit works within him simultaneously with Christ's Spirit; such things as sorrow over sin as sin, and an upright seeking after consolation, a hungry desire for Christ and his merits: furthermore, I do not think it is impossible for a born-again person to feel the first descent of the Spirit into the soul, for such a thing can bring its own feeling with it so that it can easily be discerned, although we do not always see it, nor perhaps see it ordinarily; it is true that the giving of spiritual life and the giving of such feelings are two distinct workings of the Spirit; but who can deny that these two workings could not go together, even though they do not always go together; but however it may be, it can nevertheless be felt in such persons, even at the beginning of regeneration, that they are in the state of regeneration: this conclusion stands firm, namely: *they can know what has been wrought in them, but how it was wrought, that they cannot know.*

-> # Looking unto Jesus <-

...of Christ with us, we call a hidden and spiritual union; but although it is hidden and spiritual, it is nonetheless a true, actual, essential, and self-subsistent union, through which the person of the believer is inseparably united with the glorious Person of the Son of God. For our better instruction, we may (if it please you) note a threefold union: either of Persons in one nature <note>The Trinity: three Persons in one divine nature</note>, or of the natures in one Person <note>The Hypostatic Union: the divine and human natures in the person of Jesus</note>, or of the natures and Persons in one Spirit <note>The Mystical Union: Christ and His Church</note>; in the first there is one God, in the second one Christ, in the third one Church with Christ. Our union with Christ is the last of these, through which He and we are all spiritually united to make up one spiritual body. Oh, what an advantage this is! A poor, believing person—let him be ever so lowly and miserable in the eyes of this world—is nonetheless one with Christ, just as Christ is one 
<margin>1 John 1:3</margin>
with the Father; **our fellowship is with the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ.** Every one of the Saints is a co-partner with Christ; there is a kind of similar proportion between Christ and His Saints in all things. When we look at all that Christ is—what He is in His Person, in His glory, in His Spirit, in His gifts of grace, in His Father’s love, and in the access He has to His Father—in all these things we are, in a certain way, co-partners with Christ; only with this distinction, that Christ in

<column-break/>

all things has the pre-eminence. Everything comes from the Father first to Christ, and everything we have, we have through the marriage <note>A common metaphor for the union between the soul and Christ</note> with Jesus Christ. Christ has all good things through His union without measure, but we have them through our union in a certain measure, according as it pleases Him to share them with us. But if we are like Christ in this—either in His union with the Father, or in His union of the two natures in one Person of the Mediator—if we come to this conformity through "looking unto Christ," to be one with Jesus Christ, oh, what an advantage this is! If we did not have good assurance of such a great status, it would be nothing but a blasphemous boldness for us to want to claim for ourselves the Royal blood of Heaven. But the Lord has been pleased to so dignify a poor earthworm <note>A traditional term of humility used to emphasize the distance between humanity and the divine</note> that every one of the believers can say with truth, *I am one with Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ is one with me.*

To make this union even more delightful <note>The original Dutch 'smakelijcker' suggests something that can be 'tasted' or enjoyed by the mind</note> for our thoughts, I shall make known to you the advantages that bloom from it, and let these awaken you to this conformity.

From this it comes that Christ lives in us, and that Christ gives us both life and is our life:
<margin>Colossians 3:4</margin>
<margin>Philippians 1:21</margin>
<margin>Galatians 2:20</margin>
**When Christ, who is our life, shall appear; for me to live is Christ; I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.**

### The Fourth Book. Part 1. Chapter 2. §. 9.

There is a spiritual and a natural life; regarding the natural life, what is it other than a bubble, a smoke, a shadow, a dream, a nothing? <note>A common 17th-century metaphor for the fleeting nature of human existence.</note> But this spiritual life is a glorious life; it is wrought in us by Christ’s Spirit. The natural life differs by a whole world from the spiritual life, and this creates a distinction between that which I do as a human being and that which I do as a Christian. As a human, I have eyes, ears, movements, affections, and understanding, naturally as my own; but as a Christian, I have all of this from Him with whom I am spiritually one, the Lord Jesus Christ. As a human, I have physical eyes, and I see physical and material things; but as a Christian, I have spiritual eyes, and I see invisible and eternal things,
<margin>Hebrews 11:27</margin>
just as it was said of Moses, that he held firm as if seeing the Invisible One. As a human, I have outward ears, and I hear outward sounds of all kinds, whether distinct or indistinct; but as a Christian, I have inward ears, and so I hear Christ’s voice and the Spirit of God speaking to my soul. As a human, I have physical feet, and with them I move in my own ways of this world; but as a Christian, I have spiritual feet, and upon them I walk with God in all the ways of His commandments. And as a human, I have natural affections—

<column-break/>

—and so I love beauty, and fear punishment, and hate my enemy, and rejoice in outward happiness, and so forth. But as a Christian, I have renewed affections, <note>In this context, "affections" refers to the inner inclinations and desires of the heart.</note> and so I love goodness, and hate nothing but sin, and I fear above all the displeasure of my God, and I rejoice in God’s favor, which is better than life. Certainly, this is a blessed life; and as soon as I am united with Christ, then I live—yet not I, but Christ lives in me. First, Christ is conceived, then He is prepared, and then He is born; and thereafter Christ grows in me to a blessed fullness.
<margin>Galatians 4:19</margin>
**My little children, for whom I labor again in birth until Christ is formed in you:** the preparation follows the conception, and the labor signifies the birth,
<margin>1 Corinthians 3:1</margin>
and according to that, we are young children in Christ, or Christ is like a young child in us; from there we grow up to the strength of youth;
<margin>1 John 2:14</margin>
**I have written to you, young men, because you are strong;** and finally, we come to the perfection of the Gospel—yes, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.
<margin>Ephesians 4:13</margin>
And is this all? No; but if my union is firm, and Christ lives in me, then I go forward, and in this condition I have

**died with Christ,** and I am
<margin>Romans 6:4, 11</margin>
**buried with Christ,** and I have become alive again to God in
<margin>Colossians 3:1</margin>
**Christ Jesus,** and I am raised with Christ, and I am
<margin>Romans 8:17</margin>
**glorified with Christ;** yes, even more...

<margin>Deuteronomy 6:4.</margin>
Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord. The last word, *one*, signifies the Unity; the three words, *The Lord your God*, look toward the Three Persons; and the middle phrase, *your God*, aptly describes the second Person who has taken on our nature. How well it came to pass, then, that at the beginning of the new world, the new Law, and Christ’s Baptism, the Three Persons revealed themselves; especially since He ordained that Baptism should be administered in their most holy name, bap-
<margin>Matthew 28:19.</margin>

This was the greatest manifestation that has ever been on earth: each Person of the Trinity gives a sensible testimony of their presence there.

Regarding the second point: why in the form of a Dove, rather than in any other form? Several reasons are given for this; such as:

1. To show Christ’s innocence, purity, simplicity, lovability, and love.

2. To show what innocence and blamelessness ought to be in those who are baptized.

3. To fulfill the pre-

<column-break/>

figurement <note>original: "voor-beeldt," referring to a biblical 'type' or prophetic symbol</note> of Noah’s flood; for just as a Dove at that time brought the message that the waters had subsided, so the Dove has now also brought the message of the diminishing of God’s wrath through the preaching of the Gospel. The first Dove we find in the Bible is Noah’s Dove with an olive branch in her mouth, proclaiming peace; the next is David’s Dove, whose wings are covered with silver, thus signifying uprightness; following that is Isaiah’s Dove cooing with her voice, representing patience; and the last is Christ’s innocent and spotless Dove. Now all these characteristics are found together in this Dove, the Holy Spirit. I could add several more things here, but I am eager to move on to some edifying instructions.

<margin>The Use.</margin>
From this Baptism of Christ, we can learn a practical and necessary <term>doctrine</term><note>A formal piece of religious teaching</note>; there are people who speak against Water-baptism, and they do so on this ground: they believe it was solely John’s own work to baptize with water, and Christ’s work to baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire. # The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 1. §. 4.

He baptizes all His holy ones with the Holy Spirit and with fire; but beyond all this, He commanded John—and not only John, but all His Apostles and their successors—to **Baptize** with water for all time. And they have done so, and continue to do so in obedience to Christ's command, which were the final words Christ spoke on earth. And although Christ Himself did not baptize with water <note>original: "Christus selve met water niet gedoopt en heeft," likely referring to the observation in John 4:2 that Jesus’ disciples performed the baptisms rather than Jesus himself</note>, yet Christ was (as we see here) Himself baptized with water. He Himself entered through the door through which His disciples should always follow Him; and truly, He entered through the door of **Baptism** to sanctify the entrance He had made for the house He was now about to build. And regarding the distinction that people make between the **Baptism** of Christ and that of John, what purpose does it serve? We all know that in **Baptism** there are two parts: an outward part and an inward part. You may call these (if it pleases you) the outward **Baptism** and the inward **Baptism**. The outward **Baptism** is performed by the minister, but the inward is from Christ. But must we separate these? Or rather unite them (since in the ordinary course they must go together), just as we find them in Christ, and as we wish they may be in us? I cannot see otherwise than that our **Baptism** and John’s **Baptism** are one in nature and in essence, <margin>Mark 1:4.</margin> and the same. For 1. John preached the baptism of repentance

<column-break/>

unto the forgiveness of sins; they had, therefore, the same teaching and the same promise. 2. The **Baptism** administered by John belonged to the <margin>Matthew 3:15.</margin> fulfillment of all righteousness, and Luke testifies that the tax collectors <margin>Luke 7:29, 30.</margin> and the people, having been baptized by John, justified God; but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not being baptized. But herein lies the difference: that John **Baptized** into a Christ who was yet to die and rise again; but we **Baptize** in the name of a Christ who has died and is risen. There is a difference in respect to the circumstances, but not the essence. O, then, take care that you do not reject the **Water-baptism** on the mere pretense of the **Baptism** with fire! Christ (as we see) has joined them together; no one, then, should separate them. Christ Himself was baptized with fire, and yet Christ Himself was also baptized with water.

# Looking unto Jesus. #

taught us to pray, "lead us not into temptation," and yet He Himself is now led into that very temptation against which we must pray; surely this happened for our instruction. We must not give ourselves over to temptation: Christ Himself did not wish to enter the battle uncalled and unbidden. What then could we poor, weak humans trust in regarding any of our own abilities? Who would dare to wrestle with the Devil in their own strength? Oh, be on your guard! If we must pray not to be led into temptation, we have much more need to pray that we do not *run* into temptation before we are led into it. And yet, for the comfort of God's people, if it should happen that we are led into temptation—whether through divine permission or the prompting of the Holy Spirit—and find ourselves involved in some business or way of life in which we encounter many temptations and little comfort, oh, let us regard these as a consequence of divine providence. In this, we must glorify the Lord our God, and not see it as a sign of God's disfavor or lack of love. And why is that? Because Christ Himself, who could have driven the Devils away with the breath of His mouth, was nevertheless led by the Spirit of His Father to be tested by the spirit of darkness. *Consider it pure joy, my brothers,* (says

<column-break/>

<margin>James 1:2, 3.</margin>
James) *whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance.*

3. The purpose <term>original: "eynde" — literally 'end,' referring to the goal or ultimate objective</term> of Christ being led by the Spirit into the Wilderness was either immediate or distant <note>original: "verschooven" — literally 'shifted' or 'postponed'; here meaning the secondary or ultimate outcome</note>. Regarding 1. The **immediate purpose**, that was to be tempted by the Devil; to that end Christ was brought there so that the Devil would tempt Him. You might think here that this is a completely strange plan—that the Son of God should be brought to the Wilderness to be besieged by all the Devils of hell; but God also had a **further or distant purpose** in this, and that was His own glory and our benefit.

1. **His own glory** has been revealed in this: if Satan had not tempted Christ, how then would Christ have conquered Satan? The first Adam was tempted and conquered; the second Adam <note>A theological title for Jesus, contrasting him with the first man, Adam, in the Garden of Eden.</note>, to repay and mend that blow, was tempted and conquered the tempter. Now, through this, Christ's power was markedly revealed; the Devil, having let the chain loose, let it fly at Christ with all his might; and Christ—who could not obtain victory without a struggle <note>original: "slagen" — literally 'blows' or 'strikes'</note>—through this violent assault of Satan, has both conquered him and triumphed over him. And through this, Christ's graces are shown quite gloriously: how are Christ's faith, patience, humility, zeal, and strength there...

4. The time and opportunity of the Devil’s attack: it was when he had fasted for forty days and was finally hungry. Some (as you have heard) 

<column-break/>

say that during all the forty days that Christ was in the wilderness, he was only tempted invisibly; for Satan during all that time did not take on a visible form, as they say he did at the end of the forty days. My intention is not to argue over this. Although there is a difference of opinion regarding his temptation, there is none regarding his fasting for forty days and forty nights. We have had several examples of this before Christ came into the world: thus Moses fasted forty days at the giving of the Law, and Elijah <note>The Dutch text uses "Elias," the Greek/Latin form of the Hebrew "Elijah."</note> fasted forty days at the restoration of the Law. To fulfill the time of both these examples, Christ willed to fast forty days at the completion of the Law and the preaching of the Gospel. By fasting so long, Christ showed his almighty power; and by fasting no longer, he made known the truth of his humanity and his weakness. To prove that there was no difference between us and him except for sin, he willed both to fast and also to be hungry. We know quite well that Christ could have lived without food, and he could have fasted without hunger; it would have been quite easy for him to sustain his body without any means of nourishment or life. ### 1. His cunnings are very many / and very dangerous : as : —

In spiritual and religious works, all outward relations stand still; matters of miracles concerned only His Divinity, and in this case it was: "Woman, what have I to do with you?" <note>Jesus' response to His mother Mary at the wedding in Cana is often interpreted by theologians not as a rejection, but as a clarification that His miraculous power belongs to His divine nature, not His human relationship to her.</note> We must not refuse love or dutiful obligations to our kin; but in God's matters, natural friendships must transition into spiritual ones, and like stars in the presence of the Sun,

wine that the last draught of it was the most pleasant of all. The world gives us beautiful promises of pleasure, honor, and advancement, but in the end, there is bitterness; all sin smiles upon us at its first approach, but when we have drunk deeply, then comes that which is worse. Only Christ changes our water into wine; if we fill our water-pots with water—if, like David, we drench our beds with our tears over our sins—then Christ will come to us at one time or another with the wine of joy, and He will give the best wine at the last. O how sweet shall that new wine be, which we shall one day drink with Christ in the Kingdom of His Father.

### §. 6.

2. If by Christ’s presence we understand his spiritual presence, then the question is: what is this spiritual presence? For if we say that it is his presence as he is God, then I would ask: how can God be said to be more present in one place among men than in another? God in his essence is perfectly everywhere, but contained nowhere; Heaven is his throne, and the earth his footstool, and yet neither the earth, nor the heaven, nor the heaven of heavens is able to encompass him. Since we speak of Christ’s presence in the assembly of his people spiritually, we cannot

Christ in his Spirit is in the midst of us, awakening and moving our spirits; or the Spirit of unity is with the united spirits. <margin>Matt. 23:10</margin> I. Christ’s titles in respect to his Prophetic ministry were these: 1. Sometimes he is called **Teacher** or **Master**: *Neither be called masters, for one is your Master, even Christ.* The word used is *Leader* <note>original Greek: Καθηγητής (Kathēgētēs)</note>, which signifies a Teacher, an Instructor, a Master-teacher, or a Guide.

In this case, <margin>Isa. 33:22</margin> God is our Judge: *The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he will save us.* In our consciences, we must hear no voice other than God’s; no other doctrine in the Church but Christ’s. No ministries, institutions, or forms of worship must be permitted except those he has established. Therefore, when men bring in strange teachings, it is said <margin>Col. 2:19</margin> that they *do not hold fast to the Head* <note>Meaning they have lost their connection to Christ, the source of authority</note>.

3. Sometimes he is called a **Counselor**: <margin>Isa. 9:5</margin> *And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor*; *Counsel and sound wisdom are mine*, says Christ; <margin>Prov. 8:14</margin> *I am understanding, I have strength.* Christ gives men counsel through his ministry on how they must flee from sin, how they must please God, how they must escape hell, and how they must be saved.

4. Sometimes he is called the **Apostle of our profession**: *Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider <margin>Heb. 3:1</margin> the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus.* God has sent him as his Ambassador to make his will known; he did not come without being sent—the word itself signifies a sending: <margin>Rom. 10:15</margin> *How shall they preach, except they be sent?* Let all those who have knowledge of this take heed, who run before they are sent, for Chri- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Chri-", likely continuing "Christ" on the next page.</note>

Miracles are generally outcomes that are wrought above the course and the power of nature; such were the miracles of *Christ*, and such were the miracles of the *Prophets* and of the *Apostles* of *Christ*; for all that they did was above nature; and the only difference between theirs and *Christ's* miracles was this, namely, that they did not work them in their own name and power, as *Christ* did.

Regarding the second, why did they happen? Various reasons have been given for this, of which I have previously given some indication, but in relation to the Scripture (which is the great master over all disputes), this is the common and true reason: that the miracles were performed for the grounding and confirmation of some divine truth or teaching at its first presentation. To this end, the miracles were like *Trumpets* <note>original: Basuynen</note> or *Heralds*, through which the *Gospel* was first commended to us; just as the *Law* was first strengthened by many miracles performed on Mount *Sinai* and in the *Wilderness*, which thereafter ceased when they approached the promised land and came into its possession; so also the *Gospel* was first strengthened by various miracles, but its sound having now gone through the whole world, these miracles have ceased: if in every...

After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Some would have it that this was the feast of Pentecost; and to tell the truth, most of our interpreters are at home with that view. Others take this for the feast of Passover, and they do so more readily because John counted the time of Christ's public ministry by the various Passover feasts. Now, if this was not a Passover feast, then we cannot find as many Passover feasts in the Gospel as would make up the three and a half years of Christ's ministry. On this ground, I join myself to the latter opinion; and thus I end here the second year of Christ's ministry, and come to the third, and to his works in the same in relation to the salvation of our souls.

### The Fourth Book. Second Part. Chapter 3. Section 2.

...day had come, he called his disciples to him, and chose twelve from among them, whom he also named Apostles. Until now, Christ has taught alone; but since after his Ascension <note>The event where Jesus was taken up into Heaven.</note> he would necessarily need a ministry to continue until the end of the world, he first wished to choose some who, during the time of his ministry, would attend to him on every occasion until he was taken up into Heaven. In this election or appointment, the following points are first to be noted: 1. The Person by whom they were chosen: Jesus Christ. 2. The place where they were chosen: namely, on a Mountain. 3. The time when they were chosen: after this vigil and praying the whole night through, and when it had become day. 4. The company from which they were chosen: these were his disciples, and from among them he made this choice. 5. The number of those whom he chose: they were twelve, no more and no less. 6. 1. The Person by whom they were chosen is Jesus Christ. They did not choose themselves, but Christ chose them; this calling was immediate <note>A direct calling from God without human intervention.</note>, and therefore most glorious; but nowadays we are not to look for such direct callings, and therefore I shall not dwell on this point; note only in passing that the ministers of the Gospel must be servants of Christ, being

If you only want to sit down at God’s table, if you only want to have the honeycomb with the honey, if you only want to drink of his Wine with his Milk, if you only want to drink—yes, if you only want to drink abundantly from the flasks of the new Wine of his Kingdom—well then, come! Come to the waters; come to me and drink. *Christ’s* arms are spread wide everywhere to receive sinners; he calls and knocks, he calls and waits, he calls and begs; every word here has so much sweetness and loveliness in it that it clearly testifies he is willing and ready to receive you, if you only will come.

### §. 4. Of Christ’s gentle yoke, and light burden.

<margin>Matthew 11:29, 30.</margin>
III. Regarding the gentleness of Christ’s yoke and the lightness of his burden: Christ has dealt with this in these words; *take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, — for my yoke is gentle, and my burden is light.* Notice the works of Christ from this year in relation to the healing of our souls. 1. He gives his Disciples the task of calling in the sinners. 2. He stands ready to accept them, if only they are willing to come. 3. He softens for them the way of a Christian walk, once they have entered. The hearts of men are full of fear and anxiety over the difficulty, hardness, and severity of Christ’s teachings; and to set this objection aside, he tells them quite clearly that such is not the case, but rather the opposite: *for my yoke is gentle, and my burden is light.*

<margin>1 John 5:3</margin>
*My yoke*, that is, my commandments; so has the Apostle John explained it, *His commandments are

<column-break/>

not heavy.* *My yoke is gentle*, that is, my commandments are without any discomfort; the difficulty of the yoke is not in its weight, but its discomfort. And Christ speaks quite well: *my yoke is gentle, and my burden*, that is, my teachings; this word refers primarily to the draft or ballast of a ship, which carves through the waves as if it had no weight at all, and yet without this burden, the ship could not remain safe. <note>original: "φορτίον παρὰ τὸ φέρεσθαι, à ferendo" — a burden from 'carrying,' or rather, something carried in a ship to ensure it moves steadily and safely.</note> *My burden is light*; the yoke of the law was hard, and the burden of the Pharisees was heavy, but Christ’s yoke is gentle, and his burden is light, in every way sweet and pleasant.

The Christian Religion and its practice is entirely sweet, light, and pleasant; *my yoke is gentle, and my burden is light.*

<margin>Isaiah 40:4, 6</margin>
The Prophets, foretelling this, spoke thus: *every valley shall be raised up, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and what is crooked shall be made straight, and what is bumpy shall be made into a valley.* The meaning is that the ways of our Christian walk shall be smoothed and made level, and that all obstacles and hindrances shall be removed from the path, so that the way to Heaven should fall so much lighter and easier for us: to this end serves yet another prophecy; and there shall be an exalted
