The reasons for the lightness, sweetness, and delightfulness of the Christian religion and its practice, I shall reduce to these points.

1. The Christian religion is entirely reasonable. If we look into the very best laws which the wisest men of the world have followed, we shall find that Christ has brought the best of all those into this one Law; the highest peak of reason is no more than a spark, a candle, a small light, which is enveloped and swallowed up in the body of that great light which is kindled by the Sun of Righteousness. Some have noted that Christ’s teaching is the summary of all the wisdom of the best of men, and a pure exemplar <note>original: "exemplar"; a perfect model or pattern</note> and transcript of his Father’s wisdom; nothing is found in the laws of the Christian religion but that it serves to the perfection of our spirit, as a worthy means to obey God, and to fulfill our duties, and to do good to all kinds of people on all occasions.

3. It provides a peace everywhere / it commands all duties of friendliness / politeness / love / gentleness / lowliness / humility of the heart toward others; and such sweet inclinations are often received with love / and with all neighborly kindnesses;

<term>Christ</term>: The central figure of the faith, seen here as the source of grace that subdues chaotic emotions.
<term>Peace</term>: Not just the absence of war, but an internal "tranquility of the soul" and domestic harmony.
<term>Laws</term>: The moral teachings of Jesus, presented as a guide for practical living rather than a set of legalistic rules.
<term>Passions</term>: In the 17th century, these were powerful, often conflicting emotions like greed, anger, and lust that were thought to "enslave" the ungodly.
<term>Wicked</term>: Those who live without God's law, characterized here by their internal conflict and restlessness.
<term>Household</term>: The primary social unit where Christian virtues like patience and kindness are first tested and displayed.
<term>Humility</term>: A core virtue that leads to "peace everywhere" by preventing social friction.
<term>Psalmist</term>: A reference to King David, traditionally credited with writing the Psalms.

<summary>This page contrasts the internal and domestic chaos of the "wicked"—who are torn apart by conflicting passions—with the profound peace and harmony experienced by those who follow Christ's laws. It emphasizes how Christian virtues transform a man into a gentle leader within his home and a kind neighbor in society.</summary>

### The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 3. Section 4.

Truly there are burdens that do not weigh down the bearers at all, like the burden of feathers on a bird's back; it is in no way heavy for them, but rather lifts them up; and the burden of gold and silver on the back of a man (suppose that it is the reward for his service, and the wage for his labor) is also in no way heavy for him, but rather gives him courage and makes him light on his feet. Men, brothers, Fathers, if we only want to come and unite ourselves with Christ, then the Spirit is given to us to make us capable, and Heaven is promised to us to give us courage; the one gives strength, and the other awakens our movements <note>The "movements" or "stirrings" of the soul toward God.</note>; and how could we then complain that the burden presses upon us? ### The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 3. Section 4.

surrender to the offerings of the Gospel, finding that everything the world can offer has now been outbid. You know that when someone comes and bids a certain amount for a property, and another comes and outbids him, the latter walks away with the prize. In the same way, while the world, lust, and sin offer this or that satisfaction, Christ comes and outbids them all; upon that, the bargain is struck, and Christ carries away the heart. So it may be said of many Christians, if they are so strict <note>The original Dutch "naeuw geset" refers to "precisians" or those who live by a very strict moral and religious code.</note>, that they are seldom happy and joyful.

But I answer—1. Christians who truly hold themselves to the rule are mostly all grave and stately, and the world looks upon them as melancholy.

2. It may be that they are not "in their element" except in the works of religious devotion, and therefore they cannot express their spiritual joy elsewhere. A fish cannot enjoy itself on land, but it does so in the water; a bird does not sing down

on the earth, but only when it is taken up into the air. God’s people can take no pleasure in sin, as drunkards and gamblers do; but when their hearts are engaged in religious exercises and in communion with God, then they are joyful and gladdened.

3. It may be that they are in the company of those who make them sad. Worldly people reproach the saints, saying they are sad, sullen, and melancholy people; but meanwhile, they do not consider that their own swearing, barking <note>original: "baffen" — a term for loud, coarse, or insulting talk.</note>, and dishonoring of God’s name have made the godly so sad. <margin>Genesis 6:6</margin>
in His heart, as it is said in Genesis 6:6. And so it is no wonder that the godly cannot rejoice in your sinful company; you are the cause of their sadness. But let them once come into the company and the communion of the saints, and then they will certainly know how to be glad.

4. If it is the case that they are often sad and mournful, that is not because of their religious devotion, but because they are not yet *more* religious—because they still find so much lack of godliness in their own hearts. This was the cause of Paul’s sadness:
<margin>Romans 7:24</margin>
> O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?

## CAP. IV.

### Sect. I.

#### Of the fourth year of Christ's ministry, and in general of his actions in the same.

This was the last year of Christ's ministry, in which a thousand things occurred. The Evangelist <term>John|The Gospel writer John, often noted for his theological depth</term> relates more of Christ in this year than in all the preceding ones; and if I did not seek to be brief, we could dwell longer on what he did for us this year than we have done from the beginning of his ministry until now. Now it was that he was changed in appearance <note>referring to the Transfiguration</note>, and that he instituted the Sacrament that is called the Lord's Supper; now after the Supper he delivered his farewell sermon, being wondrously mixed with sorrow and joy, and being wrought with mysteries as if with emerald stones <note>original: "Smaragdus-steenen"</note>: now it was that after his Sermon he blessed his Disciples, and prayed for them, and having sung a song of praise, he went out to the Mount of Olives, where he in a garden

<column-break/>

began his suffering. On these actions I had thought to dwell somewhat longer, but I see that the book is swelling under my hands <note>an idiomatic way of saying the manuscript is becoming very long</note>; and as I now approach Christ's suffering, I shall touch upon only one piece, which I have skipped until now, being a matter that contains more within itself than any discourse I can present.

There are many questions regarding Christ's holiness, or righteousness, or obedience. Such as: does it concern us as well? And is it the substance of our <term>justification|The process by which a person is made right or "just" before God</term>? And was Christ obliged to keep the Law of works as <term>Mediator|One who acts as a go-between or advocate for humanity before God</term>, or merely as a simple man? And are we not justified only through the righteousness of Christ's suffering? And since we are now treating Christ's deeds in relation to our souls' salvation, we cannot skip this great work, of which many things pertain as much to Christ's life as to his conception, or birth, or death, or suffering.

This same distinction is given by others with these words: Christ’s righteousness is either His original conformity <note>The inherent alignment of His nature with God's will</note>, or His active and passive obedience to the Law. His original conformity is that gracious inherent disposition in Christ, whereby He was conformed to the Law of God in a holy manner; and this original righteousness answers for our original unrighteousness. His active obedience is His performing of legal obedience according to the commandment; and His passive obedience is His suffering of the punishment which we deserved with our sins. --- I shall expand just a little further upon this distinction of Christ's righteousness, and present it thus: namely, the righteousness of Christ is either negative (if I may speak so) or positive. By the negative, I understand the absence of all sins and blasphemies which are forbidden in the Law; by the positive, I mean a presence of all virtues and duties which are required for a perfect fulfillment of the Law, as well as a willing suffering of the punishment to satisfy the threat and the curse of the Law.

1. The negative righteousness is that which we call the innocence <term>innocence|The Dutch "onnooselheydt" here refers to being "harmless" or "without guilt," rather than a lack of knowledge</term> of Christ; we often read in Holy Scripture that He was blameless and unspotted: 1. Blame-

<margin>1 Pet. 1:19</margin>

2. The positive righteousness of Christ is twofold: His perfect fulfillment of all things that are commanded, and His perfect satisfaction of the threatened punishment. The first is the holiness of Christ, which is also twofold: the holiness of His nature, and the holiness of His life and conduct. The first is that which we call His habitual righteousness <note>Refers to righteousness as an internal quality or state of being (from the Latin 'habitus')</note>; the latter we call His active obedience. And thus much for the distinction of the righteousnesses of Christ.

### §. 3.
### Of the holiness of Christ’s nature.

<margin>Psalm 45:2</margin>
Now, in the first place, regarding the holiness of His nature, of which the Psalmist says: *You are much fairer than the children of men, grace is poured into your lips.* This is one and the same as the description of Christ given by the Bride <margin>Song of Sol. 5:10</margin> in the Song of Solomon: *My beloved is white and ruddy, and bears the banner above ten thousand.* Just as in the most excellent beauty there is a mingling of these two colors—of white and red—so also in Christ there is a gracious mingling and composition of all the graces of the Holy Spirit. There is in Him a sweet mingling of meekness, purity, righteousness, loveliness, humility, and what not? In <margin>Col. 2:3</margin> Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; and I may well add: the treasures of all other gifts, endowments, and graces. There is no grace that was not in Christ, and that in a more excellent way than in any of the saints of the whole world; and therefore He is said to be fairer than the children of men. Note: there was more habitual grace <term>habitual grace|Theological term for "gratia habitualis," referring to the permanent, inherent holy disposition and qualities infused into the soul</term> in Christ than there ever was, is, or shall be in all the elect, whether Angels or men. If we look upon anything in Heaven or on earth that we consider excellently beautiful, the Lord Jesus is represented by that thing in the Scriptures in regard to His inward beauty. # Looking unto Jesus.

§. 2.

### Of meditating on Jesus in this regard.

II. Let us meditate on Jesus, as he took upon himself the great work of our salvation during his life. It is not enough that we study and know, but we must also ponder, and deliberate, and meditate upon it, until we have brought it to some useful outcome. By pondering on Christ, we can feel or perceive a certain insensible change, though we know not how: just as someone standing in the Sun for other reasons feels that he is being enlightened and warmed; so also can our souls, in a holy pondering, be changed and turned in a hidden and insensible way; there is a power accompanied by an earnest meditation, a changing and turning power; and therefore look further, O my soul, have strong imaginings of all these different places of Christ’s life.

1. Meditate on the Preaching of John the Baptist: we talk much of precision <note>original: "precijsicheydt," referring to strict religious discipline</note>, but show me once among all the worshipers or saints in our times such a pattern of holiness and extraordinary strictness: the content of all his preaching was repentance, the leaving of sin, and the bringing forth of fruits of repentance worthy of life. In the continuation of

<column-break/>

this teaching, he was a sharp rebuker of the Pharisees, and Sadducees, and <term>Tax-collectors<gloss>original: "Tollenaers," those who collected Roman taxes and were often seen as traitors or extortionists</gloss></term>, and the Soldiers, and in truth of all men; but especially of those who continued in their impenitence, for to such he proclaimed the judgment and the unquenchable fire. O, he had an excellent zeal and a fiery spirit in preaching, and the best interpretation of all his Sermons was his own life; he was clothed with Camel’s hair, and he ate locusts and wild honey; he despised the world and resisted temptations, he desired to receive no vain honor, and in all things he was an outstanding example of self-denial and <term>mortification<gloss>original: "doodinge," the spiritual practice of subduing one's sinful desires</gloss></term>: and by these means, he made a glorious and fit preparation for the coming of the Lord. O my soul, if you would only sit for a little time at the feet of this Preacher, or if you would only <term>ruminate<gloss>original: "herkauwen," literally to "chew the cud," a metaphor for reflecting deeply on the Word</gloss></term> as the beasts do: meditate on his Sermons of repentance, and righteousness, and temperance, and of the coming judgment, and see what inspirations these have upon your soul; <margin>Acts 24:25.</margin> when Paul preached such things before Felix, it is said that he became very afraid: a Sermon of the chaff being burned with unquenchable fire is powerful enough to make your heart tremble, if it is handled with power and received with emotion; but see what effect it

->The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 5. §. 2. 425<-

has on your heart and life? Do you feel in yourself a spirit of mortification <note>original: "doodinge," the theological concept of "killing" or subduing one's sinful nature</note>? Do you, along with the Baptist, die to the world? Do you deny your own will regarding all your natural sinful desires? Do you refrain from fleshly lusts and pleasures, so that the flesh, being brought under the spirit, may both walk together in the service of God? Do you kill the desires of the flesh by removing all food and fuel for those cravings? This is the work of meditation; it first employs the understanding to reflect on things, and then the will to accept those things, and both of these are directed toward grace and a godly life. That meditation which ends only in knowledge, or in the mere contemplation of knowledge, is like the sunshine in Winter, which shines but does not warm. Oh my soul, think and think upon the preaching of this forerunner of Christ, until you feel that this meditation has brought some warmth into your heart and some influence upon your life, toward holiness, self-denial, and mortification.

2. Meditate on the Baptism of Christ; he who had never sinned was made sin for us, and so it befitted Christ to receive the Sacrament of sinners, or of the conversion from sin; but he was especially baptized so that, through that sign, he might cleanse our nature, whose stains and guilt he had taken upon himself. Meditate

<column-break/>

on this, Oh my soul, and bring this closer to your heart; surely every soul that lives the life of grace is born of water and spirit, and to that end, Christ, who is our life, descended into the water of Baptism, so that we, descending after him, might find its effects, such as the forgiveness of sins, acceptance into the covenant of grace, and holiness of life. If Christ had not been baptized, what power would there have been in our baptism? Just as it befitted him to fulfill all 
<margin>Matth. 3:15.</margin>
righteousness, and he therefore necessarily had to be baptized; so he did not accomplish that for himself, but for us. Christ’s obedience in fulfilling the Law is credited to all who believe unto righteousness, as if they themselves had fulfilled it; so also, Christ having been baptized, the power of his baptism has come down upon us. Oh, the sweetness of this meditation! Christ was baptized, and while being baptized, the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended, and a voice from Heaven proclaimed him to be the Son of God, and the one in whom his Father was well pleased. And the same anointing that was poured out upon the head of our High-Priest <note>A reference to Psalm 133:2, where the sacred oil flows down the head and beard of Aaron</note> has descended onto his beard, and further fell upon the edge of his garments; for just as Christ felt these workings in the revelation, so we also believe that through Christ we feel similar workings in our baptism.

The heavens are then also (so to speak) opened for us, and the Holy Spirit then descends upon us; and then we are sealed for the inheritance of the sons, in whom the Father, through His Son, also takes a good pleasure. Oh my soul! What abundance of blessing is in Christ’s baptism? And how could you suck and be satisfied, if you would use your meditations rightly? Christ’s baptism is like a field of flowers, in which there is a world full of benefits, such as **justification**, **adoption as children**, **rebirth**, **sanctification**, and **glorification** <note>These terms describe the various stages of a believer's spiritual journey in 17th-century Reformed theology</note>. Oh, then set your soul at least upon some of these flowers, and do not leave them until you have drawn some honey from them; if you are in Christ, then you are baptized into His death, and baptized into His baptism; you enjoy both the fruit and the operation of His death, and life, and baptism, and everything.

3. Meditate upon Christ’s fasting and temptation in the Wilderness. Now we see what kind of adversary we have, how he fights, how he is resisted, and how he is overcome: in the first attack, Satan sought to bring Christ to despair in His Father’s providence; in the second, to presumption upon His Father’s protection; and when neither despair nor presumption could have any effect on Christ, he tempted Him with honor; and so he also deals with us. If he cannot strike us down through

<column-break/>

despair, then he labors to lift us up through presumption; and if neither of these has power, then he comes forth with luxury, profit, and honor, which are truly the most dangerous temptations of the "right hand" <note>Temptations of the "right hand" are those that appeal to our desires for success and comfort, whereas those of the "left hand" involve suffering and fear</note>. Oh my soul, as long as you are in this conflict, here is your state; temptations, like the waves of the Sea, follow one after another. If the Devil has treated Christ so roughly, what hope can you have to be spared? How can you judge that the turning away of one temptation merely paves the way for another? But take heart; here is your strength: you have such a <margin>Heb. 4:15, 16.</margin>Savior, *who in all things, just as we are, was tempted, yet without sin*. With what boldness can you then go to the throne of grace to obtain mercy, and find grace to be helped in a timely hour? Christ was tempted so that He might be able to come to the aid of those who are tempted; you are never tempted, Oh my soul, but Christ is with you in the temptation; He has sent His Spirit into your heart to make intercession there for you; and He Himself is in Heaven to pray for you there as well; yes, His own experience <note>original: "onderbindinge," meaning the personal undergoing or subjection to the trial</note> of the temptation has so worked in His heart that His love and kindness are most active when you are most tempted. Just as kind fathers are always moved by their children, but especially when they are sick, and weak, and not feeling well

**5.** Meditate on Christ’s scourging of the buyers and sellers out of the Temple. Sometimes, O my soul, you are alone in secret, and sometimes you are in the gatherings of God’s people; and when you are performing your duty, wherever you might be, meditate on Christ’s special presence. And what is that other than the presence of His Spirit and of His Angels?

**1.** The presence of His Spirit; we know it through His working in us. Surely the Spirit does not only hover over us, but He works in us: and how in us? I answer: through His life-giving, raising up, nurturing, healing, softening, soothing, and comforting. In this way He works in us when we are in His <term>ordinances — religious practices or rites ordained by God, such as prayer, preaching, or the sacraments</term>. Well now, He is (as I hope) riding in triumph in the midst of this gathering; now He is on His chariot, on His throne, and in the hearts of His people. And therefore away, away with all buyers and sellers out of this Temple of the Holy Spirit!

**2.** The presence of Christ is the presence of His Angels; just as a King is where His Court is, so is Christ the King of Kings especially present where His blessed Angels pitch their camp. And the presence of the Angels, O my soul, is well worthy of your meditation. Surely they are ministering spirits who have their work to perform

<column-break/>

upon your inward man. But to depart a little from our <term>propoost — the subject or theme of the current discussion</term>, it is a fine thing to know how the Angels can speak to us, and how we can know when they speak to us, and how we can distinguish what is spoken by the immediate <note>original: "inblasinge" — literally "breathing-in" or inspiration</note> of the Spirit, or through the medium of the Angels.

3. But how shall we distinguish what is spoken through an *immediate* inspiration of the Spirit, or through a *mediate* inspiration of the Angel? Here we must stand with the truth; and I know no better way to answer this than Master Calvin <note>original: "Calvinus" — John Calvin (1509–1564), the French theologian whose work formed the basis of the Reformed tradition.</note>, that in such hidden mysteries we must use the rule of modesty and moderation, and that we must neither speak nor think, nor desire to know anything other than what is taught to us through God's word. I do not know if this question has any great utility, and therefore I will not weary my mind to give a full account of it; only this stands to be noted as certain truth: 1. That the things communicated to our inner man (I mean those internal movements and inspirations toward holiness and obedience) often and commonly occur through the ministry of Angels. 2. That these same things, which are communicated to our inner man, always originate primarily and principally from Christ’s Spirit, and it is for this reason that we record them all on the same tally-stick <note>original: "kerf-stock" — a notched stick used for bookkeeping; the author means we credit both to the same ultimate source.</note>; we attribute them all to Christ’s Spirit. 3. ### The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 5. § 3.

<margin>Galatians 4:4.</margin>
In relation to yourself. God has sent forth His Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that He might redeem those who were under the law, and that we might receive the adoption as children. <note>original: "aen-neminghe tot kinderen"</note> **It is a sweet observation of Dr. Andrews,** <note>Lancelot Andrewes (1555–1626) was a prominent English bishop and scholar who helped oversee the translation of the King James Version of the Bible.</note> Christ was placed under the Law; that is, He was placed under one half of the law (which is the governing part) and satisfied it through the innocence of His life, without breaking one jot or tittle of the law, and so He answered that part as the principal party. He was also placed under the other half (which is the punishment) and satisfied it by suffering an unjust death, which He in no way deserved or owed, and so He answered that part as one who had forfeited. But when we now ask, for whom was all this? It is for us alone, so that we might be redeemed and adopted as children; redeemed from all evil, and adopted to have a share in all good. **Since this is so, oh, who would want to miss the influence and the benefit of Christ’s active obedience <note>original: "doenlijcke gehoorſaemheydt" — referring to Christ's perfect adherence to God's law during His life.</note> for a world full of gold? Meditate upon this, O my soul, until you feel some power from Christ's life entering into yourself.**

If the crumbs of his bread are so sweet, what then must the great bread, Christ himself, be? Christ is wonderful in his works and in his person; but above all, his person is most wonderful. No creature in the world displays God in such a way as the person of Jesus Christ; <margin>Hebrews 1:3.</margin> he is the express image of his Father’s substance. Just as the impression of the seal upon the wax is the expressed image of the seal itself, so is Christ the highest representation of God; he is the likeness of Him who is otherwise without any likeness. ### §. 4.
### *On hoping in Jesus in this regard.*

VI. Let us hope in Jesus, as he has taken upon himself the great work of our salvation in his life. But I do not speak here of a wavering, wobbling, or doubtful hope, but of a certain hope, of a hope that is well-grounded. The main question of a soul is whether Christ's life also belongs to me: whether all these opened passages of his life also concern me? Whether the indwelling righteousness and actual holiness of Christ is also imputed to me for righteousness? And what are the grounds and certainties upon which my hope is built? The Apostle tells us 
<margin>2 Thess. 2:16.</margin>
that God gives good hope through grace. If the hope is well and good, it will manifest itself through the workings of saving grace. Oh, look into your soul! What gracious workings of the life of Christ are there? Certainly, his life is not without all influences upon our spirit, if we are indeed his members and he is our head. The head, we say, communicates life, and feeling, and movement to the limbs; and so Christ also communicates a spiritual life, and feeling, and movements to his members. Oh, the glorious workings flowing from the life of Christ into the souls of the believers! I shall present these as follows: When—

1. If Christ’s life is mine, then I am delivered from the **Law of sin**; this was the Apostle’s

I cannot think otherwise, despite the influence of Christ's life upon me, but that sin constantly remains in me; I am and remain a sinner in respect to the

*that sin should not reign in your mortal body, to obey it in its lusts.*

...kindle affections? Forbes <note>Likely referring to John Forbes (1593–1648), a Scottish theologian whose works were popular in Dutch Reformed circles.</note> reminds us that God's word has three stages of operation in the hearts of his elect. First, it falls upon the ears of men like a **sound of many waters**, a very great and tumultuous sound, generally bringing neither fear nor joy, but nonetheless an amazement and a confession of a strange power and more than human strength. This is the operation that many felt when hearing Christ, 
<margin>
Mark 1:22, 27.
</margin>
<margin>
Luke 4:32.
</margin>
<margin>
John 7:46.
</margin>
when they were astounded <note>Dutch: *versloegen*, literally "beaten" or "struck," used here to mean being overcome with awe.</note> by his teaching; for he taught as one having authority. "What new teaching is this? Never has a man spoken like this man." The next operation is the **voice of thunder**, causing not only amazement but also fear, filling not only the ear with a sound but also moving and terrifying the conscience. The third operation is the **sound of the harp**, when the word not only carries one away through amazement and strikes the conscience with fear, but finally fills it with a sweet peace and joy. 

Allow me now to ask: O my soul, have you been brought to astonishment by the mighty miracles and Divine teaching of Jesus Christ? Do you fall down and worship him as your Lord and God? Do you believe in him and trust in him for your life and salvation? Are you obedient to him, and do you **follow the Lamb** wherever he goes? Do you begin to act from the principles of grace in newness of life and holiness of conduct?

<column-break/>

...do you walk according to the commandments of Jesus Christ, or is there at least an earnest effort in you to walk so, and is this a concern for your soul when you notice your stumbles; and do you rejoice in your Spirit when you are led by the Spirit? Well then, here is yet another ground of hope: that a power from Christ's life has gone out into your soul.

If Christ's life is mine, then **I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.** Paul spoke this testimony: *I am crucified with Christ, yet I live*, etc. <note>original Latin/Dutch: "ick ben met Christo ghekruyst, doch ick leve &c." – a reference to Galatians 2:20.</note> He has placed Christ’s death and Christ’s life together in one and the same soul—that is, no one knows the benefit of Christ’s death except he who feels the power of his life. There is no certainty of Christ's death for us, except when we feel the life of Christ in us; when the power of Christ's death kills my lusts, then the power of the life of Christ shall make my soul alive. 

But what does he mean to say with this: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me*? It seems to be a paradox <note>Dutch: *wonder-spreucke*, literally a "wonder-saying" or a miraculous statement that seems contradictory.</note>—*I live, yet no longer I*—but a good explanation takes away all difficulty: such as this: I live for God, and not for myself; I live for Christ, and not for the world; I live according to the will of God, and not according to my own lusts and imaginings; or (as some would have it) I live under grace, and not under the law. <column-break/>

as one who has become subject to the law, having not only taken on our nature, but also our debts; our nature as a human,
<margin>2 Corinthians 5:21.</margin>

### The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 5. §. 5.

...ness <note>continuing from "holiness" on the previous page</note> holiness and blessedness, sanctification <note>original: "heyligh-makinge"</note> and justification <note>original: "rechtveerdigh-makinge"</note>. If Christ’s garments were powerful enough to heal, how much more so great and essential a part of Christ—even half of Christ, so to speak; for such is the life of Christ? There is a strong presumption that the true reason why so much is spoken of Christ’s death, and so little in comparison of His life, is either this: that we do not yet understand the fullness of His life, or because we are carnal <note>fleshly or worldly</note> and lovers of ourselves, seeking more after freedom from Hell than after Holiness on earth, seeking more of Christ’s benefits than conformity <note>likeness</note> with Christ. O come! behold the fullness of Christ’s life! In relation to our sanctification, was it not a completely perfect pattern of perfection? A most exquisite <note>original: "curieuse," meaning carefully crafted or remarkable</note> representation of the entire word of God? An express image and manifestation of the whole mind of God? A perfect example for all others to walk, work, and live by? And in relation to our justification, is not Christ’s life the object of faith and of justification? Yes, is not Christ’s life the object of justifying faith, just as much as Christ’s death, resurrection, Ascension, sitting at the right hand of God, and intercession for us? The teachers of Christ’s active <note>original: "doenlijcke"; Christ’s perfect following of God's laws</note> and passive <note>original: "lijdelijcke"; Christ’s willing suffering of the penalty for sin</note> obedience for

<column-break/>

us can tell us of two things in which the law is fulfilled: the first being the primary one, namely obedience; and the other being the second, namely the curse at the bottom of obedience; so that once sin is committed, a double act is required for justification: the suffering of the curse, and a fulfillment of righteousness anew. The one is the satisfaction for the wrong that we have done to God as our judge; and the other is a fulfillment of the service we owe to God as our Creator. Oh, how broad and full and all-encompassing is this life of Christ?

2. Meditate on the excellence and glory of this object: Christ’s life is glorious; and therefore Christ’s righteousness is the most glorious garment that God’s saints have ever worn.

# Looking unto Jesus

The sign of love is to not like being in debt: and (O my soul) is there within you neither grace, or at least a good nature? O that hardened heart! Wake up! ### §. 7.
### Of rejoicing in Jesus in this looking [unto Him].

<margin>21.</margin> VII. Let us rejoice in Jesus, just as He bore the great work of our salvation for us during His life. But what is there in Christ’s life, or in all the dealings of His life, that can stir us to joy? I answer that His entire life, and all the dealings of His life, being properly <term>appropriated</term> <note>original: "toe-eyghent"; the theological act of claiming the benefits of Christ's life and death for oneself through faith.</note>, are an excellent subject for the awakening of our affections: certainly, the power of the work consists in the appropriation of the life of Christ. If we wish to rejoice in Christ in a spiritual manner, we must bring the object and the soul’s power together: and this union of the object and the soul’s power is commonly sought through contemplation, or through trust, or through enjoyment. I shall stay here only a little while, so that we may finally come to rejoice in Christ; yes, if it were possible, to rejoice always.

Come then, stir up your memory; <margin>7.</margin> let us be steadfast men; let us often spend our thoughts upon this blessed object; the reason why we <margin>8.</margin> lack our joy is because we have so little reflection upon our Jesus. # Looking unto Jesus.

### A prayer and thanksgiving.
1. We must pray that all these dealings of Jesus during his life, or during his ministry on earth, may be ours; we hope that it is so, and we believe that it is so, but above all this we must pray that it may be so; there is no contradiction between hope, and faith, and prayer, but rather much agreement, <margin>Mark 9:24.</margin> 
> *Lord, I believe, yet help my unbelief,* or *let it happen to me according to my faith,* however weak it may be, which is to say the same thing.

2. We must thank God for all these dealings in Christ’s life. So did the multitude, <margin>Luke 19:37, 38.</margin> 
> *they praised God with a loud voice, because of all the mighty works they had seen, saying, Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord, peace be in heaven, and glory in the highest places.*

What (my soul), has Christ done all this for you? Has he come under the law to redeem your soul, and adopted you as his Son to inherit Heaven? Has he come down from Heaven; and traveled so many miles on earth, to free and win your heart? Has he spoken so many words, and performed so many wonder-works <note>miracles</note>, to work faith in you? Oh, how you ought then to praise, prize, and glorify his Name! How you ought to break out into that blessed song of praise: to him who

<column-break/>

loved us, and who has made us Kings and Priests to God, and his Father, to him (I say) be the Glory and the power into all eternity, Amen! <margin>Rev. 1:5, 6.</margin>

### §. 9.
->Of conformity with Jesus in this looking.<-

IX. Let us be conformed to Jesus in what he has done for us in his life. The looking unto Jesus has this especially as its goal; we must look upon him just as someone looks upon his pattern <note>original: "patroon", meaning a model or blueprint to be followed</note>; just as the sailors on the sea, in order to hold a straight course, keep their eye on that ship which carries the lantern; so we also in the race <note>original: "loop-bane", referring to the spiritual course of life</note> that is set before us, must keep our eye on Jesus, as our blessed pattern. This must be our constant question: is this the course that Jesus steers? Or to present this somewhat more broadly—
In this matter I shall examine these three questions: 1. In what must we be conformed to him? 2. Why must we be conformed to him? 3. How must we be conformed to this life of Jesus?
Regarding the first, in what we must be conformed, I answer—
1. By way of exclusion <note>original: "beneeminghe", here used to set aside or exclude things that are not applicable to human imitation</note>; we must not, nor can we, be conformed to Christ in those works which belong to his Divinity, such as the performing of wonder-works: I do not deny that wonder-works are as a privilege and dispensation...

# Looking unto Jesus.

->a prayer and thanksgiving.<-

1. We must pray that all these dealings <note>original Dutch: *verhandelinghen*, referring to the events and teachings of Jesus’s life discussed in the text</note> of Jesus during his life, or during his ministry on earth, may be ours; we hope that it is so, and we believe that it is so, but above all this we must pray that it may be so; there is no contradiction between hope, faith, and prayer, but rather a great agreement. <margin>Mark 9:24.</margin> *I believe Lord, yet help my unbelief*, or let it be done to me according to my faith, however weak it may be, which is to say the same thing.

2. We must thank God for all these dealings in Christ's life. So did the multitude; <margin>Luke 19:37, 38.</margin> *they praised God with a loud voice, because of all the mighty deeds they had seen, saying, Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord, peace be in Heaven, and glory in the highest places.* What, (my soul), has Christ done all this for you? Was he made under the law, to redeem your soul, and accepted you as his Son to inherit Heaven? Did he come down from Heaven; and travel so many miles on earth, to call and win your heart? Has he spoken so many words, and performed so many wonderous works, to work faith in you? Oh, how you ought then to laud, praise, and glorify his Name? How you ought to break out into that blessed song of praise, to him who us

<margin>Rev. 1:5, 6.</margin> loved; and who has made us Kings and Priests to God, and his Father, to him (I say) be the Glory and the power for all eternity, Amen?

### §. 9.
### Of the conformity with Jesus in this looking.

IX. Let us be conformed to Jesus <note>To be "conformed" means to be shaped or modeled after someone’s likeness</note> in what he has done for us in his life. Looking unto Jesus has this especially as its aim; we must look upon him just as someone looks upon his pattern <note>original: *patroon*, meaning a model or blueprint</note>; just as sailors on the Sea, in order to keep a straight course, keep their eye on the ship that carries the lantern <note>In the 17th century, the lead ship of a fleet carried a lantern at night to guide those following behind</note>; so must we also, in the race-course that is set before us, keep our eye on Jesus, as our blessed pattern. This must be our constant question: is this the course that Jesus steers? Or to present this somewhat more broadly. — 

In this matter I shall examine these three questions: 1. In what must we be conformed to him? 2. Why must we be conformed to him? 3. How must we be conformed to this life of Jesus?

Regarding the first, in what we must be conformed, I answer —

1. By exclusion <note>original: *beneeminghe*, a logical term for defining something by what it is not</note>; we must not, nor can we, be conformed to Christ in those works which are proper to his Divinity, such as in the performing of miracles: I do not deny that miracles are granted as a privilege and dispensation

5. In respect of all his works, deeds, and duties of moral obedience <note>The author distinguishes between 'moral' (everlasting) and 'ceremonial' (temporary Jewish) laws.</note>: We find in the life of Christ var-

<column-break/>

ious particular actions and deeds of obedience toward his Heavenly Father, of which some were moral, others ceremonial: now all these are not for our imitation, but only such moral deeds, regarding which we have both his example and his command; come, let us observe this one rule, and we need no more: everything he commanded, and everything he did, being of close morality, therein we are bound to follow his footsteps. I put his commands and deeds together, because in those things which he did and did not command, we have no need to be conformed to him; but in those things which he did and commanded, we are bound to follow him; in this case his laws and works differ only as a map and a guide; a law and a judge; a rule and a precursor.

In respect of all these particular parts, and especially in respect of Christ’s moral obedience, the whole life of Christ has been a teaching, a living, visible, and exemplary command to men; and for this reason we find that such names are given to him in Scripture which signify not only an excellence but also an example: thus he is called a Prince, <margin>Dan. 9:25.</margin> a Leader of the peoples, <margin>Isa. 55:4.</margin> a Guide, <margin>Matth. 2:6.</margin> the Chief Shepherd, <margin>1 Pet. 5:4.</margin> a forerunner or leader into glory, <margin>Heb. 6:20.</margin> and a light for the Jews.

Regarding the second point—why we must be conformed to Him: by what motives? I answer: 1. Because Christ Himself performed and suffered many things for this very end and purpose. I have often wondered why Christ chose to do and suffer so much, as the Evangelists relate of Him? This I believe: that Jesus was perfect God and perfect man; and that every deed of His life, and a single hour of His suffering and death, would have been sufficient for the satisfaction <note>The legal payment of the debt of sin.</note> and reconciliation of ten thousand worlds; but now I have my answer: that all these patterns of holiness, and all these types of virtues, and all these degrees of His suffering, and all those sheddings of His blood, were partly for this reason: that He might become an example to us, that He might be a light for all ages and generations of the wor—

<column-break/>

—ld, and that He would thus be a Lodestar <note>original: *Leydt-sterre*</note> and a beacon-fire <note>original: *bier-baken*</note> for them on their journey toward Heaven. O my soul, how this calls to you to be conformed to Christ! What? That far less expense would have been enough for your justification <note>Being declared righteous before God.</note>, and yet the entire storehouse <note>original: *magazijn*</note> of your sanctification <note>The process of becoming holy in practice.</note> cannot bring it about? That for a smaller sum of obedience God might have forgiven your sins, and yet for a larger sum you do not want to do as much as follow His holiness? If in the dark night a will-o'-the-wisp <note>original: *dwaes-licht*</note> should go before you, you would be so captivated by that small flame that you would be inclined to follow it and lose yourself; and yet do you not wish to follow the Glory of the Sun of Righteousness, who calls out to you through so many examples, and who wishes to bring you into a safe harbor and secure you against all hardships that can be imagined? God forbid! If it had not been for your imitation, I cannot think that Christ would have lived so many years on earth, and would have performed so many gracious, meritorious works. O, ponder this.

### Looking unto Jesus

...as a pattern for others; now Christ is the firstborn / Christ is the head of all who were previously ordained / just as the firstborn was formerly the head in every household. The ancients used to say, *According to the example of the King, etc.* <note>original: "Regis ad exemplar &c." This refers to the Latin proverb *Regis ad exemplar totus componitur orbis*, meaning "The whole world is formed after the example of the king."</note> Even a deformity was once considered an honor if it was done in imitation of a Prince; it is told of Nero that, because he had a crooked neck, people were so eager to follow the court in this that it became the fashion and beauty of those times to hold one’s neck crooked: and shall not Christ, the King of His Saints, be followed much more by His Saints? Christ is <margin>Colossians 1:18.</margin> the head of the body; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things He might be the first; and it is a common rule that whatever is best and first in certain things is itself the rule and measure for all the others. Well, such a one is Christ / O, let Him then also be the Guide of our life and our conduct.

3. Because Christ not only gives us an example, but He also maintains, supports, and helps us through His gentleness, good pleasure, and His likeness toward us. Someone has very sweetly remarked that Christ’s holiness (which we must follow) is level, steady, irreproachable, and consistent with human society, without any dread of the leader, and without any examples of miraculous and strange deeds greater than those that could be

<column-break/>

followed by men. We are not commanded to follow a life whose account speaks of raptures in prayer, of withdrawals of the senses, of uncommon fasting to the weakening of our spirits, and to the making of our souls unfit for all works: No, no; but a life of righteousness, and temperance, and chastity, and godliness, and love, and devotion; such a life without which human society cannot exist. — And it is very noteworthy that, besides the ease of this imitation, there is still a power and working in the life of Christ; a merit and an obtaining in various actions of Christ's life, to work out our imitation of Him. <margin>Colossians 3:12, 13.</margin>

<margin>1 Peter 1:15, 16.</margin>
--- and as He who has called you is holy, so be you yourselves also holy in all your conduct, because it is written, *be holy, for I am holy.* But here some would object: how can we be holy just as Christ is holy? First, the matter is impossible; and second, if we could, then no Christ would be necessary. But I answer to the first: if the matter is correctly understood, it is not impossible; we are commanded that we shall

<column-break/>

be holy as Christ is holy—not in respect of equality in degree, as if our holiness must be of the same height as Christ’s holiness; but in respect of quality. Our holiness must be of the same substance and sincerity as Christ’s holiness was; for example, the Apostle <margin>Romans 13:9.</margin> says that we shall love our neighbor as ourselves. The meaning of the Apostle is not that we shall love our neighbor in the same degree <note>The author distinguishes between the 'nature' of love (sincerity) and the 'degree' of love (intensity).</note> as ourselves, for the Law permits certain steps in love, according to the degrees of relationship <margin>Galatians 6:10.</margin> in the things beloved: *let us do good to all men, but especially to the household of faith.* Love for a friend may, without reproach, be greater than love for a stranger; or the love for one’s wife or children can, without sin, be greater than the love for a friend. But nonetheless, in everything our love toward others must be of one and the same nature—indeed, as true, and active, and heartfelt, and sincere, and steadfast, as the love toward ourselves: We must love our neighbor as ourselves, that is, sincerely and without hypocrisy.

# Looking unto Jesus.

<columns>
...[Chri]st, going upward for the satisfaction of His Father; the second is the work of His Spirit and His grace, going downward toward the sanctification of His church. In the one, He has bestowed His righteousness upon us through imputation <term>imputation: the theological concept where Christ’s righteousness is legally credited to the believer</term>; in the other, He has crafted His image within us through renewal—and how! O my soul, do you wish to undo the purpose of Christ’s coming in the flesh, or do you wish to miss the end for which Christ came with regard to your best interest? O, may God forbid!

Again, consider the examples of the saints before you; if their holy ambition consisted in this—that they wished to be like Jesus—then follow them in this, for this is a holy desire for imitation. It is noteworthy how even the Heathens <note>The author refers to classical Greek and Roman philosophers as "Heathens."</note> taught themselves a rule that comes very close to this. Seneca’s advice 
<margin>Seneca, Epistle 2</margin>
was that every person should set before themselves the example of a certain wise man and virtuous person, such as Cato, Socrates, or another; and in deed undertake his life as a guide for all his actions. But is not the life of Jesus far more precious, and in an infinite way more worthy to be imitated? 

We read in the histories of a certain virgin, Cecilia <note>Saint Cecilia, a 2nd-century Roman martyr.</note>, who had accustomed herself to the contemplation of Christ in order to follow Him; and to that end, she always carried in her bosom some portions of the Gospel, which she had gathered together from all the Evangelists, and she always meditated or

<column-break/>

pondered upon them by day and by night. This work she took upon herself in such a cycle that she finally became perfect in it, and thus had Christ and the Gospel for her delight, not only in her breast, but also in the secret places of her heart. This was evident from her love for Christ, her trust in Christ, and her intimacy with Christ, as well as from her contempt for the world and all its glory for Christ’s sake. 

There is something similar in the Bride <note>A common allegorical name for the Soul or the Church in 17th-century divinity, drawn from the Song of Solomon.</note>, when she concludes of Christ: *He shall lie all night between my breasts*
<margin>Song of Solomon 1:13</margin>
as if she said: "He shall be as close to me as possible; my thoughts of Him (and consequently my imitation of Him) shall be constant and without ceasing, not only by day, but He shall even lie all night between my breasts." 

What, O my soul, has this been the practice of the saints? And do you wish to have no fellowship with them in this? O, God forbid! Let us therefore move and awaken our souls to this conformity: let us rouse, incite, spur on, kindle, and sharpen our wicked, slow, sleepy, and sluggish souls. Let us strengthen our faint, weak, slack, stumbling, dripping <note>original: "druppende" - likely meaning failing or leaking away like a guttering candle</note>, and powerless affections, desires, and efforts. Let us, with a doubled diligence, bind and encourage our regressing and negligent spirits to this duty of conformity...

### The Fourth Book. Part 2. Chapter 5. Section 9.

...not because of any imperfection in the object (especially in such an object as **Jesus Christ** is), but because it is not properly appropriated <note>In a religious context, "appropriated" means taking a spiritual truth and making it one's own through personal belief and application.</note>, and through meditation laid upon the heart, until it performs its work upon the same. It is true that the manner of this working can be secret and imperceptible; nonetheless, if we follow it, we shall feel it in the end. The beholding of Christ is a powerful beholding; a changing and recreating power flows out from Christ through looking upon Him. Can we indeed think on His humility and not be humble? Can we think on His gentleness and the kindness of the Spirit, and yet continue in our self-absorption, stubbornness, and fretfulness of Spirit? Can the proud, self-absorbed heart grasp a gentle and humble **Jesus**? No, no; the heart must be made suitable to the things that are to be grasped, otherwise it is impossible. Truly, if the sight is to be effective, there must be a correspondence between the heart and Christ. Sight even works upon the imagination in irrational creatures: when Laban’s sheep looked upon the speckled rods, their lambs were also like that <note>A reference to Genesis 30:37–39, where Jacob used a visual technique to influence the breeding of Laban’s livestock; the author uses this as an analogy for how what we "look at" shapes what we "produce" in our character.</note>. Now, if sight can work upon the imagination, and the imagination can work an actual change in nature, is then the eye of the soul (especially the eye of faith) not much stronger and more powerful? If I only

<column-break/>

write according to a model <note>original: "voorschrift," referring to a calligraphy practice sheet or a copybook used by students to learn handwriting</note>, in time I shall also write in that manner. If I seriously think on an excellent subject, an impression of it will remain in my soul. If I but read of the life and death of some exceptionally graced holy people, the same softens, restores, and changes my heart, and makes it conformed to them. Even so, and much more so is it in this matter; since the eye of faith works in that material which is in itself working and powerful, it must necessarily work more than if there were only a simple imitation and bare thought. Oh, let us then set the model of **Christ’s** life (as described before) before us, and let us look upon it with both eyes: with the eye of reason and with the eye of faith.

But how shall we keep the eye of our faith upon this blessed object until we perceive this conformity in ourselves? I answer: —

1. It may be that we are sometimes busy in our civic calling <note>One's daily work, business, or social duties</note>, and then is not the time; but when those things are done and the day begins to decline, let us then—along with our secret prayers—fall to this duty of looking unto Jesus through a true faith. Oh, what a blessed time this shall be!

DE The Sun of Righteousness <note>Sun of Righteousness: A title for Christ drawn from Malachi 4:2, representing His light and healing power.</note> having risen with healing, we shall now see it set in a red cloud. And in this part—just as in the preceding one—we must first present the object, and then instruct you how to look upon it.

The object is Jesus, having taken upon Himself the work of man's salvation <term>salvation: the deliverance from sin and its consequences, believed by Christians to be brought about by faith in Christ</term> during the time of His suffering: But in the whole treatment of this time, we shall regard it as if it were carried out consecutively in these few hours of His suffering and death.

<column-break/>

Just as this work of man’s salvation was great, so it is necessary for us to observe how each part of it was carried out at its proper time, even from eternity to eternity. Even the time of Christ’s suffering did not depend on any man’s will, although His enemies often sought to kill Him; as did Herod in His childhood years (Matthew 2:16); the Jews in His adult years, when they sometimes took up stones to stone Him (John 8:59); and at another time they wanted to throw Him off a steep mountain to break His neck <note>original: "den hals te breken," referring to the attempt on His life in Nazareth mentioned in Luke 4:29.</note>.

<margin>Exodus 12:2, 6.</margin>
the fourteenth day of the month **Abib** <note>Also known as Nisan, the first month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical year, occurring in Spring.</note>, or called **Nisan**: during the full Moon, in the evening, or "between two evenings" <note>This Hebrew idiom refers to the period between the sun's decline (around 3:00 PM) and its final setting.</note>: some believe that this month corresponds with our March, others with our April; we shall not examine this too closely, as it is not worth the effort: but I must nonetheless note this, that on the same day when the Lamb had to be slaughtered, our **Passover Lamb** also had to begin His suffering: and just as it was then the full Moon, so it indicates to us the **fullness of time** <term>fullness of time: the moment ordained by God as the perfect time for Christ's mission</term> which had now come; and just as it was in such a month that the light overcame the darkness, and all things begin to live and sprout again; so Christ by His suffering has driven away our darkness and death, and brought back to us the light and revival and a blessed sprouting of grace and glory; and just as it was slaughtered in the evening, or between two evenings; so Christ, the true Passover Lamb, had to be offered at nearly the same hour as the prefiguring Lamb was slaughtered.

To understand this, we should know that the Jews divided their full day into four parts: from six to nine, from nine to twelve, from twelve to three, and from three to six; this last part was considered the evening of the day: and

<column-break/>

the following three hours the evening of the night. Now, in this last part of the day, it was customary for the **Passover Lamb** to be slaughtered, and after it was slaughtered, some time was taken to prepare it entirely for the **Lord's Supper**; likewise Christ, in the fourth part of the day, at their ninth hour—that is, at three o'clock by our clock in the afternoon—between two evenings, crying out with a loud voice,
<margin>Matthew 27:50.</margin>
gave up His spirit.

Regarding the entire time of Christ's final suffering, I shall bring it down to somewhat less than a natural day; or if we may take the whole day before us, consisting of 24 hours, and beginning with the evening, following the beginning of the natural days of creation (of which it is said, there was
<margin>Genesis 1:5.</margin>
evening, and there was morning, the first day) in this cycle of time I shall note these particular actions.

2. Around eight in the evening, He washed His disciples' feet, and then leaning on the table, He pointed out **Judas**, who would betray Him, and this lasted until nine o'clock.

B. C.** of our Christianity (as **Bradford** <note>Likely referring to John Bradford (1510–1555), an English Reformer and martyr known for his writings on the "A.B.C." of Christian faith.</note> said) that we learn the lesson of taking our cross upon us, and following **Christ**. -># Looking unto Jesus.<-

You might say, "That is a hard word; who can bear to hear it?" It comes to my mind that when Jesus spoke with his Disciples about his suffering—that the same must be fulfilled in Jerusalem—that Peter took the liberty to advise his Master against it, <margin>Matthew 16:22.</margin> *Lord, be merciful to yourself; this shall not happen to you*; but Christ called him for that reason a **Satan**, judging that there is nothing that fights so much against the marks of God and Christ as to advise us against suffering.

There is still more than too much of Peter’s nature remaining among us. Oh, this doctrine of tribulations cannot be digested by the **Libertines** <note>Free-thinkers or those who believe grace exempts them from moral restraint.</note>, **Antinomians** <term>Antinomians<gloss>From the Greek 'anti' (against) and 'nomos' (law); those who believe that under the gospel of grace, the moral law is of no use or obligation.</gloss></term>, and others of such kind; and for this reason, I believe that our gatherings are so small compared to some of theirs. They who can break the yoke of obedience, and loosen the bonds of discipline, and preach an easy religion, and a Heaven on earth made of nothing but roses, and strew palm branches and clothes on the road, and give great freedom to live in sin, and unite eternity with these present pleasures—they have their schools full of Disciples. But those who preach of the **Cross**, and of suffering and tribulations, and of a strict and holy life, they have no other lot than their blessed Savior; that is, people think ill of them, they are abandoned, and they are spoken against.

Well, if Christ has then 

<column-break/>

led us along this way, while others remain at rest in **Sion** <note>Zion, here used to represent a place of false security or ease.</note>, let us follow him into the valley, and over the brook **Cedron** <note>The Brook Kidron.</note>.

Thus far we have considered Christ on the road, as well as his crossing over Cedron; we now proceed to the garden, into which he entered with his Disciples.

### Of the Garden into which Christ entered.

<margin>Matthew 26:36.</margin> Matthew writes of it thus: *Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane*, as a plot of land <note>original Greek: ὡς χωρίον</note>, which specifically signifies a field or a village, but more generally, a "place," just as we have translated it. Various mysteries are locked within this word, and I believe it happened not without reason that our Savior entered into a garden. For:

— 1. Because gardens are solitary places, the right places for meditation and prayer; to that end, we find that Christ was sometimes on a mountain, and sometimes also in a garden.

2. Because gardens are suitable places to rest and be still: Christ [having come] from preaching...

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 1. §. 3.

...having become renowned for wonders and works of grace within Jerusalem, he then departed to this garden. 3. Because the garden was the place of our fall, and therefore Christ chose a garden to begin the very greatest work of our redemption: in the first garden was the beginning of all evil, but in this garden was the beginning of the restoration of all evil; in the first garden, the first Adam was overwhelmed by Satan, but in this garden, the second Adam has conquered, and Satan himself is brought to nothing by him; in the first garden, sin was committed, and we became debtors to God through our sin, but in this garden, the sin was paid for by that costly and precious price of the blood of God: in the first garden, man was confounded <note>Original: *verbaest*, meaning stunned or terrified by the consequences of the act.</note> by the eating of the forbidden fruit, but in this garden, Christ himself in a wondrous way broke into a sweat, even a bloody sweat; in the first garden, death made its first entry into the world, but in this garden, life has entered, to restore us from death into life: in the first garden, Adam’s freedom to sin brought himself and us all into slavery, but Christ, being bound and fettered in this garden, has thereby freed us and brought us back to liberty. I could thus expand upon this further in regard to every circumstance, but this is the summary: in a garden, sin first took its beginning, but in this garden, first 

<column-break/>

the suffering began—that great and meritorious work of our Redemption. 
4. Christ specifically entered into this garden so that his enemies would find him more easily. <margin>John 18:2.</margin> The Evangelist tells us that this garden was a place into which our Savior often entered with his disciples, so that Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often gathered there with his disciples. It is certain, then, that he did not go there to hide himself, but much more to expose himself and, like a brave champion <note>Original: *kamp-vechter*, a combatant or gladiator appearing in the arena.</note>, to be the first to appear in the field and await his enemies. Thus it is revealed to the whole world how willing Christ was to meet his <margin>Isaiah 53:12.</margin> death. He has *poured out his soul unto death*, says <margin>Galatians 1:4.</margin> the Prophet: *he gave himself for our sins*, says the <margin>John 10:17, 18.</margin> Apostle: indeed, he himself told us, *Therefore my Father loves me, because I lay down my life: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself: I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.* But I shall not hold you at the gate; let us follow Christ into the garden, and behold his prayer and suffering there.

In the garden, we must first notice his prayer, and secondly his suffering.

I. He commits himself to that great means, which he himself, as the sovereign Physician of our souls, has commanded to all the world; he worships his Heavenly Father; he kneels down, and not that alone, but he falls flat upon the earth; he prays indeed as intensely as his distress was great, and yet with such a willing submission, as if the cup had been the most ordinary <note>Original: *middelmatigste*, meaning something of little consequence or average.</note> thing in the world. His prayer

<margin>Matt. 26:39.</margin>

reads thus: *My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will.* In this prayer, these particular things are to be noted: 1. the person whom he called upon, *My Father*. 2. the matter for which he prayed, *Let this cup pass from me*. 3. the condition of the prayer, *If it is possible*, and, *if you will*.

1. Concerning the person to whom he made his prayer, the same is his Father; just as Christ did not pray in his Divinity, but according to his humanity, so he never made his prayer to himself as God,

<column-break/>

but to his Father, the first person in the Godhead; for this reason, some have noted that the Father, saying, *This is my beloved Son*, does not speak to himself, but to the Son: so the Son, often saying, *My Father*, did not make his prayer to himself, but to the Father.

2. Regarding the matter of his prayer, *Let this cup pass from me*: some explain this thus; let this cup pass me by, oh that I might not drink it: But others in this way: let this cup pass from me; although I shall have to taste it, yet oh that I may not be visited by it for too long, or too slowly. The introduction to this explanation is given in the words of the Apostle,

<margin>
<note>Original Latin: "Quod dicit, transfer calicem istum a me, non hoc est, non adveniat mihi: nisi enim advenert, transit, sed sicut quod praeterit, nec intactum est, nec permanens: sic salvator leviter invadentem tentationem flagitat pelli. Sic. Dionys. Alexandr. Heb. 5. 7."</note>
When he says, "transfer this cup from me," it does not mean "let it not come to me"; for unless it comes, it cannot pass; but just as something that passes is neither untouched nor permanent, so the Savior asks for the temptation that attacks briefly to be driven away. Thus says Dionysius of Alexandria on Hebrews 5:7.
</margin>

Christ has, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications to him who could deliver him from death, with strong crying and tears, and he was heard because of his fear. <note>Hebrews 5:7.</note> How was he heard? Not by the removal of the cup, for he drank it entirely, but in respect to the slow damage or agony of the cup; for although it made him sweat drops of blood, although it caused him sadness and pain, and caused him to cry out, *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* although it made him fall asleep <note>A common scriptural euphemism for death.</note> and laid him dead in his grave, and sealed him there for some time; yet he was nevertheless immediately, within the time of forty hours...

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 1: §. 4.

Some even distinguish the guilt of sin / so that there is *reatus culpæ* <note>original Latin: "guilt of the fault"</note>, the guilt of the sin as sin / and this is the sin itself / being the true essence / the soul / the formal nature of the sin; they call it a foundational / or potential guilt; and there is *reatus pœnæ* <note>original Latin: "guilt of punishment"</note>, *reatus personæ* <note>original Latin: "guilt of the person"</note>, *reatus actualis* <note>original Latin: "actual guilt"</note>, the guilt or obligation to the punishment / the actual guilt / or the actual obli-

It is known to us all that sweat more resembles water than blood. ### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 1. Section 5. 503

<margin>Aristotle, Book 3 of the History of Animals, Chapter 19. <note>The original text cites Chapter 29, but this refers to Aristotle's observations on blood in Book 3, Chapter 19.</note> Augustine, City of God, Book 14, Chapter 24.</margin>
...clotted, thick, gathered, and curdled sweat; this bloody sweat did not come from Christ like a thin dew, but in great drops; they were drops, and indeed great drops of blood, coarse and thick drops. From this it is judged that it happened in a supernatural way; for although some might naturally be said to sweat blood, as Aristotle points out, and Augustine admits to having known a man who could sweat blood as often as he wished; in weak bodies, subtle and thin blood can indeed penetrate through the pores <note>original: "sweet-gaten," literally "sweat-holes."</note> of the skin like sweat. But that through these same pores thick, coarse, and great drops of blood would bleed out—that has never been, nor can it be, without a miracle. Some call them grains, others little balls of blood; it is certain that they were great drops, as large as if they had burst through his skin, only to be followed by the overflowing streams and rivers of his cross.

3. Here is yet another progression <note>original: "op-klimmingh," a rhetorical deepening of the description.</note>, since these great drops of blood did not merely drip; they flowed down. A stream flowed down as strongly as if it had bled from a completely mortal wound: they were *great drops of blood falling down to the ground*. Here is both greatness and quantity; there were great drops, and in such a multitude, so abundant, that having penetrated through his clothes and through everything, they bled down

<column-break/>

onto the earth. Now it was that his garment was dyed with crimson-red; that word of the Prophet, although spoken in another sense, may nevertheless in a certain respect be applied here: <margin>Isaiah 63:2.</margin> *Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the wine-press?* O, what a spectacle was here! His head and limbs were all bloody with sweat; this sweat poured down and covered his clothes, which appeared like a new firmament beset with stars, foretelling and bringing a great storm. Nor did it stop there, but fell down to the earth: O happy garden, to be watered with such tears of blood! How much better are these rivers than Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus—yes, better than all the waters of Israel, even than all those rivers that watered the Garden of Eden?

1. This points out to us the heavy burden of sin, under which Christ so groaned that he sweated and bled. When the first Adam committed the first sin, this was the punishment: <margin>Genesis 3:19.</margin> *In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread*; but now the second Adam <note>A theological title for Jesus, contrasting him with the biblical Adam.</note> has taken all the sins of all believers of the whole world upon himself; he did not only sweat from his face, but over his entire body. O, how disfigured must this face have been, standing thus full of drops—and those not drops of watery sweat, but of thick blood. We see in other men that when they are disturbed by fear and anxiety...

3. Regarding **Christ’s binding**, the Evangelists recount to us that the band, and the captain, and the servants of the Jews seized **Jesus** and bound him,
<margin>John 18:12</margin>
<term>ἔδησαν</term> <note>original Greek: "edēsan"; meaning they bound or tied.</note>; they bound his hands with cords; the prototype of this was *Samson*, whom *Delilah* bound with ropes; thus they also bound him with ropes and snares, wishing to say thereby that he would have to die, as it was not their custom to bind anyone with ropes or snares except those whom they had firmly intended to crucify.

Others also speak of certain circumstances of this binding: that they bound him with thick cords, and with such violence that they caused the blood to burst from his tender hands; it is certain that they

<column-break/>

lacked no malice, and now they also lacked no power, for the Lord had delivered himself into their hands. Binding is a proof of unworthiness: histories testify of King *Alexander*, that having been shot with an arrow, and it needing to be pulled out, his physicians judged that he must be bound, because the slightest movement (according to them) would be harmful to him; but he gave as an answer: *That no kings should be bound, since the royal power is always free and unbound.*
<margin>It is not fitting for a king to be bound, since the king's power is free and always intact. <note>original Latin: "Non decet vinciri regem, cum libera sit regis & semper salva potestas. Bern. serm. de pass."</note></margin>
And *David* in his lament for *Abner* said: *Did Abner then die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound, nor your feet put into bronze fetters.*

<margin>2 Samuel 3:33-34.</margin>
Foolish people and slaves were customarily bound, and likewise thieves; it is proper that those who open their hands to steal the goods of others should have their hands bound and made fast; but was our Savior also placed among the number of these? Oh yes! At that same hour *Jesus* spoke to the multitude:
<margin>Matthew 26:55.</margin>
*Have you come out as against a murderer, with swords and clubs, to capture me?*
<margin>Philippians 2:7.</margin>
He emptied himself, having taken the form of a servant: <note>The Dutch "vernietigt" literally means "annihilated" or "brought to nothing," reflecting the theological concept of kenosis or Christ's self-emptying.</note> O wondrous humiliation and emptying of *Christ*! He who was exceedingly righteous is regarded as a thief; he who was equal to God has become a slave; he who was stronger than *Samson*, and who [could snap] his cords from his arms...

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 1. §. 7.

<margin>Verse 75.</margin> Or he went out, and wept bitterly; the Rooster was the preacher, and the look of Jesus was the grace that made the preaching powerful. O, the loving-kindness of Christ! He looks back at the one who had forgotten Him; He awakens the memory of His servant to remember the words of his Master; He sends him outside to weep bitterly, so that He might thus graciously restore him to His former favor.

<margin>Application.</margin> Let us learn from this to have a modest and humble opinion of ourselves; indeed, let him <margin>1 Cor. 10:12.</margin> who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall! If Peter could first hesitate, then lie, then swear, and finally blaspheme and curse—O, then let <margin>Rom. 11:20.</margin> us not be high-minded, but fear. And should we also happen to fall as Peter did, let us nevertheless not despair like Judas, but let us trust firmly in the Lord in our conversion. When Christ looked upon Peter, he wept bitterly; notwithstanding that our sins are great, a look from Christ is nonetheless very powerful, and sufficient to make us melt into tears. O, let us not sink into despair, but look up to Him, so that He may look down upon us again. <margin>Pliny, Natural History.</margin> Plinius <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> tells us of certain rocks in Phrygia <note>An ancient region in what is now Turkey.</note> which, when shone upon by the Sun, give off drops of water as if they were weeping tears; "Peter" signifies a "rock," and

<column-break/>

as long as Peter remained in his sin of denying Christ, his heart was as hard as a rock; but when Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, looked upon him, his heart became soft and dropped tears without ceasing. So powerful is the sight of Christ; it changes the rocky stone into a <margin>Ps. 114:8.</margin> flood of water, and the flint-stone into a water-fountain. Finally, we must not deliberate too long over our conversion, but put it into practice at the first opportunity, taking it in hand and carrying it out; is there not a master of the Gospel here?

# The Fourth Book. 3rd Part. Chapter 1. § 7.

...the face of Christ / which in Heaven is so highly honored and worshipped / has been made so foul and ugly by their spit! Oh, that no other place could be thought of to receive and carry away their filth than the blessed Face of Jesus Christ!

<margin>Isaiah 50:6.</margin>
I did not hide my face (says Christ) from shame and spitting: I used no mask to protect my beauty <note>Original Dutch: "wit", literally "white," referring to his pure complexion or beauty</note>, although I was fairer than the children of men; I did not preserve my beauty from their ugly slime, but I set my face open and presented it as a target for them to cast their scornful spit upon.

2. They struck him with fists; we have previously noted that one of the servants struck Jesus with the palm of his hand, but now they have struck him with fists. Some note this distinction between <term>rhapisma <note>Original Greek: ῥάπισμα; a blow with the open hand</note></term> and <term>kolaphos <note>Original Greek: κόλαφος; a blow with the closed fist</note></term>; that one happens with an open hand, and the other with a closed fist. And thus they treated him at this time; they struck him with their fists, and so the blow was greater and hit harder. By this means, they caused his face to swell and become covered in lumps everywhere.

<margin>By the fists his whole head was a swelling, his face perhaps bruised and blue, and his teeth knocked out. <note>Original Latin: "Colaphis illi tuber totum caput, facies livida forte, & excussi dentes."</note></margin>
Someone has spoken of it thus: *By these blows of their fists his whole head was swollen, his face became black and blue, and his teeth were loosened so as to fall out of his jaws.*

<column-break/>

It is indeed likely that with their powerful blows they made him stagger and stumble back and forth, that they made his mouth, nose, and face bleed, and caused his eyes to start in his head from fear.

<margin>Mark 14:65</margin>
3. They covered his face: several reasons are given for this: 1. To strike him more boldly and shamelessly. 2. To have no object of pity in his face; it is held that even the sight of his wondrous beauty, being so miserably mistreated, would have softened the hardest heart under Heaven, and therefore they covered and blindfolded that moving and attractive face. 3. So as not to see their own filth in his face; although his beauty was outstanding, they had nevertheless so stained it with their beastly spit that they were revolted to look at him: it was a loathsome sight (someone says) and powerful enough to make anyone vomit who only looked at it.
