-># Looking unto Jesus.<-

To pass the difficult night, they took turns making fun of him; first one, and then another, gave him a blow to the jaw (we often call that a box on the ear) and being blindfolded, they commanded him to guess who had struck him. Some have considered these insults to be among the bitterest treatments of his suffering: for even in the greatest misery, there is nothing more miserable than being mocked by one’s enemies in the midst of it. This was then the lot of our Savior, that they used this spite for their pastime: with a wanton and playful malice <note>Original Dutch: "broodt-droncken," literally "bread-drunk," meaning insolent or reckless with plenty</note>, they further aggravated their injustice through this mockery, as if they had said, "Come now, you are Christ the Son of the living God, and therefore it is to be believed that you are omniscient, you know all things; tell us then, who is it that has struck you; we have blindfolded you, so that you cannot see us with the eyes of your body, let your Divinity then now guess, surmise, tell, and prophesy, who is he now, who last struck you? who gave you that blow?" O godlessness without example! Truly, if his patience had been anything less than infinite, then even these wickednesses would have been greater than his patience. But to apply this somewhat to ourselves.

Those cover his face, who so reluctantly and unwillingly confess their sins, who with ornate excuses belittle their weaknesses and imperfections. --- 4. Those insult and mock Christ, who mock and despise his messengers and servants; 
<margin>Luke 10:16</margin>
"he who rejects you, rejects me," says Christ. Oh, that we would lay these things to our hearts, and pay good heed and notice how we stand guilty of this sin, so that we may repent.

<margin>Revelation 4:4</margin>

But we shall leave these mysteries aside; **Herod's** intention was not so much to show his excellence or innocence, as his folly and simplicity; certainly he regarded him as nothing else than a fool, an ignoramus, a common, simple man. The **Philosophers** (says **Tertullian** <note>Early Christian author, c. 155–220 AD</note>) have depicted him as being dressed by **Herod** like a fool, with long donkey ears, whose fine nails were plucked off, and who had a book in his hand, etc.

-># Looking unto Jesus.<-

Wondrous madness! O those strange errors of men! In his life they judged that *Jesus* was a glutton, a <margin>Matt. 11:19</margin> wine-drinker, a friend of sinners; a blasphemer, a sorcerer, <margin>Mark 2:7</margin> and one who casts out devils through *Beelzebub* the prince <margin>Matt. 12:24</margin> of devils; yes, and one who himself <margin>John 8:48</margin> had the Devil. And now, before his death, he was bound like a thief; in the house of *Caiaphas* he was beaten like a haughty and bold rogue; before the Great Council <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial body in ancient Judea</note> he was accused of blasphemy; before *Pilate* he was brought as an evil-doer, a rioter, a deceiver, a rebel, as one who sought the kingdom; to *Herod* he was sent as a charlatan <note>original: "guychelaer," meaning a juggler or street performer who uses trickery</note> to show some tricks; and now, to conclude it all, he is held by *Herod* and his soldiers to be a fool, a know-nothing, a beast, not having any human understanding. But gently, *Herod*; is *Christ* a fool because he remains silent? And are you wise because of the multitude of your words and all your questions? *Solomon*, a much wiser man than *Herod*, is of another <margin>Prov. 10:19</margin> opinion: "In the multitude of words sin is not lacking; but he who restrains his lips is wise." And <margin>Prov. 17:27, 28</margin> again: "He who has knowledge spares his words, and a man of understanding is of a cool spirit; even a fool who remains silent shall be esteemed wise, and he who shuts his lips, intelligent." Oh, poor *Herod*, consider these words for once, and then tell me, who is the fool?

<column-break/>

What? You, who speak many words and ask about many things—which in due time shall increase your damnation—or *Christ Jesus*, who chose to remain entirely silent for the world's eternal salvation? *Paul* was of another spirit and of another judgment concerning *Jesus Christ*; in him was knowledge, but that is not yet all; in him was wisdom and knowledge, and even that is not yet all; in him were the treasures, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in him are hidden <margin>Coloss. 2:3</margin> all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; and even that is not yet all. In him is not only wisdom, but he is Wisdom itself (for that is his name and title in the book of *Proverbs*), and yet by *Herod* and his courtiers, he is regarded, dressed, and mocked as a truly simple man.

2. They sent him away; in this posture they sent him back again to *Pilate*, adding to all their previous mockery that he was now presented as an object of ridicule for the boys in the streets. *Herod* was not satisfied that he and his soldiers alone should mock him, but he sent him through the most public and magnificent streets of *Jerusalem* in his white garment, to be mocked by the people as well, to be spat upon by wicked men; and in this was fulfilled that which was foretold of *Christ*: <margin>Lam. 3:14</margin> "I have become a laughingstock to all my people."

Around nine o'clock (which the Jews call the third hour of the day) Christ was stripped, scourged, clothed with purple, and crowned with thorns: in this hour his suffering came upon him heavily: I must divide that into two parts, and speak of each in particular.

<margin>Matthew 27:26, 27.</margin>

# Looking unto Jesus

<columns>
...was naked) how ashamed and red in his face must Christ then have been, when he stood entirely naked in the Judgment Hall <note>The "Judgment Hall" refers to the Praetorium, the residence of the Roman governor.</note> before the eyes of the entire band or company of soldiers? 
<margin>Psalm 44:16</margin>
*My confusion is continually before me, and the shame of my face hath covered me*, said David in the person of Christ <note>The author views David’s lament in the Psalms as a prophetic first-person account of Christ’s own feelings.</note>. In Church history, it is recounted that two female martyrs and holy virgins (named Agnes and Barbara) were stripped entirely naked before their execution. It is said that God had compassion for their great shame and distress, and to cover their nakedness, He created a covering of light for them, bringing them thus to a quiet and desired death. But our Savior Christ—having chosen every kind of shame and contempt in order to reconcile His Father’s wrath through perfect suffering, and to sanctify all kinds of suffering and insults for us—willed to endure the shame of nakedness at the time of His scourging. Behold here a naked Christ, and behold therein Christ’s loving-kindness toward us; like the Good Samaritan, He has bound us up when we were left lying stripped, wounded, and half-dead. And so that we might be covered, He willingly suffered His own clothes to be pulled off Him; He took upon Himself the state of the sinning Adam and became naked, so that we might first 

<column-break/>

be clothed with righteousness, and then with immortality. Oh, what a glorious use we ourselves can make of Christ’s nakedness!

**2.** Pilate delivered Him to be scourged; some believe he did this for no other purpose than that the Jews, being satisfied and appeased by this pain, might hold themselves content and think their grievance was now sufficiently avenged, and thus cease desiring His death. That He was scourged is beyond doubt, for the Evangelists recount it: *Then Pilate took 
<margin>John 19:1.</margin>
Jesus and scourged Him*; and that Pilate may have delivered Him to be scourged on such an account is very probable, because after the scourging he brought Him out to the Jews, crying out: 
<margin>verse 6.</margin>
*I find no fault in him*; and before His scourging, he had said it even more explicitly: 
<margin>Luke 23:15, 16.</margin>
*Lo, nothing worthy of death is done unto him. I will therefore chastise him, and release him.* Added to this is the fact that, although it was a custom that those who were to be crucified had to be scourged first, nevertheless, if they 
<margin>Jerome, on Matthew, vol. 9.</margin>
were condemned to death <note>original: "Hierom," referring to St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate.</note>, their lashes were to be fewer; but if they were to be released, they had to be scourged with more lashes. And as Pilate attempted to preserve His life, they scourged Him beyond measure, even unto the point of death.

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 2. § 4.

1. On the shame. 2. On the pain.

<margin>Acts 22:25, 26</margin>
1. Regarding the shame: it was so great that the Romans exempted all their citizens from it. "Is it lawful for you," said Paul, "to scourge a man that is a Roman?" <note>In the New Testament, the Apostle Paul invoked his rights as a Roman citizen to avoid being flogged without a trial.</note> And when the centurion heard that, he went and told the chief captain, saying, "Take heed what thou doest: for this man is a Roman." The Romans regarded this as the most shameful punishment, which ought to belong only to thieves and slaves, and not to free-born or enfranchised Romans. Even the Jews themselves would not permit more than a certain number of lashes, so that a brother should not be held as contemptible in their eyes. <margin>Deut. 25:2, 3</margin> "If the wicked man be worthy to be beaten, the judge shall cause him to lie down... forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee." 
Scourging is such an unworthy manner of punishment that usually only children, slaves, and rogues are punished with it—especially when they are struck with more than forty lashes. <margin>2 Cor. 11:24</margin> Having been treated thus, Paul tells us that from the Jews he five times received "forty stripes save one." <note>original: "veertigh slagen min een"</note> Theophylactus <note>A 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> says that they did not want to exceed that number so that Paul would not be physically ruined or made unfit for any public service 

<column-break/>

after that time; and hoping that they might yet win him back, they did not want to brand him with such a mark of permanent shame. O, if then a single lash above forty was considered so shameful among the Jews, what shame, what dishonor was this, when so many welts—hundreds and thousands of lashes (as some count them)—were given to Jesus Christ? And yet our Lord did not hesitate to suffer such things for us; He bore in His body those wounds and blows that we had deserved with our sins.

2. Concerning the pain: this kind of punishment was not only shameful but also terrifying. No sooner had the soldiers received their orders than they burdened and weighted Him with such bloody blows, as if He had been the greatest evildoer and the most wretched slave in the world. Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century church historian.</note> calls these scourgers <margin>Niceph. Book 1, Ch. 3</margin> "bloody executioners" who, through their fierce scourging, had caused many a man to die under their hands. -># Looking unto Jesus.<-

"...two others scourged him with ropes or scourging cords, braided and knotted like a farmer’s whip; and when those were also weary, two others scourged the very skin off him with iron wire or small iron chains; and so they continued, until with alternating and succeeding turns they gave blow upon blow, and wound upon wound—the last upon the first, and the new upon the old—so that he was everywhere covered in clotted blood."

<margin>Isaiah 53:5</margin> The Scripture tells us that he was wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. He was wounded, bruised, punished, and scourged with blows. If you wish to know with how many blows? Some count them according to the number of the soldiers: six hundred and sixty, or a thousand blows. Others count them according to the number of bones that are joined together in a human body—which the anatomists <note>original: "ontleders." The text reflects historical anatomical belief; the author notes a count of 260 bones, whereas modern anatomy identifies 206 in an adult.</note> say are two hundred and sixty—and Christ, having received three blows for every bone according to the threefold manner of his scourging, the total rises to seven hundred and eighty blows. Others count as many as five thousand and forty, beyond which the Jews were commanded they must not proceed.

—And it is the truth, if the entire company of soldiers scourged Christ (as some understand it), then I cannot see it otherwise

<column-break/>

than that his blows may well have been more than these. When the son of the Israelite woman <margin>Leviticus 24:14</margin> had blasphemed God, the Lord said to Moses: *Bring the curser out beyond the camp, and let all who heard him lay their hands upon his head, and then let the whole congregation stone him.* Now, Christ had said before the entire company that he was the Son of God, which they called blasphemy; and why then (according to this law) should they not all have been allowed to lay their hands on him and attack him? And if not with stones (which was now changed to scourging), then surely with rods, scourging cords, and small chains?

I will not dispute the number of his blows; but this is certain, that the soldiers executed their charge with power and with their hard hands. They tore his flesh so that the pillar and the floor were purple-red with excessive blood; and if we may believe Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a medieval mystic whose writings on the physical suffering of Jesus were very popular in the 17th century.</note>, "they struck his back with their scourges and made long furrows, and afterward they turned his back toward the pillar and scourged his belly and chest so long that no part was left free, from his head to his feet." A scourging that is enough to kill a man, and which would also have killed him, had he not been preserved by his Divinity, in order to [undergo] yet a shame—

<margin>The Use</margin> We can read here a lesson of God's infinite love in Christ toward us poor <term>Gentiles<note>original: "Heydenen." Historically used here to refer to all non-Jewish peoples whom the author believes were brought into God's favor through Christ.</note></term>; he was scourged for this reason, that he might unite us with himself, and never again reject or cut us off. We read of a certain law in Moses, that if a man, having taken a wife, should then hate her, and lay a charge of misconduct against her, and wrongly give her an evil name, <margin>Deuteronomy 22:18, 19.</margin> then the elders of that city should take that man and chastise him—she should then be his wife, and he may not let her go all his days. In this ceremony lies a great mystery, for that man (some say) was Christ, who through his incarnation had betrothed himself to the Church of the Gentiles; but he seemed to hate her, and to provide cause for gossip against her, and to bring an evil name upon her, <margin>Matthew 10:5.</margin> as when he said, *Go not into the way of the Gentiles, nor enter into any city of the Samaritans;* <margin>Matthew 15:26.</margin> and *It is not fitting to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.* And now he is accused before the Elders; now he is scourged and chastised, and charged by his Father to take her as his wife, and not to let her go all his days. I know well that there is a great disparity in this mystery, for Christ was not scourged because he had called the church an adulteress

<column-break/>

who in truth was chaste; but he was scourged in order to present the Church to his Father as a pure Virgin, she who in truth was adulterous. Oh, he has loved the <term>Congregation<note>original: "Gemeynte." This refers to the collective body of believers or the Church.</note></term>, and has given himself up for her. —— <margin>Ephesians 5:25, 27.</margin> *that he might present her to himself in glory, a Congregation that has no spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, but that she should be holy and blameless;* this was the meaning of Christ's scourging. <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> *The punishment that brings us peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed.*

Come then and let us learn to read this <term>love-letter<note>original: "minne-brief." A poetic term used in 17th-century Dutch divinity to describe the Gospel or Christ's wounds as a message of love from God to humanity.</note></term> sent from Heaven in bloody letters. Christ, who clothes the lilies of the field, is scourged; Christ is bound hand and foot; his hands that multiply the loaves, and his feet that were weary from seeking the wandering sheep. <margin>Isaiah 1:6.</margin> Christ is scourged all over, because we were all over full of wounds, and gashes, and swollen sores; and there was no means to heal our wounds except through his wounds, our bruises through his bruises, our sores through his sores. ### §. 6.
### Of Christ’s Crucifixion and its Circumstances.

Around eleven they made themselves ready in all haste for the execution; in the course of this hour, these various points are for us to note: 1. Their stripping off of his robe, and re-clothing him in his own

<column-break/>

clothes. 2. His leading away from Gabbatha <note>The Hebrew name for the stone pavement where Pilate sat in judgment</note> to Golgotha. 3. His carrying of the cross with Simon, who helped carry it after him. 4. His consolation to the women who followed him weeping as he went. 5. How they gave him vinegar mixed with gall to drink. 6. How they crucified him, or fastened him to the cross, upon which he died.

<margin>Matthew 27:31</margin>
1. The Evangelists repeat to us: *they took the robe off him, and put his own clothes on him.* Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> has noted that they took off the robe, but they did not take off the crown of thorns; they constantly observed whatever could serve their own advantage <note>Likely referring to the mockery or the preservation of the soldiers' property</note>, but nothing at all for the relief or mercy of the sorrowful Son of Man. It is held that this small task could not have been done without great pain: after his cruel scourging, his blood had congealed and thereby stuck to his purple robe, so that in the stripping off of the robe and the putting on of his own clothes, it could have been nothing other than a renewal of his wounds.

<margin>Matthew 27:31</margin>
2. *They led him away.* Some say that they threw a rope or chain around his neck, with which they led him out of the city toward Mount Calvary, and that all along the way a great multitude of people watched for him, and a herald went before him

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 2. §. 6.

...the principal purpose is to glorify God, and to preserve my lineage with all faithfulness, and I elevate these two purposes above all worldly advantages, whatever they may be?

Oh, what a blessed reformation would then be among us! And if this is not the case, what are you other than so many Pilates? For if you are merely threatened in a verdict, you would rather condemn Christ than yourself for fear of enmity against the Emperor <note>Referring to the biblical scene where the crowd warns Pilate that releasing Jesus would make him no "friend of Caesar."</note>; and your cry will be such: "Let him be crucified, and let me be exalted."

Much more could still be said, but the bell strikes again; Pilate has now risen, the court has adjourned, and Jesus is handed over into the hands of the Jews to be executed. How that proceeded, we shall speak of in the next hour; may God only prepare your hearts to listen attentively and to earnestly reflect upon what Jesus, the great Savior of the world, has suffered for you.

### §. 6.

->Concerning Christ’s crucifixion and its<-
->circumstances.<-

Around eleven o’clock they made their preparations for the execution in great haste; in the course of this hour, we are to observe these several parts: 1. Their stripping off his robe and re-clothing him in his own

<column-break/>

clothes. 2. Their leading him away from Gabbatha to Golgotha <note>Gabbatha is the Aramaic name for the "Stone Pavement" where Pilate judged; Golgotha is "the place of the skull" where the crucifixion occurred.</note>. 3. His carrying of the cross with Simon <note>The text refers to "Simeon," commonly known as Simon of Cyrene.</note>, who helped him carry it. 4. His comforting of the women who followed him weeping as he went hence. 5. How they gave him vinegar mixed with gall to drink. 6. How they crucified him, or fastened him to the cross, on which he died.

<margin>Matthew 27:31.</margin>
1. The Evangelists tell us that they took off the mantle and put his own clothes on him. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> noted that they took off the mantle, but they did not take off the crown of thorns. That which could serve to their advantage <note>Meaning, to further mock or humiliate him.</note>, they constantly observed, but they did nothing at all for the mitigation or pity of the sorrowful Son of Man. It is believed that this small task could not have been done without great pain: after his second scourging, his blood had congealed and by this means caked onto his purple mantle; thus, in the stripping off of the robe and in the putting on of his own clothes, it could be nothing other than a renewal of his wounds.

<margin>Matthew 27:31.</margin>
2. They led him away. Some say that they threw a rope or chain around his neck, with which they led him out of the city to Mount Calvary, and that all along the way a great multitude of people looked out for him, and a herald went before him...

# Looking Unto Jesus.

...gone forth, proclaiming before all the hearers the cause of his death; namely that *Jesus of Nazareth* was a deceiver, a blasphemer, a sorcerer <note>original: "swarte-konstenaer," literally a practitioner of the black arts</note>, a false teacher, saying of himself that he is the *Messiah*, a *King of Israel*, and the *Son of God*.
<margin>John 19:17</margin>
3. He carried his cross. So John has related: before it carried him, he first had to carry it; and thus they made their double cry true, "crucify him, crucify him": first they crucified him with it as with a burden, and thereafter they crucified him with it as with a cross; these shoulders that before were so unmercifully beaten with rods are now again tormented with the heavy burden of the cross. Like a true *Isaac* <note>In the Book of Genesis, Isaac carried the wood for his own sacrifice upon his shoulders</note> he carried the wood for the sacrifice of himself; or like *Uriah* <note>Uriah the Hittite unknowingly carried the letter from King David that commanded his own death on the battlefield</note>, he carried with him the actual tool of his sorrowful death. O the cruelty of this dealing! they had hardly left him so much blood or strength that he could carry himself, and must he now still carry his heavy cross? yes, until he fainted and sank down, so long he had to carry it, and he would have had to carry it even longer, if they had not feared that he would have died with less shame and pain than they had intended; and to prevent that, they forced a
<margin>Matt. 27:32. Mark 15:21</margin>
*Simon of Cyrene* to carry his cross after him. How faithfully they can here again

<column-break/>

swallow a camel and strain out a gnat? The cross was a death sentence used by the Romans, and thus an object of their abominations; therefore they themselves did not want to touch this tree of shame, so as not to defile themselves. But to touch the anointed of the Lord, to crucify the Lord of glory—of that they made no difficulty at all. But why did another have to carry this cross, if not to lay this duty upon man: that we must come into the fellowship of the sufferings of *Christ*? If any man
<margin>Matt. 16:24.</margin>
*will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.* — and
<margin>1 Pet. 2:21</margin>
*Christ has suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow his footsteps.*
4. He comforted the women who followed him weeping as he went along. And
<margin>Luke 23:27, 28.</margin>
a great multitude of people and women followed him, who also wept and bewailed him; but *Jesus* turning to them, said, *You daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves, and over your children.* In the midst of his misery he did not forget mercy: in the midst of all their torments and loud outcries of ignominy, of blasphemy, of mockery, he can hear the weeping of his following friends, and forgets all his own suffering to comfort them: "do not weep over me." He had more compassion for the women who [followed] him weeping

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 2. Section 6.

...weeping followed; yet with himself thus torn apart, and staggering along the way, fainting and bleeding almost unto death, he felt the tears that ran from their eyes more than all the blood that bled from his own veins. We have heard above that he did not deign to give a single word to Pilate, who threatened him, nor to Herod, who entreated him; yet, without being requested, how mercifully did he turn his holy, bleeding face toward these weeping women, honoring them with his sight and also with words, both of compassion and of comfort: *You daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but for yourselves.* But note that he did not turn his face toward them until he heard them weeping; nor should we think that we shall ever see his face in glory, unless we first bathe our eyes in repentance <term>boet-veerdigheyt: a 17th-century term for "penitence," implying not just regret but a transformative sorrow for sin</term>.

<margin>Psalm 126:5, 6.</margin>
It is a wonder to me that anyone in our age would disparage tears, repentance, sorrow, and the brokenness of the heart; how many saints do we find in both the Old and New Testament who have refuted this proud sentiment with their deeds? The promise tells us that *those who sow in tears shall reap in joy*; he who follows Christ, *going forth and weeping, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.*

But what does this mean, *weep*

<column-break/>

*not for me?* Are we not permitted to weep over Christ’s death?
<margin>Deuteronomy 34:8.</margin>
Do we not find in the Scripture that all the people wept for the death of Moses?
<margin>Acts 8:2.</margin>
That the entire congregation wept for the death of Stephen? That the women lamented the death of Dorcas? And if all the works of Christ are instructions for us (I do not mean his miracles, nor his works of merit, but his works of love), did not Christ himself weep over Lazarus and over Jerusalem? Indeed, did he not weep a downpour of blood here as he went along the way? and should we not be allowed to let a tear fall over all these red puddles of his? ♃ What is the meaning of: *weep not for me, but weep for yourselves?*

I answer that these words were spoken not absolutely, but by way of comparison. Christ did not simply forbid us to weep for our friends; but much more, he desires that we change our worldly sorrow into a Divine concern over sin as sin. Christ has herein directed the women to the true cause and subject of all their concern, which is their sins; and thus we have cause enough to weep. Oh! our sins were the causes of Christ’s suffering; and in this regard, oh, that our heads were water, and our eyes fountains of tears! <note>original: "sprinck-aders," literally spring-veins or fountain-heads, a reference to Jeremiah 9:1</note> Oh, that our tears were as our food and drink! Oh, that we, with David, made tears our bread, and that the Lord would [give] us abundant tears...

<meta>The catchword "wilde" (would) indicates the sentence continues on the next page, likely asking God to grant abundant tears.</meta>

# Looking unto Jesus.

...would give to drink! O, that the Lord would strike (as he did of old at Rephidim <note>A site mentioned in the Book of Exodus where Moses struck a rock to bring forth water for the Israelites.</note>) the rock-stone of our hearts with the rod of sincere repentance, so that water might spring forth! O, that we would thus mourn over Jesus, whom we have pierced, and would bitterly wail for him, as one bitterly wails for a firstborn!
<margin>Zechariah 12:10.</margin>

<margin>Matthew 27:34.</margin>
5. No sooner had he come to the place of execution than they gave him vinegar to drink mixed with gall. That they gave him something to drink was a proof of their courtesy; this was a custom among Jews and Gentiles, that they always gave the condemned wine to drink:
<margin>Proverbs 31:6.</margin>
*Give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those who are bitterly grieved in soul.* But that they gave him vinegar mixed with gall to drink was a proof of their cruelty and malice.
<margin>Theophylact on Mark.</margin>
Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107), a prominent Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> says plainly that vinegar mixed with gall is poisonous and deadly; and therefore, when Christ had tasted it, he would not drink, preferring rather the death of the cross, to which he was appointed by his Father, over any poisonous death.

<margin>Application.</margin>
Ah brothers, are we not inclined to have evil thoughts of the Jews because they gave Christ such a bitter drink at this time of his death? And yet, how little do we consider that when we sin, we do the very same thing.

<column-break/>

<margin>Deuteronomy 32:32, 33.</margin>
See how God himself compared the sins of the Jews to poison: *for their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and from the fields of Gomorrah; their grapes are poisonous grapes, they have bitter berries; their wine is the fiery venom of dragons, and the cruel poison of asps.* In this "looking unto Jesus," we must certainly think as poorly of ourselves as of the Jews; for as often as we sin against God, we do nothing other than mix a hot poison and bring it to Jesus Christ to drink.

<margin>Matthew 27:35.</margin>
6. They crucified him—that is, they fastened him to the cross and then set it upright. There is disagreement among the learned whether Christ was fastened to the cross before it was raised, or while it still lay on the ground. I shall not stir up these delicate matters too much, yet it is more likely that he was fastened to it while it still lay on the ground, and afterward
<margin>John 3:14.</margin>
*just as Moses lifted up a serpent in the wilderness, so also must the Son of Man be lifted up.* We may here express the manner of their doing and of his suffering, as a certain learned brother <note>Likely referring to Joseph Hall (1574–1656), an English bishop and devotional writer whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> has done for us:
<margin>Hall's Contemplations on Christ’s Passion.</margin>
Now those barbaric, cruel thief-leaders <term>dief-leyders: a term for the officers or executioners who led criminals to their death</term> have come and begun to loosen his hands; but how? Alas, it was not for the sake of the slightest freedom, but for those worse bonds of the nails; then they stripped off his clothes which were completely stuck to him, and with them, without a doubt, no small part of his torn skin and flesh,

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 2. Section 6.

...as if it were not enough to crucify him as a thief, but they must also fill <note>The original Dutch *vullen* means "to fill" or "to stuff," likely referring to the bitter drink offered previously or perhaps a typo for "loading" him like a beast of burden.</note> him like a beast; furthermore, they stretched him out like a second Isaac upon his own burden, the cross, in order to take the measure of the holes; and although the imprint of his blood had given them his length, how harshly did they nevertheless stretch him out longer than he actually was, in order thereby to crucify and torment him at once? That he was thus stretched and tormented upon his cross, David gave more than probable indication: *I could count all my bones*; and again, *all my bones have separated from one another*; which, how could it have happened otherwise than by such a violent stretching and pulling? Whereby it seems that they made of him a living dissection <note>Original: *ontledinge*, meaning an anatomical study or autopsy performed on a living subject.</note>; nor was it in the least sensitive parts of his body where they drove in their large nails, from which his whole heavy body had to hang; but in the hands and feet, the most sinewy <note>Original: *zenuwachtighste*, referring to the concentration of nerves and tendons in the extremities.</note>, and consequently above all others the most sensitive fleshy parts; and how roughly and painfully they dealt with him in this is also apparent from the saying of David: *they have pierced my hands and my feet*, they have made wide holes as if with a spade, as if they had dug in a ditch. We have the unseemly and uncommon size of these nails from venerable antiquity; of Constantine the Great, it is said that he had both a helmet and a bridle made from them.

<column-break/>

...How could I write, so that my tears would not wash away that which I write, since no other has been so ill-treated as he, who has wiped out the handwriting of requirements <note>Original: *handt-schrift der insettingen*, a biblical term referring to the record of debt or legal demands against humanity.</note> that was against me?

# Looking unto Jesus.

...although [he] does not speak of the crucifixion, he has nonetheless included it under the general category of hanging on the tree; and some understand that Moses, speaking of the curse <note>Moses refers to the "curse of God" on anyone hung on a tree in Deuteronomy 21:23.</note>, foresaw what manner of death the Savior would die.

2. Concerning the pain, it was a painful death, as appears in various ways: 1. His legs and hands were violently stretched and pulled out to the place where they were fastened, and there they were pierced through with nails. 2. By this means, he was deprived of the use of both his hands and feet, and so he was forced to hang motionless on the cross, having no power to turn himself anywhere for relief. 3. The longer he lived, the more he also endured, for by the weight of his body his wounds were opened and enlarged further, his veins and sinews were torn and pulled apart, and his blood continually flowed out more and more. 4. He died limb by limb (so to speak) and not all at once; the cross was a slow death, having held him for a long time on the rack <note>The author uses the term *pijn-banck*, comparing the cross to a judicial torture device.</note>; there were three whole hours between Christ's hanging and his passing, and it would have lasted even longer if he had not willingly and voluntarily given up the spirit. It is recounted that the Apostle Andrew hung on the cross for two whole days before he died, and just as 

<column-break/>

long Christ might also have lived thereon, if God had not in a supernatural way increased his pain to greater degrees.

I may add here, as surpassing all this, the pain of his soul while he hung on the cross; for there Christ also had his anxieties and soul-struggles. <margin>Acts 2:24</margin> These were those <term>pains of death</term> <note>original Greek: *ōdinas thanatou*</note>, those pains or sorrows of death from which Peter tells us Christ was released. The word <term>pains</term> <note>original Greek: *ōdinas*</note> properly signifies the birth-pangs of a woman who is in labor; such were also the pains of Jesus Christ in his death. <margin>Isaiah 53:11</margin> The Prophet called it the labor of his soul; <margin>Psalm 116:3</margin> and the Psalmist called it the terrors of hell: *The bonds of death had encompassed me, and the terrors of hell had struck me.* The anxieties or snares of death had encompassed his body, and the terrors of hell had struck his soul. And these forced from him that mournful complaint: <margin>Matthew 27:46</margin> *My God, My God, why have you forsaken me?* He complained of that which felt much more grievous to him than ten thousand deaths: *My God, my God, why have you taken away your usual presence, and left my soul as if in the terrors of hell?*

### The Fourth Book, Part 3, Chapter 2, Section 7.

...the arched back, the torn cheeks, the pierced hands and feet, and then consider that my sins are the cause of all this: it seems to me I need no other arguments to be struck with terror by them of my own accord! Oh Christians! Would your heart not rise up against one who murdered your father, mother, brother, wife, husband, the dearest friends in the whole world? Oh, how then ought your hearts and souls to rise up against sin? Truly your sins have murdered Christ; they have killed him who is better than all friends, who is a thousand and a thousand times dearer than your father, mother, wife, child, or whoever they may be; it seems to me that a single thought of this ought to be enough to make you say <margin>Job 42:6</margin> with Job, *I loathe myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.* Oh, what is the cross on Christ's back? My sins. Oh, what is the crown on Christ's head? My sins. Oh, what is the nail in Christ's right hand, and the other in his left hand? My sins. Oh, what is the spear in Christ's side? My sins. Oh, what are these nails and wounds in Christ's feet? My sins. With the spiritual eye, I see no other instrument of torture <note>original: *werck-tuygh*; literally "work-tools," referring to the implements used for execution.</note> that torments Christ; no other Pilate, Herod, Annas, or Caiaphas who condemn Christ; no other soldiers, servants, Jews or Heathens <note>original: *Heydenen*; here referring to the Romans and other non-Jewish participants in the execution.</note> bringing Christ to execution, but sin alone; my sins, my sins, my sins!

<column-break/>

2. Let us comfort ourselves with the end <note>The author uses "end" in the sense of the ultimate purpose or final goal (*finis* in Latin).</note> and aim of Christ's death; <margin>John 3:14, 15</margin> *As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.* The purpose of Christ's crucifixion is the reason why it occurred; and therefore the purpose must be noted as well as the deserving cause; without this observation, the beholding of Christ's death, or the contemplation of the narrative of Christ's suffering, can be nothing other than entirely fruitless; <margin>John 12:32</margin> but what was the purpose? Christ is lifted up, so that he might draw all <note>The Dutch text implies "all things" or "all people."</note> to himself. <margin>1 Peter 2:24</margin> Christ hung upon the wood, so that he might bear our sins on the wood: this was the design that God, with an eternal purpose, had in view in the crucifixion of Christ, and so our faith must take it up; truly our comfort depends upon this; the intention, the mark, and the aim of Christ in his suffering is that pleasant news <note>The author refers to the "glad tidings" or the core message of the Gospel.</note> and the true spirit of the Gospel. Oh, keep this in memory! Christ is crucified, and why? *That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.*

We are now at the height of Christ's suffering, and the Sun is now at its midday, or its highest ascent; I shall no longer count the hours; for from <margin>Matthew 27:45</margin> the sixth hour until the ninth hour (that is, from twelve until three in the afternoon), there was—

# Looking unto Jesus

...darkness over the whole earth. But of this and of what follows, we shall speak in the next section.

### §. 7.
### Regarding what followed Christ's Crucifixion.

I shall handle the following matters briefly. As thus: —
1. Around twelve o’clock, when the sun usually shines at its brightest, it began to grow dark. This darkness was so great that it spread over the entire Jewish land—some even believe over the whole world, as we translate it <margin>Luke 23:44</margin> in Luke: *and there was darkness over the whole earth.* Many Heathens <note>original: *Heydenen*; meaning non-Jewish people, particularly the Romans and Greeks.</note>, besides the Jews, noted this as a great miracle. Dionysius <margin>Suidas, in the life of St. Dionysius.</margin> the Areopagite <note>A judge of the Athenian Areopagus who, according to tradition, witnessed the eclipse in Egypt and was later converted by St. Paul.</note> (as Suidas relates) could say upon its first appearance, *“Either the world is at an end, or the God of nature is in suffering.”* This very darkness was the cause for that altar erected <margin>Acts 17:23.</margin> at Athens and dedicated to the "Unknown God." Amos prophesied this: <margin>Amos 8:9.</margin> *“And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord God, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.”*
The cause of this darkness is explained differently by various writers. Some believe that the Sun, through Divine <margin>Jerome on Matthew 27.</margin> power, withdrew and held back its rays. Others

<column-break/>

say that the darkness was <margin>Origen, tractate 35 on Matthew.</margin> caused by certain thick clouds that arose in the air in a miraculous way and spread across the entire earth. Others judge <margin>Dionysius, epistle 7 to Polycarp.</margin> that this darkness came through a miraculous positioning of the Moon, which was full at that time, but by a miracle placed itself between the earth and the Sun <note>A solar eclipse is naturally impossible during a full moon (Passover), hence the author emphasizes this as a supernatural event.</note>. But whatever the cause may have been, it lasted for the duration of three hours, as dark as the darkest winter nights.
2. Around three o’clock (which the Jews called the ninth hour), the Sun began to regain its light, and Jesus cried <margin>Matthew 27:46.</margin> with a loud voice, *Eli, Eli, lama Sabachtani*, which is, *My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?* — And after this, so that the <margin>John 19:28, 30.</margin> Scripture might be fulfilled, he said, *“I thirst.”* — And when he had taken the vinegar, he said, *“It is finished.”* — And at last, <margin>Luke 23:46.</margin> crying with a loud voice, he said, *“Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit”*; and having said that, he gave up the ghost. I cannot linger now upon the seven words that Christ spoke on the cross; fine words were always pleasant, but never more pleasant than at this time. We find in no human books or writings, in no annual chronicles or registers of men, such suffering, nor such words as these last words and wounds were—this speaking and suffering of Jesus.

**Christ.** — And having said this, he gave up the ghost <note>original: *geest*; meaning his spirit or breath of life</note>. Or as John relates it, bowing his head, he gave up the ghost: he did not bow his head because he was already dead, but first he bowed, and after that he died. The meaning is that he died willingly, without compulsion; joyfully, without murmuring. What a wonder is this? Life itself gives up its life, and death itself dies through his death; Jesus Christ, who is the master-craftsman of life, the God of life, has laid down his life for us, and death itself lies forever firmly nailed to that bloody cross in the place of Jesus Christ. And now we may remember that he was before the gates of Paradise, calling out with his last words that they should be opened, so that the King of Glory might enter therein.

---

Behold him entering into the Garden of Gethsemane; in a Garden Adam had sinned, and in this Garden Christ had to suffer, so that the same place which had been the nest to hatch sin would now be the childbed <note>The author uses "kraem-bedde" (birthing bed) to contrast the "nest" of sin with the "birth" of grace.</note> of grace and loving-kindness; he had no sooner entered this Garden than he began to be greatly distressed; all his inward powers and passions were in a conflict. Meditate, O my soul, how suddenly a strange fear came upon him: never was a man so afraid of the pains of hell as Christ (standing in our place) was for his Father’s wrath: fear is always powerful to dismay a person, and never has any man been able to so perfectly understand the cause of fear as Jesus Christ; and he was not only afraid, but also very sorrowful;
> My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.

His sorrow was consuming and

<column-break/>

deadly; it caused his soul to melt away bit by bit, just as wax melts through the heat; it remained with him until his last gasp, his heart was like burning wax during the entire time of his suffering, and

<margin>Psalm 22:15</margin>
finally it melted in the midst of his bowels.

<margin>Mark 14:33</margin>
Nor did he only become anxious and sorrowful, but he also began to be greatly amazed <note>The original "verbaeſt" implies a state of being stunned or terrified by a great sight.</note>; this signifies a general standstill of all the powers of the soul, each in its particular work; we commonly call it a consternation; it is like a clockwork that is hindered in its movement for a time by one hand or another being laid upon it; or if it was not a total standstill, it was at least an amazement, such a movement of the mind by which he was, for the present, made unable to grasp anything else in his mind but the terrible feeling of the wrath of God.

O, what a struggle this was! O, what a wrestling suffering mixed with sorrow! What distressing and dismaying movements occurred under the sight and feeling of exceeding danger in this struggle?

# The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3. Section 3.

Nothing so greatly cools and refreshes a repentant, sorrowful, and thirsty sinner as the blood of Jesus Christ. It was this that caused a certain poor woman to cry out so earnestly: "I have a husband, and children, and various other desirable things, but I would willingly give them all, and all the goods I shall ever see in this world and the world to come, so that my poor thirsty soul may be refreshed with that precious blood of the Lord Jesus Christ."

But what is there in Christ’s blood or death that is so desirable? I answer:

<margin>Hebrews 1:3</margin>
1. In it is Christ’s **Person** / He who is the God-man / and man-God / the radiance of His Father’s glory, and the express image of His person; it is He who has died. Every drop of His blood was not only the blood of an innocent man / but of one who was as much God as man.
<margin>Acts 20:28</margin>
*God has purchased the Church through His own blood*; now, surely everything that is in God is most desirable.

2. In it is a **worth**, or price; when Christ is considered under the name of a sacrifice, He is of an infinite worth; now, this sacrifice (says the Apostle) He has offered.
<margin>Hebrews 9:28</margin>
Hebrews 9:28. He offered it / not in Heaven / as the <term>Socinians</term> <note>A group of non-trinitarian Christians who denied the pre-existence of Christ and argued His sacrifice was purely exemplary or completed in heaven.</note> claim / by presenting Himself before His Father / but on earth / namely / in His suffering on the cross. No riches, neither in Heaven nor on earth, were powerful enough to redeem a single soul except for this; and therefore

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Peter 1:18, 19</margin>
the Apostle has set this against all perishable things / such as silver and gold, which are things held in such high regard by worldly men; *You were not redeemed by perishable things, such as silver or gold — but by the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.*

<margin>Ephesians 1:6, 7</margin>
3. In it is a **merit** and **satisfaction**; it is true that Scripture does not use these words explicitly / but it contains the sense and meaning of them; as in those words / *He has made us accepted in the Beloved, in whom we have redemption through His blood.* I know that there is a different meaning in these words; for "merit" properly looks toward the good that shall be obtained / but "satisfaction" looks toward the evil that is turned away; but in Christ we do not dwell on this distinction / because His merit was satisfaction / and in His satisfaction was merit. A great dispute has recently arisen / whether Christ’s death is a satisfaction to God’s justice? But even the words "redemption" and "purchase" prove clearly / that a satisfaction was given to God through the death of Jesus;
<margin>Titus 2:14</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 6:20</margin>
*He gave Himself for us, that He might redeem us*;
<margin>Revelation 5:9</margin>
*you are bought at a price*; and what kind of price was that? what? His own blood. *You were slain, and have purchased us for God with Your blood*, that is / with Your death and suffering. ### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3. § 4.

...any hope? Not all hope is a well-confirmed hope; the full assurance of hope is a high degree of hope, and every Christian must strive and labor for it. Now then, in order to do so, and to distinguish clearly that our hope is not a bastard hope <note>A "bastard hope" refers to a false or illegitimate spiritual confidence that does not come from a true relationship with God.</note>, but one well-born—that the foundations of our hope are not deceptive, but of the right sort—I shall set down these identifying signs: —

1. If Christ’s death is mine, then Christ’s life is also mine; and conversely, if Christ’s life is mine, then Christ’s death is also mine. Christ’s active and passive obedience <term>active and passive obedience: A theological distinction where 'active' refers to Christ’s perfect keeping of God's laws during his life, and 'passive' refers to his willing suffering and death.</term> cannot be separated. Christ is not divided. We must not seek one part of our justification in his birth, another in his inherent holiness, another in the perfection of his life, and another in the obedience of his death. Those who labor to separate Christ’s active and passive obedience greatly diminish Christ and make him but half a Savior. Was Christ not our surety? <note>original: "borge," meaning a legal guarantor or bondsman who takes on another's debt.</note> Hebrews 7:22. And was he not thereby bound to fulfill all righteousness for us? That is, to suffer in our place, and also to obey in our place. Oh, beware that you do not set or divide Christ’s death and life against one another; either we have Christ entirely, or we have no part in Christ. Now,

<column-break/>

since these two go together, one can serve as a sign of the other. Examine yourself then and test yourself, O my soul: do you have any part in Christ’s life? ### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3. Section 4.

...which is only removed from one sin to another; or sin can seem to be killed when the nourishment and the power of sin is killed, just as a lamp goes out when it is either not refilled with oil, or when the oil itself is taken away. Now, so that we may get to the root of the matter in this investigation, and understand the truth and certainty of our <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "doodinge." In 17th-century theology, this refers to "mortification of sin," the spiritual process of killing the influence of sin in one's life.</note>, the same can be proven by these rules:

<margin>Matthew 7:18</margin>
1. True mortification springs from the root of faith. All worldly things have one cause or another from which they originate; and if the cause is good, the result must also necessarily be good; but if the cause is evil, the result must also necessarily be evil: *a good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit; nor can a bad tree bring forth good fruit.* Let us then investigate the cause in this case; if we can establish that we believe in Christ, that we cast ourselves upon Christ to obtain life and salvation, and that we now begin to feel the decrease of sin within us, then we may conclude from the cause or the origin that this decrease of sin is true mortification. Truly, the sin has already received its death-wound; it is a blessed result, proceeding from a good, upright, and proper cause.

2. True mortification is universal; not one sin alone,

<column-break/>

but all sins are killed in a sincere believer. Just as death is to the members of the body, so is mortification to the members of sin; now, death overcomes all the members—it leaves no life in a single member of the body—likewise, mortification leaves no life in a single member of sin. I mean to say, that it takes away the ruling power of sin in all members:
<margin>Colossians 3:5</margin>
*Mortify your members which are upon the earth,* says the Apostle; *your members*, not just one member, and then he provides examples: *fornication, uncleanness, shameful movements* <note>original: "schandelijcke beweginge." Often translated in English Bibles as "inordinate affection" or "passion."</note>, *evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry.* Christians who have their share in Christ’s death must not only abandon pride, but also lust; not only uncleanness, but also greed; sin must not only be killed in the understanding, but also in the will and the emotions. Mortification is universal.

You might say: this is a hard word; is there any person, any believer, who leaves all sins? Yes, in respect to the ruling power, he leaves all sins; all great sins, and all other sins; yet with this distinction: [he leaves] all gross sins, and all stumblings and weaknesses that involve consent and inclination. It is very useful that we observe the steps of mortification; the first is to take away the practice of gross and offensive sins in words and works; if anyone

The third is being free from all established <term>lust</term> <note>original: "lust." In this context, it refers to any illicit or sinful desire, not just sexual desire.</note> or any evil movement; not only refusing consent and the will, but even refusing the thoughts and imagination, so as to take pleasure in sin with settled intent and deliberation. I know that being free from all evil movements of the flesh, or from all hasty inner agitations, or from all sudden pleasures in sin, or from all deadness and hesitation toward good things in respect to sin, is a higher peak than any man in this world can reach; for as long as we live, the <term>law of the members</term> <note>A biblical reference to Romans 7:23, describing the internal struggle between one's spiritual desires and one's fallen human nature.</note> will work, and we shall find cause enough to complain about a "body of death." However, when we—as soon as these movements first arise—immediately labor to quench them, to reject them, to loathe them, and to put them away from us, that is a sincere <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "doodinge." The theological process of "killing" or subduing sinful impulses.</note>; and this far we must see to it that we forsake all sin.

3. True mortification is not without present conflict, although it ultimately triumphs; for a long time the

<column-break/>

corruption may break out, and the desire can be strong and powerful; but that powerful desire is only for that time, whereas an unmortified desire always reigns. It is with sin in a believer as it is with a man who has received a deadly wound from his enemy; he will not run away immediately, but will rather charge with even greater violence at the one who wounded him; yet, however vehement he may be, he will nevertheless sink down in the midst of his fury because he has received a deadly wound. 

So it is with the sin of a believer and with mortified desire: it may rage somewhat in the heart and seem to reign for a short time, but the power and strength of the sin is nonetheless killed; it sinks down and has no power to overcome. By this sign we can know whether the corruptions and agitations of our hearts come from a mortified or an unmortified desire. A mortified desire may still rage for a time, but it cannot prevail; it may struggle, but it cannot overpower. It may be in the heart like a thief in a house—not to stay and dwell, but to come for a night and pass through. And (as should always be noted) after its sway and outburst, a soul that has given it place has a loathing of it in dust and ashes, calling out with power to God for mercy and forgiveness,

### The Fourth Book, Part 3. Chapter 3. Section 4.

...and repairing the damage with a stronger resolution and with an invincible alertness against future attacks. But an unkilled desire possesses the heart, and rules and reigns in the soul; it stays there and knows nothing of departing. I do not want to deny that there can be a cessation of its workings for a time, but this is not through a lack of good will, as they say, but only from a lack of material, means, opportunity, prompting, company, lure, or the like. After such a pause or postponement, the heart embraces the same sin again with greater greed; it leads and delights itself again as much in it as it did before. It hardens itself therein quite stubbornly, as if it were impossible to leave the same, or to live without it in any comfort.

4. True <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "doodinge." The theological practice of "putting to death" sinful desires and habits.</note> is a painful work. ### The Fourth Book, Part 3, Chapter 3, § 5.

Women followed him, weeping; but because this weeping was not properly spiritual and elevated, he said to them: *Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves.* The way of faith, drawing some power from Christ's death, is primarily to pay attention to the aim <note>original: "oogh-gemerck," literally "eye-mark," meaning the objective or target.</note> and intention of Christ in his suffering. Just as God, in prayer, looks primarily at the intentions of the Spirit, so faith also looks primarily at the intention of Christ in his suffering. And do not misunderstand me; my intention is by no means that we should be ignorant of the narrative of Christ's death, or of the manner of his suffering; you see that we have opened the same in the second part, and have followed it very closely from the beginning to the end. But we must not remain stuck there; in all of this, we must primarily look upon Christ's mind and heart. There are those who have noted that we find this order in both the Old and the New Testaments: first the narrative, and then the mystery; first the manner, and then the intention of Christ’s suffering. As in the Old Testament: we have first the narrative in Psalm 22, described by David; and then the mystery in Isaiah 53, described by Isaiah. And in the New Testament, we have first the manner of his suffering described in the second part by all the Evangelists; and then the meaning, described by the Apostles in all their epistles. Now, the works of faith correspond here

<column-break/>

likewise; we must first look at Jesus as he is lifted up, and then at the end and the intention. What was this, Jesus being thus lifted up? Well, you might then ask, what was the end, the aim, and the great intention of Christ in this looking up?

I answer that some ends are remote <note>original: "verschoven," literally shifted away or distant, referring to secondary or ultimate outcomes.</note>, and others are somewhat more immediate. But passing over all these remote ends—his glory and our salvation, and so forth—I shall only answer these things.

#### The Fourth Book. Part 3, Chapter 3, Section 5. 589

...not willing the death of the sinner, and for no lesser purpose <note>The original Dutch uses "eynde" here to mean "goal" or "final cause."</note> has willed the death of His Son, whom He loved more than the entire world. It cannot be anything other than a great matter for whose sake God has consented to the death of His Son; and this could be nothing less than to take away that which He hated most, and that was sin. Here then is another purpose of Christ's death: the forgiveness of sin, which is a large part of our justification <term>justification: being declared righteous or "in the right" before God</term>.

<margin>Romans 6:12</margin>
3. Another intention of Christ's death was to kill our "members" <note>In a biblical context, "members" refers to the parts of our body or our earthly, sinful nature.</note> that are upon the earth. Not only did He want to forgive sin, but He also wanted to bring it to nothing—to kill and to crucify it. He did not want sin to reign in our mortal bodies, nor for us to obey it in its lusts. The Apostle expressed this aim in these <margin>1 Peter 2:24</margin> words: *He bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness.* Christ did not only intend to deliver us from the guilt of sin through His death, but also from <margin>Galatians 6:14</margin> the power of sin. *Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.* Paul was a dead man—dead to the world and dead to sin—but how did he become so? He attributed this to the cross of Christ, to the

<column-break/>

death of Christ. The death of Jesus was the cause of this death in Paul. <margin>Hebrews 9:14</margin> *How much more shall the blood of Christ—cleanse your consciences from dead works to serve the living God?* In the death of Christ, there is, firstly, a worthiness <note>Meaning merit or legal value.</note>, and secondly, a power. The first is for our justification, and the latter is for our sanctification <term>sanctification: the ongoing process of being made holy and being changed into the likeness of Christ</term>. Now, sanctification has two parts: the "dying-away" <note>Often called "mortification" in older theology.</note> and the "making-alive." Christ’s death, or His passive obedience, is specifically useful for the former; His life, or His active obedience, for the other. For this reason, believers are said to have *become one plant with Christ <margin>Romans 6:5</margin> in the likeness of His death.* There is a certain similarity between Christ and Christians: Christ died, and the believing Christians die; Christ died a natural death, and a Christian dies a spiritual death; Christ died for sin, and a Christian dies *to* sin. This was another purpose of Christ's death: from His death proceeds a killing power, causing the death of sin in the soul of a believer—a great part of our sanctification.

O my soul, look upon this! Herein lies the "pit and marrow" <note>A Dutch idiom meaning the core or the very essence.</note> of Christ's death. And if you will now only put your faith to work and practice it in this regard, how shall you bring the power and application of this death into your soul? # Looking unto Jesus.

...prompt me to draw down the power of Christ's death and to feel the same in my soul for the dying away, crucifying, and killing of sin?

I answer, 1. Through prayer, meditation, self-examination, receiving the Lord’s Supper <term>Lord's Supper: also known as Communion or the Eucharist</term>, and so forth: I must present myself and my soul before the Lord Jesus Christ, just as He took upon Himself and accomplished that bitter and painful work of suffering, even unto His death, yes, even the death of the cross, as it is presented in the account of the Gospel. 2. I must indeed and steadfastly believe, and certainly assent, that all this suffering of Christ—thus discovered and revealed—was indeed, truly, certainly, and in every way without doubt within Himself. I must look upon this sorrowful, bitter, cruel, painful, and altogether shameful, cursed, and blasphemous suffering of Christ as a completely strange and wondrous matter; noting especially the spiritual part of His suffering, namely the feeling and the apprehension of God’s abandonment, which grieved Him in the day of the heat of His wrath. Over this I must be greatly dejected and amazed: what? That the Son of God had to lay His head upon the block <note>The author uses the imagery of a literal executioner's block to describe Christ's submission to divine justice.</note> under the blow of God’s justice? That He placed Himself under the wrath of His Heavenly Father? That He had to enter into the conflict of God's sorrowful displeasure, and had to

<column-break/>

be deprived of the feeling of His love, and kindness, and usual comfort: how can I be anything but amazed at this altogether wondrous suffering of Jesus Christ?

4. I must consider and note what the cause of all this was, namely, sin—yes, my sin—yes, this and that sin in particular. This comes somewhat closer to us, and from this I must now bring in these following conclusions. As—

1. It was Christ's intention that through His suffering He would give a satisfaction for sin to the infinite justice of God. 2. The meaning and the intention was (at least in the second place) to give to the world a very remarkable and glorious example and demonstration of the dreadfulness, hatefulness, and horribleness of sin, since nothing less than this, indeed, nothing other than this could serve the cause of reconciling and settling it. 3. It further demonstrates that, just as sin is horrible in itself, it also must grieve and provoke Christ beyond measure; Oh, it cost Him so much, it brought Him to all these pains and torments, it made Him cry out:

> *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?*

How can it be otherwise: must it not provoke Him above everything, above all things in the whole world? 4. If there is then any spark of Christ's love in me, or anything that resembles Christ; or if I want Christ—

# The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapters 3, 4, 5.

...Christ has any affection, love, esteem, and regard for me, then it will entirely befit me by all means to have a loathing of sin and to cast it away from me; to cry out against it, to wash my hands of it, and to loosen my heart from it. It is the truth that I can perhaps give no greater proof of my sincere love, inward affection, consideration, conformity, demonstration, and compassion with Christ, than that I exert all force and use all holy severity against sin, even for His sake.

Now, the heart being thus exercised, God will without doubt meet us through His Spirit: the desire and labor of our soul to weaken and kill sin in the soul is not without reward; but especially when sin is rejected in this way and by this means of the soul’s affection, and is brought into hatred and contempt, it perishes and dies of its own accord; for it only lives and grows through the warm affections, good thoughts, and good feelings that sin receives from the soul. So, as these things thus touch the heart, the flow <note>original: "invloepinge," referring to an inward flowing or influence that nourishes a condition.</note> that feeds and strengthens sin is cut off, and it withers gradually until it is finally and completely destroyed.

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3. Section 5.

The core object: Christ crucified. There is an infinity of worth in Christ's death; and this arises first from the dignity of His person, for He was the God-man <note>original: "Godt-mensche," referring to the doctrine of the Hypostatic Union, where Christ is both fully divine and fully human.</note>. If the deaths of all angels and men were placed together, they could not compare to the excellence of the death of Christ. Be amazed at your own blessedness, O believer! You have gained by your loss: you lost the righteousness of a mere creature, but the righteousness of an infinite person has now become yours. For this reason, it is frequently called <margin>Romans 10:3</margin> the righteousness of God; both because Christ is God, and because it is such a righteousness by which God is fully satisfied <term>satisfied: "voldaen," a legal term meaning a debt has been paid in full</term>. He looks for nothing better; indeed, there can be nothing better. 2. This worth lies not only in the dignity of His person, but also in the price that was given. Oh, it was the blood of Christ, of which a single drop is worthier than thousands of gold and silver. It was this blood, <margin>Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 1:18</margin> that purchased the entire Church of God, a feat which the riches of a thousand worlds could never have accomplished. 3. This worth is found not only in the person and the price, but also in the manner of the offering. Christ had to die upon the cross, just as it was decreed. The price in itself is not enough unless it is arranged and suited to the pleasure of the one who must be satisfied: <insert>100</insert>

<column-break/>

If someone were to give an infinite sum of money for a captive person—a sum sufficient in itself to redeem a thousand—yet if the payment did not happen in such a way, nor upon such conditions as the lord of the captive had prescribed, then it could not be called a true satisfaction. Now, this was the condition: that Christ had to die, and die the death of the cross. Having accepted and fulfilled this, a luster, glory, excellence, and worth were placed upon His death. Oh, the dignity! Oh, the excellence of this death of Christ! Many are ready to complain, "Oh, the impurity of my sins! Oh, the offenses and ingratitude that have been present in my iniquities!" It is not my own misery or my ruin that torments me so much as the fact that God is angry. Dear soul! Turn your eyes hither: certainly, this death of Christ is more powerful to satisfy God than it is possible for all your sins to displease Him. There was a much sweeter aroma in Christ's sacrifice <note>original: "offerhande"</note> than there could be offense in all your sins. The excellence in Christ’s death to make someone righteous is far more abundant than the impurity of sin to make someone a sinner. Come then, and hold fast to Christ with this encouragement: there is a worth and excellence in this object of faith—Christ crucified.

### §. 6.
#### On loving Jesus in this looking.

VI. **L**et us love Jesus, as He has taken upon Himself the great work of our salvation in His suffering and death. Why did He suffer, and <margin>John 15:13</margin> why did He die? No one has greater love than this, that someone lays down his life for his friends.

<margin>Romans 5:8</margin> But God confirms His love toward us, that Christ died for us while we were still sinners; truly here is a proof of love. What else can we do but love Him, who has loved us so? To pursue this, I have nothing more to do but to show 1. The love of Christ toward us, and then 2. how we must exercise our love toward Him.

1. Concerning His love toward us; has not God Himself spoken of it, and does Scripture not speak of it? Who would have believed our words? Yet Christ has done it, and it is well worth our effort to weigh and consider it in holy meditation <term>meditation: "gepeyns," meaning deep, pious reflection or pondering</term>. — Indeed, how can I do less than in an

<column-break/>

ecstasy of my soul, behold the Lord Jesus, who from eternity was clothed with glory and Majesty, but was now draped with old rags, and rocked in a manger, and suffered hunger, thirst, weariness, reproach <note>original: "gebaer," likely referring to gestures of mockery or the physical toll of His state</note>, contempt, poverty, blasphemy, scourging, and wrath? But not to dwell on this; what a stirring comes over me, seeing that the Judge of the entire world is accused, condemned, and damned? Seeing the Lord of life die on the shameful and cursed wood <note>Referring to the cross, which was considered a "cursed" form of execution in biblical law.</note>? Seeing the eternal Son of God struggle with His Father’s wrath? Seeing Him who had said, *I and my Father are one*, sweat drops of blood in His struggle, and hearing Him cry on the cross, *My God, My God, why have you forsaken me?* Oh, to what lengths has His love for mankind brought Him! Had He only sent His creatures to help us; had He but sent His Prophets to instruct us in the way to heaven; had He only sent His Angels from the heavenly court to look after us and serve us—it would have been a great work of mercy <term>mercy: "barmhertigheyt," meaning heart-felt compassion for the miserable</term>. Or, if it had to be so, had Christ Himself come down from heaven only to visit us, or had He but come and wept over us, saying, *Oh, if only you also knew, even in this your day, the things that belong to your peace!* Oh, if only you had paid a little better attention...

### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3. §. 7.

I do not know how it will turn out, for either free grace must save me, or it is all over for me.

Do not speak so / for through this death of Christ, both free grace and justice are your friends. Although some do so / it is nonetheless certain / that you have no need to appeal from the court of Justice to the throne of grace; in this mystery of godliness there is surely as much comfort when we stand before the tribunal of justice / as before the throne of grace / that is / when we stand there in and through the Lord Jesus Christ; yes / this is the Gospel-way / that we go to God the Father / and offer Him the active and passive righteousness <term>Active and passive righteousness: "Active" refers to Christ's perfect obedience to God's law during his life; "passive" refers to his voluntary suffering and death on the cross.</term> of His Son Jesus Christ as a reconciliation and satisfaction for our sins / in this way the comfort of justification is brought near; if we go to God by any other way / that is no more than a natural way / and not through the right way of the Gospel. A person may know by nature well enough / that having sinned / they must plead with God for mercy; but to seek reconciliation with God with a price in our hands / and to offer the merits of Jesus Christ as a satisfaction to divine justice / that is a mystery of faith.

Yet I do not speak against trusting in God's mercy for forgiveness / but what need have we to appeal from justice to

<column-break/>

mercy / since we can offer the death of Christ through faith / and thus be accepted even by God's justice? Come, my soul / and let me say to you for your confidence / if you have any part in Christ's death / then you have two strongholds to hold your reconciliation and salvation: mercy and justice; free grace and righteousness; mercy in respect to you / and justice in respect to Christ; not only is free grace ready to release you / but a complete price has also been paid to discharge you from all your sins: So that when the Prince of this world <note>The "Prince of this world" is a biblical title for Satan (John 14:30).</note> now comes against you / you can say in a certain way with Christ / *He has nothing in me*, for how can he accuse me, since Christ is my surety? <term>Surety: A legal guarantor who takes responsibility for another person's debt or obligations.</term> since the handwriting <note>original: "handt-schrift" — referring to the "handwriting of ordinances" or debt-bond mentioned in Colossians 2:14.</note> is canceled, and Jesus Christ did not wish to leave a single penny unpaid? Just as Paul said to Philemon concerning Onesimus, *if he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to me*, so says Christ to God, *if these have wronged your Majesty, or owe you anything, charge that to me.* Paul immediately added / *I, Paul, have written it with my own hand*, but Christ speaks thus / *I, Jesus, have ratified and confirmed it with my own blood.*

<margin>Gen. 2:17.</margin>

## §. 9.

->On conformity with Jesus in this looking.<-

IX. Let us become conformed <note>To be "conformed" means to be shaped or molded into the likeness of something else.</note> to Jesus in respect of his suffering and dying; looking unto Jesus is very powerful for this; the objects of our gaze have an attractive power to make things like unto themselves. I have read of a woman who, setting the power of her imagination on a Moor <note>In the 17th century, "Moor" was a general term for North African or Black people. ### The Fourth Book. Part 3. Chapter 3: §. 9.

Herein I shall examine these questions: 1. In what way we must become conformed to him. 2. What is the cause of this conformity? 3. What are the means thereof on our part?

Concerning the first: in what way must we become conformed? I answer that we must become conformed to Christ in his graces, suffering, and death.

<margin>John 1:16</margin>
1. In his graces, which shone most gloriously in his bitter suffering; his life was truly a life of grace; he was full of grace, and from his fullness we have all received, even grace upon grace <note>original: "genade voor genade"</note>; but his graces shone most clearly and gloriously in his death; just as a lily among the thorns appears most beautiful, so his graces shone most excellently in his suffering. I shall give some examples of this, such as:

1. His humility was very deep: what? That the Most High God, that the only-begotten and eternal Son of God, was willing to humble himself so far that he was willing to be despised, and that he was willing to be esteemed less than Barabbas, a murderer? That Christ was willing to be crucified on a cross between two thieves, as if he were the ringleader <note>original: "roer-vinck," meaning a troublemaker or chief instigator</note> of all evildoers: Oh, what humility was this!

<margin>1 Peter 2:20, 21, 23</margin>
