<meta>This page continues the comparison between Christ’s physical death on the cross and the spiritual "mortification" (dying away) of sin in the believer. While the previous page discussed death being voluntary and violent, this page moves to the third characteristic: that it is a lingering or slow process.</meta>

->### Looking unto Jesus. ###<-

<margin>Matthew 27:45</margin>
"from the sixth hour until the ninth hour," says Matthew: that is, from our twelve o'clock until three, before he gave up his spirit. Likewise, our dying away <note>The author uses the term *afstervinge*, which in 17th-century theology refers to "mortification," the lifelong process of killing off one's sinful nature.</note> is also a slow death; sin is not killed all at once or entirely, but it gradually loses its power more and more. Herein is noted that great distinction between justification <term>Justification: being declared righteous before God through faith, which happens instantly.</term> and sanctification <term>Sanctification: the gradual process of becoming more holy throughout a believer's life.</term>; the first is a perfect work, admitting no degrees or stages, but the latter is different. Although a believer is perfectly freed from the guilt of sin, he is nonetheless not yet freed from its power; sin dwells in us, despite it not reigning over us.
<margin>Romans 7:17</margin>
"It is no longer I that do it, but sin that dwells in me"; like a rebellious tenant <note>original: *huerlingh*; literally a hireling or tenant who refuses to leave.</note> keeping possession in spite of the owner, until the house is cast down over his head. It is truly so, that the "body of sin" in a reborn person has received its death-wound, and in that respect it can be said to be dead; but it is not yet entirely dead; it still moves and stirs constantly, dying only by degrees. What the Apostle says of the renewal of the "new man," we can also say of the wasting away of the "old man": the inward man is renewed day by day, and the old man is corrupted <note>or "decays"</note> day by day. Or as Paul said of himself,
<margin>1 Corinthians 15:31</margin>
"I die daily," and that in respect of his afflictions; so may we say of

<column-break/>

a Christian in respect of his sins: there is none of the holiest on earth who does not still have some remnants of corruption in him, which God, according to his wise providence, permits for the testing, exercise, and humbling of our souls, and to make the riches of his own grace—in the renewal and multiplication of forgiveness—the more glorious.

And here is a ground of comfort for a languishing and dejected soul. Such a person cries and complains, "Alas, I feel the stirrings and powerful workings of sin, and I fear that my sin is not yet killed."
<margin>Genesis 25:22</margin>
Just as Rebecca said, feeling the children struggling together within her, "If it be so, why am I thus?" So, if sin is killed, says the soul, why am I thus? But, troubled soul, do not become despondent; Jesus Christ was not dead immediately as soon as he was fastened to the cross. But have you dealt with the "body of sin" as the Jews did with the body of Christ? Have you accused it, have you indicted it, have you condemned it, and have you fastened it to the cross? Have you accused it before the tribunal <note>original: *vierſchare*; an old Dutch term for a court of justice</note> of God’s judgment? Have you indicted it in the manner of a humble and hearty confession? Have you condemned it on its own account, pronouncing a sentence of eternal damnation over yourself? And have you fastened it to the cross, beginning its execution and the killing thereof...

I have not yet resisted unto blood <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:4: "Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin."</note>, and even if I had, what is this in comparison to his extreme suffering? ***Christ*** died in his suffering; his passive obedience <term>Passive obedience: The theological concept that Christ submissively accepted the suffering and death ordained by God for the salvation of humanity.</term> was unto death, even the death of the cross; he hung on the cross until he bowed his head and gave up the spirit; he died unto sin once:

Again / a likeness to ***Christ*** in his death / shall cause a likeness to ***Christ*** in his glory;
<margin>*Romans 6:5*</margin>
*if we have become one plant with him in the likeness of his death, so shall we also be in the likeness of his resurrection*; just as it is with a graft and a trunk / the graft appearing dead with the trunk in winter / becomes living again with the same in the spring / after the death of winter it shares in the resurrection of the spring; so it is also between ***Christ*** and us / if we die to sin with ***Christ*** / then we shall also be raised with ***Christ*** to glory; being conformed to him in his death / we shall also be in his resurrection. Let us thus stir up and incite our soul to this conformity.

5. Let us pray to God / that he will make us conformed to ***Christ***. Do we lack grace? let us pray to him / that from that fullness which is in ***Christ*** / we may receive, according to our measure, grace for grace.

# Looking unto Jesus.

...set into work; surely there is a conduit of healing, strengthening, and refreshing power flowing into our souls while we look and fix our eyes upon the crucified **Christ**; upon the exalted **Christ**; and this comes from that hidden presence of **God**; blessing our looking up to **Christ** in this way, as an ordinance <note>An "ordinance" refers to a religious practice or ceremony established by God—such as prayer or the sacraments—meant to be a means of receiving grace.</note> to which He has attached a powerful impression upon the heart. We must not curiously investigate how this can happen; first principles (as we say) require no proof; simply accept that **God** has said it, and that experience <note>original: "onderbindinge" — referring to practical or experimental knowledge of faith.</note> has discovered it: that when faith has the opportunity to work upon some suitable holy object, **God** does not fail to answer the same through His **Spirit**; in such an opportunity, He fills the soul with more comfort, blessing, and strength; He causes to return upon the soul (through the working of faith) the very thing upon which faith has looked. Surely no one else knows this except those who feel it, and no one who knows it is able to express it; just as there is something in fire (the heat, the warmth, and the light) that no painter can express; and just as there is something in a face (the heat, the warmth, and the life) which no painter can represent; so there is something that flows into the soul while faith is working upon the death of **Christ**, which regarding its origin, or

<column-break/>

way, or manner of its working, is beyond the reach of the tongue to speak, of the pen to write, or of the brush to draw. Come then, if you desire grace, suffer afflictions, die to sin, grow in the dying away <term>Dying away: "Afstervinge" in Dutch, or mortification; the process of the old, sinful nature losing its power over the believer.</term>: let us often return to our duty of looking upon **Jesus**, or believing in **Jesus**, just as He was exalted.

---

And yet, after all is done, let us not think that sin in us will completely die and cease, for such is a higher perfection than this life will produce; only through the use of the means <note>The "means of grace" are the tools God provides for spiritual growth, such as scripture, prayer, and worship.</note> and through **God’s** blessing may we expect it to go so far that sin shall not reign; that it shall not wear the crown; that it shall not sit upon the throne; that it shall not hold parliament; that it shall not establish laws within us; we shall not serve it, but we shall die to its dominion through the power of this death of **Jesus Christ**. And this He desires to give to us, He who died for us. Amen, Amen.

---

->Thus far we have looked upon **Jesus** as our **Jesus** in His suffering and death.<- Our next task is to look upon **Jesus** as He took the great work of our salvation upon Himself during the time of His resurrection and His stay on earth, until He was carried up and taken into **Heaven**.

->Concerning the manner of Christ’s resurrection.<-

III. How he was raised: regarding the manner of his resurrection / we can observe it in these points. —

1. ### Looking unto Jesus.

In this regard, the Apostle makes a comparison between Adam and Christ; now, we know that Adam, before his fall, was regarded as a representative head <note>original: *ghemeen hooft-persoon*, a theological and legal term for one who represents a whole group</note>, standing not individually or for himself alone, but as representing the entire human race that would descend from him; so also Jesus Christ is regarded for us, both before, in, and after his death, as a representative head, not living, not dying, or rising individually or for himself alone, but as representing all the believers in the world. And for this reason, Adam is called <margin>1 Cor. 15:47</margin> *the first man*, and *Jesus Christ* is called *the second man*; as if there had never been more people in the world, or ever would be, than just these two. And why? As if these two held the entire rest of the children of men bound to them as if on a cord: Adam had all the children of men coming into this world, and being called *earthly men*, enclosed within him; and Christ had all his elect, whose names are written in the heavens, and who are therefore called *heavenly men*, enclosed within him; so that now everything that Christ has done is counted by God as if it were done by us and for us. Christ rising, rose as our head and as a representative person, and in God's estimation we have risen with him and in him. Just as among all the sheaves in the field, there was one sheaf that, in the name and the

<column-break/>

place of all the others, was lifted up and waved before the Lord; so also, we being all dead, Christ was raised as the firstfruits from the dead, and by this act of his resurrection all the elect from the beginning of the world until its end have risen with him and in him. 
<margin>1 Cor. 15:20</margin>
He is *the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep*; notwithstanding that the holy ones still sleep, they are nevertheless already powerfully raised with Christ because he is their firstfruits. Let us always remember this: that Christ was raised as the firstfruits, as the second man, as a head, as a representative person.

2. That Christ was raised by his own power; regarding this he looked, saying, <margin>John 2:19</margin> *Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.* He does not say, you destroy it and another shall raise it up; no, no, but I, I myself shall do it; yes, and I shall do it through my own might and power. Here is a clear proof of Christ's Divine nature, for no one has ever done this, or can do this, except God himself. There were some raised before Christ's incarnation <note>original: *menschweerdinghe*</note>, but not a single one by himself or through his own power. God had indeed shared some power with certain Prophets for that time and occasion, and so such people were raised; but Christ was raised not by any power given to others, but by his own power. ### The Fourth Book. Part 4. Chapter 1: Section 3.

raised by Elijah, and that of the Shunammite woman <note>A reference to 2 Kings 4, where the prophet Elisha restores a woman's son to life.</note> by Elisha; both of these were raised by others, and those others did not raise them by their own power, but by a power that was given to them from above. For this reason, although they raised others during their lives, they themselves, once dead, were not able to raise themselves. But Jesus Christ not only raised others during his life, but even while dead and lying in his grave—weighted down with stones, guarded by soldiers, and held by the entire host of darkness—he nevertheless, as a conqueror, made himself alive again through his own power. He acted through the strength of his own arm, ensuring that all things had to clear a path for him. <margin>John 10:18</margin> *I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again;* he possessed a power to take it up equal to his power to lay it down.

But here an objection might be raised: <margin>Acts 5:30. Chap. 2:24</margin> *The God of our fathers has raised Jesus—having loosed the pains of death.* Since in various places Christ's resurrection is attributed to his Father, how then can he be said to have raised himself by his own power?

I answer that it is the truth that the Father raised him, and yet it does not contradict the fact that he raised himself. For

<column-break/>

<margin>John 5:19</margin> *whatever the Father does, that the Son does also,* says Christ. Christ’s resurrection is the indivisible work of the Holy Trinity; it is a common work of all three persons. The power of the Father and of the Son is but one, so that it is the truth of both: the Father raised him, and the Son raised himself.

3. That Christ was raised <margin>Matthew 28:2</margin> with an earthquake; *and behold, there was a great earthquake, for the Angel of the Lord descended from Heaven.* The earth trembled at his death, and now it trembled again at his resurrection, stating clearly that it could neither endure his suffering nor prevent his resurrection. Just as it is said of a Lion that with his roaring he makes his lair <note>original: *leger*, meaning a lion's den or resting place</note> in which he lies tremble, so also was this Lion from the tribe of Judah <note>A traditional title for Christ, referencing his strength and kingly lineage from the tribe of Judah.</note> powerful enough to make his bed (the earth in which he lay) tremble with his voice or his appearance. He had no sooner moved himself than he moved the earth; at his first movement, the earth moved itself, and the prophecy <margin>Psalm 114:7</margin> was now fulfilled: *Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.*

It does not befit us to curiously investigate the causes of this earthquake; certainly the cause exceeded the reach of nature. It was not some hollow wind released from the innermost parts of the earth, but it was caused either by Christ’s resurrection or the Angel’s descent. The earth [trembled] either from joy—

### Looking unto Jesus.

joy leaped up that Christ was resurrected, or it trembled with fear that men would not believe in Christ’s resurrection. The Evangelist seems to attribute it to the Angel, for the Angel of the Lord descended from Heaven: certainly, the power of the Angels is very great; they can move all physical things even in the blink of an eye; they can cause a storm to rise, and move the earth and the waters, yet all their power is subject to God’s will: <margin>Psalm 103:20.</margin> *Praise the Lord, you his Angels, you mighty heroes, who do his word.* It was God’s will that the Angel should now take hold of the pillars of the earth and make them tremble; no wonder then <margin>Matthew 28:4</margin> that the guards were greatly terrified and became as dead men. And since an Angel was powerful enough to make the earth and the guards tremble—those armed soldiers who were stationed to guard the grave—what then will Christ himself do when he shall return for judgment with many thousand times thousands of angels? Oh, how terrible and fearful his coming shall be! Just as at Christ’s resurrection, so also at the final resurrection <margin>Matthew 24:7 <note>The source text cites Matthew 28, but the context of "earthquakes in various places" refers to the signs of the end times in Matthew 24.</note></margin> there shall be earthquakes in various places. 4. That as Christ was rising, the

Angels served him. An <margin>Matthew 28:2.</margin> *Angel approached, and rolled away the stone from the door, and sat upon it.* Christ’s power was not enclosed in the grave, nor in the earth, but extended into the Heavens and their hosts; however much the High Priests <note>The religious leaders of the Jewish Sanhedrin.</note> and Pharisees <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional laws.</note> conspired together to shut him in the earth, to seal the stone, and to set a guard, and to secure everything as best they could; nevertheless, the Angels of Heaven were ready to attend to him as their highest Lord. An angel descended to roll away the stone; not as if Christ were powerless to do that himself; he moved the earth, and would he not be able to lift a stone? Oh, yes! But in this way, he wished to display his power, proving his authority over the mighty Angels; he had only to speak to his Angel, "Do that," and he does it. I find some difference among the interpreters <note>Theologians or biblical commentators.</note> as to why an Angel had to roll away the stone; some believe that it happened only for the sake of the women, so that they might enter the grave and see the empty tomb, and thus be assured that Christ was not there, <margin>Matthew 28:6.</margin> but had risen, just as they said, *Come, see the place where the Lord lay*; others believe it was their bounden duty to serve Jesus Christ, to make a way for his body to come out of the grave without having to pass through any other physical matter; as for me, I side with these latter ones, although it is not...

Some believe that they died again, but it is more likely—since they rose to prove the life-giving power of Christ’s resurrection—that they were also glorified with Christ; and just as they rose with the rising Christ, so they also ascended into Heaven with the ascending Christ.

### Looking unto Jesus

...some answer <note>Continuing the thought that the angels’ positions corresponded to the places where Mary had previously anointed Jesus</note> that just as Maria Magdalene had anointed his head and feet, so these angels sat in both these places to acknowledge this, as it were, on her behalf. Others think that it serves for the consolation of us all; that if we are but in Christ, we shall go to our graves in white and lie between two angels, who are said to guard our dead bodies themselves and to bring them back to life on the day of resurrection.

But in this appearance, we see further a question and an answer. **1.** The angels ask Mary, "Woman, why do you weep?" May I speak these words a bit more broadly? It is as if they had said:

> O Mary! what reason have you for your tears? If the angels rejoice, it surely does not fit that a woman should weep; previously you could arm your feet with a manly courage to run between the swords <note>A reference to the dangers of visiting the tomb of a condemned man guarded by Roman soldiers</note> when you came to the tomb, and are you now so faint-hearted <note>original: "wijfachtigh," meaning "womanish" or "weak," reflecting the 17th-century view that excessive weeping was a lack of spiritual fortitude</note> that you cannot restrain your eyes from weeping? O woman, why do you weep? If your Christ were here in his grave, under this stone, then we might think that your grief over the dead would squeeze the tears from you; but now that you find this grave to be a place of the living, why then do you stand here weeping over the dead? Are your tears tears of love, as your love is well-known? Then spare your tears. Are they tears of anger? Then they must not be shed 

<column-break/>

here, where all anger is taken away and buried; are they tears of sorrow or duty? They are spent in vain where the dead has already become living again; and therefore, O woman, why do you weep? Would our eyes be dry if such floods of tears were becoming for us? And have the angels not always, in their visible appearances, shown their Lord's invisible pleasure? Adjusting their appearance to the aim of his inclinations? As for example: when God is angry, they brandish swords; and when he is reconciled, they put them into the scabbard; when God wishes to protect, they show themselves as warriors; and when he wishes to alarm, they take on a fearsome appearance; and when God wishes to comfort, one sees joy in their eyes, sweetness in their face, kindness in their words, favor and grace, and loveliness in their presence. Well, why do you weep then, seeing that we are glad? Do you think that we have cast off our nature, or that we have forgotten any of our duties, though our state knows no change nor any wrongdoing? Are you more zealous in your love, or do you have a closer understanding of God’s eternal counsel than we who stand daily before the throne of his glory? O woman, why do you weep? This by way of explanation.

<margin>John 20:13</margin> She said to them, "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him."

A small remnant of Christ being lost is a very lamentable loss. Mary had recently enjoyed the presence of the whole Christ; she had his presence; she heard his words; she saw his divinity in his miracles, and in the casting out of seven demons from her own body; but now she had lost Christ entirely. His presence was gone, his preaching was gone, his Divinity <note>original: "Godtheydt," referring to His divine nature</note> was gone, his humanity was gone, his soul was gone, and last of all, his body was gone. <margin>Question.</margin>
But does Christ ever leave his own entirely and completely?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I answer: not in fact, but only in feeling. In times of abandonment, a Christian may, according to his own feeling, find nothing at all of Christ; and this was the state of Mary Magdalene. Whether Christ truly and in truth abandons a soul (for abandonments are sometimes in appearance and sometimes in fact), yet he does not forsake his own both in fact <margin>1 Sam. 12:22</margin> and entirely. *The Lord will not completely forsake his people, for his great name's sake.* The workings of his love <note>The author distinguishes between the "feeling" of being loved and the actual "existence" of that love.</note> may be withdrawn, but his love <margin>Jer. 31:3</margin> is always the same; it is an eternal love. # Looking unto Jesus.

There was a double presence of Christ / one perceived / and one unperceived; the perceived presence is / when it graciously pleases Christ to let us know of it / and this is a Heaven on earth. The unperceived presence / is that hidden presence / when Christ seems to pull us on one side / and drive us away on the other. Thus he dealt with the **Canaanite woman** <note>Also known as the Syrophoenician woman in Matthew 15; Jesus initially appears to reject her request to test and ultimately strengthen her faith.</note> / he seemed to chase her away / but at that same time he worked through his Spirit in her an increase of faith / and by that means he drove her toward him. Thus a soul can think that Christ is lost / and seek and weep / and weep and seek / and yet Christ is present nonetheless.

<margin>John 20, 15.</margin>
2. Concerning Mary’s inquiry / she, **supposing him to be the gardener**, said to him, *Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.*

In these words, two things are to be noted: 1. her mistake, and 2. her speaking based on her mistake.

1. Her mistake / she supposed that he was the gardener. O Mary! had Christ lived so long / done so much / and shed so much blood / to come to no higher esteem than a gardener? This was a great mistake: yet in some ways / and also in a good sense, Christ may be called a gardener; As 1. he is the one who gardens all our souls / who plants therein the seed of righteousness

<column-break/>

who waters them with the dew of grace / and makes them fruitful unto eternal life. 2. He is the one who made his own dead body living again / and he shall also change all our graves into a garden-plot / <margin>Isaiah 26, 19.</margin> *Your dead shall live, even my dead body, they shall arise; awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew shall be as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the deceased.* Beyond that, there is a mystery in her mistake. Just as **Adam** <note>According to the Book of Genesis, Adam was the first man, placed in the Garden of Eden to tend it.</note> in the state of grace and innocence was placed in a garden / and his first assigned task was to be a gardener; so Christ’s first appearance was in a garden / and he showed himself in the form of a gardener. And just as that first gardener was a father of sin / a destruction of the human race / and a cause of death; so is this gardener the ransom for our sin / the restorer of our fall / and the healer of our life. In some sense then / and in a hidden way, Christ was a gardener; but Mary’s mistake consisted in this / that she thought he was only the gardener of that place; and not the gardener of our souls. Souls in a state of abandonment commit one mistake after another, although in their mistakes there are sometimes certain mysteries.

See how quickly everything, both outwardly and inwardly, has changed; now here was a new world; Christ’s resurrection was also the resurrection of Mary Magdalene; in a moment she became alive again / being raised, as it were, from death and sorrow / to a living and joyful state.

   2. She said to him *Rabboni*, which is to say, Master. Just as she was swept away by his voice / so she took the word from his mouth without delay / and at his first and only word / she answered with but one other / *Rabboni*, which is to say, Master: It is a wonder that in this verse only two words passed between them / for which some give this reason: that a sudden joy, touching all her affections, prevented her from continuing in her own words, nor did she let him continue in his words. Love would have spoken / but fear commanded silence. Hope prepares the words / but doubt smothers them in their coming forth / her internal thoughts made them emerge / but her voice trembled / her tongue stammered / her breath failed / such indeed is the state of those / who are sick with an abundance of sudden joy; her joy was so sudden / that no more words could be spoken / than *Rabboni*, which is to say, Master. <column-break/>

astonished at such good news. Just as in the sea after a storm / there always remains an internal working and rolling; so also in the mind of man / once fear is driven out / and silence has come / there always remains a *movement of trembling* <note>original: "Motus trepidationis". This refers to the psychological aftershock or "vibration" felt after a traumatic or overwhelming event has passed.</note> / or a careful jealousy <note>In this 17th-century context, "jealousy" refers to a protective anxiety or a fearful suspicion that something so good might not be real or might be lost.</note> regarding that which we enjoy. And thus may have been the state of Mary; although she answered Christ immediately / upon the first recognition of his voice / yet since the novelty was so strange / his person so changed / his presence so unexpected / and so many wonders appeared to her astonished eyes at once / she felt something like a riot in her thoughts; her hope suspected the best / but her fear thought it was too good to be true; and these objections and answers thus coming between them / she sees him all the better / but because of the present moment she can speak no more than this one word *Rabboni*, that is to say, Master.

### The Fourth Book. Part 4. Chapter 1. Section 5: 653

<margin>John 20:17.</margin>
5. Regarding the events following his appearance; Jesus said to her / **do not touch me**, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.

In these words, we can observe a prohibition and a command: the prohibition is / **do not touch me**; the command / **but go to my brothers, and tell them** etc.

1. **Do not touch me.** It seems that Mary had now fallen at his holy feet / she was now ready to kiss with her lips his formerly sorrowful / but now very glorious wounds. Such is the nature of love, that it not only desires to be united, but if it were possible, it would be transformed from itself into the beloved thing. Mary was not satisfied / that she saw her Lord / nor was it enough for her / that she heard her Lord / but she had to touch him / embrace his feet / and kiss them a thousand times. Oh, how she hung and clung to his feet! Or at least how ready she was to fall upon him! — But immediately he rebukes her forwardness <note>The Dutch "voorbarigheydt" suggests Mary was acting too quickly or prematurely in her excitement.</note> / **do not touch me**.

What a mystery is this! Mary, while a sinner, touched him / and now being a believer / is she not permitted to do so? She was once allowed to anoint his head / and is she now unworthy to touch his feet? What does Christ

<column-break/>

have in mind to keep her from such a desired duty? She had seen Christ first / and heard his words first after his resurrection / and could she not have the advantage of his first embrace? There is something wonderful <note>In this context, "wonderful" means "full of wonder" or "mysterious."</note> in these words / and that causes many to wonder; and various explanations are given to take away the wonder: I shall present some of them to you / though I hold only with the last.

<margin>John 16:7. <note>original Latin: "Quia nondum sanctum Spiritum miserat ideo & tactu suo Mariam prohibebat, dicens nondum ascendi in cælum, unde ipse Spiritum sanctum ad vos mittet. Cyril. l. 12. in Joan. c. 50."</note> Because he had not yet sent the Holy Spirit, he therefore forbade Mary from touching him, saying: I have not yet ascended into heaven, from whence I will send the Holy Spirit to you. He had died in weakness and dishonor, but he rose in power and glory. He intended to say: although I have not yet ascended to my Father, yet I shall ascend shortly; therefore, do not behave toward me according to the place where I am, but according to that which belongs to me; and if you indeed wish to fall down, do it rather from afar, than that you should seem to touch me with such familiarity: therefore, do not touch me.

1. *From now on we know him no longer [in that way]*; if we had any earthly, physical thoughts of Christ—like the other Jews—that he would begin an earthly, temporal kingdom as a King in Israel, and that we would enjoy all kinds of earthly, physical advantages, such as honor, wealth, and power, then we nevertheless know him so no longer; we have cut off all such physical imaginings of his Kingdom. Paul’s ministry was esteemed less by some people than that of the other Apostles because he had not lived with Christ in the flesh; to which Paul wishes to answer: "Away with this physical knowledge; from now on we know no one according to the flesh." Our way of interacting with Christ is in a spiritual manner; indeed, this way carries the blessing, and not the other. <margin>John 20:29</margin> *Blessed are those who shall not have seen, and yet shall have believed.* Of his mother Mary, it is said that she received Jesus Christ twice: once in her body, and then in her soul; the first was indeed a greater miracle, but the second was a greater benefit. ### The Fourth Book. Part 4, Chapter 1, § 5.

->**[Column 1]**<-

This was Christ’s command; instead of touching him, she had to go with a message to his Apostles, and this was a greater blessing for them both. Besides the Angels, Mary Magdalene was the first who preached of this resurrection; she, out of whom seven demons had once been driven, now had the Holy Spirit within her. She, who was but a woman, was now made by Christ into an Apostle, an *Apostle of the Apostles* <note>original Latin: "Apostolorum Apostola"</note>, for she was sent to them. And the message she was to deliver was Christ’s Resurrection and <term>Ascension (Hemel-baert)<gloss>literally "heaven-journey," referring to Christ's return to the Father</gloss></term>; and what was this other than the Gospel—indeed, the very pith and core of the Gospel? This was the first sermon ever given by any human being regarding Christ’s resurrection. And some have compared this deed of hers to Eve’s sin; a woman was the first messenger of this, our joy, because it was through the service of a woman that sorrow was first brought upon us.

But what does he mean to say by speaking of his Ascension, while we are still only at his resurrection? I believe this was done to prevent her misunderstanding <note>The Dutch "mis-slagh" implies a mistake in judgment or an error in expectation.</note>, as she might have thought: "Since Christ has now risen, we shall enjoy his company again just as before." No, says Christ, I have not risen to stay with you, or to dwell with you on earth as I did previously; my resurrection is in relation to my

<column-break/>

Ascension. See, the stars do not rise so quickly without immediately climbing upwards; so too, Christ had no sooner risen than he was at once occupied with his Ascension.

But where does he wish to go? To his Father and our Father, to his God and our God. Each word is a step or rung of <term>Jacob’s ladder<gloss>A reference to the ladder seen in a vision by the patriarch Jacob, connecting Earth to Heaven</gloss></term>, by which we can climb up into Heaven. As, 1. *Father* is a name of good affection; in it are the <term>depths of compassion (inghewanden van mededoogentheyt)<gloss>literally "the bowels of compassion," an archaic way of describing deep-seated, gut-level mercy</gloss></term>. Oh, what kindness is in a Father! And yet, how many fathers lack the means to express their good affection toward their child? Therefore, *God* is added here, so that we might not think he will lack the means. Oh, blessed message! This is the voice of the Father to his Son: <margin>Luke 15:31</margin> *all that is mine is yours*. Now, since this Father is also God, and since all that is God's is also ours, what more can we desire than all that God has? Or all that is worthy of God? But oh, here is the question: is this Father and God also ours? That he is Christ’s Father and Christ’s God is beyond all doubt; but that his Father should also be our Father, and his God our God—oh, that is a true Gospel! Oh, what a Gospel this is then!

# The Sight of Jesus.

...have become ours, and ours have become his again. It is not strange that Luther once said that the best divinity consists in pronouns <note>original Dutch: "voornamen," referring here to possessive pronouns like "mine" and "ours." Martin Luther famously argued that the power of the Gospel lies in the personal application of God's promises.</note>; for just as there is no comfort in Heaven without God, and in God no comfort without a Father, so too is there no comfort in Father, Heaven, or God without the word *Our*, to give us a sense of ownership in them all. Oh, that joyful news that Christ said to Mary, and Mary to us: *I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.* Oh, what dull hearts we have, that we are not moved more by this joyful message! No sooner had Christ risen than he was careful to appear first to Mary; and no sooner had he appeared to her than he immediately sent her to the others: *go hence to my brothers, and tell them*; he wanted both Mary and the other Apostles to hear of the sweetness of his loving-kindness early in the morning. Oh, alas! A few days ago they were stricken with care and fear, but now he has provided them with joy; and no sooner had they heard this message <margin>Isaiah 9:3</margin> than they were glad, just as one rejoices in the harvest, or as one is joyful when dividing the spoils. Christ’s resurrection was a reason for unspeakable joy for them; and how can we hear of the same joyful message and not be moved more by it? Come, Christians, since this

<column-break/>

opportunity extends to us as well, and concerns us just as much, let our hearts also turn to this key; that just as we may weep with those who weep over Christ’s absence, we may also leap for joy over his return and rejoice with those who are glad. So much for the first appearance.

# The Fourth Book. Part 4. Chapter 1. § 6.

...to them that evening; and so that the day would not be missed, it was on the evening of that same day, being the first day of the week.

1. It was the same day, that is, the very day of the resurrection; he could not bear for them to remain in doubt for long; the sun was not allowed to set before the Sun of Righteousness <note>A traditional title for Christ, drawn from the book of Malachi 4:2.</note> had shone upon them again. On the same day that he had appeared to Peter, to the two disciples going to Emmaus, to the women coming to the grave, and to Mary Magdalene—as we have already understood—on that same day he also appeared to the ten disciples. Oh, what a blessed day was this! It was the day of his resurrection, and the day of these various appearances.

2. It was on the evening of that same day. Both in the morning, at noon, and in the evening, Christ showed himself alive through various infallible signs. Early in the morning he appeared to Mary, and immediately thereafter to the three Maries, who touched his feet and worshipped him. Around noon he appeared to Simon Peter: in the afternoon he walked with two of his disciples toward a village called Emmaus, nearly eight miles—namely sixty stadia <term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance; sixty stadia is roughly 7 miles or 11 kilometers</term>—being about two and a half hours' walk; and in the evening of the same day he returned from Emmaus to Jerusalem. At all times of the day, Christ is ready and active to prepare grace for his people.

<column-break/>

3. It was on the evening of that same day, being the first day of the week: "on the first of the sabbaths" <note>original Greek: τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων (tē mia tōn sabbatōn)</note>, that is, on one of the Sabbath days. However, the Greek words are a Hebrew way of speaking, and it is very common among the Hebrews to signify "the first" by saying "one" <margin>Genesis 1:5</margin>, as in Genesis 1:5: "and the evening and the morning were the first day" <note>In the original Hebrew and the Dutch text here, it literally reads "day one."</note>. And when the Greek words say "on one of the Sabbaths" <note>original Greek: τῶν σαββάτων (tōn sabbatōn)</note>, that must either be understood literally as "Sabbaths" or figuratively for the entire week. This manner of speaking was common among the Jews, just as Luke presents the words of the Pharisee <margin>Luke 18:12</margin>: "I fast twice on the Sabbath" <note>original Greek: Νηστεύω δὶς τοῦ σαββάτου (Nēsteuō dis tou sabbatou)</note>, that is, twice a week, for it is impossible to fast twice in a single day. For this reason, the translator has rendered it thus: "on the first day of the week" <note>original Latin: *primo die hebdomadis*</note>. In this, we have a revelation of his kindness: Christ did not postpone showing himself to his Apostles for several days—indeed, he did not postpone it for even a single day—but did so on that very first day. When Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, he did not do so at the first opportunity, and yet he dealt with them kindly and quite excellently; but oh, Christ’s friendliness far surpasses that of Joseph, for on the first day of the week, on the very day he had risen, he appeared to them. This concerns the timing.

### The Fourth Book. Part 4, Chapter 1, Section 6.
Oooo 3

...the doors being closed. I know that it is against the nature of a body that one should pass through another while both bodies remain whole, and it is a rule in **Philosophy** <term>Philosophy: In this context, the author refers to "natural philosophy," what we would now call physics or the natural laws of the material world.</term> that the penetration of bodies is entirely impossible; however, as for me, I shall not argue against God's omnipotence. This answer is sufficient for me against all objections, whether from **Papists** <note>original: "Papisten," a common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note> or **Lutherans**, that the creature must give way to its Creator, and that the Creator does not need to pass through the creature. Christ entered while the doors were closed, doing so either because the door gave way before him—the disciples not knowing how—or otherwise by changing the substance of the door so that his body could pass through it without damage. I know nothing else than that He who solidified the waters to carry his body could also have thinned the door to make a way for his body.

3. The persons to whom he appeared were his disciples; they who were locked in an inner room, not daring to come outside the doors for fear of the Jews, to them he has now appeared. It is Christ’s common way to appear to those who are full of fear and sadness, and in the greatest difficulties; <margin>Isaiah 43:2.</margin> when you go through the water, I will be with you, and through the rivers, they shall not overflow you. <margin>Psalm 23:4.</margin> Even though I walked in a valley of the shadow of death, I would fear no evil (says David) for you are with me. He was with Joseph in the prison, with Jonah in the deep, with Daniel in the lions' den, with the three youths in the fiery furnace: Look, I <margin>Daniel 3:25.</margin>

<column-break/>

see four men (said **Nebuchadnezzar**) walking free in the midst of the fire, and the form of the fourth is like a Son of the Gods. So he was also with Paul, standing <margin>2 Timothy 4:16, 17.</margin> before Nero: although all men have forsaken me, yet the Lord Christ has stood by me and strengthened me. And do his appearances on this day not also mean this? When Mary was full of sorrow, Christ appeared to her; the disciples going to **Emmaus**, speaking of all those things that had happened and being sad, then Christ appeared to them; and all the Apostles, fearing the Jews and therefore closing the doors so that no one should come in, then Christ appeared to them; it was to his disciples, his dejected, dismayed, and fearful disciples, that he appeared.

4. The manner in which he appeared consists of these things: 1. He stood in the midst; 2. He said, "Peace be unto you"; 3. He showed them his hands and his side.

1. He stood in the midst. In this, he showed himself here as a "common good"; things standing in the middle are common to all. And he stood in the midst as a **Universal Savior** <note>original: "gemeene Salighmaecker," referring to a Savior who belongs equally to all believers.</note>, and for this reason our faith is called a common faith: <margin>Titus 1:4.</margin> to Titus, my true son according to the common faith. And our <margin>Jude verse 3.</margin> salvation is called the common salvation: I make every effort...

But I notice that there is even more to it, that he stood in the middle; for the middle is Christ’s place by nature; he is the second person in the **Trinity**; and the middle is Christ’s place through his ministry; he acts between God and man; and the middle is Christ’s place in regard to his person: he is the **God-man**, one who has his part in both parties; it had to be the middle person who was the **Mediator**, who took this mediation between God and us upon himself. We read in Roman history that when the Romans and Sabines <note>A reference to the legendary "Intervention of the Sabine Women," who stepped between their Roman husbands and Sabine fathers to stop a war.</note> wanted to go to war with one another, the women—being daughters of the one side and wives of the other—placed themselves between the two and settled the dispute; and through their intervention, since they had their own kin on both sides, those who previously stood in the highest enmity against one another were thereafter united into one body and state. God and we were enemies, but Christ stood in the middle to reconcile us with God and to kill this enmity; and for this reason Christ is called **the Mediator** <note>original Greek: "μεσίτης" (mesitēs)</note>, a word that is unique to the Scripture and is not found in any worldly writers. Oh, what a comfort is here, that we see Jesus Christ standing in the middle? # Looking unto Jesus.

1. Some believe that these scars or impressions were like trophies of victory; there is nothing so pleasant for a lover as to bear the scars of the wounds he received for his beloved; and for a soldier, nothing is more glorious than to show the wounds he received in service to the Fatherland; what are these other than so many proofs of his courage and signs of his victory?

<margin>Bede on Luke.</margin>
This was the judgment of Bede <note>original: "Beda." Referring to the Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note>; Christ kept these scars, not because he was not powerful enough to heal them, but to spread the glory and triumph of his victory over death and hell.

2. Others believe that these scars and impressions served to present Christ’s luster and beauty, just as in slashed or embroidered garments the underlying silk cloth shines through all the more; so, from within Christ’s wounds, a much greater beauty shone forth. Aquinas says that even in the places of Christ’s wounds, there is a special comeliness. And Augustine remembers that even the martyrs shall keep some scars of their wounds in glory, because in them there is no ugliness, but dignity; and besides a certain beauty, they shall shine in their bodies according to the virtues in which they have shone.

<margin>Thomas [Aquinas], Part 3, Question 53, Article [5].</margin>
<margin>Augustine, [Book] 22, [On the] City of God.</margin>

3. Others recall that Christ kept these scars to pray for us through them;

<column-break/>

over these words, *we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous,* they make this very declaration: that God is reconciled through Christ’s presentation to him of the impressions and scars of his human nature.

<margin>1 John 2:1</margin>
<margin>Thomas [Aquinas] on 1 John 1, 2</margin>
Christ’s wounds are like so many open mouths, which cry for mercy before the <term>Vierschare</term> <note>original: "Vierschare." A traditional Dutch term for a tribunal or court of justice.</note> of his Father, just as Abel’s blood cried for vengeance.

4. Others judge that Christ kept these scars to shame the Jews with them on the Last Day, and all the ungodly in the world. It is Augustine’s judgment that just as Christ showed his hands and side to Thomas because he would not believe otherwise, he shall likewise show his wounds to all his enemies on the Last Day, saying,

<margin>Augustine, Book 2 on the Creed, Chapter 8.</margin>
> Come and see the man whom you crucified; come and see the marks of the nails and the mark of the spear; these are the hands and feet that you nailed to a piece of wood; this is the side that you pierced; for you and because of you it was opened, but you did not wish to enter therein to be saved.

And for this sentiment, they bring forward this passage of Scripture:

<margin>Revelation 1:7</margin>
> Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Even so, Amen.

### §. 7.
### Regarding Christ’s appearance to all his Apostles.

<margin>John 20:26, 27.</margin>
Immediately after this appearance to the ten Apostles, followed the appearance to all his Apostles, not one being absent; and after eight days his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them, and Jesus came, while the doors were closed, and stood in the midst, and said, "peace be unto you"; <margin>Verses 28, 29.</margin> after that he said to Thomas, "bring your finger here, and see my hands, and bring your hand, and thrust it into my side, and be not unbelieving, but believing": and Thomas answered, and said to him, "my Lord, and my God": Jesus said to him, "because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are they who shall not have seen, and yet shall have believed."

In this entire narrative, we have Christ’s appearance and its fruits.

1. In the appearance we have, as before: 1. the time. 2. the place. 3. the persons to whom he appeared, and then 4. the manner in which he appeared.

1. **The time**, "and after eight days"; it was on the same day, seven nights after the first appearances, being the first day of the week, which now, because of his resurrection and appearances, was called the Lord’s Day; <margin>Revelation 1:10.</margin> *I was in the spirit on the Lord’s day*: this serves (in my judgment <note>original: "na mijn oordeel"</note>)

<column-break/>

greatly for the esteem of the Lord’s Day; the first gathering of the Apostles after Christ’s death was on the first day of the week; and the second church assembly <note>original: "kerckelicke vergaderinghe"</note> that we read of was again on the first day of the week. "And after eight days"; a sign that the <term>Lord's-Day-Sabbath</term> <note>The author is referring to the theological shift of the day of rest from Saturday (the Jewish Sabbath) to Sunday (the day of Resurrection).</note> was instituted on the first day, and that the solemn assemblies of God’s people would henceforth be on the Lord’s days. It is a common observation that things and persons called *of the Lord* are sanctified and honored to a high degree; such as the grace of our Lord, Romans 16:20 <note>The source OCR says Rom 16:32, but as Romans 16 only contains 27 verses, this is likely a printer's error or a reference to a different numbering system.</note>; the Spirit of the Lord, 2 Corinthians 3:17; the beloved of the Lord, Romans 16:8; the glory of the Lord, 2 Corinthians 3:18; the word of the Lord, 1 Timothy 6:3; the cup of the Lord, 1 Corinthians 11:27. <margin>Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostles*, Sermon 15. <note>original: "Aug. de verb. Apo. fol. Serm. 15." Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) was a foundational Christian theologian.</note></margin> Augustine tells us that "the resurrection of the Lord has promised us an eternal day, and that it has sanctified the Lord’s day for us." This day, then, truly ought to be a holy and solemn day among us Christians. Now it was that, just as the rising of the Sun drives away the darkness, so Christ, the <term>Sun of Righteousness</term> <note>A common title for Christ based on Malachi 4:2, representing his role as the source of spiritual light and truth.</note>, shines into the world through the light of his resurrection; and for this reason we read that the Apostles observed this day above all others; *On the first day of the week, when the disciples had come together to break bread,* <margin>Acts 20:7.</margin> Paul spoke with them.

# The Fourth Book. 4. Part. Cap. 1. §. 7.

<margin>1 Cor. 16:1, 2.</margin>
...as I have ordered the churches in Galatia, so do you also: on every first day of the week, let every one of you lay something aside for himself, storing up a treasure, according as he has prospered. Charitable collections <note>original: *Liefde-schatten*, literally "love-treasures"</note> and church gatherings were customary on the first day of the week—that is, on the Lord’s day. This is proof enough for me against all who oppose this holy truth: that the first day of the week is our Christian Sabbath. For Christ rose on that day, and appeared several times before his Ascension <term>Ascension (translated from the old Dutch *Hemel-baert*, literally "heaven-journey")</term>; and after his Ascension, Christ sent the Holy Spirit down on that very same day; and after the sending of the Holy Spirit, the Apostles preached, the congregation gathered, the charitable collections were gathered, and the Lord's Supper was held. Christ's first appearance was on that day, and once that day had ended, he did not appear again until that day had come again eight days later.

2. The place is said to be "within"; it was possibly the same house in which the first appearance occurred; the house where Christ held the Passover and instituted the Lord’s Supper, 
<margin>Mark 14:15.</margin>
in which a large upper room was prepared for Christ. In this upper room, immediately after Christ's Ascension, was that famous gathering of all the Apostles, as we have understood. And in this upper room was that other famous 

<column-break/>

gathering of all twelve, when the Holy Spirit descended upon them in fiery tongues at the feast of Pentecost; and if we may believe the traditions, the seven Deacons (of whom Stephen was one) were chosen and appointed in this upper room. And in
<margin>Acts 6.</margin>
this upper room, the Apostles and Elders of the church at Jerusalem held that Council—being the pattern for all Councils—to settle the question: Must the believers from among the gentiles be circumcised? In
<margin>Acts 15.</margin>
this upper room, the Apostles were often gathered together to offer prayers and supplications; indeed, they were all gathered there with one accord in prayer and supplication;
<margin>Acts 1:14.</margin>
and for that reason Cyril, being Bishop of that place, called it <term>the upper church of the Apostles <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἀνωτέρα ἐκκλησία τῶν Ἀποστόλων"</note></term>, the mother-church of the Apostles. But of this upper room and its closed doors, we have spoken before.

3. And why Thomas with them? Was Thomas not one of them? Was Thomas not just as much a disciple of Christ as all the others? I admit that. <margin>Rom. 14:9</margin>
...having become alive again, he has become a Lord of both the living and the dead; for to this end Christ also died, and rose again, and lived again, so that he might rule over both the dead and the living. <note>original: *weder lebendigh gheworden* — This refers to the resurrection and the restoration of life.</note> And thus he is a Lord in two ways: 

**1. A Lord in authority,** to command whom and what he wants; he alone is a Lord over our persons, over our faith, over our **consciences**; and to him alone must we say, *Lord, what do you want me to do? Lord, save us, or we perish.* 

**2. He is a Lord in power;** he has the power to forgive and to cleanse; he has the power to make righteous and to make holy; he has the power to give life, and power to save completely <note>original: *volkomen saligh te maken* — to make perfectly or eternally blessed/saved.</note> all those who come to God through him; he has the power to hold his sheep fast, and power to cast out the accuser of our brothers; he has the power to defeat all his enemies, and power to subject all things to himself; in respect of all these things, Christ is a Lord. # Looking Unto Jesus.

<margin>Exodus 7:1, Exodus 4:16</margin> Is he God? Not only by communication, likeness, or in some respects, just as Angels and men are called gods; but simply, absolutely, and essentially, without any limitation. Sometimes we read in the Scripture that men or Angels, both good and evil, are called gods. Then the Lord said to Moses, *I have set you as a god over Pharaoh, and you shall have Aaron as a god.* <margin>Ezekiel 31:11</margin> Thus Nebuchadnezzar is called the "Mightiest," or the "God of the Heathens"; <margin>2 Corinthians 4:4</margin> and Satan is called the "god of this age." Likewise, the Rulers <note>original: *Overheden* — magistrates or civil authorities</note> are called gods; <margin>Exodus 22:28</margin> *you shall not curse the gods.* *I have said, you are gods;* <margin>Psalm 82:6</margin> the Angels are called gods; <margin>Psalm 138:1</margin> *in the presence of the gods I will sing Psalms to you.* But in all these instances, there is a limitation, or an improper <note>original: *oneyghentlicke* — meaning a figurative or metaphorical use of the word</note> way of speaking. Moses is called Pharaoh's god and Aaron's god, not absolutely, but with limitation to Pharaoh and Aaron; Nebuchadnezzar is called the "god of the heathens," and Satan the "god of this age"—not absolutely, but with relation to the heathens and this age. The Rulers and the Angels are called gods, not absolutely, but in respect of some ministry or excellence that has been shared with them by God. Only Jesus Christ is called God without any limitation, and not only in respect of some ministry or likeness, but absolutely, essentially, and properly; as being from all eternity God of God,

<column-break/>

as being God in essence from the Father before all the world. What? Is Christ only God in the way an Angel is a god? I wish to challenge all slanderers <note>The author is likely targeting groups like the Socinians or contemporary Arians who denied Christ's eternal divinity.</note> here: <margin>Hebrews 1:5</margin> to which of the Angels has he ever said, *you are my Son, today I have begotten <note>original: *gegenereert*</note> you*? Or to which of the Angels has he ever said, <margin>verse 8</margin> *your throne, O God, is for all eternity*? Or to which of the Angels has he ever said, <margin>Romans 8:3</margin> *you are my Son, my own Son, my only-begotten Son*? To which of the Angels has he ever said, *this is the true God, the great God, <margin>John 5:20, 1 John 5:20, Titus 2:13, Romans 9:5</margin> God to be praised above all for eternity, Amen*? To which of the Angels are these Divine properties given, such as eternity, immutability, omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence? But all these are ascribed to Christ. ### §. 2.

->Of meditating on Jesus in this looking [unto him].<-

II. Let us meditate on Jesus, as he has performed this work of our salvation for us in his resurrection. It is not enough that we know the necessary soul-saving truth, but we must also digest it, and we must draw the power from it for the nourishment and refreshment of our poor souls. Just as a person can chew and receive into his stomach as much food in half an hour as he needs at least seven or eight hours to digest, so a person can grasp more doctrines in his understanding in one hour than he is able to digest in many; what good these people would seem to obtain from sermons or teachings, who know nothing of pondering, I cannot see. Many have

<column-break/>

noted that this is the reason why so many sermons among us are given in vain; why the listeners, who run from one sermon to another and are not weary of reading and hearing, nevertheless have such faint and dead souls, because they will not set themselves to pondering. <margin>Josh. 1:8</margin>
well, this is the duty upon which I now insist; when you know these things, meditate, chew the cud <note>The author uses the Dutch term "her-knauwt," literally "re-chewing," a metaphor common in 17th-century divinity for the slow, repetitive process of spiritual meditation, much like a cow digesting grass.</note>, ponder, and weigh them back and forth. This was the sweetest sound she had ever heard; many times had she been called by that name, but never had she heard such a powerful, inwardly working, and sensitive voice as at this time; through this the cloud was driven away, and the Sun of Righteousness <note>original: "Sonne der gerechtightept," a common biblical title for Christ derived from Malachi 4:2, symbolizing his healing and life-giving power.</note> broke through; this one word, **Mary**, enlightened her eyes, dried her tears, refreshed her heart, and made her like-dead spirits living again. Christ’s single word wrought such a powerful change in her, as if she were entirely renewed, merely by being named. # Looking unto Jesus.

...to say, "Master, is it You?" With many briny tears I have sought You, and are You unexpectedly so close! Your absence was a hell to me, but Your presence is nothing less than a heaven: Oh, how my soul is ravished by Your voice? If the child leapt in the womb of Elizabeth, hearing only the greeting of Mary, how can my heart do otherwise than leap at Your greeting? I feel that I am entirely outside of myself. Instead of a sorrowful heart and a troubled spirit, I now feel a sweet and lovely stillness of mind; You are my comfort and soul-refreshment; whom have I in Heaven besides You? And whom should I desire on earth beside You? But yet I am not yet satisfied; it is not only the enjoyment of You, but the union with You for which my soul longs; not Your presence alone, but Your embraces—or my embraces of You—can satisfy me. Come then, and permit me, O my Lord, my God, that I may run to the handling of my highest delight, that I may fall at Your holy feet and wash them with the tears of my joy: O my Jesus! I cannot live with You in any other way than the Bride <note>A reference to the Bride in the Song of Solomon, often interpreted as the individual soul or the Church.</note> lives with You; now that I have found You, whom my soul so heartily loves, I shall hold You fast and not let You go. <margin>Song of Sol. 3:4</margin>

I find in all the divine books no soul who was more dejected by sorrow and more lifted up by joy than this one: O, reflect on this! When Christ is away, everything then is night; but Christ appearing 

<column-break/>

turns everything back into a bright day. There is no sorrow like that which is sensitive to Christ’s loss; and therefore this is noted in hell as the most grievous pain. Of these two, it is the greatest torment (say the theologians) to lose God and Jesus Christ, rather than to suffer all those flaming scourges, the unquenchable fire, the unbearable cold, and the hideous stench. On the other side, there is no joy in Heaven like this, which feels Christ’s presence; <margin>Psalm 16:11</margin> fullness of joy is in Your presence; pleasures are at Your right hand forevermore. I would rather be in hell with Christ (said someone) than in Heaven without Christ. <note>This sentiment is famously attributed to St. Bernard of Clairvaux, emphasizing that Christ's presence defines paradise, while His absence defines hell.</note> This is the true height of Heaven’s joy, the essence of glory, the highest blessedness of the saints.

O my soul, seek as Mary did; yes, seek and weep, and weep and seek, and do not rest until Christ has appeared. If you only occupy yourself in the use of the means <note>Technical term: "Means of Grace," referring to practices like prayer, scripture reading, and the sacraments through which God communicates with the soul.</note>, then He will appear sooner or later; or even if you should never see a joyful day on earth, a single sight of Christ in Heaven will make it all good. Truly, if you knew the joy of Christ’s presence, you would run through death and hell to come to Christ; <margin>Philippians 1:23</margin> Paul’s word was: *I have a desire to be departed and to be with Christ, for that is far better*; he regarded no death if he only [came] to Christ.

2. Think on this appearance to the ten disciples: when the doors were shut for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them, "Peace be unto you." Through His appearances, He sought to address the sorrow and fear that had completely taken hold of their hearts; sometimes they wandered outside and were grieved; and sometimes they kept themselves inside and locked the doors, being full of fear. In such a state comes Jesus Christ (as one who best knows the time and opportunity for grace and comfort) and stands in the middle of their gathering; He came in, though they knew not how, and no sooner was He inside than He greeted them: "Peace be unto you."

This was the first of all His wishes; no sooner had He risen than He wished peace to all His Apostles; no sooner did He come to them than these words opened His lips; these were the first words, at the first meeting, even on the first day. This is a sure sign that peace was in the heart of Jesus Christ; although with us it may be peace or war; there is a republic <note>The author uses the term "republic" (republijck) to describe the kingdom or commonwealth of Christ, reflecting the political language of the 17th-century Netherlands.</note> where Christ is King, and there is peace—yes, nothing but peace. Come, see, prove, and examine yourself: are you, O my soul, a member of this body? A subject of this republic? Has the influence of Christ's peace (sought and proven by His resurrection) any power over you?

Now we must know that a short prayer offered in faith, with a broken heart, and looking toward Christ’s honor, proves the growth of grace more than prayers of a whole day, even if they are eloquent, without such qualities. In every duty we must look at its end and goal; for if we humble ourselves in the feeling of our own wretchedness, and emptiness, and unfitness, and if we eye God's honor, power, praise, and glory, it is a good sign of growth; we call this the spiritual part of duty, as it comes from God, through God, and to God.

4. We grow when we are more rooted in Christ; thus the Apostle describes it: *growing up into him in all things.* So the Scripture speaks; the growth of grace is generally expressed through growing in Christ,
<margin>2 Peter 3:18.</margin>
*but grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.* It is just as if growing in grace were nothing at all without him, as indeed it is not. The philosophers, civic-minded men, and others may grow in virtues, but not in Christ. Come then, and let us examine and test whether we are more rooted in Christ; when trees are first planted, they have no deep roots in the earth; they can be pulled up by hand; but once the tree has shot up in height, it also makes its roots deeper and deeper in the earth, and it cannot be moved by any force; so it is with us too; we do not have such a firm and close union with Christ at the first stages, upon the first union; but the longer we live in him—like good trees spreading out in the sight of all men and bringing forth fruits of righteousness—the more we shall also root downwards through a stronger faith and firmer trust. <column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual growth, specifically exploring how believers advance through different stages of grace and how the quality of their spiritual practice matures over time. It follows a section describing how faith strengthens like a growing child.</meta>

<page-num>706</page-num>
<header>Looking unto Jesus.</header>

...and graces; although all graces can be habitually <note>In 17th-century theology, a "habit" referred to an internal quality or state of being rather than a repetitive action.</note> planted in him, yet the exercise of them is not all at once, but in stages. Thus the church speaks to Christ,
<margin>Song of Sol. 7:13.</margin>
*at our gates are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, O my beloved, which I have laid up for you;* she has all kinds of fruits which she has kept for Christ; new and old; she has young converts and those who are more rooted confessors than others; or she has new and old graces like others; she adds grace to grace; she was led from the exercise of one grace to another new grace. Just as the ungodly are led from one sin to another, and thus become worse and worse, so also the godly are led from one grace to another, and thus they grow,
<margin>Rom. 5:3, 4.</margin>
knowing that *tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.*

2. **We grow** when we find that new degrees of the same grace are added; as when love becomes more fervent, when knowledge becomes more abundant and better understands spiritual things; when a person's faith proceeds from throwing oneself upon Christ to finding sweetness in Christ, and so to the full assurance of faith; when godly sorrow proceeds from repenting over sin as something that strives against God’s holiness, to

<column-break/>

repentance for the same because it strives against him who loves us: which generally follows upon assurance; when obedience widens its borders and we become more and more abundant in the work of the Lord. *I know your works* (said Christ to the church of Thyatira) *and love, and service, and your works, and that the last are more than the first.*

3. **We grow** when the fruits and duties that we perform become riper, and more spiritual, and more to Christ’s honor; it may be that we do not pray more, or longer than we once did; it may be that our prayers do not have more understanding or memory than before; but that they are nevertheless more savory <note>meaning more spiritually pleasing or sincere</note>, more spiritual, and more to Christ’s honor than before. Now we must know that a short prayer offered in faith, with a broken heart, and looking to Christ’s honor, proves the growth of grace more than prayers of a whole day, though they be ever so eloquent, without such qualities. In every duty we must look at its end and aim; for if we humble ourselves in the feeling of our own wickedness <note>original: "snoodheydt," meaning vileness or lowliness</note>, and emptiness, and unfitness, and if we look to God’s honor, power, praise, and glory, it is a good sign of growth; we call this the spiritual part of duty, as it comes from God, through God, and to God.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 706 regarding the progression of spiritual maturity. While the previous page focused on adding new types of graces, this page focuses on the "rooting" process—how a believer's union with Christ deepens over time, moving from a fragile beginning to an unshakeable stability.</meta>

<page-num>707</page-num>
<header>The Fourth Book. Part 4. Chapter 2. Section 4.</header>

<margin>Ephesians 4:15</margin> 4. We grow when we are more rooted in Christ; so the Apostle describes it, *growing up into him in all things.* So the Scripture speaks; the growth of grace is generally expressed through growing in Christ, but grow up in the grace and know- <margin>2 Peter 3:18</margin> ledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Just as if growing in grace were nothing at all without him, as indeed it is not. The Philosophers, civic-minded people, and others may grow in virtues, but not in Christ. Come then, and let us examine and test whether we are more rooted in Christ: when trees are first planted, they do not have deep roots in the earth, and one can pull them up by hand; but once the tree has shot up in height, it also makes its roots deeper and deeper into the earth, and it cannot be moved by any force. So it is with us also; we do not have such a firm and close union with Christ at the first steps, upon the first union; but the longer we live in him—like good trees spreading themselves out in the sight of all people and bringing forth good fruits of righteousness—the more we shall also root downwards through a stronger faith and firmer trust.

Our union corresponds with that which unites us; now, at first, faith is but weak, like a smoking flax-wick <note>original: "roockende vlas-wieck" – a biblical metaphor from Isaiah 42:3 and Matthew 12:20 referring to a faith that is barely flickering but not yet extinguished.</note> and a poor bruised reed; but when faith draws the Spirit from Christ, the

<column-break/>

more it is exercised, the stronger it becomes. Just like young children: their strength is very weak at first, but the more they are nourished and exercised, so much more do they increase their strength in all their workings. Once Peter’s faith was so weak that Peter was unsettled at the voice of a servant girl; <note>This refers to Peter's denial of Jesus in the courtyard of the High Priest (Matthew 26:69-75).</note> but after having walked in Christ for a long time, he was so rooted that no threats, scourgings, imprisonments, appearances before the great and powerful, or any other thing could move him. You might object: "If we are not rooted in Christ at first, can a weak faith easily be overcome, and can we fall away?" It is true, if we are not rooted in any way; but we are indeed rooted at our first grafting into Christ through faith. Only this of which I speak is a higher degree of rooting, which not only excludes falling away, but even excludes shaking and wavering to a great degree. Certainly, every believer is not so situated; no, no, such is only the state of those who have walked long in Christ, who have become great in grace, holiness, and vivification <term>vivification: the theological concept of the "making alive" of the soul, where the believer is increasingly energized by the Holy Spirit to live for God.</term>.

O my soul, now test the growth of your vivification by these few signs: are you led to the exercise of new graces, adding grace to grace? Is your love more fervent, your faith stronger?

### V. Let us believe in Jesus
as he has carried out the great work of 

<column-break/>

our salvation for us in his resurrection. This is a chief article of our faith: *risen on the third day from the dead*; and this I now present as an object of our faith. Oh, let us believe this; let us believe our part and portion in it. And to that end, let us look upon Jesus as a <term>representative person</term>; <note>original: "ghemeen persoon" – in 17th-century theology, this refers to Christ acting as a legal representative or "public person" for all believers, much as a proxy acts for a group.</note> under whatever consideration he appears to us, it is in our place, and in that regard we must consider ourselves as his partners. Fearful souls might object here: "Is it possible that Christ is raised, and that I shall be raised with him, and in him? Is it possible that Christ died as a representative person for my sins? And that Christ is raised, and that he is justified through his resurrection as a representative person in my place?" Oh, the mystery of this redemption! Without all doubt, the <margin>1 Timothy 3:16</margin> mystery of godliness is great: *God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit.* <note>original: "Godt is geopenbaert in den vleesche, is gerechtveerdight in den Geest" – 1 Timothy 3:16. Here, "justified in the Spirit" refers to Christ being vindicated or declared righteous by his resurrection.</note> It is a mystery beyond my reach that Christ, who is God in the flesh, had to be justified in the Spirit for our justification; that Christ had to die in my place as a condemned man, and that having finished his work, he had to be raised again in my place as a righteous person. These things are unfathomable and surpass faith; oh, what shall I do? I find it to be a hard, yes, a very hard thing to believe this.

-> # Looking unto Jesus <-

the <note>This "the" completes the sentence from the previous page: "It seems to me that the least of the..."</note> Christian’s state is a joyful and comforting state: Zion’s children have the greatest cause for joy. <margin>Zephaniah 3:14</margin> Sing joyfully, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel; be glad and leap for joy with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem. And why indeed? A thousand reasons could be given, but here is one—one of the first: <margin>1 Corinthians 15:20</margin> Christ is raised from the dead and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The account of Christ's resurrection has always been a means of finding joy in God.

Someone might say, "What does Christ's resurrection have to do with me?" It is true: if you have no part in Christ, then Christ's resurrection does not concern you at all. But if Christ is yours, then you are raised with Him and in Him; then everything He has done was performed in your name and for your sake.

Others might object: "Even assuming that Christ's resurrection is mine, how am I bettered by it?" How? Do not all Christ’s privileges flow as much from the power of His resurrection as from His death? Tell me, what is your condition—what could be the state of your soul—from which you could not draw sweetness from Christ's resurrection? For instance:

1. Is your conscience disturbed over your sin? <margin>1 Peter 3:21</margin> The Apostle tells you that the appeal of a good conscience toward God is through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

2. Do you shrink back in fear of damnation? The Apostle tells you that

<column-break/>

He was delivered up for our sins, <margin>Romans 4:25</margin> and raised for our <term>justification</term> <note>original: "rechtveerdigh-makinge"; the legal act where God declares a sinner righteous through faith.</note>.

3. Do you doubt your <term>rebirth</term> <note>original: "weder-geboorte"; the spiritual renewal or being "born again."</note>? <margin>1 Peter 1:3</margin> The Apostle says that He has caused us to be born again through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

4. Are you everywhere distressed, persecuted, and tormented? <margin>2 Corinthians 4:10, 11</margin> The Apostle tells you wherein your confidence, comfort, and courage then consist: namely, in Christ's life, in Christ's resurrection. We always carry about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus might also be revealed in our body; for we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus might also be revealed in our mortal flesh. And thus <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> explains these following words <margin>verse 14</margin>: knowing that He who raised up the Lord Jesus shall also raise us up through Jesus. That is, to a "civil resurrection" <note>An outward or metaphorical resurrection referring to being lifted out of earthly misery.</note> from our torments. Paul was imprisoned and partially tortured, but through the power of Christ's resurrection, he foresaw his deliverance. Beza grounds this explanation on the following and preceding words, in which Paul compares his persecution to a death and his deliverance from it to a life, just as he had done previously in Chapter 1, verses 9 and 10.

5. Do you fear apostasy or falling away? Well, remember that the immutable power and endurance of the new covenant is established through the resurrection of Jesus Christ—

Away, away with all restless, doubtful, and anxious thoughts! Ponder what joy there once was in the foreseeing of Christ's resurrection, but especially what joy there was throughout the whole world when he was raised again from the dead. Then the angels came down from Heaven and appeared in white
