<margin>
Luke 24:41.
The Apostles, cheered by the Lord's Day, not only wanted it to be a most festive occasion, but also determined that it should be observed every week. <note>original: "Apostoli die dominico exhilarati, non solum ipsum festivissimum esse voluerunt, verum etiam per omnes hebdomadas frequentandum esse duxerunt."</note> Innocent I, Epistle to Decentius, book 1, chapter 4.
</margin>
than before! How I am assured that the disciples rejoiced greatly when they saw the Lord; yes, so joyful that they did not believe it for joy. It is noteworthy to see how all the ancient saints were taken up with these glad tidings, and for that reason even with the day on which Christ rose. Some call it "the first day of joy and gladness," and because of the joy that occurred on that day, the Apostles (they say) hallowed the first day of the week in honor and service of Jesus Christ. Augustine applied the words of the Psalm to this day: "This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it." (Psalm 118:24). Ignatius, who lived in the times of the Apostles and was a disciple of John, called it "the Queen, the Princess, and the Lady" by way of excellence among the other days of the week. Chrysostom calls it a "Royal day," and Gregory Nazianzen (Oration 42) says that it is higher than the highest, and wondrously above other days. Truly, the Lord’s day was held in high esteem by the early church, and the primary reason was Christ's resurrection from the dead. Oh, that on these days we could rejoice in the Lord, and rejoice again! Someone has remarked /

## §. 9.
### On Conformity with Jesus in this Looking.

IX. Let us become conformed to Jesus in respect of his resurrection. In this matter, I shall examine these questions: 1. In what must we become conformed? 2. How is this conformity wrought? 3. What are the means of this conformity on our part?

<margin>Rom. 6:4.</margin> 1. In what must we become conformed? I answer in a word: In our quickening <note>original: *levendighmakinghe*; a 17th-century term for "vivification" or being made spiritually alive through grace</note>. There is a likeness between our quickening and Christ’s resurrection; and if we wish to know what this consists of in particular, the answer of the Apostle is clear: just as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we also shall walk in newness of life. Christ’s resurrection was unto newness of life; it was a new life, distinct from his preceding life: and so our quickening is also a new life; a life from a new principle, of new works, of a new state, of a new relation, of new income <note>original: *inkomsten*; refers here to spiritual "in-flowings" or the graces received from God</note>, of a new sort or manner.

<column-break/>

<margin>Ephes. 2:2.</margin> 1. It is a life from a new principle. Before our quickening, our principle <note>the fundamental source or driving force of one's actions</note> was the flesh, the world, or the devil; in time past you walked according to the age of this world, according to the Prince of the power of the air, of the spirit that now works in the children of disobedience; but now we have a new principle: the Spirit of holiness, or of sanctification, the Spirit of God. It is the very same Spirit that dwells in Christ’s human nature and which raised him up; "if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you"; it is an indwelling Spirit; <margin>Rom. 8:11.</margin> just as the soul dwells in the body, so the Holy Spirit dwells in the soul of a reborn person, causing them to breathe, work, and live. This is the new principle that God places in us after our quickening.

<margin>Rom. 8:5.</margin> 2. It is a life of new workings. As our principle is, so also are our workings; those who are after the flesh mind the things of the flesh, but those who are after the Spirit mind the things of the Spirit. Some people, hearing of a good proposal <note>a worldly or business plan</note>, love it; they feel their soul pressing toward it with great activity; there is something in them that corresponds with what is proposed. But when they hear of divine love, and of the riches of grace, then their soul is still, immovable, and dead; there is no attraction to those things. But on the other hand, those who are made alive, they direct their strength, more or less according to their principle...

death; he shall not come under the dominion of sin, nor shall he fall entirely away from grace; that incorruptible seed through which he is born again shall always remain in him. <margin>Rom. 8:10</margin> *If Christ be in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness*; the body is indeed subject to physical death because of the remnants of sin, but the **Spirit** is life; even that small spark of grace is—because of the most perfect imputed righteousness of **Christ**—life here, and shall be life hereafter, yes, into eternity. And in this, our quickening corresponds with **Christ’s** resurrection; <margin>Rom. 6:4</margin> *just as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, raised to a new life, so we also must walk in newness of life.*

Regarding the second question: how is this quickening or conformity <note>Being made in the likeness of Christ</note> sought? I shall answer only regarding the state <note>the condition of the soul</note>, and thus our quickening is generally sought in this manner: 1. in the understanding, and 2. in the will.

# Looking Unto Jesus.

...to have Jesus Christ as an example. This example of Christ / although it is not for us / as it is for the Socinians <note>Followers of Socinianism, a 16th-century theological movement that emphasized Jesus as a moral example and human teacher, while denying His divine nature and the traditional doctrine of the atonement</note>, the *whole of Christ* <note>original: "totum Christi"</note>, it nevertheless helps much toward our quickening; who would deny that working after a pattern is very beneficial? Come then / and if we wish to lead a godly life / let us live just as Christ did after His resurrection. But how is that done? I answer /

1. See that we return to the grave no more; guard yourselves against any returning to our former state; you might say / what purpose does this warning serve? Has Christ not said / he who lives and believes in Me / shall not die for all eternity? Or not fall away? I answer / it is so / that they shall never wholly and finally fall away / yet they can fall hideously and terribly; they can lose that strength and power / that feeling / which they once had / they can touch so close to the grave / that they are reckoned both by themselves and by others with those who go down into the pit, set apart among the dead, as Heman <note>Heman the Ezrahite, the biblical figure traditionally identified as the author of the sorrowful Psalm 88</note> has testified of himself.
<margin>Psalm 88:5</margin>
The Apostle says something that would make a Christian person shudder; he speaks of some who have once been enlightened (through the Word) and have tasted the heavenly gifts (some flickerings of inward joy and peace) and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit (the common gifts and graces of the Spirit <note>In 17th-century theology, "common gifts" referred to spiritual experiences or abilities, like preaching or temporary joy, that could be felt even by those who were not truly saved</note>) and have
<margin>Hebrews 6:4, 5, 6</margin>

<column-break/>

tasted the good word of God (have found some taste in the sweet and salvific promises of the Gospel) and the powers of the age to come (they have had some rapturous understandings of the joy and glory in heaven); and yet fall away (through a total apostasy). Christians! how far this goes! I know that this is said only to those / who have the name that they live / and nothing more; but certainly it warns us all / not to approach the slope / the edge of the grave; and let us not give a single sin access / to live in it / or to continue in it.

walk as children of light. Walk / that is / direct yourselves in the works of God;

We see that the night is intended for rest / and that God, governing all things gently / has therefore drawn a curtain of darkness before us / so that we might rest kindly; like a wet-nurse <term>minnemoer: an archaic term for a nanny or wet-nurse</term> wishing to put her child to sleep / throws a cloth over its face / and hides the light everywhere: But when this natural Sun rises / then people go out to their labor; so also we / though we have slept in the darkness of the night in sin / we must nevertheless now awaken ourselves / since the Sun of the spiritual world has risen over us.

### The Fourth Book. Part 5. Chapter 1. Section 1.

<margin>Rom. 10:14, 17, 18.</margin>
He was not suddenly snatched away from them like Elijah; nor taken away in secret and hiddenly like Enoch, but in the presence of them all—His apostles as well as His disciples—He ascended into Heaven. But why not in the sight of all the Jews, so that they might know that He had risen and ascended into Heaven? Certainly, this was the intent: God preferred that the chief articles of faith should be learned through hearing rather than through seeing. Although Christ’s own disciples were taught through seeing, in order to better teach others who would not see, nevertheless the ordinary means to come to faith is hearing: *How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?* <note>original: "hoe ſullen ſy in hem gelooven , van welcken ſy niet gehoort en hebben ?"</note> --- So then faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. ### § 3.
#### Concerning the reasons why He ascended.

IV. As to why He has ascended, these are the reasons:

1. From Christ’s side: that He, through His suffering, should pass into glory; *ought not the Christ to suffer these things, and so enter into His glory?* <margin>Luke 24:26</margin> I will not enter into the dispute of whether Christ earned this for Himself; this is beyond dispute: that through His suffering (I will not say strictly "earned," but) He obtained this glory because He humbled Himself so greatly. God has exalted Him above the grave in His resurrection, above the earth in His Ascension, and above the heavens, seating Him at His right hand. And He ascended so that all prophecies concerning this would be fulfilled: *You have ascended on high.* <margin>Psal. 68:19</margin> <margin>Zach. 14:4</margin> And His feet

<column-break/>

shall stand in that day upon the Mount of Olives, which lies before Jerusalem toward the East. The types <note>In historical theology, "types" are Old Testament people or events that foreshadow Jesus.</note> of this were Enoch’s being taken up, Elijah’s ascent, Samson’s carrying of the gates of Gaza to the top of the mountain, and the High Priest’s entrance into the Holy of Holies; *Since we have a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, namely Jesus the Son of God.* <margin>Hebr. 4:14</margin> Truly, all these types, shadows, and prophecies had to be fulfilled, and therefore it was necessary on His part that Christ should ascend and enter into Heaven.

2. The reasons on Christ’s behalf are these: ---

1. That He might triumph in our place over sin, death, and hell. In His resurrection He conquered, but in His Ascension He triumphed; it was now that He led sin, death, and the Devil behind the wheels of His chariot as if in a triumph. <note>A "triumph" refers to the ancient Roman custom where a victorious general paraded through the city with his captives in tow.</note> And this is what the Psalmist and the Apostle mean when saying, *When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive:* <margin>Eph. 4:8</margin> He has conquered all our enemies and triumphed over them; He has overcome the world, bound the devil, plundered hell, weakened sin, and brought death to nothing; and now He has made a public display of triumph over them in His own person; He has led the captives bound to His chariot wheels, just as was the custom in the Roman Triumphs <meta>catchword: so=</meta>

### Of God’s right hand, and of Christ’s sitting there. ###

II. Regarding Christ’s sitting at God’s right hand / being a consequence of his Ascension / I shall examine / 1. What is God’s right hand? 2. What is the sitting there? 3. In what nature does Christ sit there? 4. Why does he sit at the right hand of God his Father in glory?

And just as in the natural, so also in the economical kingdom, the Father reigns immediately through the Son as Mediator: and from this it is that the Son as Mediator alone is said to sit at God's right hand, because the right of active administration, or immediate execution of the highest power, is uniquely proper to the Son, specifically as Mediator between God and men. <meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding Christ's session at the right hand of God, specifically addressing the completion of the sentence from the previous page concerning the cooperation of his two natures. It then enters a polemical defense against the Lutheran doctrine of the "communication of properties" (communicatio idiomatum).</meta>

Looking unto Jesus.

...that of the flesh; Christ is Mediator as God and man, and the glory has come to him as God and man, and living in his glory he rules and governs his Church as God and man; in his human nature he truly ascended alone into Heaven, but he sits at the right hand of God as Mediator in respect of both his natures. The Lutherans <note>Followers of Martin Luther’s theology, who in the 17th century held specific views on the physical presence of Christ’s body.</note> attribute this sitting at God’s right hand only to Christ’s human nature; they say this sitting is nothing other than an exaltation of his human nature to a perfect and free use of some of the divine attributes, such as omnipotence <note>All-powerfulness</note>, omniscience <note>All-knowingness</note>, and omnipresence <note>Being everywhere at once</note>. The ground of this error is that they think that upon the union of the two natures in Christ follows an actual communication of the divine attributes; so that the human nature is truly made omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. They claim this happens not through any mixing of the attributes, nor through any mere fellowship or convergence of the same toward one and the same operation—where each nature does its part with the fellowship of the other (this we allow)—but through an actual communication <term>communicatio idiomatum: the theological doctrine that the properties of the Divine Word can be ascribed to the human nature of Christ</term>, through which the divine attributes so become the attributes of the human nature that the human nature, through them, can work no less than the divine nature itself for its own perfection. Against this view

<column-break/>

we have these reasons: 1. The union cannot cause the human nature to have a greater share in the divine attributes than it causes the divine to have in the attributes of the human. 2. If a true and actual communication of the divine attributes were to follow, then it would necessarily have to include all attributes, such as eternity and infinity, seeing these are the divine essence itself, which can in no way be divided. 3. Infinite perfections cannot make finite natures perfect, any more than rational perfections can make irrational creatures perfect. 4. To what purpose would the created gifts serve—those which Christ received "above measure"—if much more glorious [divine] attributes had already entered into Jesus Christ and been communicated to him? Many other reasons are given, but I intentionally keep myself from all such points of contention.

# Looking unto Jesus.

<margin>Hebrews 1:6</margin> ...but having entered into the world, the Angels of God worshipped him; but because through his sitting at the right hand of God the Divine nature is revealed, and the human nature exalted to that dignity and glory which it never had before, therefore now especially, and from that time on, the honor and dignity of worship has been shared with him as God and man. And therefore the theologians generally establish this as a result of *Christ’s* sitting at God’s right hand: namely, that *Christ*, as both God and man, is the object of divine worship.

<margin>Chrysostom, Homily 5 on Hebrews <note>original: "Christ. hom. 5. in Hebr." — Refers to John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note></margin> O, it is a great matter, and wonderful, and full of amazement, that the man *Christ* sits here above at the right hand of God, and is worshipped by the Angels and Archangels. The grace of the union <note>This refers to the "hypostatic union," the theological doctrine that Christ's divine and human natures are united in one person.</note> was already given to *Jesus* beforehand, and so he was worshipped even before his suffering; but after he <margin>Philippians 2:8, 10, 11</margin> humbled himself, being obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, then (yes, and for that reason) God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name, so that in the name of *Jesus* every knee should bow, of those in Heaven, and those on earth, and those under the earth, and every tongue should confess that *Jesus Christ* is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. He was a Lord before, because he is the Son of God; but now he is a Lord again through the power of his humiliation and his sitting at God’s right hand.

<column-break/>

And do not trouble yourself with the objections of those who say that if *Christ* must be worshipped as God and man, then the human nature itself is being worshipped. The person who is worshipped is man, but the humanity itself is not the specific object of worship. There is a distinction between the composite <note>The person of Christ as a whole.</note> and the abstract <note>The human nature viewed in isolation.</note>; although the man *Christ* is God, nevertheless his humanity is not God, and consequently must not be worshipped with that worship which is properly and essentially divine. Truly, if worship were appropriate for *Christ’s* humanity alone, then his humanity could help and save us; but *Christ’s* humanity cannot help and save us [on its own], because <term>every action belongs to the person</term> <note>original: "omnis actio est suppositi" — A philosophical rule stating that actions are performed by an individual person (the subject), not by a nature or an abstract quality.</note>, and the human nature of *Christ* is not a <term>suppositum</term> <note>original: "suppositum" — A technical term for a self-subsisting individual or person; here it means the human nature does not exist as a separate person from the divine Word.</note>, not a self-standing or personal being.

He is seated at the right hand of God as a High Priest, or Minister, to pray for us; for *Christ* has not entered into <margin>Hebrews 9:24</margin> the sanctuary made with hands, which is a copy of the true one, but into Heaven itself, now to appear before the face...

And there is yet another ground for hope; not only shall we sit with Christ in his glory, but we even now sit with him in glory: Christ has not only entered into Heaven to prepare a place for us, but he sits in Heaven in our place, and God looks upon him as that great image of that whole body, of which he is the head, and he delights himself seeing them all glorified as in his Son. Christ is now exalted in our nature; this is that wonderful thing, about which Chrysostomus <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> stood amazed, that the same nature, of which God said, *thou art dust, and shalt return to dust*, shall now sit in Heaven at God's right hand: yet not only the human nature, but Christ sits there in his person as a representative person <note>original: "gemeene persoon" — a legal or theological term for one who acts on behalf of others, like a head of state or a proxy.</note> in our place; he is on his throne, and we sit with him in the super-celestial places. Oh, what grounds and pillars of hope arise from this!

Among the ancients it was a custom that in days of great joy and on feast days, they gave presents and distributed honors among the people. When the walls of Jerusalem were built, it is recounted that all <margin>Neh. 8:10</margin> the people went their way to eat, and to drink, and to send portions. And on the feast of Purim <margin>Esth. 9:22</margin> they made days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor. So also has Christ, in the days of his Majesty and homage, in that great <margin>Ephes. 4:8</margin> and glorious triumph—when he ascended up on high—led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.

Regarding this sending of the Spirit, or these gifts of Christ to his Church, I shall treat their fulfillment as it reveals itself in these words:
<margin>Acts 2:2, 3, 4</margin>
> *And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.*

In these words we shall notice these particular points: the time when; the persons upon whom; the manner how; the measure according to which; and the reasons why the Holy Spirit was sent.

We find in the Scripture special, memorable things presented with the number of fifty. Such as the fifty days from Israel’s departure out of Egypt until the day of the giving of the Law. And in the fiftieth year was the great Feast of the Jubilee year <note>A year of biblical celebration where debts were forgiven and slaves set free.</note>, being the time of the remission of debts and of the restoration of men to their original state. And fifty days was the correct appointed time for the Jews' Harvest, being defined as it were by two famous days, of which the first was the beginning and the second was its end; the beginning was the second day of the Passover <note>original: "δευτέρα τὸ πάσχα" (deutera to pascha)</note>; the end was Pentecost <note>original: "πεντηκοστή" (Pentēkostē)</note>, the fiftieth day thereafter, called Pentecost <note>original: "Pinxter"</note>. On the second day <margin>Levit. 23:10</margin> they offered a sheaf of the firstfruits of their harvest; at the feast of Pentecost they offered <margin>Verse 17</margin> two wave-loaves. The sheaf being offered, all fruits in the entire field were sanctified; and the two loaves being offered, it was a sign that the harvest was ended and done. The Spirit blows wherever he wishes.

4. He came like a mighty rushing wind; just as the wind is sometimes of such force that it splits and cleaves mountains and rocks, uproots trees, and blows down buildings; so also are the workings of the Holy Spirit; he breaks everything down before him, he takes captive various high thoughts, he overcomes the world, beginning from Jerusalem, and spreading over the whole earth; he is powerful in his workings, making the boldest and most courageous men shake and tremble, and even crushing stony hearts; certainly our words without this Spirit are but a weak breeze; we can exhaust ourselves, and yet not soften any souls;

# Looking unto Jesus.

<margin>Psalm 84:5, 11.</margin>
David says, "Blessed are those who dwell in your house; — I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than to dwell for long in the tents of wickedness." <note>The author is quoting Psalm 84:10, emphasizing the blessing of being in God's presence.</note> Those who remained in this house <note>Referring to the "Upper Room" in Jerusalem where the disciples gathered.</note> were under the promise that the Holy Spirit would come, and now the promise was fulfilled for them, for he filled the entire house where they sat. I say, "where they sat," to signify that none of all the other houses in Jerusalem felt this mighty, driving wind; there was no assembly of the Saints in any corner of the city except in this house alone; or if there had been any other assembly, this Spirit did not blow upon any of them where these people were not; that house, and only that house, did he fill where they sat. And this blowing upon a specific place is a true characteristic of the Holy 
<margin>John 3:8.</margin>
Spirit; "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know from where it comes or where it goes; so is everyone who is born of the Spirit." The Spirit blows where he wishes and upon whom he wishes, and they shall feel it enough, while others around them feel nothing at all: do we not sometimes have the experience of this in our own meetings? A sound is heard, a wind blows, and it may be that only one or two hear the sound and feel the blowing inwardly to their salvation; it may be that one person here and another there feels the Spirit, and is thereby sensibly 

<column-break/>

moved and touched; but twenty on this side and forty on the other side of him remain sitting quite still and go their way, being no more moved than when they first came into God’s presence. Oh, that it would please this Spirit of the Lord to come daily and constantly into our meetings! Oh, that he would blow upon this person, and that person, and that one! Oh, that he would fill all souls in the gathering with the heavenly blowing! Come, O Holy Spirit; awake,
<margin>Song of Solomon 4:16.</margin>
O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, that its spices may flow out.
6. He came down in the form of tongues. As someone aptly said, this wind brought tongues—indeed, a whole downpour of tongues. The Apostles were not only breathed upon for their own benefit, but they were given gifts to share this blessing with many others. But why did the Holy Spirit appear in the form of tongues? I answer: 1. The tongue is a sign of the proceeding of the Holy Spirit from the Word of the Father; <note>In traditional Christian theology, the Spirit is seen as proceeding from the Father and the Son (the Word).</note> just as the tongue has the closest fellowship with the word and is moved by the word of the heart to express it through the sound of the voice, so also the Holy Spirit has the closest fellowship that can exist with the Word of God, and he is the expresser of his voice and the speaker of his will.
2. The tongue is the only instrument of knowledge, which conveys it from one person to another.

2. 3. Yet there is a distinction in the measure of his sending. At first, he was only sent with drops and like a dew, but now he is poured out in a downpour and abundance; the Holy Spirit, says Paul <margin>Titus 3:6</margin>, is richly poured out over us through

<column-break/>

Just as there are degrees in the wind <note>original Latin: "aura, ventus, procella"</note>—a cool breeze, a wind, and a storm—so also we cannot deny the degrees in the Spirit. The Apostles received the Spirit at Christ’s resurrection, but now they are filled with the Spirit; then it was only a cool breeze, but now it was a mighty wind. And in truth, never was the Spirit given to men in such a measure as at this time; the Fathers before them, and we and our fathers after them, have only (so to speak) a hin <term>hin: an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, roughly 6 liters, used here to represent a small portion</term> of the Spirit compared to their epha <term>epha: a much larger Hebrew dry measure, about 36 liters, used here to represent the vast abundance of Pentecost</term>; such a Pentecost as this never was, neither before nor after; it was Christ’s coronation day, the day of his seating upon his throne, when he gave these gifts to men, and therefore on that day all glory was shown, above all other days. Thus far concerning the measure of the Spirit, which is now given to Christ’s church.

# Looking unto Jesus.

Not that they were previously devoid of the Spirit, but now they were more filled with the Spirit than they had been before; and they spoke with other tongues—different ones than they had learned. It is probable that until this time they had known no other than the **Syriac** tongue <note>The author refers to Aramaic, the common language of Judea at the time</note>, but now in the blink of an eye, they could speak **Greek**, **Latin**, **Arabic**, **Persian**, **Parthian**, and what else? God’s wisdom and loving-kindness can clearly be seen here: that the means of different languages, which had been the cause of **Babel’s** confusion, must here be the very same means given to the **Apostles** to bring about **Zion’s** building up. Thus, the curse being taken away, a blessing comes in its place; the confusion of languages is united for God’s glory. This was the result of the tongues: that no speech or language on earth would exist where His name, glory, and Gospel would not be heard among them.

And here there is even more to note: that they spoke with other tongues, just as the Spirit gave them utterance. The word "utterance" in the original language is <term>to speak out clearly<note>Greek: ἀποφθἐγγεσθαι (apophthengesthai)</note></term>; you have likely heard of <term>Apophthegms<note>Wise and weighty sayings</note></term>, which refers to the speaking of wise and significant proverbs. <column-break/>

of our redemption, of **Christ’s** merits, of the glory and riches of His grace, and of the honor we owe His Name because of all His loving-kindnesses. Others add that they spoke of the wondrous works of the **Trinity**, such as our creation, redemption, and sanctification, and what generally pertains to human salvation. Their words were not the <gloss>crudities</gloss> of their own brains, nor poor, trivial, and common matter; but <term>Great Things<note>Latin: Magnalia</note></term>, large and high matters, <term>Apophthegms</term> or divine oracles, just as the Spirit gave them to utter. But these reasons are far from us <note>meaning these specific miraculous gifts are distinct from common experience</note>.

### The Fourth Book. Part 5. Chapter 1. Section 11.

...some were appointed who were full of the Holy Spirit; and it is said of **Stephen** that he was full of the Holy Spirit; and **Barnabas** was called a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is commonly said to fill believers; but whether this is the person of the Holy Spirit, or the impressions <note>The outward effects or influences</note> of the Holy Spirit, is a very great point of difference. As for me, I am inclined to side with those who say it is not only the impressions of the Spirit, the qualities of holiness, the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit, or—as some think—<term>habitual grace<note>A theological term referring to a permanent disposition or "habit" of holiness infused into the soul</note></term> in a special way; but that the Holy Spirit himself fills, and dwells, and reigns in the hearts of all reborn people. And this seems clear to me: 1. From Scripture. 2. From logical arguments.

<margin>John 7:38, 39</margin>
**1.** The Scripture passages are these: *He that believeth on me, as the Scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.* And this he spoke of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. Regarding these words, *out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water*, by the "living water" is understood grace; by the "rivers of living water," the manifold graces of the Spirit; by the "flowing" of these rivers, the overflowing and sharing of these graces from one person to another; and by the "belly" from which these rivers would

<column-break/>

flow, is understood the heart clothed or filled with the Holy Spirit. Now the spring-head and the rivers, the fountain and the streams, are different things and must be distinguished; the one is the cause, and the other the effect; the one is the tree, and the other the fruit. The Holy Spirit filling the hearts of believers is the origin and the fountain from which all these streams of living water flow; and therefore the Evangelist says expressly, *this he spoke of the Spirit, which they that believe in him should receive*. Of what Spirit? Even of the Holy Spirit, who was not yet given in full measure, because Jesus was not yet glorified. It is the same Spirit whom believers receive, from whom all these streams of living water flow; but these streams do not flow from habitual grace, nor from any of the individual graces of the Holy Spirit, but from the Holy Spirit himself.

<margin>John 16:13</margin>
Again: *When the Spirit of truth is come, he will guide you into all truth—and he will show you things to come.* Now, the "habits" or dispositions of grace cannot lead, nor teach, nor announce things to come to a person; the habits of grace cannot speak nor hear; just as it is written there: *he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak.* This can be no other than the Spirit in his own person; this is the **Comforter** <note>Also known as the Paraclete; the Holy Spirit acting as an advocate or helper</note>, who hears and speaks and leads into all truth.

<summary>This page argues that the Holy Spirit dwells personally within believers, rather than just acting as a vague influence or a set of holy qualities. The author uses the metaphors of a fountain and its streams to distinguish the Spirit's personhood from the graces He produces.</summary>

This union is by way of appropriation <term>the logical or theological attribution of a property to a person without changing their essence</term> / and not by way of mingling; if a heap of wheat and a stone were joined together / there is a union / they make but one heap / but the wheat cannot say / I am a stone, nor can the stone say / I am wheat, because this union is only by way of appropriation; but when wine and water are united with each other / then each part can say / I am water, and I am wine, because this union is not just through appropriation / but through mingling. There is surely a great union between the Spirit and a believer's soul / nevertheless the believer cannot properly say / I am the Spirit, or I am like God, because their union is only through appropriation / and not through mingling.

->Looking to Jesus.<-

<margin>*1 Cor. 2:12.</margin> [We have received] not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. The things given to us may indeed be received by us, and yet the receiving of them may not be known to us; therefore the Spirit comes for our further consolation, and places his hand and seal upon our reception; he shines upon our graces, or enlightens our graces, whereby we may know that we believe, and that we live. In truth, this is something special in God’s own people; sometimes (notwithstanding this seal) we can be in such a state as Paul was with his company in the ship <margin>Acts 27:20</margin> when neither sun nor stars appeared to them for many days; so it can also be for a long time that neither sun nor stars appear to us; neither light in God's countenance, nor light in our souls; no grace descending from God, nor grace bringing our soul to God; yet if we do in this dark state as Paul did with his company—that is, if we cast out the anchor even in the dark night of temptation, and wish and pray for the day to come—then God will appear, and everything will light up; we shall finally see the light from without and from within; surely the Morning Star shall rise in our hearts.

5. There is an operation of joy and consolation; and this seal is yet a further gift of the Spirit; we see that the operations of the Spirit are of two kinds: either in us through the im-

<column-break/>

printing of sanctifying grace, or upon us through the shining upon our souls, and through the sweet feeling of joy; habitual grace <note>original: "hebbelicke genade," a theological term referring to a permanent disposition or quality of the soul rather than a fleeting emotion</note>, or sanctifying grace, is somewhat more steady and always like itself; but the operation of consolation and joy is of the nature of those benefits of God which he sometimes gives, and sometimes does not; and from this it follows that a Christian may well have grace, and may know that he is in the state of grace, and yet in the matter of consolation, God is not with him. So it was with Job; he knew that his Redeemer lived, and he had resolved to trust in Him even though He should slay him; he knew that he was no hypocrite <note>original: "gheveynsde"</note>, and that his grace was sincere; notwithstanding all the objections and accusations of his friends, they could not move him from his integrity with their arguments: *I will hold fast to my righteousness, and will not let it go* <margin>Job 27</margin>; but for that time he nonetheless saw no light from Heaven, but he was in a sad and distressed state, until it pleased the Lord to reveal His favor to him again in a special way. Now this operation of joy generally does not come but after faith, and after many experiences of God's love, and after much waiting upon God. These are the various operations of the sealing of the Spirit.

# Looking unto Jesus.

...to learn and to know for yourself. Learn 1. Christ’s Ascension: how, and to where, and why he has ascended. 2. Learn the sitting of Christ at God’s right hand; O the depths and riches of that spiritual Heavenly knowledge! 3. Learn the sending of the Holy Spirit; there is not a single circumstance in it that is not worthy of your diligence; worlds full of riches (ten thousand times better than gold, or silver, or precious stones) are found in the digging of these mines. Have not many students exhausted their brains over much lesser subjects? What great labor has been spent to crawl into the secrets of nature? What great books have been written on Physics, Metaphysics, and Mathematics <note>The Dutch terms are "Natuur-weet" (Natural science), "Over-natuur-weet" (Metaphysics), and "Wis-konst" (Mathematics).</note>? And is this subject not Christ? Is not each of these subjects—Christ’s Ascension, Christ’s sitting, Christ’s sending of the Holy Spirit—of greater worth, preciousness, and usefulness than all of these? Come and study in that part of the Bible in which this is described; there is not a single rule or expression of Christ in the Scripture but there is matter enough to write about for an entire century. You do not need to leave old principles for new revelations <note>A common 17th-century warning against "enthusiasts" or radical groups who claimed direct prophecy outside of the Bible.</note>, for even in these matters you can continually find sweetness for all eternity.

§. 2.

->On the meditating upon Jesus in this looking.<-

II. Let us meditate on Jesus, as he has performed the great work of our salvation in these things for us. We must not only learn to understand these things, but we must ponder them until they have descended from the head into our hearts. Meditation is the weight that moves all the wheels; it would be of little use if we were commanded to long, to hope, to believe, to love, to rejoice, etc., if we would not first think. It is in meditation that the understanding works, that the will is inclined to follow, that attention is awakened, faith increased, hope confirmed, and love ignited. And therefore begin here, O my soul; it is a proper meditation that gives both life, and light, and movement to all your workings in all dealings.

# Looking Unto Jesus

When the Spirit shines upon our graces, then he seals us: O, meditate upon this shining, sealing work, and do not cease until the Holy Spirit radiates upon you with a spiritual light, and gives you a revelation, knowledge, and assurance of your effectual calling <note>This "effectual calling" refers to the theological concept of God's internal call to a person's soul that leads to salvation.</note>; there are many other reasons for the sending of the Spirit, but among them all, O my soul, meditate and contemplate these few; think on Christ’s Ascension, his session <note>original: "sitten". In theology, "the session of Christ" refers to his sitting at the right hand of God the Father.</note>, and the sending of the Spirit; but let every thought be attentive, fruitful, and specific; say, "Christ has entered into Heaven for my sake; he sits at the right hand of God for my sake; and he has sent down his Spirit into my heart." Oh, what workings will be within you, if you are but lively and active in the contemplation of these various acts!

->§. 3.<-

->Of Longing for Jesus in this Looking.<-

III. <column-break/>

saints, would not cry out, "Come, Holy Spirit; O Christ, give me your Spirit! You who give gifts to me, come and bestow these gifts upon me, yes, upon me." A believing soul cannot hear of any true revelation of his grace and glory without necessarily sending many sighs after him: "Oh, that Christ were mine! Oh, that I had some part in this work!" It is true, these actions are all in the past, but their power remains forever; and according to the power, might, and influence <note>original: "inbloeijinghe". A 17th-century term for the "in-flowing" of divine grace into the soul.</note> of these actions, so must also be the object of our desires; but now, what is the power of Christ’s Ascension other than that we also may ascend? And what is the power of Christ’s sitting, other than that we also may sit with him on his throne? And what is the power of the sending of his Spirit, other than that we also should have a part in the Holy Spirit? Oh, let these be the objects of our desires; come, let us pant and sigh for these things. As:

2. There is a testimony of the Spirit which the Spirit sometimes inspires and witnesses to a sanctified conscience with a hidden, quiet, soul-ravishing sound in this or a similar manner: *you are a child of God, you are among the number of those who shall be saved, you shall inherit eternal life*; and that indeed as surely and comfortingly as if that Angel from Heaven should say to you, as to Daniel: *O man greatly beloved*—powerful and noteworthy was the working of the Spirit in this manner upon the heart of that noble Martyr Robert Glover, at the first sight and appearance of the stake, when he cried out: *He is come, he is come.* <note>Robert Glover was an English Protestant martyr burned at the stake in 1555; he famously struggled with spiritual desertion until the moment he saw the stake.</note> Such an immediate coming of the Spirit was in the heart of Master Peacock <note>original: "Meester Pauw" — Thomas Peacock (c. 1564–1611), a Fellow of Brasenose College whose deathbed struggle with despair and eventual triumph was a famous example of Puritan piety.</note>, who after many days of the utmost terror confessed that the joy he

felt was unbelievable. Such an immediate working was also in the heart of Mistress Brettergh <note>Katherine Brettergh (1579–1601), known for her piety and her intense spiritual battle against the "terrors of hell" on her deathbed before finding peace.</note>, who after the return of her beloved [Lord], immediately cried out: *How wonderful! How wonderful! How wonderful are the loving-kindnesses of the Lord! Oh the joy, the joy, the joy that I now feel in my soul!* We feel and know through daily experience that Satan inspires immediately; and should the Holy Spirit then not also, in His Holy and Heavenly way, sometimes thus breathe in immediately?

Just as in the eye there is **innate light** <note>original: "lumen innatum"</note>, a certain in-born light to make the eye see external lights and colors; and just as there is in the ear **internal air** <note>original: "aer internus"</note>, a certain in-born sound and air to distinguish the sound that is external; so there is in a graced heart <term>graced heart</term> <note>A heart that has been transformed by God's saving grace.</note>, a new nature, a habitual inspiration from Heaven to distinguish the comforts of God's Spirit, witnessing immediately that we are God's children; there are some hidden and inexpressible features of the image of the Maker in this child, which the renewed soul recognizes and claims at the first blush <note>The Dutch "roodtheydt" literally means "redness," but here refers to the "first blush" or immediate recognition.</note>. the here is the life of faith: to fix one's eyes on Christ's intention in all his actions. 2. Christ is seated so that we should sit with him in Heaven; what is the end of Christ's sitting other than that he should clothe all his saints with the same advantage? For a right prayer in words requires not only gracious assistance in the actual deed, but also a new state of adoption as children and of sonship. Many speak words to God who do not pray; many recount their sins who do not confess their sins to God; many speak well of God who do not praise God; many thousands speak of a Fatherhood who have no sonship, nor any ground in the matter itself. A new nature is alone the best ground for prayer, ensuring that the name of God is not used in vain. Now this is the fruit of the Spirit, and one of the ends <note>purposes</note> of the Spirit’s sending.

2. That he might lead us into all truth; I understand this as all necessary, fundamental, and soul-saving truth; in this respect, we have need of the Spirit in these days. He has new thoughts, new intentions, new desires, new hopes, new love, new delights; he carries on, as it were, a new trade in this world for the sake of the other world; **he has become in Christ a new creature; the old has passed away, behold, all has become new.** And from this we can firmly conclude the truth of our doctrine. Now, they judged this a greater favor (given the circumstance of such a person acting in such a manner) than if he had actually given them full pay or reward. Oh, they valued such a chain much higher than a great quantity of similar gold; even the person of the Emperor hung upon the chain as such a precious jewel, whose worthiness in the martial imagination no million in gold could match. Oh my soul! If an Emperor could thus win the affections of men, how could you do otherwise than love Jesus Christ, that great Emperor of Heaven and earth? It was he who gave you his Spirit; it was he who set aside <margin>Num. 11:17</margin> a portion of the Spirit that was upon him (as God spoke to Moses) and laid it upon you; and would not Christ’s person, Christ’s worthiness, increase the price of this gift?

# Looking unto Jesus

just as all gifts are tokens of love, so must the love of a great personage—and the gifts proceeding from such love—be held in higher esteem than the gifts of any other lesser persons.

2. Another circumstance is the greatness of the gift; this proves the greatness of the good will, and consequently deserves a corresponding return of affection. Now, what greater gift did Christ have in his treasury <note>original: "Magazijn" – used here in the sense of a royal storehouse or spiritual treasury</note> than the giving of his own Spirit? The Spirit proceeds from him and is of the same essence with him; the Spirit is the third person of the true and only Godhead, proceeding from the Father and the Son; and is co-eternal, co-equal, and co-substantial <note>The author uses "gelijck-wesigh," the Dutch equivalent of the Latin *consubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance" or "essence."</note> with the Father and the Son. This is evident from the Divine attributes that are attributed and communicated to the Holy Spirit: Such as 1. **Eternity**; God was never without his Spirit. *In the beginning* <margin>Gen. 1:1, 2</margin> *God created the Heaven and the earth—and the Spirit of God moved upon the waters.* 2. **Omnipotence**; because he, together with the Father and the Son, created and maintains all things. *By* <margin>Job 26:13</margin> *his Spirit he hath garnished the heavens.* — <margin>C. 33:4</margin> *The Spirit of God hath made me.* — <margin>1 Cor. 12:11</margin> *And all these things worketh that one and the self-same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.* 3. **Omniscience**; or knowledge of all things, <margin>1 Cor. 2:10</margin> *For the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.* 4. **Immutability**; *Men and brethren,* <margin>Acts 2:36</margin> <note>While the margin cites Acts 2:36, the quote "this Scripture must be fulfilled" is found in Acts 1:16.</note> *this Scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost spake before.*

### §. 9.

### Of the conformity with Jesus in this looking.

<margin>Coloss. 3:1, 2.</margin>
IX. Let us become conformed to Jesus in the aforementioned regards. An attentive beholding of Jesus in His ascension, sitting, and the sending of His Spirit is enough to change us into the same image from glory to glory. It was a sweet saying of a pious believer: "Behold the glorified Christ, see Him as in that relation and state, and you shall immediately have in your hearts the sparks <note>Original: "sprancken," referring to small flashes or reflections of light.</note> of the same glory." Christ is now exalted; He is now in glory at the right hand of God. venly walking. Seek the things that are above; mind those that are above. Well then, if we have been powerfully raised with Christ, and have ascended and been seated with Him in Heaven, let us then spiritually ascend and sit with Him in these regards; certainly there is a conformity in our heavenly walk. O let then our walk be in Heaven!

In the continuation of this, I shall examine these questions: —

1. What do we understand by our walk in Heaven?
2. Why must our walk be in Heaven?
3. By what means can we come to this heavenly walk?

1. By our walk in Heaven, I understand our striving after Heaven. Just as Heaven is our home, so are our eyes directed toward it; all that we do, our end, our aim <term>mark</term> <note>Original: "wit," a term for a target or mark in archery, meaning the goal one shoots for.</note> is to prepare ourselves for Heaven and to set our course toward Heaven. O, let us not be so base as to set our affections on earthly things, but much rather on God and Christ; and this is our walk in Heaven.

6. By our walk in Heaven, I understand our dealings and commerce <note>Original: "koopmanschap," suggesting the metaphor of a merchant trading for goods.</note> for Heaven, even while we are on earth: the word in the original language means this; *for our citizenship is in heaven* <note>original: "ἡμῶν γὰρ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς" (Philippians 3:20)</note>; our business is in Heaven; although our bodies are not there, yet our business is there; we conduct ourselves and present ourselves in this life as Citizens of the city of Heaven; our City in which we are Citizens, and to which we have a right, is above in Heaven; in this respect our business is not with trifles, as it is with other men, but we deal in great things, in high things; we trade for Divine pearls, yes, for God, and for Christ, who sits at the right hand of God. We see now what we understand by our walk in Heaven.

2. Why is the saints' walk in Heaven?

1. Because they know full well that the Origin of their soul is from God and Heaven; the body is indeed from the dust of the earth, but the soul is the breath 

<column-break/>

<margin>Gen. 2</margin> of God; thus it is said of the first man, God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and so man became a living soul. The Origin of the soul is more Heavenly and Divine than any other creature here below in the world; and when God works His grace in the soul, and she thus begins to know herself, and to return to herself again, then she looks down upon all things here below as base and contemptible things; then she looks upward, and begins to converse with those things that correspond with her Origin.

Just as it is with a noble-born child, being carried away to a foreign land and held there as a slave, and set to clean stinking gutters or (like the prodigal son) to tend the swine; as long as he is there and has no knowledge of his lineage, he thinks of nothing but his food and doing the work he was assigned; but if he once comes to know where he is from, that he is a lawfully born heir of such a Prince in such a land, O, his thoughts, his mind, and his desires will then very quickly change: Oh, that I were in my country! Oh, that I were with my Father in his court! So it is also with the souls of men; they are the offspring (so to speak) of that great King of Heaven and earth; and although through man's fall they have become as slaves of Satan, nonetheless, when it pleases God to convert the soul, then He reveals

In this work of Christ in Heaven (if we wish to follow Him), we must go from glory to glory <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18, suggesting a progressive spiritual journey where the believer becomes more like Christ by beholding Him.</note>; no sooner do we depart from one place of glory than we immediately enter into another, every bit as glorious as the former. The saints can do nothing else (if it pleases them) but lift up their hearts through the changing of the Heavenly light and comfort that proceeds from the bosom of Jesus Christ. ->Looking unto Jesus,<-

As in the previous section, I shall first present the object, and then guide you to look upon it. The object is Jesus carrying out the great work of our salvation in His intercession; in which I shall essentially examine these things:

1. What this intercession of Christ is?
2. According to what nature Christ prays for us?
3. To whom Christ’s intercession is directed?
4. For whom He prays?
5. How Christ’s intercession corresponds with the intercession of the High Priests of old?
6. What is the difference between Christ’s intercession and the intercession of the High Priests?
7. What are the properties of this intercession of Jesus Christ?
8. In what, specifically, does Christ’s intercession consist?
9. How powerful and prevailing this intercession of Christ is with His Father?
10. What are the reasons for this great transaction of Christ’s intercession for His people?

### § I. What is Christ’s intercession?

Some describe it as follows: Christ’s intercession is that part of His priestly ministry <note>original: "Priesterlicke bedieninge"; referring to the three offices of Christ—Prophet, Priest, and King.</note> through which Christ is an Advocate and spokesman with God the Father for the believers; I state it thus: Christ’s intercession is His gracious will, fervently and unmovably desiring that, by the constant power of His sacrifice, all His members may be acceptable to the Father, both in their persons and their duties. 1. I call Christ’s intercession His own gracious

<column-break/>

will; for we must not think that Christ, in His intercession, casts Himself down upon His knees before His Father’s Throne, speaking some humble words or prayers; that would not befit the Majesty of Him who sits at God’s right hand. Even while on earth, the content of His intercession for His Saints was in <margin>John 17:24.</margin> this manner: *Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am;* <note>The author emphasizes the word "will" (Greek: *thelo*) to show that Christ’s prayer is an exercise of His divine authority, not just a petition.</note> and how much more is this now the form of His intercession in Heaven: *Father, I will this, and I will that.* 2. The ground of Christ’s intercession is the sacrifice or death of Christ; and for this reason, we identify two parts of Christ’s Priesthood, or sacrifice: the one is atoning, when He suffered on the cross; and the other is presenting, when He appears in Heaven before God for us. The one He accomplished on earth, suffering outside the gate <note>A reference to Hebrews 13:12; just as sacrificial animals were burned outside the camp, Christ suffered outside the city walls of Jerusalem.</note>; the other is accomplished in Heaven, now that Christ is in the City. The first was truly a sacrifice; the second is not so much a sacrifice as the reminder of a sacrifice. The first was an act of humiliation, and this latter is an act of glory. The first was accomplished once for all; this latter is done without ceasing. The first was the obtaining of redemption, and this latter is for the application of redemption; so that the former is the ground of the latter. Christ prays to His Father fervently and unmovably, by reason of and for the sake of the power of His sacrifice. 3. The subject matter for which He prays is that all the Saints and their service may be acceptable to God.

<summary>This page defines Christ's heavenly intercession not as a humble plea, but as an authoritative "will" based on His completed sacrifice on the cross. It distinguishes between the atoning work finished on earth and the ongoing presentation of that work in heaven to ensure believers remain acceptable to God.</summary>

### §. 3.
### To whom Christ’s intercession is directed.

<margin>1 John 2:1</margin>
### III. To whom is Christ’s intercession directed?
I answer: immediately to God the Father. *If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father.* In the work of intercession, three Persons are involved: the injured party, the injuring party, and the intercessor, who is distinct from both. The injured party is God the Father; the injuring party is the sinful human; and the intercessor, distinct from both, is Jesus Christus, acting as the middle Person between God the Father and us humans. The Father is God and not man; and we who believe in Christ are men and not God; and Christ is both man and God, and therefore He is the Intercessor and Mediator between God and men.

Should someone object that not only the Father is wronged by sin, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that consequently there must also be a Mediator for them; the solution is easy. Christ’s Intercession is made immediately to God the Father, but since God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one single and un-

<column-break/>

-divisible essence, and thus also one will, it follows that when the Father is reconciled through Christ’s Intercession, the Son and the Holy Spirit are also reconciled with Him and in Him.

I do not deny that Christ’s Intercession is made to the entire Trinity, yet it is made immediately and legally to the first Person, and through Him to the others. — But if this is so (say our opponents), then Christ’s Intercession is in a way made to Himself, which cannot be, because in all intercessions there must necessarily be three parties. This point has caused much difficulty in the Roman Church <note>original: "Roomsche Kerche"; referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, so much so that to resolve it, they have known no other way than to concede that Christ is our Intercessor only as a man, and not as God. This is in no way true; for just as both natures come together in the work of satisfaction <note>term: "voldoeninge" (satisfaction); the theological concept that Christ’s death paid the legal debt or penalty for human sin.</note>, so they also both come together in the work of Intercession. It is an old and accepted rule

<margin>Names of the office apply to both natures.</margin> <note>original: "Ap. con- tun- cur utra- nat."; an abbreviation for "Appellationes concreti tribuuntur utrique naturae." This is a technical rule in Christology stating that titles describing Christ's work apply to His entire person, encompassing both His divine and human natures.</note>

that the names of the offices given to Christ, such as Mediator, Intercessor, etc., fit Him according to both natures. And how could the act of Christ’s Intercession be an act of Christ’s humanity alone? What? To hear prayers and to offer them up? To receive and present the prayers and thanksgivings and other spiritual offerings of all believers in the entire world? To handle all of these at one and the same time, according to the diversity and multitude of their particular circumstances? Truly, this is and must be the work of an infinite, and not of a finite, Agent.

### §. 4.

<margin>Luke 23:34.</margin>
> *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do;*

But this may be seen as a common duty as a man, in which respect He subjected Himself to the Law of God, which demands that we shall forgive our enemies and pray for those who persecute us—and not through His special office as <term>Mediator</term> <note>A 'Mediator' is a go-between or legal advocate who reconciles two parties.</note>. According to this view, His prayer was heard when so many of the Jews were converted at Peter’s Preaching (Acts 2:41). But what more do we need? His own words are clear: that Christ’s intercession is not for the World, or the reprobate. So much regarding the negation.

And in truth, this part of his Priesthood is the most excellent of both; indeed, it is the peak and the highest point of his Priesthood; and for that reason, it is presented to us in the examples of both those two orders of Priesthood that existed before him and prefigured him: both that of Aaron and that of Melchizedek. 1. ...and the intercessions of the Old High Priests? There is no doubt that, although they agree in some respects, Christ nevertheless serves in a far Higher and more Glorious way than any of the High Priests before him; but the difference between Christ and them, and between Christ's intercessions and their intercessions, appears in these points: —

VII. **W**hat are the characteristics of these Intercessions of Jesus Christ? I answer:
1. The same is **Heavenly** and **Glorious**; as evidenced by these points:
1. Christus does not fall upon his knees before his Father, as in the days of his humiliation <note>The 'status humiliationis' refers to Christ's time on earth in human form, prior to his exaltation in heaven.</note>; for that does not befit his Glory which he has received; he only presents his will to his Father, to the end that He might hang his Seal upon it and consent to the same.
2. Christ does not pray through a private love, just as the Saints in this life pray for one another, but through the public ministry of the Mediatorship,
<margin>1 Timothy 2:5.</margin>
For there is one God, and there is also one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

<column-break/>

3. Christ does not pray out of lowliness, as one might present requests for unmerited things, but out of Authority, by which he desires things just as he has the right above all others to bestow them, as well as to desire them.
4. Christ does not pray merely as an Advocate, but also as a reconciler; Christ’s Spirit <note>Referring here to the Holy Spirit as the Paraclete.</note> is an Advocate, but only Christ is an Advocate and a reconciler; Christ’s Spirit is our Advocate on earth, but only Christ in his Person assigns his merits to us in Heaven, and promotes the cause of our salvation with his Father in Heaven. In each of these respects, we can see that Christ’s intercession is Heavenly and Glorious.
2. The same is always powerful and worthy; just as he has the power to pray for us, so he has the power to give us that for which he prays for us.
<margin>John 14:16. Chapter 16:7.</margin>
I shall pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter <note>original: 'Trooster', a traditional Dutch term for the Holy Spirit as Advocate or Consoler.</note>. If I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you, but if I go hence, I shall send him to you. If Christ, praying on earth, was always heard, then we can be assured that praying in Heaven, the Father also hears and answers him there; Christ, praying as a man for himself, was heard in that which he feared; but Christ now as Mediator prays for us, and he is always heard even in the specific things that he desires for us. # Looking unto Jesus.

<margin>Heb. 9:1, 13:12</margin> Not only did the Priest have to slaughter the bullock outside the Holy of Holies, but he had to go with the blood into the Holy of Holies, and there within sprinkle the mercy-seat <term>versoen-decksel: the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, where God met his people</term> with it; truly these were foreshadowings <note>original: "voorbeeldingen"</note> of the things that had to be done in Heaven. Christ, who was slaughtered and crucified outside the Gate, has carried his own blood into the Holy of Holies, <margin>Heb. 9:12</margin> or into the Heaven of Heavens; for by his own blood he entered once into the Sanctuary, having brought about an eternal redemption; and having arrived there, he sprinkled it, as it were, upon the Throne of Grace; that is, he has applied it <note>original: "toe-ge eygent"</note> and through it obtained grace; through Christ’s blood, God’s loving-kindness and justice are reconciled in themselves, and reconciled for us. Christ has sprinkled his blood upon the Throne of Grace seven times; seven is a sign of perfection <note>In biblical numerology, seven represents completeness or the divine finish</note>; where Christ’s blood is sprinkled upon a soul, that soul is assured that it is washed from all impurity, and shall finally be made perfect and completely saved. On earth Christ’s blood was poured out, but his blood is sprinkled now that he is in Heaven. Is any soul sprinkled with Christ’s blood? Surely this sprinkling has come from Heaven; so speaks the Apostle: <margin>Heb. 12:22, 24</margin> *But you have come to Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, to the Heavenly Jerusalem, — and to the Mediator of the New Testament*

Well, this is the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better things than Abel. #### IV. Book VI. Part. Chapter I. Section 5.

...fills Heaven and earth with its sound; indeed, the ears of the Lord are so filled with it that it drowns out all other sound and rings without ceasing in His ears.

2. The difference <note>The author is contrasting the "cry" of Abel's blood with that of Christ's.</note> lies in these things: Abel's blood cried out for vengeance against Cain, but Christ's blood speaks of grace over all believers. Abel's blood was shed because of his offering, and because he and his offering were acceptable <margin>Gen. 4:4, 10</margin>; but Christ's blood is shed so that He Himself might be offered, and that we, through His offering, might become acceptable. Abel's blood cried out thus: *Look, Lord, and avenge*; but Christ's blood cries out thus: *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do* <margin>Luke 23:34</margin>. And even to this very time, Christ's blood cries for forgiveness, and that is our comfort: if God hears the servant <note>Abel</note>, He will much more gladly hear His Son; if He hears the servant regarding destruction, He will much more gladly hear the Son regarding salvation. However, so that I may speak literally and not figuratively <note>original: "Figuerlich"</note>, I do not mean to say that the physical blood itself, which Christ shed on the Cross, is now in Heaven, or that it speaks in Heaven; these are all metaphorical <note>original: "overdraghtige"</note> words. Yet I maintain this as actual and literal: that the power, the merits, and the strength of Christ's blood are presented by our Savior <term>Salighmaerker: literally 'Heal-maker' or 'Blessedness-maker'</term> to His Father, both as a public satisfaction for our sins and as a public price for the obtaining of our glory.

<column-break/>

in the presentation of His will, of His request and desire for us, grounded on the power of His glorious merits <margin>John 17:24</margin> for us: *Father, I will that where I am, those also whom You have given Me may be with Me, that they may behold My glory which You have given Me.* This was a portion of Christ's prayer on earth, and some say that it is the essence of Christ's Intercession for us now in Heaven in His glory. He prayed on earth just as He intended to pray once He had entered Heaven; He indicated this at the beginning of His prayer, for He spoke as if all His work on earth were already finished, and as if He then wished to begin His work <margin>John 17:4, 5</margin> in Heaven: *I have glorified You on earth, I have finished the work You gave Me to do: and now, Father, glorify Me with Yourself, with the glory I had with You before the world was.*

#### The Fourth Book. Part VI. Chapter 1. § 9.

<margin>Heb. 5:4, 1.</margin>
**C**hrist did not glorify himself to become High Priest; no, no: but he was called by God just as Aaron was. God the Father selected <note>original: "uyt-geleygt," meaning set apart or appointed.</note> him for this, he prepared him for it, and has confirmed him in it: *The Lord has sworn, and it shall not repent him, you are a Priest for*
<margin>Ps. 110:4.</margin>

We have often thought of God the Father as being just and stern, and that Christ his Son is more gentle and kind; but this cannot be, for there are not two infinite wills, nor two infinite kindnesses—one in the Father and another in the Son; but one will and one kindness in both. And consider to that end only the willingness of God the Father to honorably receive Christ into Heaven, to perform the work of the High Priest there; no sooner had Christ entered through the gate into the city of Heaven than God immediately said, *Sit at my right hand*—but to what end? <margin>Heb. 8:1.</margin>

*Of the knowing of Jesus, as carrying out the great work of our salvation in his Intercession.*

I. <note>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral and foliate scrollwork</note>et us know Jesus as carrying out the great work of our salvation in his Intercession. And is it not a noble knowledge, when we now on earth know what Christ does for us in Heaven? If I had a great <term>lawsuit<note>Original: *proces*. I dare say on behalf of all the believers in the world, that Christ is now busy praying for us at the right hand of God; from the time of his <term>Ascension<note>Original: *Hemel-baert*, literally "Heaven-journey."</note></term> he has been occupied with this work; it is a work of over <note>original: "sestien-hondert jaren"</note> sixteen hundred years; and summer and winter, night and day, without weariness of Spirit, Christ is constantly busy praying for us; Christ's love has absolutely no standstill, no ceasing; yes, even now while you are reading this, Christ is acting as an <term>Advocate<note>Original: *Voorspraake*. A legal term for one who speaks on behalf of another in court.</note></term> for you. Christ has carved your names as a Seal upon his heart, and standing directly before the eye of his Father, the eye of God falls at the first glance upon the breast of Jesus Christ; and is it not worthy to know this well? O my Soul, leave your <term>muddy studies<note>Original: *poele studien*. Refers to "swampy" or "miry" intellectual pursuits that lack spiritual depth.</note></term> of na-

O the excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ; such knowledge (if it is sincere) is nothing less than soul-saving. Come and learn of the Intercession of Christ in all the preceding parts. I have run through them, for the work has <term>grown under my hands<note>A phrase indicating the author found more to say than originally intended as he wrote.</note></term>, and I must now shorten it: only remember that in Christ's Intercession there are various mysteries which we on this side of Heaven must not yet know; oh, beware of entering this labyrinth without the key of the Word; above all, pray for the leading of the Spirit to enlighten your darkness, and whatever you then know, know it for yourself.

God understands the eloquence of your sighs just as well as your cries. But what is so desirable about **Christ’s Intercession**? I answer:

1. In **Christ’s Intercession** lies the present dealing <note>original: "verhandelinghe"; referring to an ongoing transaction or business</note> regarding the salvation of our **Soul**. The things we have spoken of until now are finished and past; the dealings of eternity reached their end when time began; the dealing of **Christ’s** promise ended with the incarnation <note>original: "mensch-werdinghe"</note> of **Christ**; the dealings of **Christ’s** birth, life, death, resurrection, and **Ascension** are now already over sixteen hundred years old. I know that the power and influence of all these dealings remains, and shall remain continuous throughout all eternity, but the various actions themselves have reached their end; only **Christ’s** sitting, the sending of his **Spirit**, and his blessed **Intercession** were, and still are, the true present business of **Jesus Christ**. If it were possible for us to see into **Heaven**, if we could with **Stephen** keep our eyes toward **Heaven** and see the **Heavens** opened; if our eyes were drawn by an uncommon power through that blue sky, and through everything until we came into the **Holy of Holies**, and to **Jesus Christ** in his **Glory**, what would we see other than **Christ** praying for us, **Christ** being busy with his **Father** in the cause of his poor **Saints**? Now he prays, now he displays his **Person**, merits, and intercession, as if he said: "Father, here are a group of rebel-

<column-break/>

lions <note>original: "rebellen"</note>, having justly fallen under your wrath; they have deserved to be eternally separated from you, but I must necessarily have them reconciled and received into your bosom; come, and state your demand, let your justice demand even the greatest satisfaction, I have paid a sufficient price for all, and powerfully for them; give them whatever laws you please, I undertake that they shall keep them; and therefore go, go **Holy Spirit**, go to such and such **Souls**, make them capable of their duties, yes, make them capable in their duties, and sanctify them thoroughly in their souls, bodies, and spirits." Well, this is the present business of **Jesus Christ**, and therefore very desirable. It seems to me that I long to know what **Christ** is doing now for my **Soul** in **Heaven**, and is it not this? Does he not spend all his time either in completing the reconciliation for his redeemed, or in presenting their prayers, or in pleading for them? Truly, he is every day occupied with his **Intercession**; that is the present work for our **Souls**—O, most desirable work!

2. Faith must meditate on this: that it is God's aim and Christ's intention that this **Intercession** shall be for the benefit of those who are given to Christ. Oh, there is enough in Christ, enough in Christ's Intercession to bring about fellowship, the Spirit, protection, free access to the throne of grace, the spirit of prayer, the forgiveness of sins, perseverance in grace, and the salvation of the souls of the Saints and God's people throughout the whole world; and this is God's intention, that Christ's intercession shall be like the fountain from which all streams shall flow and be brought over to us.

3. Is there, then, any desirable end in Christ's Intercession that we look upon? Oh, let us exercise faith in total dependence; let us lean, stand, or rest upon Christ himself for this end; let us roll ourselves <note>original: "wentelen"; a 17th-century theological metaphor for casting all one's weight and worldly cares onto Christ</note>, or cast ourselves upon the intercession of Jesus Christ. It seems to me that this love of *Christ* ought to transform my *Soul* into a lump of divine love for *Christ*, as by the *Spirit of the Lord*. 2. Another motive for our love for *Christ* is our ownership in *Christ*; *you are not your own*, says the *Apostle* <note>Paul, in 1 Corinthians 6:19</note> of us; should anyone ask, how can that be? I answer, that the *Soul* in loving *Christ* is no longer its own, and in respect of love, *Christ* is not his own; the one gives himself over to the other, and the right of self-ownership ceases on both sides. *My beloved is mine, and I am his*, says the *Bride*; not as if *Christ* should cease to be his own, or to be a free God, when he becomes ours; no, no; but he bears himself so in respect of his love as if he were not his own; he enters into such relations, and takes on such offices and obligations, as if he were entirely for us, and not at all for himself. Thus he is called a <term>Savior</term> <note>original: "Salighmaecker"</note>, a <term>Redeemer</term> <note>original: "Verlosser"</note>, a *King*, a *Priest*, a *Prophet*, a *Friend*, a *Leader*: a *Head*, a *Husband*, a *Keeper*, a *Ransomer*, an <term>Intercessor</term> <note>original: "Voorbidder"</note>, and what not of this kind?
