### Of conformity with Jesus in this respect.

VIII. **L**et us become conformed to Jesus in respect of his intercession. I cannot think otherwise but that in every act of Christ there is something imitable <note>The author uses "na volgelicks" to mean "worthy of imitation," reflecting the "Imitation of Christ" tradition popular in 17th-century devotion.</note> for us. And regarding this work, I will only point to these few points. As—
1. Christ appears in Heaven for us: let us appear on earth for him. Is there not as much equity as conformity in this duty? O my soul, consider what your Jesus does, consider in what Christ's Intercession consists! and is this not the first part thereof? Well, he appears in Heaven before the Saints, before the Angels, and before God his Father for you; and would you be fearful to appear before worms <note>original: "wormen" — a common 17th-century metaphor for humans to emphasize their frailty and mortality compared to God.</note>, before mortals, dust and ashes in his cause and for his truth? Shall Jesus Christ know you in Heaven; and do you not want to know Jesus Christ here in the world? Shall Jesus Christ your great High-Priest, even bear your name on his breast <note>This refers to the "Breastplate of Judgment" worn by the High Priest in the Old Testament, which was set with stones engraved with the names of the tribes of Israel.</note> in the presence of God? and do you not want to bear Christ's name, and present it in confession and practice before all men? Oh what a strong obligation is here, to stand by Christ, and to appear for Christ, and to stand up for his cause in these apostate times; since Christ sitting at the right hand of God, is willing and ready to appear for us in

<column-break/>

his Person, both as Mediator, and Surety, and Reconciler, and Advocate, and Ambassador?
2. Christ spends all his time for us and our salvation, let us also spend all our time for him, and in his service; the Apostle tells <margin>Heb. 7:25.</margin> us, that he always lives to pray for us; it is not for a day, or month, or year, but he lives always in this respect; always, that is, from the time of his Ascension until the end of the world; he is always busy praying for us; he spends all that time for us: and shall we think it too much, if we spend those few days for him, which we have to live here on earth? someone judges this to be the greatest reason in the world, to make us walk in unity with God in Christ; he spends of his eternity for us, and shall we not spend of our whole time for him? Certainly men do not consider what Christ does for them in Heaven; if you believers only seriously considered, that Christ is at his work this Sabbath, this day of rest; that he, without any weariness or ceasing, from morning till evening, and from evening till morning, always, always prays for you, how would this bind you to his service? Oh Christians! if you should without ceasing pray, thank, read and hear this entire day: Oh how tired would you be! # Looking unto Jesus.

We cannot judge otherwise than that this is most just: that those who live should henceforth live not for themselves, but for him who always lives to pray for them.

4. Christ takes our prayers, mixes them with his own prayers, Intercession, and incense, and brings them in this way—as a combined work—to God the Father. Oh, let this also be our concern: to send up all our prayers to God in the name of Christ, and to rest ourselves upon Christ’s Intercession. When everything is done, let us seek the acceptance of our prayers not for our own sake, nor for the sake of our prayers, but for the sake of him who makes our prayers sweet-smelling, mixing them with his own prayers. Many a sorrowful Soul is long afraid to pray to God, for lack of proper meditation on this conformity <note>The "conformity" mentioned here is the spiritual practice of aligning one's internal life and actions with the pattern of Christ's life.</note>; such a person comes to prayer, and they focus on the prayer exactly as it lies upon their own heart, or as it originates from themselves; and then they cry out, "Oh, what a poor, weak, sinful, and imperfect prayer is this!" Well, but once your weak prayer is mixed with the glorious and Heavenly prayer of Jesus Christ, that weakness will soon disappear, and your prayer will find favor with God the Father. It is with your prayers and duties just as it is with your beer; your kitchen-beer <note>original: "keucken-bier" — a low-alcohol beer brewed at home for daily use. I answer: These objections would have some strength if there were no intercession of Christ upon which to rest ourselves and our prayers. 6. Christ makes us perfectly saved through his Intercession; O let us also serve him perfectly; truly, all that we can do is too little to respond to such a love as this is. Oh Christians! why should it be considered an unnecessary thing to have a tender conscience and to walk with total caution? Matthew 7:13. O come and learn this lesson of Christ: he makes us perfectly saved, so let us also serve him perfectly, with our whole heart, with our whole Soul, and with all our strength.

And the seventh Angel sounded his trumpet, and there were great voices in Heaven. If we may believe the **Commentators** <note>Dutch: *Uyt-leggers* — scholars who interpret and explain the meaning of Holy Scripture.</note>, these are the voices of the blessed souls and the holy Angels in Heaven; no sooner does Christ give the command than the Angel sounds the trumpet. I say, no sooner has Christ commanded than the Angel has sounded; but immediately, because of the joy of this command, all voices in Heaven gave a shout: "Well, this is the long-awaited day!" The day of the full number of the Saints; the day of the union of the souls and bodies of the believers; the day of the gathering together of all generations, both of believers and Angels, under one roof; the day of the bringing of the Bride to the Lamb, and of the completion of the **Marriage** <note>The "Marriage of the Lamb," a biblical metaphor for the final union between Christ and His Church.</note> in its highest state; and therefore it is no wonder that because of these new things, great voices and shoutings occurred in Heaven, just as sailors and grape-harvesters are accustomed to do. # Looking unto Jesus.

Regardless of who they may be, we find that they are so gladdened by these new things—namely, that Christ shall now judge the world—that they immediately rose from their thrones and fell down on their faces; and first they gave thanks, and then they worshipped. 1. They thanked God that He has taken His power for Himself; until now, Christ has looked through His fingers, as it were, at the power of His enemies; not Christ, but the **Antichrist** <note>In the theology of this period, the Antichrist was often identified with the Papacy or any power opposing the "true" Gospel.</note> seems now to rule and to sit in the Temple of God; but now Christ has resolved to rule Himself and to make all enemies His footstool, and therefore we thank You now, Lord God Almighty. 2. They prayed that Christ would proceed to the judgment: 1. I know that these words were spoken to Christ at His **Ascension** <note>Dutch: *Hemel-vaert*. The event where Jesus ascended to heaven forty days after his resurrection.</note>; but that does not prevent God from speaking the same to Christ once again; for we do not yet see (says the Apostle) that all things are subject to Him, and God’s intention was that Christ should rule until He had subjected all things under His feet. Indeed, why not speak these words now rather than before? Christ has always ruled in deed since His Ascension, but now He shall reveal His Kingdom even more particularly; for now He shall execute justice among the heathens, now He shall fill the places with dead bodies, now He shall overcome Popes, Turks <note>In the 17th century, "Turks" was a common term for the Ottoman Empire and the broader Islamic world, often viewed as a primary adversary of Christendom.</note>, and all His enemies, and He alone with the Father and the Holy Spirit shall rule over His chosen Saints and Angels. In this they all agree: that in the last days Christ shall be perfectly glorified in His kingly power; for a long time Christ has been greatly glorified in His **Prophetic** and **Priestly** offices; yet not so much in His **Kingly** one; but now He shall be perfectly glorified in His Kingly office; now especially the kingdoms of the world must become our Lord’s and His Christ’s, and so He shall rule for all eternity. ### Of Christ’s coming to the judgment.

Regarding Christ’s coming to judgment; as soon as Christ was prepared and everything was ready, he descended from his Royal Throne to the seat of judgment. In this discourse, I shall note these specific things.

### The Fourth Book. Chapter 1. Section 3.

...the Heaven. Allow me to pause here a while, so that we may reach a more complete understanding of these words. In them, the coming of *Christ* is presented in three ways: with a shout, with a voice, and with a trumpet. Some believe these are one and the same thing expressed in different ways, but I am of a different opinion. Most agree that the events of the giving of the Law on Mount *Sinai* were a preview of the events that will occur on the great day of judgment; now, in that event, we read of a threefold sound: the voice of God, the voice of thunder, and the sound of the trumpet, **Exod.** 19:16, compared with **Exod.** 20:1. And in this manner we also find that the Apostle speaks of a threefold voice: of the voice of *Christ*, of the voice of Thunder, and of the sound of a Trumpet.

1. The Lord himself shall descend with a shout. *Arias Montanus* <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598) was a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note>, and the common translation, render this as "with a command." *Lyra* <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan teacher whose literal interpretation of the Bible influenced the later Reformation.</note> and others believe this is the voice of *Christ* himself, saying with a loud voice: "Arise, you dead, and come to judgment." 
<margin>John 11:43</margin> 
Thus *Jesus* cried with a great voice: "Lazarus, come forth"; and with such a voice shall he call to the dead on the last day. 
<margin>John 5:25</margin> 
So much *Christ* himself has taught us: "The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and they that have heard shall live." The hour *is* now, because in his first coming he awakened some

<column-break/>

through his voice; and the hour *is coming*, so that he shall awaken all people in a similar manner on the last day. And do not wonder at this, says *Christ* in verse 28, for the hour is coming in which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice and shall come forth. Just as he said at the creation of the world, "Let there be light," and there was light; so shall he also say at the end of the world: "Let the dead arise, let the Sea give up its dead that are in it, let death and Hell give up their dead that are in them," and so it shall be.

2. The Lord shall descend with the voice of the Archangel. <term>Archangel: derived from the Greek, meaning 'chief messenger' or highest-ranking angel.</term> Two questions arise here: 1. Who is this Angel? 2. What is this voice?

1. Concerning the first, some say that this Angel is *Gabriel*, others *Raphael*, others *Michael*. The Jews have an old tradition that there are seven Head-Angels who serve before the Throne of God, who are therefore called Archangels. The Scripture seems to speak much regarding this, 
<margin>Revelation 4:5; chapter 6</margin>
calling them seven fiery lamps burning before the Throne: and seven horns, and seven eyes of the Lamb: and the seven Spirits of God sent out into all lands: 
<margin>Zechariah 4:10</margin>
the seven eyes of the Lord, which shall range through the whole land; 
<margin>Revelation 8:2</margin>
and even more clearly: seven Angels, who stood before God. Now, which of these seven is the Archangel spoken of here is not easily determined; it is only probable that all the Archangels and all the Angels are understood through this, as being included under that one, with which

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the nature of the "shout" (the first of the three sounds mentioned in 1 Thessalonians 4:16), this page examines the "voice of the archangel" and the "trumpet of God," drawing parallels between the Second Coming and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai.</meta>

# Looking unto Jesus.

...corresponds with Matthew 24:31. Master Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622) was an English Nonconformist theologian and scholar known for his annotations on the Pentateuch.</note> has observed that when an act is performed by many, of whom one is the leader, that deed is often attributed without distinction either to the multitude or to the one who is their head. 
<margin>2 Kings 11:12.</margin> 
For instance, it is said that Jehoiada brought forth the king’s son and put the crown upon him; or that "they" brought forth the king’s son and "they" put the crown upon him, 2 Chronicles 23:11. So also, David offered burnt offerings, 2 Samuel 6:17, or "they" offered burnt offerings, 1 Chronicles 16:1. And in the same way, "He shall descend with the voice of the Archangel," or "He shall send his Angels with a great sound," Matthew 24:31. That there are seven Chief-Angels <term>Hoost-Engelen</term> <note>Referring to the traditional concept of the seven archangels who stand before God.</note> is confirmed by Master Mede <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638) was an influential English biblical scholar and student of prophecy.</note>, and that there is one who is called "the Archangel" in a pre-eminent way. Some others say that just as among the Devils there is one who is the Prince of Devils, who is called so by name, and therefore it is said that the fire 
<margin>Matt. 25:41</margin> 
is prepared for the Devil and his angels; so also from this text in 1 Thessalonians 4:16, Daniel 10:13, and Jude verse 9, some conclude with probability that the good Angels have a Leader, namely Michael, whom Jude calls the Archangel. But let us go no further into this: may the Lord 
<margin>Coloss. 2:18</margin> 
preserve me, so that I do not intrude into those things which I have not seen; the day itself shall reveal it; and here I shall leave it, as having said enough for those who are wise unto moderation.

2. Regarding the second point: what this voice of the Archangel is: I believe that we must understand it to be the thunder. Here is, as we have said, a clear reference to the proceedings

<column-break/>

at the giving of the Law. Now the voice expressed there—besides the voice of God and the voice of the trumpet—is the voice of thunder: *And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders.* In this sense, some explain these words of the Apostle in which it is said that the Law was spoken by the Angels, because the Angels stirred up this uncommon thunder, which was perhaps the material substance of that clear voice in which the Lord spoke to Israel. Or, if the Law was spoken by Christ—as I have declared my opinion elsewhere—he being the Angel of the Covenant, Malachi 3:1, and the Angel of his presence, Isaiah 63:9, it nevertheless does not prevent the created Angels from also being able to speak the Law; if not in respect of a clear articulate voice, yet in the voice of the thunder, being accompanied thereby. Thus the thunder is often called "the voice of God," and "the voice of his majesty," Job 37:4–5, Psalm 29:3, 9.

3. The Lord shall descend with the trumpet of God. Such a voice was also present at the giving of the Law, Exodus 19:16 and chapter 20:18; and so it shall be now also, when men shall be called to give an account of the keeping or breaking of the same. To understand this, our translation says that Christ shall send his Angels with a trumpet of great sound; but in four Greek copies, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> admits, as also in the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, and in the common translation <note>Likely referring to the Latin Vulgate.</note>, and on the margin of our latest...

### The Fifth Book. Chapter 1. Section 3.

<margin>
Exodus 19:16
-- 20:18
</margin>
In the latest translation <note>Likely referring to the Dutch Authorized Version or "Statenvertaling" of 1637</note>, it is read that Christ shall send his Angels with a trumpet and a great sound. And so the final words serve as an explanation, namely: with a trumpet, that is, with a great voice, like the voice of a trumpet; so that this reading probably proves that the "last trumpet" is to be taken as a metaphor <term>gelijckenisse</term> <note>Literally a "likeness" or "parable," used here to mean a figurative expression.</note>. <margin>Hebrews 2:2</margin> I prove this further confirmation in this way: whenever something is attributed to the Angels which does not fit their spiritual nature, and which they do not need for the execution of their service, such a thing must be taken metaphorically—unless the immediate words, or some other passages of Scripture, force the literal meaning upon us. However, a material trumpet made of silver, or copper, or other metals, does not fit the spiritual nature of the Angels, nor do they have need of such a trumpet to make a great sound in the air. <margin>Book 1, Chapter 1, Section 4.</margin> It is clear that they can make a great sound, like the sound of a trumpet, without a literal trumpet; and there is nothing at all in Scripture that should force the literal meaning of these words upon us, or give us any probable reason for it. Add to what has been said that a great sound is sometimes presented through the metaphor of a trumpet: *I heard behind me* <margin>Matthew 24:31</margin> *a great voice, as of a trumpet.* Revelation 1:10. *And the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet.* Revelation 4:1.

<column-break/>

But why is this sound, which is like a trumpet, called the **Trumpet of God**? I answer: because of its greatness. For it is customary in the Hebrew language <note>The author is explaining a Hebrew superlative idiom where "of God" acts as an intensifier.</note> that, in representing the greatness, excellence, or height of a thing, the name of God is added to the word by which the thing is signified. As in Genesis 23:6: *A Prince of God*; that is, a mighty Prince. Genesis 30:8: *Wrestlings of God*, that is, great wrestlings. Psalm 36:7: *The Mountains of God*, that is, great mountains. Psalm 80:11 <note>The OCR reads Psalm 8:11, but this refers to the "Cedars of God" found in Psalm 80:10-11.</note>: *Cedar-trees of God*, that is, very high Cedar-trees. So here, the *Trumpet of God* means a very great sound, like the sound of a trumpet. <margin>Exodus 16:19</margin> In the Law it is said: *There were thunders and lightnings upon the Mount, and a thick cloud, and the sound of an exceeding loud trumpet, so that all the people who were in the camp trembled.* And if there was such trembling at the giving of the Law, oh, what trembling shall there be on that great Day of Judgment, when sinners shall be condemned for the transgression of that Law!

Something shall happen to them that is like death, and they shall be changed. The Apostle gave the order of this from the Lord; <margin>1 Thessalonians 4:15, 16, 17</margin> *We say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord*

...shall not precede those who have fallen asleep <note>A common biblical metaphor for death.</note>: for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the Archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and those who have died in *Christ* <note>original: "Christo"</note> shall rise first: then we who remain alive shall be caught up together with them in the clouds. For the godless, I believe, shall rise like toads out of their burrows, in a black, ugly, and hideous appearance. Among the Scholastic teachers <term>School-leeraers</term> <note>Medieval academic theologians who debated precise points of doctrine.</note> it is asked whether the reprobate <term>verworpene</term> <note>Those not chosen by God for salvation; the "rejected."</note> shall rise again with all their ugliness that they had in this life? Just as some of them were blind, lame, crippled, mutilated, deaf, mute, etc. Whether they shall then rise again in that same state? As for me, I think that God, the creator of nature, wanting to restore human nature on that day, there shall therefore be no defect in the natural parts; certainly, in the damned nothing shall be lacking that would hinder the sensation of pain in any part; for the lack of any limb would hinder this general pain, which shall come upon every part of the bodies of the damned in hell: their bodies shall then be whole, but they shall be ugly, hideous, sorrowful, and senseless bodies, as being set in contrast to the glorious quali-

<column-break/>

-ties of the bodies of the saints; well, what bodies (you might say) shall they then have? I answer, glorious bodies; no sooner shall the bodies of the Saints have risen, than they shall excel with special qualities. They are sown in corruption, and are raised in incorruption; they are sown in dishonor, and are raised in glory; they are sown in weakness, and are raised in power; natural bodies are sown, and spiritual bodies are raised <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 15:42-44.</note>. The *Sun* in its glory is but a shadow of the glory of their bodies; and this shall pain the reprobate not a little, when they shall see the difference between their bodies and the bodies of the saints; *Oh!* they shall say, look, there are those whom we mocked, and now they are glorified. See a world full of *Suns* rising together from all parts of the earth; in former times we lived on earth, and we never saw more than one *Sun* rise in the *East*, but see now millions of *Suns* in the *East*, and *West*, and *North*, and *South*. *Oh*, these are those glorious Saints of Heaven; see with what swift and nimble bodies they make themselves ready to fly into the air to meet their Lord; and meanwhile we stand up with such sorrowful, clumsy, and ugly bodies, *Oh*, what will become of us? Well, this is the day of resurrection. The Angels have now been here to open our graves, to roll away the stones, and upon them...

### §. 4.
### Of the Meeting of Christ and the Saints on the Day of Judgment.

4. Concerning the meeting of Christ and the Saints on the day of judgment; no sooner shall the Saints be caught up and set before the Judge, but these things shall follow.
1. They shall see, and gaze intently, and cast forth their beams, and shed their glory upon one another. Oh, that communion! Oh! those darting forth of beams between Christ and his Saints! See, just as two wondering persons, two lovers meeting each other, their eyes glisten; they look as if they would see through one another: so shall Christ and his Saints look upon one another in the first meeting, as if they would look right through each other. And such is the effect of this looking, that they thereby enlarge each other’s luster. Was not the face of Moses shining after he had been with God? <note>Exodus 34:29–35 describes Moses' face glowing after speaking with God on Mount Sinai.</note> And shall not also the faces of the elect shine and glisten when Christ shall also look upon them? All those who believe shall burst out into wonder over Jesus Christ; they shall at the first sight perceive such an excellence in Jesus Christ that they shall be taken up with it in an infinite way; here we speak of Christ, and in speaking we stand amazed; but how they shall wonder when they shall not only speak and hear, but see and behold him who is the express <margin>Hebrews 1:3</margin> image of God, and the radiance of the Father's glory! <note>The author uses language from the Epistle to the Hebrews to emphasize Christ's divine nature and shared substance with God the Father.</note> Oh, what luster he brings forth everywhere! Does not even his body glisten more than a diamond in the sun? Yea, even more than the sun shining now at high noon? How can the saints do otherwise than wonder at this sight? This is the sign of *Christ’s* love and his esteem for his saints; as he himself ascended into Heaven, the Father said to him: *Son, sit at my right hand*; and as soon as the saints are taken up to *Christ*, he shall say the same to them: *Sit at my right hand*; *Christ* shall receive them just as the Father received him; he at the right hand of God, and they at the right hand of *Christ*; and herein consists the great exaltation of the saints. Just as *Christ*, being seated at God’s right hand, was greatly exalted by God, who gave him a name above every name; so shall the saints now also be greatly exalted through *Jesus Christ*. Now they shall be clothed with infinite perfections; now that *fullness* <note>original: πλήρωμα (pleroma)</note>, that fullness of perfection and that fullness of honor and glory shall be brought to them. At his right hand the Queen shall be set in the gold of *Ophir*, that is, in the best, most precious, and finest gold. The Lord shall now let Heavenly glory come upon his saints; he shall adorn them with all his jewelry, fitting for the Wedding Day; and in truth: this shall be the beginning of the pageantry <term>staetsye</term><note>A formal, ceremonial display of state or a grand procession.</note> of the Marriage of the Lamb. The covenant was indeed made long before, but the pageantry has been reserved for this day; and all the glory of this day is for no other purpose than to present the pageantry of the Marriage. Just as a Bridegroom on the Wedding Day comes forth in his glory, and the Bride in her finest jewels; and just as the servants,

<column-break/>

the parents, the friends, and everyone on the Wedding Day show themselves as magnificently as they can; so shall *Christ* also come on this day in his glory, with all his Angels in their glory; and the saints, the wife of the Lamb, the King’s daughter, shall be entirely glorified, inwardly and outwardly. Although the stars may lose their brightness when the Sun rises, yet the glory of the saints shall not be diminished because of the Sun of Righteousness, but rather increased. This is the day on which *Christ* shall glorify the saints in the presence of the whole world. *Come*, he shall say, and *sit at my right hand*; just as a shepherd separates his sheep from the goats, so shall I separate you from the godless outcasts; for you are those for whom the eternal counsel of my Father has wrought; you are those in whom I shall now be glorified forever; and therefore I shall now exalt, lift up, and glorify you; *sit here, or stand here at my right hand*; *O come, come here to the right hand of your Savior.*

<margin>Rev. 20:12</margin>to be; And I saw the dead, small and great, standing before God, and the books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of life. This is spoken after the manner of men, in whose public legal proceedings all documents of the trial are brought forward: examinations, and the testimony of witnesses, to show that all actions, even the most hidden, shall then be recounted and <margin>Aug. City of God, Book 20, ch. 14.</margin>discovered. Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), an influential North African theologian.</note> believes that these books are the Books of the Old and New Testaments, in which all things that must be done or left undone are prescribed by God; and that these Books shall be opened so that the sentence may be given according to them. In that <margin>Rom. 2:16</margin>day God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ according to my Gospel. Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> and most others with him understand these Books to be the books of our consciences, which are now closed and hidden from men, but then shall be opened before the whole world. Whatever these Books may be, we find here a Book opened which is specifically for the saints, called the Book of Life. In this Book stand the names of all the Elect from the first to the last; you John, and you Joseph, and you Judith, you Mary, you Elizabeth, etc.; you all stand in that Book; there is the particularity, and there you have the certainty; your names are written in Heaven, rejoice therein. Oh, what joy there is for the Saints when they see this Book once

<column-break/>

opened, and find their names written there, and engraved in letters of glory. Even this Book declares to me that God from all eternity has chosen a specific and certain number of persons to make them blessed; and that no others can be saved but those who are so chosen, and all who are so chosen cannot entirely fall away. All who worship the Beast <margin>Rev. 13:8; 17:8; 3:5</margin> have names that are not written in the Book of Life of the Lamb from the foundation of the world. And on the contrary, he who overcomes shall be written in the Book of Life, and I will by no means blot out his name from the Book of Life, and I will confess his name before my Father, and before his Angels. This is the day on which this Book of Life shall be opened, and Christ shall read out the name of every chosen one before God and the Angels; not that Christ would have need of a Book, or would literally read a name, but that his election stands so firm that he knows every chosen saint at least as well as we know the names which we have placed in our books for remembrance; and then he shall do his Saints this honor: that he will make their names known before the whole world.

<margin>Matthew 25:34.</margin> then shall the King say unto those at His right hand: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom which is prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Come)** this is the King’s invitation of His Saints to His Court; first He summoned them into His presence, and now, being near Him, He does not wish to part from them; they must come even closer, and go with Him into His inner chamber; the dwellings are prepared, the Supper of the Lamb is prepared, and now He begins the solemn invitation to His Bride:

### §. 6.

6. Concerning Christ and the Saints judging the world; no sooner will the sentence over the saints be pronounced, they shall no sooner be justified, discharged, anointed, and crowned, than they will immediately be placed upon the Throne, and sit with Jesus Christ to judge the world. To open this up, observe these points.

# Looking unto Jesus.

...see him; he whom I now see sitting on that flaming, white, and glorious Throne is *Jesus Christ*, the almighty *God*, the *Prince of Peace*, the true *Messiah*, whose precious blood was poured out like water on earth to save his people from their sins; it is he, yes, he is the same one who, while I still lived on earth, so often invited and wooed me through his faithful servants; who requested and begged me with tears of precious love that I should leave my lusts and renounce the *Devil*; who often knocked at the door of my heart to be let in, offering himself to be my all-sufficient and eternal husband, telling me that if only I had been willing to accept him, this very time would have been the ceremony of our *Wedding*, and now he would have placed upon my head with his almighty hand an incorruptible crown of salvation and glory; but I, alas! like a willful, despairing villain, forsaking my own mercy, have not deemed myself worthy of eternal life, and have wickedly and cruelly against my own soul persecuted all the means that would have sanctified me, and all *God's* servants who would have saved me as instruments in *Christ’s* hand; and now, oh, how happy I would be if I could be a hundred thousand millions of miles away from this sight of *Jesus Christ*! Oh, that these eyes in my head were holes again, just as they were a moment ago when I lay rotting in

<column-break/>

the grave! Oh, that I could turn myself away somewhere from this glorious sight! Oh, were I a stone, or tree, or something else that has no eyes! Oh, that I had no eyes within, nor intellectual power to comprehend *Christ*, or to know *Christ* as my Judge, who is now prepared to cast me into hell! Truly, such shall be the miserable wishing of the godless when they shall look upon *Christ* sitting on the Throne of judgment.

2. Regarding the holy: they shall also see the same. ### The Fifth Book. Chapter 1. §. 6.

...have a perfect vision of one another. In the <note>The Apocrypha refers to books included in some versions of the Bible but excluded from the standard Protestant canon; here, the author cites the Wisdom of Solomon.</note> Apocryphal book there is a clear description of this
<margin>Wisdom 5:1, 2, 3, 4, 5.</margin> vision: "Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him, and made no account of his labors. We fools accounted his life madness, and his end to be without honor: How is he numbered among the children of God, and his lot is among the saints!" Here is a sight that shall torment and amaze the godless; that those who were formerly their footstools shall now sit upon thrones; that poor Lazarus, who once lay at the doors of a certain rich man, shall now shine like a star next to the <term>Sun of Righteousness<gloss>A title for Jesus Christ, derived from the Book of Malachi.</gloss></term>; that those who were despised, slandered, killed, and murdered by them, shall now be their judges, being united

You men and devils, Christ shall say, fellow-

<column-break/>

heirs of Hell, fit fuel for the eternal fire, look upon us in our thrones; formerly you would not look upon us. Christ and the Christians were an abomination to your spirit; you saw us as things to be trodden underfoot, but now we have risen above you. Oh, see how great a difference there is between us and you; look upon us, look upon me, and my holy ones! See us on our thrones, see us shining in glory, and be shamed and terrified for all eternity.

4. A particularly sharp accounting shall then be demanded and given. But of what, you will say? I answer:

I. Of sins. "Come," Christ shall say, "now confess all your sins before the whole world." Formerly you covered your sins, but now every single sin shall be laid open before God, angels, and men. And now the black book of their conscience is opened, in which all their sins appear: both original and actual, of omission and of commission. For all omissions of duties shall be revealed: "Christ was hungry, and I gave him nothing to eat; Christ was thirsty, and I gave him nothing to drink; Christ was a stranger, and I did not take him in; Christ was naked, and I did not clothe him; Christ was sick and in prison, and I did not visit him." <note>This is a paraphrased reference to the Judgment of the Nations in Matthew 25.</note> And concerning the evil that was done, that shall all be revealed. # Looking unto Jesus

...blasphemy, perjury, idolatry, theft, drunkenness, impurity, godlessness, etc.; and these were my lesser sins: anger, hatred, envy, restlessness, impatience, pride, puffed-up conceit, greed for strife, instability, hypocrisy, etc.
The innumerable number of evil thoughts, words, and works that shall then be discovered! In that **black book** <note>The "black book" refers to the "Book of Life's" counterpart—the record of sins held by God or the conscience.</note> are written not only all sins that have been committed, but also all such sins that were intended; every intention of the heart, even if never fulfilled, shall then be revealed. How little people consider this! If I were to tell you of these and those intentions, which were smothered in your heart and never came to light, you would quickly say, "Wait, I never did such things; I only had an intention, or some thoughts about it, and what of that?" Well, then even these thoughts, secrets, intentions, and deliberations shall come to light; if there are any things more hidden or covered, even the inclination and state of your heart, even the leanings of your soul toward this or that evil, they shall then be made known before the whole world. Yes, even more: such sins as the sinners themselves never took notice of—neither before, nor during, nor after committing them—shall come out on this day. The **conscience** <term>conscience<gloss>From the Latin 'conscientia,' here personified as a legal official.</gloss></term> is such a remarkable <term>Notary<gloss>A public official who records legal deeds.</gloss></term> or Secretary, that it marks and registers all our actions and works, whether we pay attention to them

<column-break/>

or not; the conscience leads the pen of a ready writer, and records in brief, and with unreadable letters, as soon as you deliberate in your heart. The writing of the conscience (says someone) is not legible now, just as that which is written with the juice of a **lemon** <note>Invisible ink made from lemon juice was a common 17th-century metaphor; the writing remains hidden until the heat of a fire reveals it.</note> cannot be read by day, but against the fire at night you can read it; so the writing of the conscience cannot be read now, but on that day, when Heaven and Earth shall be set on fire, this book shall be opened, and these ciphers shall be pointed out. Oh, what a day this shall be, when not a single sin of the <term>reprobate<gloss>Those who are rejected by God and destined for damnation.</gloss></term> committed since the beginning of the world shall be missed, but all shall now be recounted.

"You who have been rich," (Christ shall say) "give an account of your stewardship; how have you invested your goods?" ### The Fifth Book. Chapter 1. Section 6.

...was given wisdom, and learning, and knowledge, and understanding, but what benefit has the Church or State had from it? Oh, remember this! If an <term>agent<gloss>Original: 'factoor.' A business representative or merchant's agent who managed trade in foreign ports.</gloss></term> having spent many years in foreign lands, should finally come home without a financial account, who would not rebuke him for his negligence? But the Master calling him to account, and finding nothing else but a ledger of expenses, so much spent on courting, so much on banquets (who would not laugh at such a foolish account?). Thus many spend the time of their lives as a season of joy, and returning to their Lord, they see that all their accounts are sins, and their profits are but vanities.

# Looking unto Jesus.

The purpose of these creatures was for the use of mankind; and since mankind will no longer use them, to what end would they then be preserved? To say they remain as a memorial of what once was; or as a dwelling place for the saints; or as a recreation spot for the saints descending from the highest Heavens from time to time to enjoy themselves here below—these are but idle imaginings and not worthy of any answer at all.

2. By proposition—by *new Heavens, and a new Earth*—is understood the *Heaven of Heavens* and the place of glory. Now these Heavens are called *new,* not because of their "new-making" <note>The author distinguishes between a physical renovation of the old sky and the arrival of a completely different spiritual realm.</note>, but because of our new possession of them as our new dwelling-place; and they are called *Heaven and Earth* because they take the place of that heavenly covering and that earthly dwelling which we now enjoy. Thus, the text can well support this interpretation: we expect *new Heavens* (that is, the highest court of God’s presence) and a *new Earth* (that is, a new dwelling-place for us) which shall, in an infinite way, surpass the comforts and blessedness of these Heavens and Earth which we now possess. <margin>Rev. 21:1.</margin> Thus says John in his Revelation: *And I saw a new Heaven, and a new Earth, for the first Heaven, and the first Earth had passed away, and the Sea was no more.* This *new Heaven and new Earth* is the place or dwelling prepared for the blessed saints and the people of God. A

<column-break/>

*new Heaven,* in which the *Moon* is more glorious than our *Sun*, and the *Sun* as glorious as He who made it—for He is the same: the Son of God, the Sun of righteousness, the Sun of glory. A *new Earth,* where all her waters shall be milk, and all her milk honey; where all her grass shall be corn, and all her corn *Manna;* where all her clods of earth and lumps of clay shall be gold, and all her gold like that of countless ships; where all her minutes shall be centuries, and all her centuries eternity; where all things in every minute are in the highest state of exaltation, as glorious as they can possibly be. Of these *new Heavens and new earth,* I can never say enough, nor know enough, until I arrive there to dwell within them. However, we shall reveal something more of this in our next divisions, for now the saints have entered in with *Jesus Christus.*

### Only a word for application.

*Christians!* what is the reason that we are so busy with this world? Just look around you; not a single one of these visible objects shall continue to exist. These houses in which we live, this *Temple* <note>The author uses "Temple" to refer to the church building or place of worship.</note> in which we gather, this City, this land, this island, and the seas and waters that flow around them—all shall be set on fire and burned to nothing. The sea shall be no more, time shall be no more, or if we look higher, that Sun, and Moon, and Stars shall be no more. That glorious Heaven which now rolls over our heads shall be rolled up like a book <note>The Dutch "boeck" here refers to the biblical imagery of the heavens being rolled up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4; Revelation 6:14).</note>, and all

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Christ’s "commission" from God the Father. # Looking unto Jesus

-sion; <note>The text continues from the previous page's word "commis-sion."</note> namely, the dominion and the execution; wearing the crown and holding the Scepter. Now, according to the first sense, Christ shall reign for eternity; the honor of the dominion and the wearing of the crown he shall never hand over to his Father, for his Father's Throne does not overthrow his own; both their Thrones exist together. <note>original: "Openb. 7. 10. 11."</note> Revelation 7:10, 11. But the duties of a King—sitting in judgment, rewarding servants, punishing evildoers, rescuing the oppressed, fighting against enemies—in this sense, Christ shall cease to reign and shall hand over the Kingdom to his Father.

More specifically, Christ is said to hand over the Kingdom in these respects:

1. Because he ceases to exercise that power which he nevertheless still possesses; just as a **Judge** leaving the **Bench** <note>The "bench" refers to the formal seat of a judge in a court of law.</note> is always a Judge, even if he gives no Judgment at that moment, but spends his time on other things; so Christ is said to hand over his place again—not that his power would be diminished, but he gives no further proof of it; for all his enemies being brought low, there is no need for any more blows to come from his kingly power.

2. Because the manner of his Kingdom after the day of judgment shall be entirely changed; he shall not reign in the same way as he has done before; in Heaven, no more good laws are needed to keep man from falling into godlessness; the orders of this life shall be changed into a new sort of government, and in this

<column-break/>

respect he is said to hand over the Kingdom.

3. Because he ceases to enlarge his Kingdom. In this world, Christ has constantly sought to win more souls for his kingdom through the **Preaching of his Word**, and so to spread his dominion further and further; but the Lord, having completed the number of his servants according to his will, shall end the world and hand over his kingdom—that is, he shall cease to broaden his borders any further; he shall allow himself to be satisfied with the number of subjects he already has.

This is the second point: Christ shall present all his commissions to his Father, handing over his **Prophetic**, **Priestly**, and **Kingly ministries** upon his first entrance into Heaven.

3. He shall present himself to his Father—not only his ministries, but Christ himself presented and subject within God. This I understand to be the Apostle's meaning when he says, *then shall also the Son himself be subject unto him that put all things under him*; the words are spiritual, and therefore it is necessary that we understand them properly according to the **analogy of faith**. <note>The "analogy of faith" is a theological rule that says individual Bible verses should be interpreted in a way that fits with the overall message of the faith.</note> The **Arians** <note>Arians were followers of Arius (c. 250–336 AD), who argued that Jesus was a created being and therefore not fully equal to God the Father—a view later declared heretical.</note> have concluded from this that the Son was not equal to the Father, because he who is subject must necessarily be lesser than the one to whom he is subject. But the answer to this is easy: Christ is regarded either as God, or as man and **Mediator** <term>Mediator: A "middle-man" or bridge-builder who works to reconcile two parties—in this case, God and humanity.</term> between God and men. Christ as God has subjected us to himself, and is subject to no one—

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of how Christ, as the Mediator, concludes his specific kingly duties after the Day of Judgment. It addresses the apparent paradox of the Son being "subject" to the Father while remaining divine.</meta>

### The Fifth Book. Chapter 1. Paragraph 8.

...ment: <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of a new sort of "government."</note> but **Christ** as man and **Mediator** is subject to his Father just as we are. Some wish to maintain that **Christ** is subject to his Father in respect of his spiritual body, the Church; and that this alone is the Apostle's meaning, that then the Church shall be subject to the Father; but I cannot hold with this interpretation, 1. Because the Apostle explicitly speaks of **Christ** and his **Kingdom**. 2. Because although **Christ** is sometimes read in the Scripture as representing the Church, or for his body, nevertheless the **Son** set against the **Father** is never so read or understood. 3. Because we read that he who must be made subject must first have all things subjected to himself. But the **Father** does not properly subject or make all things subservient to the Church of **Christ**, but to **Christ** alone, and therefore the Apostle speaks of **Christ’s** subjection to the Father. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:23.</margin>
In the same way as **Christ** hands over the **Kingdom** to his Father, he must also be made subject to his Father; but **Christ** hands over his **Kingdom** as man, and as **Mediator** between **God** and men; in these respects, as we have heard, **Christ** must no longer rule; on that day his Mediatorship shall cease; and consequently he shall, in respect of his Mediatorship, or in respect of his humanity on that day, be made subject to his Father.

You might say: is not, and was not **Christ** always subject to his Father as man, or as **Mediator** between **God** and men?

<column-break/>

Why then do we define this subjection as happening on that day? Then, says the Apostle, the **Son** shall be made subject.

I answer, this subjection shall then, or on that day, be revealed much more clearly than ever before; then he shall hand over his Kingdom to his **Father** in the presence of men and **Angels**; then he shall lay down all his offices in the sight of all; so that henceforth **God** shall not rule through **Christ's** humanity, but through himself; nor shall we henceforth be subject to **God** through a **Mediator, Christ**, but immediately <note>In 17th-century theology, "immediately" means "without a medium" or directly, rather than "at once."</note> to **God** itself; nor shall **Christ** ever rule over us again as **Mediator**; for even the glory of his Majesty shall become so glorious that all eyes shall see how **Christ's** **Divinity** is so exceedingly prominent above all creatures, yes, even above the humanity of **Christ** itself. That there shall be a greater subjection of **Christ** on that day than ever before, we can explain thus: at night the **Sun** rules over us, but through the **Moon**, for the **Moon** borrows her light from the **Sun**, although by night we see no subjection at all of the **Moon** to the **Sun**; but as soon as the **Sun** rises, the **Moon** immediately ceases her service of lighting others, and the **Sun** <note>The original Dutch text here says "Sonne" (Sun), but the theological context and the pun on "Sone" (Son) suggests the author is referring to the Son of God being revealed in his subjection to the Father's glory.</note> itself is made subject—not through a new subjection, but through a revelation of its previous subjection—so that everyone can now see what excellent glory and light the **Sun** has, both above the **Stars**

### Book Five. Chapter 1. §. 9.

<margin>1 Cor. 15:28.</margin> ...[to the Father], so that God may be all in all.
Truly, this is the meaning: Christ has subjected himself to his Father for this purpose, so that God himself may be all in all; that God should no longer rule through an ordained representative, or through a Christ <note>Meaning Christ in his specific office as Mediator or "middleman" between God and humanity.</note>, but that he should rule immediately <note>Directly, without any intervening person or ceremony.</note> and perfectly through himself, so that everyone may see him face to face. Here we enjoy God (so to speak) through means, such as in the use of the Word, the Sacraments, and the like; but when that Kingdom (of which these services are the means) shall be delivered up, then God himself shall be all in all, without means, without defect, and without end.

It is worth noting that Christ, in his **Mediatorial Kingdom** <term>Mediatorial Kingdom: The period of time where Christ reigns as the bridge between God and man to accomplish salvation.</term>, has such things that are like the means and instruments of government in the kingdoms of men; As: 1. He has his militia and laws, with threats and promises in the ministry of his Word. 2. He has his patents <note>original: *octroyen*; legal grants or charters</note> and seals, with many privileges to strengthen his people in the ordinances of his Sacraments. 3. He has his Officers and Envoys, for the arrangement of spiritual affairs in the ordinances of his ministry; but the cessation of Christ's Kingdom is the cessation of all these; and therefore he resigns his Kingdom, so that God should enter into it immediately; without any means, or without any Mediator, he himself shall be in the place of all, or all in all.

In the following, I shall explain: 1. The sense of how God is all-

<column-break/>

in all. 2. Specifically, in what
->way God is all in all.<-

1. Concerning the sense; it is an explanation of our perfect enjoyment of God; that God be all in all is as much as to say that we enjoy God alone above all things, lacking nothing, and desiring nothing outside of him; for a person who is all in all to me is to have an enjoyment of that person for all things, so that I do not want, nor do I need, to enjoy anything else besides him; thus is God for the saints in glory—he is their "exceeding great reward"; besides him they have need of nothing; even their enjoyment of **blessedness** <note>The state of ultimate happiness and peace in the presence of God.</note> is taken in without means from the fountain, and they have as much of the fountain as their souls in their greatest capacity can contain.

2. Concerning the particulars, in what specifically is God our all in all? I answer:

1. In our immediate enjoyment of God; here we enjoy God through means; he communicates himself to us either through his creatures or through his institutions; and from this it follows that we only know him in part; we see him only dimly as in a mirror; but when he shall be all in all to us, then we shall see him <margin>1 Cor. 13:12. 1 John 3:2.</margin> face to face; we shall then see God as he is, clearly and immediately. Oh, how glorious is this enjoyment above all present enjoyments here below! Just as the enjoyment of a friend in a painting, in a letter, or a token is little compared to the enjoyment of his personal pres-

All the raptures of our spirit in praying, hearing, reading, and meditating are but a tiny taste <note>original: *slopje*; a small draught or sip</note> of those rivers that we shall have in the Heavens. I know that the memory of God in a special meditation is very sweet (Psalm 104:34), and communion with God in some institution <note>referring to religious ordinances like the Lord's Supper</note> is a feast of sweetness, and marrow, and fatness (Psalm 63:5-6). There shall be light without candles, and a continuous day without a Sun; there shall be health without a Physician, and strength of body without the use of food; there shall be knowledge without Scripture, and a firm government without written laws; there shall be communion without Sacraments, and joy without promises to nourish it; the soul in glory shall

It is like the comparison made by a learned theologian: imagine that you saw a multitude of crystal globes placed in two lines opposite each other, which, because of their position, do not allow the direct rays of the Sun to pass through; and that another single globe is placed in the middle of them to transmit the rays of the Sun to all the others. By this means they all shine, though only by reflection; but if the Sun itself comes so near to them that they can receive its rays directly, then that single globe is of no more use. So it is also here: because we, through our own wisdom, cannot grasp this immediate enjoyment of God, Christ’s mediation is necessary; but when all things that cause this lack of wisdom are taken away, and we are brought into the very Inner Chamber <note>original: *Kabinet*; a private room or sanctuary</note> of God’s presence, then such a Mediator is no longer needed. Now, this is a matter in which he is our "all in all"—we shall enjoy him directly.

Here is another matter in which God is our **all in all**: we shall enjoy Him perfectly.

3. This consists in our exclusive enjoyment of God. Not as if there would be nothing else in Heaven but God alone; but that God in Heaven alone shall be **all in all**, or in the place of all things. It is God in Heaven who will make Heaven be Heaven; the blessedness of the saints and God’s own blessedness consists in the enjoyment of God Himself. The <term>Schoolmen</term> <note>original: *School-leeraers*; the scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages, such as Thomas Aquinas, who studied the nature of God and heaven</note> tell us that we shall essentially enjoy nothing else but God alone. We may have some use of the creatures <note>referring to other created beings like angels or fellow saints</note>, but no *enjoyment* <note>in the theological sense of "fruitio," finding ultimate rest and delight in an object for its own sake</note>, and therefore God is said to be all, or as good as all. And in truth, what can we think of being in Heaven that is not in God in a most excellent way?

Now, in these respects, Christ's glorified body—though it is the most radiant thing in the Heaven of Heavens—shall nonetheless be the object of the eyes of the saints, for they shall have glorified eyes in glorified bodies, moved by their glorified spirits.

4. They shall see Christ in all his glory, ways, counsels, decrees, and dealings as working toward their own blessedness <term>blessedness</term><note>original: "gelucksaligheyt"; the state of supreme spiritual happiness and union with God.</note>. Now, this is even more than what came before; there is a great difference in looking at an object as excellent in itself, and looking at it as something that serves my own happiness. It is like the difference between a stranger and an heir riding across some magnificent estates; a stranger rides through them, taking pleasure in the scenery, the rivers, trees, and fruits; but an heir looks at them in a different way. "This," he says, "is the land for which my Father paid so much, and all of it was to enrich me and to be given to me as my inheritance." So the Saints, being admitted to the glorious sight of Christ, do not just take in a view of Christ—of Christ's essential glory and Christ’s dealings as things that are excellent in themselves—but they look at all these things as being there to make them blessed. They say of Christ and all his dealings: "These are mine, and for my salvation." A stranger can look upon a King and see in him beauty, majesty, glory, and honor; but the Queen looks upon the King and his beauty as her own. So the saints look upon the King of Heaven; they see Christ, and everything in Christ, as their own.

-># Looking unto Jesus.<-

<margin>John 17:24 <note>The text cites Chapter 17, verse 24 of the Gospel of John.</note></margin>...to behold; and *Father, I will that where I am, those whom you have given me may also be with me, that they may behold my glory* <note>original: "Vader, ick wil, dat daer ick ben, oock die by my zijn..."</note>, that is, that they may **enjoy** my glory; for Christ is not only glorious in himself, but he is also a cause of glory to others; now in this respect, Christ is even more particularly our **all in all**; he is all in himself, and when we possess him, he is also our all in all. Let us look a little into the state and condition of the saints in glory regarding this possession of Christ. —

1. They shall possess Christ as their own; they go to Christ and take hold of him, saying, *You are mine*; while the Bride <note>The "Bride" is a traditional biblical metaphor for the Church or the individual soul in its relationship with Christ, the "Bridegroom."</note> was still on earth, this was her rightful language: *My beloved is mine, and I am his*; there is a right and ownership transferred to her in her betrothal with Christ, but when the state of the Wedding is completed, the possession is more perfect; once the Bride has come to behold Christ in his Kingdom, she may henceforth go with boldness to her beloved and say: *everything I see is my own; I had you formerly in hope, but hope has now vanished, and actual possession has come in its place; see, now I have you in my eye, and in my heart, and in my hands, and in my arms; and just as nothing shall now separate us, for all our enemies are trodden underfoot, so I also will not separate from you, so far as to let you out of my sight; I shall behold you continually, and in that be-*

<column-break/>

*holding, I shall possess you continually, for you are my own.*

2. They shall have the use of what they possess; and this is an infinite good for the saints; they shall not only possess Christ, but whatever use they desire, they shall have of Christ, and of everything in Christ; they shall have, according to their desire, the use of his humanity, and of his Divinity, of his glorious being, and of his glorious attributes: O wonder! that a saint shall come to Christ and say, *O my Lord, you are mine, it pleases me to use your wisdom, power, and goodness*, and that Christ shall answer and say, *welcome sweet soul, use me and all my glory according to your desire*; well then, it is as if a friend should say to his friend, *use everything I have as your own*; so shall Christ come to his saints and command them to use all his riches, glory, and excellence, as it pleases them, even to the furthest extent they can comprehend.

3. They shall have the sweetness and the comfort of all that they use; and this goes toward making a perfect enjoyment. We can have the possession of these lower things, and the use of them, but not having the sweetness and comforts of that which we use, we cannot truly and perfectly be said to enjoy these things; what help is the possession and the use of food and drink if we do not taste the sweetness thereof? ### Chapter 2. Section 1.

*Of the knowing of Jesus as carrying out the great work of our salvation in his second coming.*

What "seeing" is, and what it comprises, we have often understood; and in these regards we can look upon Jesus.

1. Let us know Jesus, carrying out the salvation of the saints in his second coming / and in taking them up into Heaven. Many excellent glorious things / many precious matters / many high and Heavenly encounters are in this transaction; And is it not a very weighty matter / that he who now sits at God's right hand and prays for us / shall come from there again to judge the world / and after the judgment take his saints with him into glory? Can we read of the various actions of this general assembly <note>original: "gemeyne vergaerschare." This refers to the "General Assembly and Church of the Firstborn" mentioned in Hebrews 12:23.</note> / and not desire to read of it constantly? yes / and is not all our reading mixed with a wonder over every action? Come! wonder, sit and muse / and pause on every word; stand and wonder / and worship that light / that shows itself in some ray of truth / and cast yourselves down at Christ's feet in wonder over the upcoming truth / and cry out / O the depth of the glory, and Majesty, and goodness, and grace that is in you! O the riches of love, that you pour yourself out in these various wonderful arrangements! <note>The author uses "bestellingen" to refer to God’s sovereign plans or ordinations for the end of time.</note> Come and be diligent in these

can well know and learn Christ, just as he knows and learns other things; he can gather great knowledge <note>The Dutch "wetenschap" here implies academic or intellectual learning.</note> concerning Christ and his coming to judgment, but he has no impression of Christ’s holiness upon his heart; and in this regard he is a stranger to Christ and all his works: alas, he learns about Christ, but he has no right, serious, and inward meditation on Christ; he does not look unto Jesus like one who looks at his pattern <note>original: "patroon," meaning a model or example to be followed.</note>, or one who looks to his refuge, hope, and help. Right and spiritual meditation is a serious matter; it is not just a few fleeting thoughts that make up this work, but thoughts that rest, dwell, and are attached and fixed on Christ, until we enjoy some profitable outcome. O, here is a different kind of business than many realize; it is a remembering with thoughts upon thoughts; it is a repetition and increase of the soul's thoughts over the proposed subject. # Looking unto Jesus.

...men can have, just like the heathens, various terrifying imaginations and thoughts about this day. Oh, to think of a time <margin>Rev. 6:12.</margin> when there shall be a great earthquake, when the Sun shall become black as a sackcloth of hair, and the Moon shall become as blood; when the stars of the <margin>13, 14.</margin> Heaven shall fall to the earth, and the Heavens themselves shall depart like a scroll that is rolled up; when the trumpet shall sound, and the earth shall tremble, and all mountains and islands shall be moved out of their <margin>v. 15, 16, 17.</margin> places: when the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich, and the captains over thousands, and the mighty, and every slave, and every free man shall hide themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains; and shall say to the mountains and to the rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of Him who sits upon the Throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of His wrath has come, and who can stand?" <note>This is a direct paraphrase of Revelation 6:12-17, describing the Day of Judgment.</note> And shall it not be terrifying? If the people were afraid when the Lord came without such a retinue to give the Law on Mount Sinai, truly such a coming in this manner shall be much more terrifying, when He shall come as an avenging judge to demand an account from the world for the neglecting or breaking of this Law.

In this regard, I am not very surprised by some weak Christians who cry out, "O Lord, You know that I have not longed for this terrifying day." A learned Jew <note>Likely a reference to a Talmudic saying (e.g., Ulla or Rabbah) expressing dread of the "birth pangs of the Messiah."</note> used to say, from a deep insight into the dreadfulness of this day: "The Messiah shall

<column-break/>

come, but O Lord, let me not live to see His coming." Now, to master this fear and to drive such slavish terror out of these souls, oh, if they would only consider this day in its entire meaning—not only as it shall be a day of distress and terror, but also as it shall be a day of rest and refreshing. Some only notice its half-meaning; they only look at it as a day of Judgment and of damnation, and so they flee from it as from a snake; but if they would take it up again and look at it from the other side, the snake would be changed into a staff. <note>An allusion to Exodus 4, where Moses’s staff turns into a snake and then back into a staff; here, it symbolizes how a terrifying prospect becomes a tool of support when viewed through faith.</note> The day that shall be so terrifying for the ungodly, and the beginning of their misery, shall for the saints be a joyful day, and the beginning of their glory.

But in what respect is this day of Christ such a desirable day? I answer in these particular things:

1. It is a day of cooling. <note>In the 17th century, "cooling" (verkoelinge) often referred to spiritual relief or refreshment, contrasting with the "heat" of sin or persecution.</note> Here the saints labor as if in an oven; He who has His fire in Zion and His oven in Jerusalem: but Christ, in His second coming (when the entire world shall burn), will let the wind, so to speak, blow upon His saints to cool them; for the ungodly it shall be a hot day, a day of eternal burning, but for the saints a day of cooling, quickening, refreshing, and reviving.

2. It is a day of the restoration of all things. Every creature is now in its workday—

To see the <term>Sun of Righteousness|A biblical title for the Messiah, usually referencing Malachi 4:2, representing light, healing, and justice</term> with all its rays united? O desirable day!

A young woman missing her husband for some years, and expecting his return from overseas lands, often goes to the shore; indeed, her heart loves the wind that shall bring her husband home again; every ship in sight draws her to the shore; it is her 

<column-break/>

new joy and new life-giving hope; she asks every traveler, "Oh, have you seen my husband too? How is he? When will he come? Has he not already gone to sea, and is he ready to return?" It seems to me the souls who are truly drawn to the Lord Jesus Christ cannot long for him any less. Oh, what a desire the Spirit and the Bride ought to have to listen for when Christ shall say to his Angels, "Prepare yourselves for the journey; let us go down, and part the air, and bow the Heavens; I shall gather my captives who have hoped in me; I cannot do without my Rachel <note>A biblical reference to Jacob’s beloved wife, here used as a metaphor for the Church, Christ's beloved.</note>, nor her weeping children; behold, I come quickly to judge the nations." It seems to me every Bride of Christ ought to love that part of the air which, being torn open, shall bring her to her husband; it seems to me she ought to love that part of the Heaven where Christ thrusts through his glorious hand, and comes riding upon the Rainbow and the clouds to take her to himself. I conclude this with the conclusion of the Bible: 
<margin>Rev. 22:20.</margin>
*He who testifies to these things says, Surely, I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.*

### The Fifth Book. Chapter 2. Section 4.

...extending toward something it loves as a future thing; only the future good, just as it is the object of hope, is difficult to obtain, and therefore it differs from desire; for desire looks upon the future good without any consideration of difficulty, but hope looks upon the future good as that which is to be obtained with effort. Lazy hope, <note>Original: *Luye hope*. The author refers to a passive or idle wish for salvation that does not involve active spiritual discipline or "use of means."</note> being unwilling to use means, even difficult ones, is no right hope; we see various desirable things set before us, of which we may say, "Oh, that we might have our part and portion in the same!" but let us go further, to examine and find out the truth of whether we have any part in them, or whether we have the hope of such things. Oh, this is well worth our labor! Come then, and let us go forward; let us not only desire that it may be so and so, but let us say upon some certain and firm grounds, we hope <margin>John 14:3.</margin> that it is thus and so; we hope that Christ shall come again, and take us to himself, so that we also may be where he is.

With truth, here is a Christian's certainty and comfort; this hope <margin>Heb. 6:19.</margin> is an anchor that is sure and steadfast, which shall hold the ship fast in the storms; but since our souls rest upon it, we must take good care that our hope may be sincere; the most wicked can say they hope to be saved as well as the best, but I fear that the hope of many shall be terribly deceived. Our Savior <term>Saligh-maker: literally "Bliss-maker," the standard Dutch term for Jesus Christ as the author of salvation.</term> relates that on the last day many shall with boldness

# The Fifth Book. Chapter 2. Section 4.

...given to the smallest members of Christ, <note>original: "leden Christi"</note> in the name of a disciple of Christ, he shall in no way lose his reward. If a Christian should doubt whether his works are of the right stamp, I give him this answer: 1. Look at the principle; is there not something there above nature? Do I not find some new light sent out from God that shows a certain glory, excellence, and beauty in good works? Is there not something in me that makes them sweet, or pleasant, or savory to me? 2. Look at the end <note>The "end" here refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of an action.</note>; natural works have no better end than self-interest and creaturely intentions; but is there not in my works some higher aim than myself? Whatever I may do, is it not in my eye that all my doing may tend to God’s honor and glory? I must carefully guard myself against self-honor and self-pleasing; the believers do not want to know of the good works they have done on the Day of Judgment; if my aim is on God, then I shall forget myself, as if everything I have done is swallowed up in God. 3. Look at the manner of my performed works; Uzza <note>A biblical figure who was struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant; used here as an example of having a "good intention" but failing to follow God's prescribed manner (2 Samuel 6).</note> had a good intention, but his work was not good because the manner was not good; are my works done according to the rule? Do they agree with God’s Law? Let everyone test his own work in this. Oh my soul, bring your works to the touchstone, the Scripture, the rule of goodness, and shall not all your gold then be found to be dross? The Scripture does not speak only of works,

<column-break/>

<margin>Titus 2:14.</margin>
but it also tells us the manner of performing them; as for example, they must be done with zeal, fervor, and readiness; thus God’s people are called a "peculiar people, zealous of good works"; a performance of holy works according to the outward form, routine, and habit lacks the right manner of performing them. What? Are my works done with zeal? Is there not far too much coldness, emptiness, and formality in my works? Well, thus I can know if my works are of the right stamp; certainly all works and duties that are not done from a gracious heart, through a gracious power, toward a gracious end, in a gracious manner, are but sins, and not such works as shall have the reward of Heaven. Someone might say, "This is a hard word; who then can be saved?" I answer 1. By concession, very few; what is the whole multitude of Christians, except for a very few (says Salvianus <note>Salvian of Marseille (c. 400–470 AD), a Christian writer who wrote "De Gubernatione Dei" (On the Government of God), criticizing the corruption of his age.</note>), other than a sewer of sin? Are only those good works which are thus and so composed? It is reason enough to make us all fear all the works we have done. But 2. this is all our hope: that Christ, in a Gospel-manner <note>original: "Euangeliums-wijse"; referring to God's judgment based on the grace of the Gospel rather than the strict perfection required by the Law.</note>, regards all our good works in their sincerity and not in their perfection; no one can bring it further than Paul,
<margin>Rom. 7:21.</margin>
who, wanting to do good, found that evil was present with him. Alas, there is a constant contradiction and struggle between flesh and spirit, so that the best spiritual person cannot do the good that he wants to do, and yet we must not conclude

<sig>Mmmm m 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: that</meta>

<summary>This page offers a guide for Christians to examine the sincerity of their good works by looking at their origin, purpose, and manner, while acknowledging that human imperfection requires the grace of the Gospel.</summary>

That there would be nothing good in us, because there is no perfect good. "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat," etc. <note>Matthew 25:34-35</note>

5. If we believe in *Christ*, so shall we live with *Christ*; if we come to him and receive him through faith, then he shall come again and take us to himself, so that we also may be where he is. Good works are good proofs, but of all, the *Gospel-works* <note>original: "Euangeliums-wercken"; refers to actions motivated by faith in the Gospel rather than legalistic duty.</note> are the clearest proofs and have the clearest promises. Come then, and let us test our obedience to the commands of faith as well as our life; let us test our submission to the *Lord* through faith as well as through doing. Certainly, the greatest work that has ever been done upon any creature is this *Gospel-work*: when, being sensible of its own unworthiness, it lets itself and its state depend upon the righteousness of *Jesus Christ*. If we were powerful enough to perform a complete, sharp, and narrow obedience to every part of the moral Law,

<column-break/>

### The Fifth Book. Chapter 2. §. 4.

O my soul, gather all these signs and test yourself by them. Every person can say that he hopes to be saved, that he hopes to meet Christ with boldness, though they have no other foundation than their own loose imaginings; but hope on a good ground is that hope which does not disappoint; say then, are you born again? do you expect and long for Christ's coming in the clouds? do you love his appearing? are you rich in good works, ready and willing to share? are you as obedient to the commands of faith as to those of life? on that last general day of judgment / how powerfully would the same work upon our souls! † <note>The dagger symbol here likely marks a pause for emphasis in the original sermon or text.</note> I truly believe that the lack of this exercise of faith is the primary cause of all evil in the world; and the exercise of faith upon this subject shall produce fruits even to the point of wonder. But how shall we believe? What directions are there to exercise our faith upon Jesus in this regard?
I answer: —
1. Faith must go directly to Christ.
2. Faith must go to Christ as God in the flesh.
3. Faith must go to Christ as God in the flesh, having been made under the Law.
4. Faith must go to Christ made under the ruling part of the Law through His life, and under the punitive part of the Law through His death. <note>The "ruling part" refers to Christ’s active obedience (living according to God's commands), while the "punitive part" refers to His passive obedience (suffering the penalty for sin).</note>

6. Faith must go to Christ as ascending into glory, as sitting at God's right hand, and as sending down the Holy Spirit.
7. Faith must go to Christ as interceding for His saints, in which work He continues until His return; all of these have been spoken of previously.
8. Faith must go to Christ as coming into this lower world to judge the living and the dead. This is the final act of faith in relation to Christ: from whence He shall come to judge the living and the dead. The coming of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, the changing of the living, the last judgment, and the glory of Christ with His saints for all eternity, is the business that must be concluded at the end of the world; and this is just as much the object of faith as the preceding points. Christ’s work is not fully finished until all this is ended: nor is our work of faith complete until it has reached its anchor-hold for the soul.

# The Fifth Book. Chapter 2. §. 5.

...will cause to come, is so far exalted and surpassing what we are now, that we do not know what we shall be; children, and more than children; and therefore the Apostle calls the last day <margin>Romans 8:23</margin> the day of adoption as children <note>original: "aen-neminge tot kinderen" - literally "the taking-on as children," referring to the theological concept of being legally brought into God's family.</note>.

4. They must be justified. I know well that they are already justified beforehand through faith; and of this justification <term>justification</term> <note>The theological act of God declaring a sinner righteous.</note> some are convinced by their own consciences; but now they shall be perfectly justified even by the living voice of the Judge; now shall their justification be gloriously and publicly declared before the whole world. The Syriac word for *to justify* <note>original: *rechtveerdighen*</note> also means *to overcome* or *to conquer*: because a <margin>Matthew 19:28</margin> person, being justified, overcomes all those writings and <margin>Hosea 13:14</margin> accusations that were brought against him. Oh, what a glorious victory that shall be over sin, death, and hell, <margin>1 John 3:2</margin> when the Judge of the whole world shall pronounce them free from all sins, and from all those wretched workings of sin, of death, of hell, and of damnation.
